Count Subarrays with Given XOR.title: Count Subarrays with Given XOR
Count Subarrays with Given XOR.problemStatement: You are given an integer array A and an integer B. A subarray is any block of one or more consecutive elements of A, pinned down by a start index and an end index; the XOR of a subarray is the value obtained by combining all of its elements with the bitwise XOR operator, left to right. Count how many subarrays of A have an XOR value exactly equal to B, and return that count as an integer. Two subarrays are considered different whenever their start and end indices differ, so blocks that happen to contain the same numbers but sit at different positions in the array are each counted separately. Single elements count as subarrays, and if no subarray reaches an XOR of B the answer is 0.

examples.explanation: The subarrays are [4, 2], [2, 2, 6], [6], and the whole array [4, 2, 2, 6, 4]. Check that last one one step at a time: 4^2 = 6, then 6^2 = 4, then 4^6 = 2, then 2^4 = 6. Note that [2, 6, 4] does NOT qualify, because 2^6^4 = 0.
The subarrays are [5] and [5, 6, 7, 8, 9] which result in XOR sum 5.

edgeCases: No subarray has the XOR sum B.
All elements are 0, and B is 0.
Array contains only one element which is equal to B.
followUps: Can you solve this in O(N) time complexity and O(N) space complexity?
What if we need to output the count of subarrays with XOR sum at most B?

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: Before reaching for any clever identity, the definition itself hands you a plan: the question asks about every subarray, so build every subarray and test it. The only thing worth being careful about is how each candidate is evaluated. Recomputing the XOR of A[i..j] from scratch means a third nested loop and an O(N^3) total, which is doing the same work over and over. The observation that removes that loop is that all subarrays sharing a start index grow by exactly one element at a time, and XOR extends incrementally just like a running sum does: once current_xor holds the XOR of A[i..j-1], a single current_xor ^= A[j] turns it into the XOR of A[i..j]. So the algorithm fixes the left end i, resets current_xor to 0 because the empty prefix XORs to 0, and slides the right end j forward, paying one operation per new subarray and checking current_xor == B each time. That gives O(N^2) time with O(1) extra space. It is easy to trust and perfectly fine for small inputs, but it starts to hurt once N reaches the tens of thousands - and it is the honest baseline that the prefix-XOR-with-hashmap solution improves upon by turning the inner scan into a lookup.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Initialize count to 0.
2. Run a loop with index i from 0 to N-1 to define the start of subarray.
3. Run a nested loop with index j from i to N-1 to define the end of subarray.
4. Maintain a running XOR sum and check if it equals B.
5. Return the count.
approaches.code:
def solve(A, B):
    # Initialize count of subarrays to 0
    count = 0
    # Loop over all possible starting indices of subarrays
    for i in range(len(A)):
        # Initialize the XOR sum for the current subarray
        current_xor = 0
        # Loop over all possible ending indices of subarrays starting from i
        for j in range(i, len(A)):
            # Update the running XOR sum by XORing with the current element
            current_xor ^= A[j]
            # If the current XOR sum equals B, increment the count
            if current_xor == B:
                count += 1
    # Return the total count of subarrays with given XOR B
    return count

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition:
The improved brute force asks the same question at every end index j: it re-walks all j+1 possible starts to test A[i..j], and nearly every test fails.

XOR cancels itself: x ^ x = 0. Let xr be the running prefix XOR (the XOR of A[0..j]). The XOR of A[i..j] is prefix(i-1) ^ xr, so it equals B exactly when prefix(i-1) == xr ^ B. The start index stops being something you search for and becomes a value you look up. With A = [4, 2, ...] and B = 6: at j = 1, xr = 4 ^ 2 = 6, target = 6 ^ 6 = 0, and the map holds 0 once, so one subarray is counted.

Nothing is skipped: every subarray ending at j has exactly one start, and the map holds one entry per prefix index before j. Inserting xr only after the lookup keeps a length-zero subarray out, and seeding {0: 1} stands for the empty prefix so subarrays starting at index 0 are counted. Storing counts rather than a set means k earlier prefixes with the same value contribute k distinct subarrays.

One pass, O(N) time and O(N) space. You trade positions for counts: it reports how many, never where.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Seed a frequency map `xr_map = {0: 1}`, standing for the empty prefix, and set `xr = 0` and `count = 0`.
2. For each value in A, fold it into the running prefix XOR: `xr ^= val`.
3. Compute `target = xr ^ B`, the prefix value a valid subarray's start must have.
4. If `target` is in `xr_map`, add its stored frequency (not 1) to `count`.
5. Only then record the current prefix: `xr_map[xr] = xr_map.get(xr, 0) + 1`, so the current index cannot match itself.
6. After the loop, return `count`.
approaches.code:
def solve(A, B):
    # Initialize prefix XOR to 0
    xr = 0
    # Dictionary to store the frequency of prefix XORs encountered
    xr_map = {0: 1}
    # Initialize count of subarrays to 0
    count = 0
    # Iterate through the elements of the array A
    for val in A:
        # Calculate the prefix XOR up to the current index
        xr ^= val
        # The target prefix XOR we look for is xr ^ B
        target = xr ^ B
        # If the target exists in our map, add its frequency to the count
        if target in xr_map:
            count += xr_map[target]
        # Update the frequency of the current prefix XOR in the map
        xr_map[xr] = xr_map.get(xr, 0) + 1
    # Return the total count of subarrays with XOR sum equal to B
    return count

complexity.time: O(N)
complexity.space: O(N)

Count Subarrays with Given XOR.tests:
assert solve([4, 2, 2, 6, 4], 6) == 4          # classic case
assert solve([5, 6, 7, 8, 9], 5) == 2
assert solve([1, 2, 3], 0) == 1                # only the whole array xors to 0
# EDGE CASE: empty array -> no subarrays at all, even for B = 0
assert solve([], 0) == 0
# EDGE CASE: zeros with B = 0 -> every one of the n*(n+1)/2 subarrays qualifies
assert solve([0, 0, 0], 0) == 6
# single element that is itself the target
assert solve([7], 7) == 1
assert solve([7], 3) == 0
prerequisites: XOR facts you must have at your fingertips: `x ^ x == 0`, `x ^ 0 == x`, and XOR is associative and commutative, so order does not matter.
Prefix-XOR: if `P[i]` is the XOR of A[0..i], then the XOR of the subarray A[l..r] equals `P[r] ^ P[l-1]` — the shared front cancels itself out.
Rearranged, `P[r] ^ P[l-1] == B` means `P[l-1] == P[r] ^ B`, which turns 'count subarrays' into 'count earlier prefixes equal to a target'.
This is the same prefix + hashmap pattern as 'subarray sum equals K'; only the operator changes from + to ^.
Seed the map with `{0: 1}` before the loop, otherwise every subarray that starts at index 0 is missed.
Store FREQUENCIES, not just presence: the same prefix XOR can occur many times and each occurrence is a separate valid subarray.

Longest Substring Without Repeating Char.title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
Longest Substring Without Repeating Char.problemStatement: You are given a string s, which may contain letters, digits, symbols or spaces. A substring is a run of characters that are consecutive inside s, so you may choose where the run begins and ends but you may not skip positions. Consider only those substrings in which no character appears more than once. Among all such duplicate-free runs, find the one with the greatest length and return that length as an integer; you return the number, not the substring itself. An empty string gives the answer 0, and a string whose characters are all the same gives the answer 1, since a single character is always duplicate-free on its own.

examples.explanation: The answer is "abc", with the length of 3.
The answer is "b", with the length of 1.

constraints: s consists of English letters, digits, symbols, and spaces.
edgeCases: Empty string s = ""
All characters are identical, e.g. "aaaa"
String with all unique characters, e.g. "abcdef"
followUps: Can we optimize the lookup time if the character set is strictly ASCII?
What if we want to print the actual longest substring?

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: Before reaching for any clever trick, pin down what the answer actually is: it is the length of some particular window of s. That means a guaranteed-correct method exists straight away — look at every window and remember the best one. So fix a start index `i`, then push an end index `j` rightwards and watch for the moment the run stops being duplicate-free, tracking the characters currently inside the window in a set called `seen`. The one observation that keeps this from being even slower is that a duplicate is permanent: the instant `s[j]` is already in `seen`, every longer window starting at that same `i` also contains that repeat, so the inner loop can `break` right there instead of scanning to the end of the string. The unsatisfying part is that `seen` is thrown away and rebuilt from scratch for each new start index, re-reading characters you have already examined — and that redundancy is exactly what a sliding window later eliminates. Cost: O(N^2) time in the worst case and O(min(N, alphabet size)) space for the set.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Initialize max_len = 0.
2. Iterate i from 0 to len(s) - 1.
3. Iterate j from i to len(s) - 1.
4. Use a set to detect duplicates. If a character is already present, break. Else, add it and update max_len.
5. Return max_len.
approaches.code:
def lengthOfLongestSubstring(s):
    # Initialize the maximum length of substring to 0
    max_len = 0
    # Outer loop to choose the start index of the substring
    for i in range(len(s)):
        # Set to store unique characters in the current substring
        seen = set()
        # Inner loop to choose the end index of the substring
        for j in range(i, len(s)):
            # If the character is already in the set, break the loop
            if s[j] in seen:
                break
            # Add the character to the set
            seen.add(s[j])
            # Update maximum length if the current length is greater
            max_len = max(max_len, j - i + 1)
    # Return the maximum length found
    return max_len

complexity.space: O(min(N, M)) where M is alphabet size

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition:
The brute force fixes a start and grows a window until a character repeats, then discards it and restarts one position later. On "abcdeaf" the run from 0 walks a,b,c,d,e before hitting the second a; the run from 1 re-walks b,c,d,e. Those re-walks are the waste.

The observation: when `right` lands on a character whose previous occurrence is at index p inside the window, every window starting at or before p and ending at right holds that character twice. The earliest start that can still work is p+1, so `left` jumps there in one assignment.

Why nothing valid is skipped: for each right, left sits at the smallest index making s[left..right] repeat-free, so the widest window ending there is measured once. A start rejected earlier stays rejected, because the duplicate pair that killed it survives in every longer window built on it - left never needs to move back.

Cost: O(N) time in one pass; O(min(N, M)) space, one entry per distinct character. The trade is that stale map entries linger, so the test compares the stored index against left rather than checking membership.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Create an empty dictionary `char_map` mapping a character to the last index where it was seen; set `left = 0` and `max_len = 0`.
2. Move `right` from 0 to len(s) - 1.
3. If `s[right]` is in `char_map` AND `char_map[s[right]] >= left` (the previous occurrence is inside the current window, not a stale one behind it), set `left = char_map[s[right]] + 1`.
4. Write `char_map[s[right]] = right`, overwriting any older index for that character.
5. Set `max_len = max(max_len, right - left + 1)`, the width of the current duplicate-free window.
6. After the loop, return `max_len`.
approaches.code:
def lengthOfLongestSubstring(s):
    # Dictionary to store the last seen index of each character
    char_map = {}
    # Initialize maximum length of unique substring to 0
    max_len = 0
    # Initialize the left pointer of the sliding window to 0
    left = 0
    # Iterate through the string with the right pointer
    for right in range(len(s)):
        # If the character is already in the window, shrink the window
        if s[right] in char_map and char_map[s[right]] >= left:
            left = char_map[s[right]] + 1
        # Update/store the last seen index of the character
        char_map[s[right]] = right
        # Update the maximum length of unique substring
        max_len = max(max_len, right - left + 1)
    # Return the maximum length found
    return max_len

complexity.time: O(N)
complexity.space: O(min(N, M)) where M is character set size

Longest Substring Without Repeating Char.tests:
assert lengthOfLongestSubstring("abcabcbb") == 3
assert lengthOfLongestSubstring("bbbbb") == 1
assert lengthOfLongestSubstring("pwwkew") == 3
# "abba" catches the bug where left jumps BACKWARDS on a stale index
assert lengthOfLongestSubstring("abba") == 2
assert lengthOfLongestSubstring("dvdf") == 3
# EDGE CASE: empty string has no substring at all
assert lengthOfLongestSubstring("") == 0
assert lengthOfLongestSubstring("a") == 1
assert lengthOfLongestSubstring(" ") == 1
prerequisites: Sliding window: keep a range [left, right] that always satisfies the constraint, extend `right` every step and only ever move `left` forward.
A dict from character to its LAST seen index lets you jump `left` past a duplicate in one move instead of shrinking one character at a time.
The guard `char_map[c] >= left` is essential: an old index that sits before `left` is stale, and jumping to it would move `left` backwards and produce wrong answers on inputs like "abba".
Window length is `right - left + 1` — an inclusive range, hence the +1.
Because `left` never moves backwards, each index is visited at most twice overall, giving O(n) time even though there are two moving pointers.
Space is O(min(n, charset)) — the map holds at most one entry per distinct character.

Remove Nth Node From End.title: Remove Nth Node From End
Remove Nth Node From End.problemStatement: You are given the head of a singly linked list and a positive integer n, where n is at most the number of nodes in the list. Delete the node that sits n positions from the tail — n = 1 means the last node, n = 2 means the one just before it, and so on — then return the head of the modified list. The catch is that the list is singly linked: every node points only forward, so there is no way to walk backwards from the tail to count off n nodes. Deletion is done by pointer surgery, making the previous node's next field skip over the doomed node. Note that the head itself can be the node to remove (when n equals the list length), in which case the returned head is different from the one you were given.

examples.explanation: The 2nd node from the end is 4. Removing it leaves 1->2->3->5.
Removing the only node leaves an empty list.

constraints: The number of nodes in the list is sz.
edgeCases: List has only 1 node, n = 1.
Removing the head node (n = length of list).
Removing the last node (n = 1).
followUps: Could you do this in one pass?
Can we do this recursively without maintaining length?

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: The difficulty is that the problem counts from the end while the pointers only let you move toward the end. Standing at some node, you have no way of knowing whether it is the n-th from the tail, because you cannot see how much list is left ahead of you. A beginner might reach for a stack or for reversing the list, but there is a much plainer fix: the position from the end and the position from the start are the same fact expressed two ways. If the list has length L, the node that is n-th from the end is the node at index L - n counting from zero at the head. So the moment you know L, the problem turns into the ordinary 'delete the node at a known index' exercise, which you already know how to do. That is why this solution walks the list twice: the first pass exists purely to learn L, and the second pass stops one node early, at index L - n - 1, because deleting requires holding the predecessor. The one case with no predecessor is L == n, where the victim is the head itself, so it is handled separately by returning head.next. The cost is O(N) time from two traversals and O(1) extra space; the only thing left to improve is collapsing those two passes into one.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Traverse the list once to calculate its total length L.
2. If L == n, return head.next.
3. Traverse up to the (L - n - 1)-th node from start.
4. Skip the L-n-th node by modifying next pointer: curr.next = curr.next.next.
5. Return head.
approaches.code:
def removeNthFromEnd(head, n):
    # Initialize a pointer to traverse the list
    temp = head
    # Variable to store the total length of the list
    length = 0
    # Count the total number of nodes in the linked list
    while temp:
        length += 1
        temp = temp.next
    # If the node to be removed is the head node
    if length == n:
        return head.next
    # Calculate the step count to reach the node before the target node
    steps_to_move = length - n - 1
    # Pointer to traverse up to the node before target node
    curr = head
    # Traverse to the target position
    for _ in range(steps_to_move):
        curr = curr.next
    # Delete the target node by skipping it in the next pointer
    curr.next = curr.next.next
    # Return the head of the modified linked list
    return head

complexity.time: O(N)

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition:
The length-first version spends a whole traversal producing one number, L, then throws the walk away and starts again from the head to reach index L - n. Nothing changed between the passes; the only thing the first bought was a count.

Two pointers held n apart make the count unnecessary. Put `fast` and `slow` on the dummy, advance `fast` n times, and the gap is frozen, since both then move one step per iteration. On 1->2->3->4->5 with n = 2, `fast` lands on 5 exactly when `slow` reaches 3, the node before the target 4.

That gap is an invariant - a fact true before and after every iteration - so `slow` is always n behind. The loop tests `while fast.next`, halting `fast` on the last node rather than on None, which leaves `slow` one node short of the target instead of on it; a singly linked list can only be cut at a node's predecessor, so the offset is the point. The dummy gives the head a predecessor too, making deletion of the first node an ordinary splice.

One pass, O(N) time, O(1) space. Traded: an explicit index, for an off-by-one gap you have to hold in your head.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Create a `dummy` node whose `next` points at `head`, so the head has a predecessor too.
2. Set both `fast` and `slow` to `dummy`.
3. Advance `fast` n times, opening a fixed gap of n nodes between the pointers.
4. While `fast.next` is not None, advance `fast` and `slow` one step each; the gap never changes, so `fast` stops on the last node with `slow` on the target's predecessor.
5. Splice the target out with `slow.next = slow.next.next`.
6. Return `dummy.next`, which is the possibly-new head.
approaches.code:
def removeNthFromEnd(head, n):
    # Create a dummy node to handle edge cases like removing the head
    dummy = ListNode(0)
    # Link dummy node to the head of the list
    dummy.next = head
    # Initialize fast and slow pointers to dummy node
    fast = dummy
    slow = dummy
    # Move the fast pointer n steps ahead
    for _ in range(n):
        fast = fast.next
    # Move both fast and slow pointers together until fast reaches the end node
    while fast.next:
        fast = fast.next
        slow = slow.next
    # Skip the N-th node from the end
    slow.next = slow.next.next
    # Return the new head node, which is dummy.next
    return dummy.next

complexity.time: O(N)

Remove Nth Node From End.tests:
assert linked_list_to_list(removeNthFromEnd(build_linked_list([1, 2, 3, 4, 5]), 2)) == [1, 2, 3, 5]
# EDGE CASE: single node removed -> empty list (must return None, not crash)
assert removeNthFromEnd(build_linked_list([1]), 1) is None
# EDGE CASE: removing the HEAD of a longer list (n == length)
assert linked_list_to_list(removeNthFromEnd(build_linked_list([1, 2]), 2)) == [2]
# removing the TAIL (n == 1)
assert linked_list_to_list(removeNthFromEnd(build_linked_list([1, 2]), 1)) == [1]
assert linked_list_to_list(removeNthFromEnd(build_linked_list([1, 2, 3]), 3)) == [2, 3]
assert linked_list_to_list(removeNthFromEnd(build_linked_list([7, 8, 9, 10]), 4)) == [8, 9, 10]
prerequisites: A dummy (sentinel) node placed before the head removes the special case of deleting the head — you always delete via some `prev.next = prev.next.next`.
To delete a node in a singly linked list you need a pointer to its PREDECESSOR, never to the node itself.
The two-pointer gap trick: advance `fast` n steps first, then move `fast` and `slow` together; when `fast` hits the last node, `slow` is exactly n+1 nodes from the end.
Starting both pointers at the dummy (not at the head) is what makes `slow` land on the predecessor rather than on the victim.
Removing the only node of a one-element list must return None, so the code has to survive `slow.next.next` being None.
The optimal version is one pass; the naive length-then-walk version is two passes but the same O(1) space.

Add Two Numbers as Linked Lists.title: Add Two Numbers as Linked Lists
Add Two Numbers as Linked Lists.problemStatement: You are given two non-empty linked lists representing two non-negative integers. The digits are stored in reverse order, and each of their nodes contains a single digit. Add the two numbers and return the sum as a linked list.
constraints: The number of nodes in each linked list is in the range [1, 100].
It is guaranteed that the list represents a number that does not have leading zeros, except the number 0 itself.
edgeCases: Lists of different lengths.
Sum results in a carry to a new node at the very end (e.g. 99 + 1 = 100).
One or both lists are 0.
followUps: What if the digits are stored in non-reversed order? (most significant digit first)
Can you solve this without creating new nodes, modifying one of the input lists in-place?

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: The most human reaction to this problem is: these lists are just numbers written backwards, so turn them back into numbers, use the addition my language already has, and write the digits out again. That is precisely what this version does. Walking l1 and prepending each digit with `num1 = str(curr1.val) + num1` rebuilds the value in normal most-significant-first order, undoing the reversed storage as it goes; the same happens for l2; the two strings become integers, get added, and the digit characters of the result are walked in reverse so the output list is once again least-significant-first. Why is this unsatisfying? It leans entirely on the language being able to hold the whole number at once. In Python that works because integers are arbitrary precision, but in Java or C++ a list of a few dozen digits overflows a 64-bit integer and the answer is silently wrong, which makes this a solution that does not port. It also builds two intermediate strings, so you pay O(N + M) extra memory for information you never actually needed to hold all at once. Time is O(N + M), but with heavy constant factors from string concatenation.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Initialise two empty strings `num1` and `num2` that will hold the digits of each list in normal reading order.
2. Walk l1 with `curr1`, prepending each digit as `num1 = str(curr1.val) + num1`, which reverses the reversed storage back into most-significant-first order.
3. Walk l2 with `curr2` in exactly the same way to build `num2`.
4. Convert both strings to integers with `val1` and `val2`, defaulting to 0 if a string ended up empty, and compute `total_sum = val1 + val2`.
5. Turn the total back into text with `sum_str = str(total_sum)`, create a `dummy = ListNode(0)` and a build pointer `curr = dummy`.
6. Iterate over `reversed(sum_str)` so the least significant digit comes first, attaching `curr.next = ListNode(int(char))` and advancing `curr` each time.
7. Return `dummy.next`, the first real node of the sum list.
approaches.code:
def addTwoNumbers(l1, l2):
    # Initialize strings to construct values of both numbers
    num1 = ""
    num2 = ""
    # Traverse l1 and build number representation in reverse
    curr1 = l1
    while curr1:
        num1 = str(curr1.val) + num1
        curr1 = curr1.next
    # Traverse l2 and build number representation in reverse
    curr2 = l2
    while curr2:
        num2 = str(curr2.val) + num2
        curr2 = curr2.next
    # Handle empty strings by converting to '0'
    val1 = int(num1) if num1 else 0
    val2 = int(num2) if num2 else 0
    # Add both integer values
    total_sum = val1 + val2
    # Convert sum back to a string
    sum_str = str(total_sum)
    # Create a dummy head for the result linked list
    dummy = ListNode(0)
    # Pointer to build the result list
    curr = dummy
    # Iterate through the digits in reverse order
    for char in reversed(sum_str):
        curr.next = ListNode(int(char))
        curr = curr.next
    # Return the sum list starting after the dummy node
    return dummy.next

complexity.time: O(N + M)
complexity.space: O(N + M) for strings

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: The reversed digit order looks like an obstacle at first, but it is actually the gift that makes the whole problem easy: the head of each list is the ones digit, which is exactly where you start when adding two numbers by hand in a column. Once you see that, there is no reason to rebuild the numbers at all. Walk both lists together, add the two current digits plus whatever carried over from the previous column, write the ones digit of that sum into a new node, and keep the tens digit as the carry for the next column. Three details make it airtight. Lists of unequal length are handled by treating a missing node as a 0 digit, so no padding is needed. The loop condition `while l1 or l2 or carry` keeps going while a carry is still outstanding, which is what produces the extra leading node for a case like 5 + 5. And a dummy head node removes the special case of attaching the very first result node, so the loop body has no branches for first-versus-later. Time is O(max(N, M)) with a single pass and no number ever held in full, and the only memory used beyond the returned list is a handful of variables.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Initialize dummy head `dummy = ListNode(0)`, `curr = dummy`, `carry = 0`.
2. Loop while `l1`, `l2` are not empty, or `carry` is not 0.
3. Sum = `carry` + (l1.val if l1 else 0) + (l2.val if l2 else 0).
4. Update `carry = Sum // 10`.
5. Create node `Sum % 10`, attach to `curr.next`, move `curr`.
6. Advance `l1` and `l2` if they exist.
7. Return `dummy.next`.
approaches.code:
def addTwoNumbers(l1, l2):
    # Initialize a dummy node to act as the head of the output list
    dummy = ListNode(0)
    # Pointer to the current node of the result list
    curr = dummy
    # Variable to keep track of the carry value
    carry = 0
    # Traverse through both lists as long as there are nodes or a carry
    while l1 or l2 or carry:
        # Sum starts with the carry from the previous step
        val_sum = carry
        # Add value of l1 if it exists
        if l1:
            val_sum += l1.val
            l1 = l1.next
        # Add value of l2 if it exists
        if l2:
            val_sum += l2.val
            l2 = l2.next
        # Calculate new carry for the next iteration
        carry = val_sum // 10
        # Create a new node with the digit value and append it
        curr.next = ListNode(val_sum % 10)
        # Advance the pointer in the result list
        curr = curr.next
    # Return the head of the sum linked list
    return dummy.next

complexity.time: O(max(N, M))
complexity.space: O(max(N, M)) for output list

Add Two Numbers as Linked Lists.tests:
assert linked_list_to_list(addTwoNumbers(build_linked_list([2, 4, 3]), build_linked_list([5, 6, 4]))) == [7, 0, 8]
# EDGE CASE: 0 + 0 must still produce one node holding 0
assert linked_list_to_list(addTwoNumbers(build_linked_list([0]), build_linked_list([0]))) == [0]
# EDGE CASE: carry propagates past the end -> answer is LONGER than both inputs
assert linked_list_to_list(addTwoNumbers(build_linked_list([5]), build_linked_list([5]))) == [0, 1]
# unequal lengths plus a rippling carry: 9999 + 999999 = 1009998
assert linked_list_to_list(
    addTwoNumbers(build_linked_list([9, 9, 9, 9]), build_linked_list([9, 9, 9, 9, 9, 9]))
) == [8, 9, 9, 9, 0, 0, 1]
assert linked_list_to_list(addTwoNumbers(build_linked_list([1, 8]), build_linked_list([0]))) == [1, 8]
prerequisites: The digits are stored in REVERSE order (units digit first), which is exactly what makes left-to-right traversal the same as school addition from the least-significant end.
Elementary addition per position: `total = carry + d1 + d2`, the new digit is `total % 10` and the new carry is `total // 10`.
A dummy head plus a moving `curr` tail pointer lets you append nodes without an `if this is the first node` branch; the answer is `dummy.next`.
The loop condition must be `while l1 or l2 or carry` — a final carry (99 + 1) creates one extra node after both inputs are exhausted.
The two lists can have different lengths, so guard every read with `if l1:` / `if l2:` instead of assuming both advance together.
Converting to int and back (the brute force) works in Python only because ints are arbitrary precision; in Java or C++ it overflows, which is why interviewers ask for the digit-by-digit version.

Delete a Given Node.title: Delete a Given Node
Delete a Given Node.problemStatement: Write a function to delete a node in a singly-linked list. You will not be given access to the head of the list, instead you will be given access to the node to be deleted directly. It is guaranteed that the node to be deleted is not a tail node in the list.

examples.explanation: You are given the second node with value 5, the linked list should become 4 -> 1 -> 9.
You are given the third node with value 1, the linked list should become 4 -> 5 -> 9.

constraints: The number of the nodes in the given list is in the range [2, 1000].
All the values of the nodes in the list are unique.
The node to be deleted is in the list and is not a tail node.
edgeCases: Deleting the head node.
Deleting the node adjacent to the tail node.
followUps: Can you delete a node if it is the tail node?
What if we need to release the memory of the deleted node in low-level languages?

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: Deleting a node normally means finding the node before it and pointing that predecessor past it, but here you were handed the doomed node directly and a singly linked list cannot be walked backwards, so the predecessor is simply unreachable. The idea people reach for first is therefore not to remove this node object at all, but to make the list read as though it had been removed. Shift every value one place to the left: `curr.val = curr.next.val` all the way down the tail. After that sweep, the sequence of values a reader sees is exactly the original list with the target's value gone, except the list is now one node too long and its final node holds a duplicate of the old tail value. Keeping `prev` one step behind lets you cut that trailing duplicate off with `prev.next = None`, which finishes the job. It is correct, but it touches every node after the target, so it costs O(N) time and O(1) space for what ought to be a purely local edit, and that waste is the hint that a constant-time version exists.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Start at the node to delete.
2. Iterate through the list, setting curr.val = curr.next.val.
3. Maintain a pointer to the previous node.
4. When you reach the tail, set prev.next = None.
5. The node is effectively deleted.
approaches.code:
def deleteNode(node):
    # Initialize a pointer to the current node
    curr = node
    # Initialize a pointer to keep track of the parent node
    prev = None
    # Traverse and copy values of next nodes to current nodes
    while curr.next:
        # Copy next node's value to current node
        curr.val = curr.next.val
        # Keep track of current node as previous
        prev = curr
        # Move to the next node
        curr = curr.next
    # Sever connection to the last node which is now duplicate
    if prev:
        prev.next = None

complexity.time: O(N)

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: The brute force copies values all the way down the tail, so the honest question is why the whole tail has to move at all. It does not. From the outside, the only things that make this node 'exist' are the value stored inside it and the fact that something points at it. You cannot touch who points at it, but you do own both the value and the outgoing pointer. So overwrite the value with `node.next.val`: the target's own data is now gone and the node is impersonating its successor. That leaves the successor's value appearing twice in a row, so splice the successor out with `node.next = node.next.next`. To any traversal, exactly one node has vanished and it carried the value that was supposed to be deleted. The problem's guarantee that the given node is never the tail is precisely what makes this legal, because `node.next` must exist for there to be anything to impersonate. Two assignments, no traversal: O(1) time and O(1) space.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Rely on the problem's guarantee that `node` is not the tail, so `node.next` is a real node; the entire method depends on that successor existing.
2. Read the successor's value `node.next.val` and write it into `node.val`, which overwrites and permanently discards the value that was meant to be deleted.
3. Observe the momentary state: that value now appears twice in a row, once in `node` and once in `node.next`, so exactly one of the two copies has to be unlinked.
4. Set `node.next = node.next.next`, bypassing the successor so the duplicate copy is dropped and the node after it becomes `node`'s new neighbour.
5. Return nothing. The edit is made in place, the caller's head pointer is untouched, and the list is one node shorter with the correct value missing.
approaches.code:
def deleteNode(node):
    # Copy the value of the next node to the current node
    node.val = node.next.val
    # Point the current node's next pointer to the next-next node
    node.next = node.next.next

Delete a Given Node.tests:
# delete a middle node (value 5) given only that node
h = build_linked_list([4, 5, 1, 9])
deleteNode(h.next)
assert linked_list_to_list(h) == [4, 1, 9]

# EDGE CASE: delete the HEAD node without owning a head reference
h = build_linked_list([1, 2])
deleteNode(h)
assert linked_list_to_list(h) == [2]

# delete the second-to-last node (its successor IS the tail)
h = build_linked_list([4, 5, 1, 9])
deleteNode(h.next.next)
assert linked_list_to_list(h) == [4, 5, 9]

# longer list, delete somewhere in the middle
h = build_linked_list([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
deleteNode(h.next.next)
assert linked_list_to_list(h) == [1, 2, 4, 5]

# the function mutates in place and returns nothing useful
h = build_linked_list([9, 8, 7])
assert deleteNode(h.next) is None
assert linked_list_to_list(h) == [9, 7]
prerequisites: You are handed only the node to delete — with no head pointer you can never reach its predecessor, so a normal 'unlink' is impossible.
The trick is to delete the VALUE rather than the object: copy `node.next.val` into `node`, then unlink `node.next`.
`node.next = node.next.next` is a pointer reassignment; the skipped node becomes unreachable and Python's garbage collector reclaims it.
This is why the problem guarantees the node is not the tail: with no successor there is nothing to copy from and the trick collapses.
The function mutates the list in place and returns None; correctness is judged by walking the list from the original head afterwards.
Any external pointer still held on the skipped node keeps observing the old value — a real aliasing gotcha worth mentioning in an interview.

Intersection of Two Linked Lists.title: Intersection of Two Linked Lists
Intersection of Two Linked Lists.problemStatement: You are given the heads of two singly linked lists, headA and headB. The two lists may merge: from some node onwards they can share the very same nodes, so that following next from either head eventually walks one common tail. Return a reference to the first node they share. Identity is what counts here, not content — two separate node objects that happen to hold equal values are not an intersection, only the same node reached from both directions is. If the lists never merge, return null. Neither list may be modified in the process.

examples.explanation: The intersected node's value is 8.
The two lists do not intersect.

constraints: The number of nodes of listA is m.
The number of nodes of listB is n.
edgeCases: Lists have no intersection.
Intersection is at the head of one (or both) list.
Lists are of equal or unequal lengths.
followUps: Can you write a solution that runs in O(m + n) time and use only O(1) memory?
What if there are cycles inside the list? How does it affect intersection detection?

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: With no clever observation yet, the definition itself hands you a plan: the intersection is the first node of A that is also a node of B, so take the nodes of A one at a time and ask whether each one appears anywhere in B. The "appears in B" test is just a full walk from headB comparing with ==, which here is reference comparison — two distinct nodes both holding 5 are not the same node, and the merge point is defined purely by shared references. Correctness follows from the shape of a merge: nodes of A before the merge point exist only in A, so they can never be found in B, while the merge point and everything after it belong to both lists. That makes the first hit in the outer scan exactly the answer, and reaching the end of A without a hit proves there is no intersection, so None is returned. The price is that each of the N nodes of A drags a complete scan of the M nodes of B behind it, giving O(N*M) time, though only the two pointers currA and currB are ever allocated, so space stays O(1). Removing that quadratic factor is precisely what the two-pointer optimal solution does.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Loop through each node A of list A.
2. In a nested loop, loop through each node B of list B.
3. If A == B, return A.
4. If outer loop completes, return None.
approaches.code:
def getIntersectionNode(headA, headB):
    # Pointer for traversing list A
    currA = headA
    # Loop over all nodes of list A
    while currA:
        # Pointer for traversing list B
        currB = headB
        # Loop over all nodes of list B
        while currB:
            # If nodes are identical, intersection found
            if currA == currB:
                return currA
            # Move to next node in list B
            currB = currB.next
        # Move to next node in list A
        currA = currA.next
    # Return None if no intersection is found
    return None

complexity.time: O(N * M)

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: The brute force re-walks the whole of B for every single node of A: node 1 of A triggers a full M-step scan, node 2 triggers another identical scan, and nothing learned in one scan survives into the next. That is N x M reference comparisons to locate one node. It never uses the only structural fact available - if the lists merge, they share one common tail, so A is (a nodes of its own) + (c shared) and B is (b of its own) + (c shared). The observation: a pointer that walks A and then continues from headB covers a + c + b nodes; a pointer that walks B and then continues from headA covers b + c + a. Identical totals. So after each has switched lists exactly once, both stand the same distance from the end and move in lockstep. That is the correctness argument too: once equidistant, they step into the shared tail on the same iteration, so the first position where pA == pB is the merge node - it cannot be passed unnoticed, and they cannot meet earlier, because before the tail the nodes belong to different lists. With no merge, c = 0 and both become None on the same step, so the loop condition fails and None is returned rather than spinning forever. Cost: O(N + M) time, O(1) space - the trade is walking the data twice in exchange for storing nothing.
approaches.algorithm:
1. If either headA or headB is None there is no tail to share, so return None immediately.
2. Set pA = headA and pB = headB.
3. While pA is not the same node object as pB, advance both by one step, with a twist: a pointer that has fallen off the end (is None) restarts at the OTHER list's head instead of advancing. Write it as pA = headB if pA is None else pA.next, and symmetrically for pB.
4. Each pointer therefore takes at most one redirect, and after its redirect it has covered a + c + b (respectively b + c + a) nodes - equal totals, so the two pointers become aligned relative to the end of the shared tail.
5. The loop exits either when both land on the same node (the intersection) or when both are None at the same moment (no intersection); return pA, which is correct in both cases.
approaches.code:
def getIntersectionNode(headA, headB):
    # If either list is empty, there is no intersection
    if not headA or not headB:
        return None
    # Initialize pointer A to the head of list A
    pA = headA
    # Initialize pointer B to the head of list B
    pB = headB
    # Traverse until the pointers meet
    while pA != pB:
        # If pointer A reaches the end, redirect to head of list B
        pA = headB if pA is None else pA.next
        # If pointer B reaches the end, redirect to head of list A
        pB = headA if pB is None else pB.next
    # Either both are None or both point to the intersection node
    return pA

complexity.time: O(N + M)

Intersection of Two Linked Lists.tests:
def _attach(head, tail_list):
    """Append the SAME node objects of tail_list to head; returns head."""
    if head is None:
        return tail_list
    t = head
    while t.next:
        t = t.next
    t.next = tail_list
    return head

# classic Y-shape: A = 4,1 -> [8,4,5]   B = 5,6,1 -> [8,4,5]
common = build_linked_list([8, 4, 5])
a = _attach(build_linked_list([4, 1]), common)
b = _attach(build_linked_list([5, 6, 1]), common)
assert getIntersectionNode(a, b) is common          # must be the NODE, not the value

# lists of very different lengths still meet at the same node
common2 = build_linked_list([2, 4])
a2 = _attach(build_linked_list([1, 9, 1]), common2)
b2 = _attach(build_linked_list([3]), common2)
assert getIntersectionNode(a2, b2) is common2

# EDGE CASE: no intersection at all -> None (and no infinite loop)
assert getIntersectionNode(build_linked_list([1, 2, 3]), build_linked_list([4, 5])) is None

# EDGE CASE: one list empty
assert getIntersectionNode(None, build_linked_list([1, 2])) is None
assert getIntersectionNode(build_linked_list([1, 2]), None) is None

# both heads are the same node -> intersection is that head
z = build_linked_list([7, 8])
assert getIntersectionNode(z, z) is z
prerequisites: Intersection means the same NODE OBJECT, not the same value — compare with `is` / `!=` on references, never on `.val`.
Once two singly linked lists share a node they share the entire remaining tail; they can never diverge again, which is what makes a Y shape the only possible picture.
The two-pointer switch trick: when a pointer runs off list A it restarts at head B and vice versa, so both pointers travel exactly lenA + lenB steps and arrive together.
If the lists never intersect, both pointers become None on the same step and `pA != pB` becomes False with pA = None — so the same loop returns None with no extra check.
The alternative is aligning the lists by their length difference; both are O(m+n) time and O(1) space, unlike the hash-set version which costs O(m) memory.
Guard for an empty list up front — a None head would otherwise crash on `.next`.

Reverse Nodes in K Group.title: Reverse Nodes in K Group
Reverse Nodes in K Group.problemStatement: Given the head of a linked list, reverse the nodes of the list k at a time, and return its modified head. k is a positive integer and is less than or equal to the length of the linked list. If the number of nodes is not a multiple of k then left-out nodes, in the end, should remain as it is.

examples.explanation: First 2 nodes reversed -> [2,1], next 2 nodes reversed -> [4,3], last node 5 is left as is.
First 3 nodes reversed -> [3,2,1], remaining 4,5 left as is.

constraints: The number of nodes in the list is sz.
edgeCases: k = 1 (no changes).
k is equal to the length of the list.
Remaining nodes at the end are less than k (should not be reversed).
followUps: Can you solve it iteratively with O(1) auxiliary space?
What if we want to reverse the remaining nodes too?

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: Reversing a linked list in blocks of k while juggling raw pointers is where most beginners get lost: you have to remember the tail of the previous block, the head of the current one, and the node that follows the block, all while the links you are standing on are being rewritten under you. The escape hatch is to notice that the hard part is not the reversal, it is the pointer bookkeeping -- and pointer bookkeeping is only hard because a linked list gives you no random access. So buy random access. Walk the list once and push every node OBJECT (not its value) into a Python list. Now the whole problem becomes array index manipulation, where reversing a block of k is a one-line slice assignment and you can see the entire structure at once. Only after the array is in its final order do you go back and write the `next` pointers, in a single clean sweep, which removes every chance of losing the rest of the chain mid-reversal. The one detail that still needs care is the ragged tail: if the list length n is not a multiple of k, the final n % k nodes must be left in their original order, which is why the reversal loop stops at `n - n % k`. The cost of this clarity is O(N) extra memory for the array, versus the O(1) the in-place pointer version achieves; time stays O(N) either way, so this is purely a space-for-simplicity trade.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Traverse the list and store node references in an array.
2. Iterate through the array in steps of size k.
3. Reverse each slice of size k.
4. Reconnect all nodes sequentially.
5. Return the new head.
approaches.code:
def reverseKGroup(head, k):  # reverse every complete block of k nodes, leave the rest
    # collect the node objects so we can reorder by index
    nodes = []  # O(n) extra space is the cost of this simpler approach
    curr = head  # walking pointer; head must stay untouched for now
    while curr:  # stops naturally at the end of the chain
        nodes.append(curr)  # store the node itself, not its value, so links can move
        curr = curr.next  # step forward before any link gets rewritten
    # Find the total number of complete groups of size k
    n = len(nodes)  # n // k complete groups, with n % k stragglers at the end
    # Loop over and reverse each segment of length k
    for i in range(0, n - n % k, k):  # n - n%k trims the ragged tail so it is never reversed
        # Reverse the sublist slice in place
        nodes[i:i+k] = reversed(nodes[i:i+k])  # the core trick: reorder the array, then relink once
    # Reconnect the nodes according to the new ordering
    for i in range(n - 1):  # n-1 links to write; the final node is handled below
        nodes[i].next = nodes[i+1]  # rebuild next pointers to follow the new array order
    # close off the chain, then hand back the new head
    if n > 0:  # guard the empty list before touching nodes[-1]
        nodes[-1].next = None  # terminate the chain; skipping this leaves a cycle
        return nodes[0]  # whatever landed at index 0 is the new head
    return None  # empty input stays empty

complexity.time: O(N)
complexity.space: O(N)

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition:
The array-of-nodes brute force buys random access by copying N node references into a Python list, then rewires links through indices. It still flips every link, so the extra array is pure overhead: O(N) memory spent to avoid remembering one pointer. What it is really compensating for is the tail-stitching bookkeeping -- after reversing a block you must reach back and connect the previous block's tail to this block's new head.

The observation that removes it: reversing a block turns the block's FIRST node into the block's LAST node. So after the k flips, `head` is precisely the tail that needs stitching, and it is already sitting in a local variable. With 1->2->3 and k=3, prev ends at 3 (the new head) and head is still 1 (now the tail). The remainder of the list is the same problem on a shorter list, so `head.next = reverseKGroup(curr, k)` stitches the tail to the answer for the rest.

Why it can never mangle a block: the counting probe runs first and walks at most k nodes. If it stops with count < k the list ran out, and the function returns `head` untouched -- exactly the rule that a leftover short block stays in original order, and the reason no block is ever half-reversed. Because the count already proved k nodes exist, the reversal loop runs exactly k times with no null checks inside, and `curr` lands on the first node beyond the block, so each block is handled once.

Cost: O(N) time -- one probe pass and one flip per link. The trade is O(N/k) stack frames, one per block, instead of the brute force's O(N) array.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Walk a probe pointer `curr` from `head`, counting up to but not past k nodes.
2. If the count came out below k, fewer than k nodes remain: return `head` unchanged.
3. Otherwise reverse exactly k nodes: with `prev = None` and `curr = head`, repeat k times -- save `curr.next`, point `curr.next` at `prev`, slide `prev` to `curr`, slide `curr` to the saved node.
4. After the loop `prev` is the block's new head and `curr` is the first node of the next block.
5. Recurse on the rest and stitch: `head.next = reverseKGroup(curr, k)`, since `head` is now this block's tail.
6. Return `prev` so the caller attaches to this block's new head.
approaches.code:
def reverseKGroup(head, k):  # recursive: reverse one block, then recurse on the rest
    # count first so a short tail is never partially reversed
    curr = head  # probe pointer; head itself must not move yet
    count = 0
    while curr and count < k:  # the count < k guard keeps this O(k), not O(n), per block
        curr = curr.next  # advance the probe one node at a time
        count += 1  # count ends below k only if the list ran out early
    # If we have at least k nodes, reverse them
    if count == k:  # exactly k nodes available, so this block earns a reversal
        # Reverse the first k nodes of the list
        prev = None  # prev trails behind and becomes this block's new head
        curr = head  # restart from the block's first node
        for _ in range(k):  # exactly k flips, so no boundary checks are needed inside
            next_node = curr.next  # save the forward link before we destroy it
            curr.next = prev  # flip this arrow to point backwards
            prev = curr  # prev slides onto the node we just flipped
            curr = next_node  # after k turns curr sits on the next block's first node
        # the rest of the list is the same problem, one block shorter
        if head:  # head is now this block's TAIL, since it moved to the back
            head.next = reverseKGroup(curr, k)  # stitch our tail onto whatever the recursion returns
        # prev is the new head of this reversed block
        return prev  # prev is the last node flipped, so it leads the block
    # If there are fewer than k nodes left, leave them as is
    return head  # fewer than k nodes left: leave them in original order

complexity.time: O(N)
complexity.space: O(N/K) recursion stack

Reverse Nodes in K Group.tests:
assert linked_list_to_list(reverseKGroup(build_linked_list([1, 2, 3, 4, 5]), 2)) == [2, 1, 4, 3, 5]
assert linked_list_to_list(reverseKGroup(build_linked_list([1, 2, 3, 4, 5]), 3)) == [3, 2, 1, 4, 5]
# exact multiple of k -> nothing left over
assert linked_list_to_list(reverseKGroup(build_linked_list([1, 2, 3, 4]), 2)) == [2, 1, 4, 3]
# EDGE CASE: k == 1 -> list is unchanged
assert linked_list_to_list(reverseKGroup(build_linked_list([1, 2, 3]), 1)) == [1, 2, 3]
# EDGE CASE: k larger than the list -> leave everything as-is
assert linked_list_to_list(reverseKGroup(build_linked_list([1, 2]), 3)) == [1, 2]
# EDGE CASE: empty list
assert reverseKGroup(None, 2) is None
assert linked_list_to_list(reverseKGroup(build_linked_list([1, 2, 3, 4, 5]), 5)) == [5, 4, 3, 2, 1]
prerequisites: Iterative list reversal with three pointers (`prev`, `curr`, `next_node`) is the building block — you must be able to write it without thinking.
Count k nodes BEFORE reversing anything: an incomplete final group must be left in its original order, and you cannot un-reverse it afterwards.
After reversing a block, the node that was the block's head becomes its TAIL, which is why the stitching line is `head.next = <result of the rest>`.
Recursion here is a clean way to express 'reverse this block, then let the same function fix everything after it'; the recursive call returns the new head of the remainder.
The value returned to the caller is `prev`, the last node processed in the reversal loop — that is the new head of the block.
Recursion depth is n/k, so a truly huge list needs the iterative variant with an explicit `group_prev` pointer.

Check if Linked List is Palindrome.title: Check if Linked List is Palindrome
Check if Linked List is Palindrome.problemStatement: You are given `head`, the first node of a singly linked list whose nodes each carry a value. Return true when the sequence of values reads the same forwards as backwards, and false otherwise. For example 1 -> 2 -> 2 -> 1 and 1 -> 2 -> 1 are palindromes, while 1 -> 2 -> 3 is not. What makes this harder than the array version is that a singly linked list can only be walked in one direction: there are no backward pointers and no indexing, so you cannot simply compare the i-th node against the one i positions from the end. A list with zero or one node is trivially a palindrome.

examples.explanation: The list is symmetric, reading 1->2->2->1 from left and right.
Reading forwards is 1->2, backwards is 2->1.

constraints: The number of nodes in the list is in the range [1, 10^5].
edgeCases: Single node list (always True).
Even vs odd length lists.
All elements are identical.
followUps: Could you do it in O(N) time and O(1) space?
How would you restore the original list after verifying?

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: The only reason this problem is awkward at all is the one-way nature of the list: to compare the first value with the last you must walk all the way to the end, and once there you have no way to step back toward the front. Arrays do not suffer from that — they can be read from either end at will. So the most direct fix is to stop fighting the data structure and copy it into one that behaves the way you need: traverse once from `head`, appending every `curr.val` into a Python list `values`, and the question turns into the easy array version of itself. Comparing `values` with its reversed copy `values[::-1]` then settles it in a single expression. This is honest O(n) time and it is very hard to get wrong, which is exactly why it is worth knowing as a baseline. The catch is the O(n) extra memory for that copy, and an interviewer who insists on O(1) space is specifically asking you to give this version up.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Create an empty list `values` that will hold a plain array copy of the node values.
2. Set a cursor `curr = head` so the traversal starts at the front of the list.
3. Loop while `curr` is not None: append `curr.val` to `values`, then advance `curr = curr.next`. The loop invariant is that `values` always contains the values of every node visited so far, in the same order the list stores them.
4. When the loop exits, `curr` is None, meaning the entire list was consumed and `values` now mirrors the list exactly.
5. Build the reversed copy `values[::-1]` and compare it to `values` with `==`, which checks the two sequences element by element.
6. Return that comparison: True when the values read identically in both directions, False as soon as any position disagrees.
approaches.code:
def isPalindrome(head):
    # List to store the values of nodes
    values = []
    # Traverse the linked list and append values to list
    curr = head
    while curr:
        values.append(curr.val)
        curr = curr.next
    # Compare the list of values with its reversed version
    return values == values[::-1]

complexity.time: O(N)
complexity.space: O(N)

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: The array copy works, but it spends O(n) memory purely to buy the ability to read backwards. You can buy that ability for free instead: if the second half of the list is reversed in place, its nodes become readable from the tail inwards, and then one pointer walking forward from the front and another walking through the reversed back half can meet in the middle over the original nodes. Two tricks make it practical. First, the midpoint is found in a single pass with tortoise and hare — advance `slow` by one node and `fast` by two, and when `fast` runs off the end `slow` is sitting at the start of the second half. Second, reversing a singly linked list in place is just re-pointing each `next` backwards using `prev`, `curr` and `next_node`, which needs no extra memory. Once reversed, `prev` is the original last node, so comparing `left` from `head` against `right` from `prev` compares first with last, second with second-last, and so on. The loop is bounded by `right`, the shorter side, so an odd-length middle node simply gets compared with itself and does no harm. The trade-off is that this mutates the input: the back half is left reversed unless you restore it afterwards.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Use slow/fast pointers to find middle of list.
2. Reverse the list starting from the middle (slow pointer).
3. Use two pointers to compare the values of first half and reversed second half.
4. If values mismatch, return False. If end of second half is reached, return True.
approaches.code:
def isPalindrome(head):  # O(n) time, O(1) space by reversing the back half in place
    # Return True if list is empty or has only one node
    if not head or not head.next:  # zero or one node reads the same in both directions
        return True
    # tortoise and hare: find the midpoint in one pass
    slow = head  # slow lands at the start of the second half
    fast = head  # fast covers two nodes for every one slow covers
    # Move fast by 2 steps and slow by 1 step
    while fast and fast.next:  # both guards matter or fast.next.next raises on None
        slow = slow.next  # one step for slow
        fast = fast.next.next  # two steps for fast; it hits the end at double speed
    # standard in-place reversal, applied from the midpoint on
    prev = None  # prev is the tail sentinel and ends as the reversed head
    curr = slow  # reverse from the midpoint; the front half stays intact
    while curr:  # run to the end of the list
        next_node = curr.next  # stash the next hop before cutting the link
        curr.next = prev  # flip the arrow to point backwards
        prev = curr  # prev advances onto the node just flipped
        curr = next_node  # step forward onto the node we stashed a moment ago
    # Loop over: prev now sits on the original LAST node, i.e. the head of the reversed back half
    # Compare the first half and the reversed second half
    left = head  # left walks forward from the original head
    right = prev  # right walks backward through the reversed tail
    # Check for value equality in both halves
    while right:  # the reversed half is the shorter side, so it sets the limit
        if left.val != right.val:  # one mismatch is enough to disprove the palindrome
            return False
        left = left.next  # advance the front pointer
        right = right.next  # halves meet in the middle, and overlapping is harmless
    # Return True if all values matched
    return True  # every pair matched; note the back half is left reversed

complexity.time: O(N)

Check if Linked List is Palindrome.tests:
assert isPalindrome(build_linked_list([1, 2, 2, 1])) == True     # even-length palindrome
assert isPalindrome(build_linked_list([1, 2, 3, 2, 1])) == True  # odd-length palindrome
assert isPalindrome(build_linked_list([1, 2])) == False
assert isPalindrome(build_linked_list([1, 2, 3, 4])) == False
assert isPalindrome(build_linked_list([1, 2, 3])) == False       # odd-length, not a palindrome
# EDGE CASE: single node is trivially a palindrome
assert isPalindrome(build_linked_list([1])) == True
# EDGE CASE: empty list is trivially a palindrome
assert isPalindrome(None) == True
prerequisites: A singly linked list cannot be walked backwards, so you either copy the values out (O(n) space) or physically reverse half the list (O(1) space).
Slow/fast pointers find the middle: when `fast` reaches the end, `slow` has covered exactly half the distance.

With this particular loop shape (`while fast and fast.next`), `slow` lands on the first node of the second half for even lengths and on the exact middle for odd lengths — both work because the middle element never has to be compared.
Reversing from `slow` gives a second chain whose head is `prev`; comparing `head` against `prev` for as long as `prev` lasts is enough, and the two chains are allowed to overlap at the middle node.
Empty and single-node lists are palindromes by definition and are handled by the early return.
This solution destroys the input; a polite interview answer mentions restoring the reversed half before returning.

Find Starting Point of Loop.title: Find Starting Point of Loop
Find Starting Point of Loop.problemStatement: You are given the head of a singly linked list, where each node stores a value and a pointer to the next node. The list may be an ordinary chain that terminates at a null pointer, or its last node may point back at some earlier node, forming a cycle that a plain traversal would circle around forever. Return a reference to the node where that cycle begins - the node the tail loops back to, which is equivalently the very first node a walk starting from head would visit for a second time. If the list contains no cycle at all, return null. The answer is a reference into the existing list rather than a copy, and the list itself should be left unchanged.

examples.explanation: There is a cycle in the linked list, where tail connects to the second node.
There is no cycle in the linked list.

constraints: The number of nodes in the list is in the range [0, 10^4].
pos is -1 or a valid index in the linked-list.
edgeCases: No cycle in list.
Cycle begins at the head node.
Entire list is a self-loop on a single node.
followUps: Can you solve it using O(1) memory?
What happens if there are multiple loops? (Not possible in standard singly-linked list).

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: The awkward part of this problem is that a cycle leaves no visible landmark. Walking the list, every node looks like an ordinary node with a next pointer, and nothing announces that you have been here before, so the beginner instinct of walking until you fall off the end simply never terminates - there is no end to fall off. What is missing is memory of where you have already stepped. The useful observation is that the entry point of the loop is precisely the first node visited twice: the nodes before the loop are each reached exactly once, and the entry node is reached once on the way in and again after one full lap, before any other node of the loop has had the chance to repeat. So carry a set called visited, and before moving from curr to curr.next, check whether curr is already in it; the first node that is already present is the answer, and if the traversal reaches a null pointer instead, no cycle exists and the answer is None. Identity is what matters here, not value - two distinct nodes may hold the same number - which is why the set stores node references rather than node values. The cost is O(N) time but also O(N) extra memory, and that memory is exactly what Floyd's two-pointer method later eliminates.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Initialize an empty set `visited`.
2. Traverse the list from head.
3. If current node is in `visited`, return it.
4. Else, add it to `visited` and move to next node.
5. If end of list reached, return None.
approaches.code:
def detectCycle(head):
    # Set to store visited nodes
    visited = set()
    # Pointer to traverse the list
    curr = head
    # Loop until the end of the list or cycle is detected
    while curr:
        # If node already visited, it is the start of loop
        if curr in visited:
            return curr
        # Add current node to visited set
        visited.add(curr)
        # Move to the next node
        curr = curr.next
    # Return None if there is no cycle
    return None

complexity.time: O(N)
complexity.space: O(N)

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: The set-based fix works by paying for it: it stores a pointer to every node it steps on, so on a list of a million nodes you carry a million entries to notice one repeat. The observation that buys that memory back is arithmetic. Run slow one step per tick and fast two; once both are inside the loop, fast closes the gap by exactly one node per tick, so it cannot jump over slow - it must land on it. Say the loop entry is L nodes from head and the collision happens k nodes into a loop of length C. Slow walked L+k, fast walked 2(L+k), and their difference L+k is a whole number of laps, so L+k is a multiple of C. From the collision point, L more steps land at position (k+L) mod C = 0, which is the entry - and L steps from head land there too. That is why resetting slow to head and then advancing both by one is guaranteed to meet at the entry and nowhere earlier: before step L the head pointer is still outside the loop, so the two cannot coincide. Cost: O(N) time, O(1) space, trading a self-evident memory proof for arithmetic you have to trust once.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Set `slow = head` and `fast = head`.
2. While `fast` and `fast.next` exist, advance `slow` by one node and `fast` by two.
3. If `slow == fast` after a move, a cycle exists - drop into the second phase.
4. Second phase: reset `slow = head`, leave `fast` at the collision node.
5. Advance `slow` and `fast` one node at a time until `slow == fast`, and return that node - it is the loop entry.
6. If the outer loop ends because `fast` or `fast.next` became None, the list terminates, so return None.
approaches.code:
def detectCycle(head):
    # Initialize slow and fast pointers to head
    slow = head
    # Initialize fast pointer to head
    fast = head
    # Traverse the list to find a collision point
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next.next
        # Collision detected
        if slow == fast:
            # Move slow pointer back to the head
            slow = head
            # Move both pointers at same speed until they meet
            while slow != fast:
                slow = slow.next
                fast = fast.next
            # Meeting point is the start of the loop
            return slow
    # Return None if no cycle exists
    return None

complexity.time: O(N)

Find Starting Point of Loop.tests:
def _make_cycle(vals, pos):
    """Build a list and link the tail back to index pos (pos = -1 -> no cycle)."""
    head = build_linked_list(vals)
    if head is None or pos < 0:
        return head, None
    tail = head
    while tail.next:
        tail = tail.next
    target = head
    for _ in range(pos):
        target = target.next
    tail.next = target
    return head, target

h, start = _make_cycle([3, 2, 0, -4], 1)
assert detectCycle(h) is start                 # loop begins at the node holding 2

h, start = _make_cycle([1, 2], 0)              # tail points back to the head
assert detectCycle(h) is start is h

# EDGE CASE: single node pointing at itself
h, start = _make_cycle([1], 0)
assert detectCycle(h) is h

# EDGE CASE: no cycle at all -> None, and the walk must terminate
h, _ = _make_cycle([1, 2, 3, 4], -1)
assert detectCycle(h) is None
# EDGE CASE: empty list
assert detectCycle(None) is None
prerequisites: Floyd's cycle detection has TWO phases: phase 1 finds any meeting point inside the loop, phase 2 converts it into the loop's entry node.
Phase 1 works because fast gains one node per step on slow, so inside a loop of length L they must collide within L steps.

The phase-2 maths: if the entry is `a` nodes from the head and the meeting point is `b` nodes into the loop, then `a` and the distance from the meeting point back to the entry are congruent modulo L — so two pointers moving one step each from head and from the meeting point meet exactly at the entry.
The loop guard must be `while fast and fast.next` because fast dereferences two links; check both or an acyclic list crashes.
Return the NODE, not a value or an index — several nodes may share the same value.
The hash-set version is far easier to derive under pressure and is O(n) time; Floyd's only advantage, but a decisive one, is O(1) space.

Flatten a Linked List.title: Flatten a Linked List
Flatten a Linked List.problemStatement: Given a Linked List of size N, where every node represents a sub-linked-list and contains two pointers: a next pointer to the next node, and a bottom pointer to a linked list where this node is head. Each sub-linked-list is sorted. Flatten the link list such that all nodes appear in a single sorted bottom-linked-list.

examples.explanation: All elements merged in sorted order.

edgeCases: Only one vertical list.
Columns have different number of elements.
Empty list.
followUps: Can we optimize the merge using a Min-Heap (Priority Queue)?
What is the time complexity of the Min-Heap approach compared to recursive merging?

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: Faced with a grid of columns joined sideways by `next` and downwards by `bottom`, the first honest thought is usually: the required output is just one sorted chain, so why preserve any of this two-dimensional structure at all? Pull every number out, sort them, and build a fresh chain. That is precisely what this version does — a worklist `queue` holds column heads, each column is walked down through `bottom`, every `curr.data` is appended to `values`, and any `curr.next` discovered along the way is pushed onto the worklist and then severed so the answer uses `bottom` only. It is easy to believe and easy to write, which is its value. What makes it unsatisfying is that it throws away information you were handed for free: each column arrived already sorted, so a general-purpose sort is re-deriving order that already existed, and the rebuild allocates brand-new nodes instead of relinking the ones you have. Cost: O(N*M) to harvest, O(N*M log(N*M)) to sort, and O(N*M) extra memory for `values` plus the rebuilt chain.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Initialize a list `values`.
2. Push the root to a queue.
3. Traverse the tree structure using `next` and `bottom` pointers, saving values.
4. Sort `values`.
5. Rebuild the list using `bottom` pointers.
6. Return new root.
approaches.code:
def flatten(root):
    # Plan: forget the 2-D shape entirely, harvest every value, sort, rebuild.
    values = []
    # A worklist of column heads still waiting to be walked downwards.
    queue = [root]
    # Keep going while some column has not been harvested yet.
    while queue:
        # Take the head of the next column (pop(0) is O(n) but this is the naive way).
        curr = queue.pop(0)
        # Walk straight down this column via the bottom pointers.
        while curr:
            # Record the value; we no longer care which column it came from.
            values.append(curr.data)
            # If this node also has a right neighbour, that is another column.
            if curr.next:
                # Remember it for later...
                queue.append(curr.next)
                # ...and cut the next pointer, since the answer uses bottom only.
                curr.next = None
            # Step one cell down inside the current column.
            curr = curr.bottom
    # Nothing was collected -> the input list was empty.
    if not values:
        return None
    # Throw away all structure knowledge and just sort the numbers.
    values.sort()
    # Rebuild one single column, chained purely through bottom pointers.
    new_root = Node(values[0])
    # Cursor for appending the remaining values in order.
    curr = new_root
    # Attach every remaining value below the previous one.
    for val in values[1:]:
        # Create the next cell of the flattened column.
        curr.bottom = Node(val)
        # Move the cursor down onto it.
        curr = curr.bottom
    # new_root is the head of the freshly built flattened list.
    return new_root

complexity.time: O(N * M * log(N * M))
complexity.space: O(N * M)

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: The wasted effort in the naive version is sorting numbers that were already in order. Every column is individually sorted, so the true task is not sorting at all — it is merging, the same linear two-pointer step you would use on two sorted arrays. That reframing is the entire insight. But there are many columns, so which pairs get merged, and in what order? The recursion answers it cleanly: collapse everything to the right of the current head first with `flatten(root.next)`, and the moment that call returns, `root.next` is guaranteed to be one single fully sorted column. From then on you are only ever merging two sorted chains, which `mergeTwoLists` handles with a `dummy` head and a `temp` cursor, repeatedly attaching whichever of `a.data` and `b.data` is smaller through the `bottom` pointer and finally hooking on whichever tail is left over. Recursing right-to-left maintains the invariant that no more than two chains are ever in play at once, and no new nodes are allocated. Cost: O(N*M) overall with O(N) recursion stack for the N columns.
approaches.algorithm:
1. If `root` or `root.next` is None, return `root`.
2. Recursively call `flatten(root.next)` to obtain a flattened right list.
3. Merge the current vertical list `root` with the flattened right list `root.next` using a sorted merge helper.
4. Return the merged list.
approaches.code:
def mergeTwoLists(a, b):
    # Dummy node so we never special-case "the merged list is still empty".
    dummy = Node(0)
    # temp always points at the LAST node of the merged chain built so far.
    temp = dummy
    # Classic two-pointer merge, except we walk with .bottom, not .next.
    while a and b:
        # Whichever head is smaller must come next for the output to stay sorted.
        if a.data < b.data:
            # Hook node a underneath temp.
            temp.bottom = a
            # temp moves onto the node we just appended.
            temp = temp.bottom
            # Advance inside column a.
            a = a.bottom
        else:
            # b is smaller (or equal), so b is appended instead.
            temp.bottom = b
            # temp moves onto the node we just appended.
            temp = temp.bottom
            # Advance inside column b.
            b = b.bottom
    # One column ran out; the other is already sorted, so attach it whole.
    if a:
        temp.bottom = a  # leftover tail of a
    else:
        temp.bottom = b  # leftover tail of b (may be None)
    # dummy.bottom is the real head of the merged column.
    return dummy.bottom

def flatten(root):
    # Base case: nothing at all, or only ONE column left -> nothing to merge.
    if not root or not root.next:
        return root
    # Recurse to the right FIRST: collapse everything after us into one column.
    root.next = flatten(root.next)
    # Now merge our own column with that single already-flattened column.
    root = mergeTwoLists(root, root.next)
    # Return the head of the merged column back to our caller.
    return root

complexity.time: O(N * M) where N is number of columns, M is nodes per column
complexity.space: O(N) recursion stack

Flatten a Linked List.tests:
class Node:                       # this problem needs data/next/bottom, not val/next
    def __init__(self, data=0, next=None, bottom=None):
        self.data = data
        self.next = next
        self.bottom = bottom

def _build(cols):
    """cols = list of already-sorted columns; links columns by .next, cells by .bottom."""
    head = None
    prev = None
    for col in cols:
        top = None
        for v in reversed(col):
            top = Node(v, None, top)
        if prev is None:
            head = top
        else:
            prev.next = top
        prev = top
    return head

def _flat(root):
    out = []
    while root:
        out.append(root.data)
        root = root.bottom
    return out

r = _build([[5, 7, 8, 30], [10, 20], [19, 22, 50], [28, 35, 40, 45]])
assert _flat(flatten(r)) == [5, 7, 8, 10, 19, 20, 22, 28, 30, 35, 40, 45, 50]

# EDGE CASE: a single column is already flat
assert _flat(flatten(_build([[1, 4, 9]]))) == [1, 4, 9]

# columns whose order must be fully interleaved / reversed
assert _flat(flatten(_build([[3], [1], [2]]))) == [1, 2, 3]

# duplicates across columns must all survive
assert _flat(flatten(_build([[2, 2], [1, 2]]))) == [1, 2, 2, 2]

# EDGE CASE: empty input
assert flatten(None) is None
prerequisites: Each node has TWO pointers here: `next` walks right to the head of the following column, `bottom` walks down inside a column — the answer must be a single column chained by `bottom`.
Every column is already sorted, which is exactly the precondition for a merge; the problem is really 'merge k sorted lists'.
Merging two sorted lists with a dummy node plus a `temp` tail pointer is the core subroutine — reuse it, do not re-derive it.

Recurse to the RIGHT first: flatten everything after the current column into one column, then merge your column into it. Merging into an already-merged result keeps each node moving only once per level.
When one list runs out mid-merge, attach the other list wholesale instead of continuing node by node — it is already sorted.
The recursion depth equals the number of columns, so O(k) stack space; the collect-sort-rebuild brute force instead costs O(total) memory and an O(total log total) sort.

Rotate a Linked List.title: Rotate a Linked List
