edgeCases: Pop from empty stack
Top/Peek from empty stack
Stack overflow if capacity is reached
followUps: How would you implement a dynamic resizing array to avoid overflow?

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: Before writing any index arithmetic, notice what a stack actually demands of its storage: all of the action happens at one single end. Nothing is ever inserted into the middle and nothing is ever removed from the middle, so the underlying container only needs cheap access to its tail. A Python list already provides exactly that — `append` adds at the end and `pop()` removes from the end, both amortised O(1) — so the simplest correct stack is a thin wrapper that renames those two operations and adds the empty guards this problem asks for, returning -1 from `pop` and `top` when `self.stack` is falsy, with `isEmpty` and `size` reading straight off `len`. Why this still counts as the brute-force answer: it leans entirely on a dynamic array that the language grows and reallocates behind your back, hiding the very mechanics an interviewer is probing when they say "using an array". Cost: O(1) per operation, O(N) space that expands on demand.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Initialize an empty list stack.
2. Push appends to the list.
3. Pop removes and returns the last element of the list, returning -1 if empty.
4. Top peeks at stack[-1], returning -1 if empty.

complexity.space: O(N)

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: The list version works, but it leaves the interesting question unanswered: how does a stack actually live inside a fixed block of memory? The realisation is that the container never needs to grow — you only need one integer that remembers where the top currently sits. So allocate `self.arr` once with a capacity of 1000 slots and keep `self.top_idx`, initialised to -1 to mean "nothing stored yet". Push becomes increment-then-write, pop becomes read-then-decrement, and no element is ever shifted or copied. Values left sitting above `top_idx` after a pop are harmless garbage because they are logically outside the stack, which is why pop can simply move the pointer instead of clearing anything. That single index is also the invariant that makes the rest trivial: `top_idx` always names the slot holding the most recently pushed element, so `size()` is just `top_idx + 1` and `isEmpty()` is just `top_idx == -1`. Cost: genuine O(1) per operation with no reallocation, paid for with O(C) memory reserved up front and a hard capacity ceiling.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Initialize a fixed-size array of size 1000 and a top_idx pointer to -1.
2. In push, increment top_idx and assign the value.
3. In pop, retrieve the value at top_idx, decrement top_idx, and return the value.
4. In top, return the value at top_idx if top_idx >= 0.
approaches.code:
class MyStack:
    def __init__(self):
        # Fixed capacity array to store stack elements
        self.arr = [-1] * 1000
        # Pointer to the index of the top element
        self.top_idx = -1

    def push(self, x: int) -> None:
        # Increment top index pointer
        self.top_idx += 1
        # Place the element at top index
        self.arr[self.top_idx] = x

    def pop(self) -> int:
        # Check if stack is empty
        if self.top_idx == -1:
            return -1
        # Retrieve top element
        val = self.arr[self.top_idx]
        # Decrement top index pointer
        self.top_idx -= 1
        # Return the popped element
        return val

    def top(self) -> int:
        # Check if stack is empty
        if self.top_idx == -1:
            return -1
        # Return top element
        return self.arr[self.top_idx]

    def isEmpty(self) -> bool:
        # Check if top index is -1
        return self.top_idx == -1

    def size(self) -> int:
        # Size is index + 1
        return self.top_idx + 1

complexity.space: O(C) where C is capacity

Implement Stack Using Array.tests:
st = MyStack()
assert st.isEmpty() is True or st.isEmpty() == True
assert st.pop() == -1
st.push(10); st.push(20); st.push(30)
assert st.size() == 3
assert st.top() == 30
assert st.pop() == 30
assert st.pop() == 20
assert st.top() == 10
assert st.size() == 1
assert st.pop() == 10
assert st.isEmpty() == True
assert st.top() == -1
print("ok")
prerequisites: A stack is LIFO: push, pop and top all act on the SAME end, which is exactly why one integer index gives O(1) for all of them.
top_idx = -1 is the 'empty' sentinel: push pre-increments then writes, pop reads then post-decrements.
Popped slots are never erased — they simply fall outside the live range 0..top_idx and become logically dead cells.
A fixed-capacity array can overflow, while a Python list grows with amortised O(1) appends; be ready to discuss doubling/resizing.
Underflow must be handled deliberately (return -1 here) instead of letting an IndexError escape to the caller.

Implement Queue Using Array.title: Implement Queue Using Array
Implement Queue Using Array.problemStatement: Build a queue — a first-in, first-out container — on top of nothing but a plain fixed-size array, without using any built-in queue or deque type. The class must expose five operations: enqueue(x) adds x at the back and reports whether it succeeded, returning False when the array is already full; dequeue() removes and returns the element that has been waiting longest, or returns -1 when the queue is empty; front() reports that same oldest element without removing it, or -1 when the queue is empty; isEmpty() reports whether any elements remain; and size() reports how many there are. The backing array in this implementation has a fixed capacity of 1000 slots, and every one of the five operations is expected to run in constant time regardless of how many elements are stored.
constraints: Values of x are in range [-10^5, 10^5]
edgeCases: Dequeue from empty queue
Front from empty queue
Queue overflow
followUps: Can you implement the queue using a dynamically resizing array?

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: One caveat before the code, because this version deliberately breaks a rule of the problem: the task says to build the queue on a plain FIXED-SIZE array whose enqueue returns False once the array is full, but a Python list grows on demand, so the enqueue below can never fail and always returns True. That is fine for a first sketch — it isolates the one lesson this approach exists to teach, namely why dequeue is slow — and the circular-array version below honours the fixed-capacity contract properly. With that said: a queue is just 'first in, first out', and a Python list already knows how to grow at one end, so the laziest implementation is to let the list BE the queue. append(x) puts a new value at the back, index 0 is always the oldest value still waiting, and pop(0) removes exactly that oldest value. Every operation reads like the definition of a queue, which is why this is the version to write first. The hidden cost lives inside pop(0): a Python list is a contiguous block of pointers, so removing the element at index 0 forces every single remaining element to slide one slot to the left. Dequeuing from a queue holding N items therefore costs O(N) work, and draining a queue of N items costs O(N^2) overall. Nothing about a queue actually requires that shuffling — the front just needs to MOVE, not the data — and that observation is what leads directly to the circular array.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Keep one Python list `queue` as the backing store; the end of the list is the rear and index 0 is the front.
2. enqueue(x): append x to the end of the list and report success.
3. dequeue(): if the list is empty return the -1 sentinel, otherwise pop(0) — which returns the oldest element and shifts everything after it one slot left.
4. front(): if the list is empty return -1, otherwise return queue[0] without removing it.
5. isEmpty()/size(): answer straight from len(queue).

complexity.time: O(1) for enqueue/front/isEmpty/size, O(N) for dequeue — pop(0) shifts every remaining element one position left
complexity.space: O(N) — the list stores exactly the N live elements and grows on demand

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: The obvious way to build a queue on an array is to keep the front at index 0: enqueue appends at the end, and dequeue removes arr[0] and shifts every remaining element one step left. It works, but that shift makes dequeue O(n), which is unacceptable for the one operation a queue exists to make cheap. The natural repair is to stop shifting and instead move a front_idx marker forward on each removal. That fixes dequeue, but creates a leak: rear_idx keeps climbing toward the end of the array while the abandoned slots below front_idx pile up unused, so the queue reports 'full' with most of the array empty. The insight is that those two problems cancel if you stop thinking of the array as a line and start thinking of it as a ring — when an index runs off the right edge, wrap it back to 0 with (idx + 1) % capacity, and the freed slots at the front are reused automatically. One wrinkle remains: on a ring, front_idx == rear_idx is ambiguous, since it is true both when the queue is completely empty and when it is completely full. That is why the class carries an explicit count field and uses it, never the pointers, to answer isEmpty, size and the full check. Every operation becomes a couple of arithmetic steps, so all five are O(1), with O(capacity) memory reserved up front.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Allocate a fixed array of `capacity` slots and keep three fields: front_idx, rear_idx and count.
2. enqueue(x): if count == capacity the buffer is full, so return False; otherwise write x at arr[rear_idx], advance rear_idx = (rear_idx + 1) % capacity and increment count.
3. dequeue(): if count == 0 return -1; otherwise read val = arr[front_idx], advance front_idx = (front_idx + 1) % capacity, decrement count and return val.
4. front(): return -1 when count == 0, else return arr[front_idx] without moving any pointer.
5. isEmpty() and size(): read `count` directly — it is the only unambiguous emptiness test, because front_idx == rear_idx happens both when the ring is empty and when it is full.
approaches.code:
class MyQueue:
    def __init__(self):
        # Fixed capacity of 1000
        self.capacity = 1000
        # Fixed capacity circular array
        self.arr = [-1] * self.capacity
        # Pointer to front element
        self.front_idx = 0
        # Pointer to rear element
        self.rear_idx = 0
        # Current number of elements in queue
        self.count = 0

    def enqueue(self, x: int) -> bool:
        # Check if queue is full
        if self.count == self.capacity:
            return False
        # Insert element at circular rear position
        self.arr[self.rear_idx] = x
        # Advance rear pointer in circular fashion
        self.rear_idx = (self.rear_idx + 1) % self.capacity
        # Increment the element count
        self.count += 1
        return True

    def dequeue(self) -> int:
        # Check if queue is empty
        if self.count == 0:
            return -1
        # Retrieve front element value
        val = self.arr[self.front_idx]
        # Move front pointer in circular fashion
        self.front_idx = (self.front_idx + 1) % self.capacity
        # Decrement element count
        self.count -= 1
        # Return dequeued value
        return val

    def front(self) -> int:
        # An empty queue has no front element to report
        if self.count == 0:
            return -1
        # front_idx always points at the oldest live slot
        return self.arr[self.front_idx]

    def isEmpty(self) -> bool:
        # count is the single source of truth: front_idx == rear_idx is ambiguous
        return self.count == 0

    def size(self) -> int:
        # count is kept in sync by every enqueue and dequeue, so this is O(1)
        return self.count

complexity.time: O(1) for all operations
complexity.space: O(C) where C is capacity

Implement Queue Using Array.tests:
q = MyQueue()
assert q.isEmpty() == True
assert q.dequeue() == -1
q.enqueue(5); q.enqueue(6); q.enqueue(7)
assert q.size() == 3
assert q.front() == 5
assert q.dequeue() == 5
assert q.dequeue() == 6
assert q.front() == 7
q.enqueue(8)
assert q.dequeue() == 7
assert q.dequeue() == 8
assert q.isEmpty() == True
assert q.dequeue() == -1
print("ok")
prerequisites: A queue is FIFO: you enqueue at the rear and dequeue at the front, so you need TWO moving indices, unlike a stack's single one.
list.pop(0) is O(N) because every element behind index 0 shifts left — that single fact is the whole motivation for the circular buffer.
Circular indexing with (idx + 1) % capacity lets front and rear wrap around the end of the array and reuse freed slots.
front_idx == rear_idx is ambiguous (it means both 'empty' and 'full'), so keep an explicit count to tell the two apart.
collections.deque is the production answer in Python, but hand-writing the ring buffer is what the interview is actually testing.

Implement Stack Using Queue.title: Implement Stack Using Queue
Implement Stack Using Queue.problemStatement: Build a class MyStack that behaves like a last-in-first-out stack, but whose only internal storage is a single first-in-first-out queue. The operations you may perform on that queue are the ones a real queue offers: append to the back, remove from the front, look at the front element, and read the current size. The class must expose push(x), which places x on top of the stack; pop(), which removes and returns the element most recently pushed; top(), which returns that same element without removing it; and empty(), which reports whether the stack currently holds nothing. In this implementation, calling pop() or top() on an empty stack returns -1 rather than raising an error.
constraints: Operations are push, pop, top, empty
At most 100 calls will be made to push, pop, top, empty
edgeCases: Pop from empty stack
Top from empty stack
followUps: Can you implement this using only two queues?

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: A queue hands you its OLDEST element, but a stack must hand you its NEWEST one, so somewhere we have to pay to reverse that order. The two-queue idea pays that price on every push and keeps it very explicit. Whenever a new value x arrives we do not put it behind the existing elements — we put it alone into the empty helper queue q2, and only then pour every element of q1 in behind it. After that pour, q2 holds x at the front followed by all the older values in their previous relative order, which is exactly the stack order we want. A single swap of the two names makes q1 the live queue again and leaves q2 empty for next time. Because the front of q1 is now always the most recently pushed value, pop and top become trivial O(1) popleft/peek operations. The cost is that every push moves the entire contents of the structure, so push is O(N) and needs a second queue's worth of scratch space.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Keep two queues: q1 is the live queue whose FRONT is the stack top, and q2 is empty scratch space.
2. push(x): append x into the empty q2 so that x sits at its front.
3. Drain q1 into q2 with popleft/append until q1 is empty, so the older values line up behind x.
4. Swap the names q1 and q2 — q1 is the live queue again and q2 is empty for the next push.
5. pop(): return -1 if q1 is empty, otherwise popleft() — the front is the newest value.
6. top()/empty(): peek q1[0] (or -1) and test len(q1) == 0.

complexity.time: O(N) for push because every existing element is moved once, O(1) for pop/top/empty
complexity.space: O(N) — the elements plus a second queue that is empty between pushes

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: The conflict is simple to state: a queue always hands back the element that has been waiting longest, while a stack must hand back the one that just arrived. The usual first fix is to keep two queues and shuttle every element from one to the other on each operation so the newest element is left alone at the front. That works but it doubles the containers and the bookkeeping. The observation that removes the second queue entirely is that a queue can rotate through itself: popping the front and immediately appending it to the back is a legal queue operation, and doing that exactly len(q) - 1 times after appending x cycles every older element around behind x, leaving x sitting at the front. Once that rotation is part of push, the invariant holds forever: the front of the queue is always the top of the stack, and the rest of the queue is in stack order behind it. That makes pop, top and empty plain O(1) reads with no rotation at all, and concentrates the entire O(N) cost into push, which is the right trade whenever reads are more frequent than writes. Memory is O(N) for the elements themselves and nothing more.
approaches.algorithm:
1. In `__init__`, create the single underlying queue as `self.q = deque()`, chosen because a deque gives O(1) append at the back and O(1) popleft at the front.
2. In `push(x)`, first append x to the back with `self.q.append(x)`, which temporarily leaves it in the wrong place.
3. Still in push, repeat `self.q.append(self.q.popleft())` exactly `len(self.q) - 1` times, moving every element that was already there around behind x. The invariant established here is that after any push, the front of q is the newest element and the remaining elements follow in last-in-first-out order.
4. In `pop()`, return -1 if the queue is empty; otherwise return `self.q.popleft()`, which by the invariant is the most recently pushed element.
5. In `top()`, return -1 if the queue is empty; otherwise return `self.q[0]`, the same element pop would return, but left in place.
6. In `empty()`, return `len(self.q) == 0`.

complexity.time: O(N) push, O(1) pop
complexity.space: O(N)

Implement Stack Using Queue.tests:
st = MyStack()
assert st.empty() == True
assert st.pop() == -1
st.push(1); st.push(2); st.push(3)
assert st.top() == 3
assert st.pop() == 3
assert st.pop() == 2
assert st.top() == 1
assert st.pop() == 1
assert st.empty() == True
assert st.top() == -1
print("ok")
prerequisites: A queue only exposes append (rear) and popleft (front), so the whole trick is forcing its FRONT to hold the newest element.
After appending x, rotating the queue len(q) - 1 times sends every older element behind x and restores the invariant 'front == stack top'.
collections.deque gives O(1) append and popleft; a plain list's pop(0) is O(N) and would ruin the analysis.
This is the 'costly push' variant: push is O(N) while pop and top stay O(1) — the two-queue version has the same asymptotics.
popleft() on an empty deque raises IndexError, so pop and top need explicit empty guards that return the -1 sentinel.

Implement Queue Using Stack.title: Implement Queue Using Stack
Implement Queue Using Stack.problemStatement: A stack is last-in-first-out: you may only push onto the top and pop from the top. A queue is first-in-first-out: the element that has been waiting the longest must come out first. Your task is to build a working queue class whose only storage is stacks, supporting four operations: push(x) adds x at the back of the queue, pop() removes and returns the element at the front, peek() returns the front element without removing it, and empty() reports whether the queue currently holds anything. The externally visible behaviour must be pure FIFO even though every underlying container is LIFO.
constraints: Operations are push, pop, peek, empty
At most 100 calls will be made to all operations
edgeCases: Pop from empty queue
Peek from empty queue
followUps: Can you optimize the operations to get amortized O(1) time complexity?

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: A stack gives back the value you pushed most recently, while a queue must give back the value you pushed first, so the oldest element has to end up on TOP of the stack. The most direct way to guarantee that is to rebuild the whole stack on every push. When x arrives we first pour all of s1 into the helper stack s2 — pouring a stack into a stack reverses it, so s2 now holds the elements upside down. We drop x into the now-empty s1, then pour s2 back on top of it. The net effect is that x has been inserted at the BOTTOM of s1 while every older element kept its relative order, which means the very first value ever pushed is sitting on top and ready to be popped. Reads become trivially O(1): pop is s1.pop() and peek is s1[-1]. The price is that a push touches all N elements twice, so push is O(N) and a burst of N pushes costs O(N^2) — the lazy two-stack version fixes exactly that.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Keep two stacks: s1 holds the queue with the OLDEST element on top, and s2 is scratch space.
2. push(x): pop every element of s1 and push it onto s2, which reverses the order.
3. Push x onto the now-empty s1, so it is temporarily the only (and bottom) element.
4. Pop everything back from s2 onto s1, restoring the old elements above x — x is now the bottom, i.e. the newest.
5. pop(): return -1 if s1 is empty, otherwise s1.pop() — the top is the oldest element.
6. peek()/empty(): read s1[-1] (or -1) and test len(s1) == 0.

complexity.time: O(N) for push because every element is moved twice, O(1) for pop/peek/empty
complexity.space: O(N) — the N elements plus the scratch stack used during a push

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition:
Rebuilding the stack on every push pours it into a helper and back so the new element sinks to the bottom: O(n) per arrival, re-reversing elements that were already ordered.

The reversal is owed only at read time, and once paid it serves every read until the pile empties. So `input_stack` takes arrivals untouched, newest on top, while `output_stack` holds the older part of the queue flipped, oldest on top. Push 1, 2, 3 and the first pop drains input into output as [3,2,1] and returns 1; the next two pops are free.

The refill guard is the correctness condition: the invariant - what holds before and after every operation - is that the queue front-to-back equals `output_stack` top-down then `input_stack` bottom-up. Transferring only when `output_stack` is empty preserves it, since everything poured in is strictly newer than everything already served. Pour into a non-empty output and the newest arrivals leave first, breaking FIFO.

Each element crosses once in its life, so m operations cost O(m) - amortised O(1), averaged over a run rather than promised per call, since one pop can still cost O(n). Space O(N).
approaches.algorithm:
1. In `__init__`, create two Python lists used as stacks: `input_stack` for newly pushed values and `output_stack` for values on their way out.
2. In `push(x)`, append x to `input_stack` and stop there; arrivals are never reordered on the way in, so push is unconditionally O(1).
3. In `pop()`, first check whether `output_stack` is empty. If it is, drain `input_stack` with a while loop that pops each element off its top and appends it to `output_stack`, reversing the arrival order so the oldest waiting element ends up on top.
4. Transfer only when `output_stack` is empty - that guard maintains the invariant that `output_stack` holds the older part of the queue reversed while `input_stack` holds newer arrivals in arrival order.
5. Still in `pop()`, if `output_stack` is empty even after the drain then the queue held nothing, so return -1; otherwise return `output_stack.pop()`, the true front of the queue.
6. In `peek()`, run the same refill check, then read `output_stack[-1]` without removing it, returning -1 when both stacks are empty.
7. In `empty()`, return True only when `input_stack` and `output_stack` are both empty.

complexity.time: Amortized O(1) for all operations
complexity.space: O(N)

Implement Queue Using Stack.tests:
q = MyQueue()
assert q.empty() == True
assert q.pop() == -1
q.push(1); q.push(2); q.push(3)
assert q.peek() == 1
assert q.pop() == 1
q.push(4)
assert q.pop() == 2
assert q.pop() == 3
assert q.pop() == 4
assert q.empty() == True
assert q.peek() == -1
print("ok")
prerequisites: Pouring one stack into another reverses the order — doing that exactly once is what turns LIFO into FIFO.
Two stacks with distinct jobs: input_stack receives every push, output_stack serves every pop, and you only transfer when output_stack runs dry.
Amortised analysis: each element moves from input to output at most once, so N operations cost O(N) total even though a single pop can cost O(N).
peek() must run the same lazy transfer as pop(), otherwise it reads a stale or empty output_stack.
empty() has to check BOTH stacks — elements can be parked in input_stack while output_stack is already empty.

Next Greater Element.title: Next Greater Element
Next Greater Element.problemStatement: You are given two integer arrays, nums1 and nums2. Every value that appears in nums1 also appears somewhere in nums2, and the values inside nums2 are distinct, so a value identifies a unique position there. The next greater element of a value x is defined by locating x inside nums2 and scanning to the right from that position: the answer is the first value encountered that is strictly larger than x. Return an array of the same length as nums1 in which position i holds the next greater element of nums1[i] as measured inside nums2, or -1 when every value standing to the right of x in nums2 is smaller than or equal to it - which includes the case where x is the last element of nums2.

examples.explanation: Next greater for 4 is 5, for 5 is 25, for 2 is 25, and for 25 is -1.

edgeCases: Array of size 1
Strictly increasing array
Strictly decreasing array
followUps: What if the array is circular? (Next Greater Element II)

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: Read the definition literally and code exactly that. For each query value x in nums1, first find where x lives inside nums2, then walk rightwards from that position and return the very first element that is strictly greater than x. If the walk runs off the end, the answer is -1. Notice the word FIRST — we stop at the first bigger element, not the biggest one, so 'break' is essential. The weakness is obvious once you write it: every query starts its own scan from scratch, and two neighbouring queries redo almost identical work. With m queries over an n-element array this costs O(m * n), but it is short, transparent, and it is the reference that proves the stack version is right.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Prepare an empty answer list that will end up the same length as nums1.
2. For each value x in nums1, locate its index in nums2 with nums2.index(x).
3. Set the running answer to -1, the value used when nothing greater exists.
4. Scan indices to the right of that position and, at the first element strictly greater than x, store it and break out of the scan.
5. Append the stored value (or the untouched -1) to the answer list and move on to the next query.
6. Return the answer list.
approaches.code:
def nextGreaterElement(nums1: List[int], nums2: List[int]) -> List[int]:
    ans = []                                       # one answer per query value in nums1
    for x in nums1:                                # handle the queries one at a time
        pos = nums2.index(x)                       # locate x inside nums2 (a linear scan)
        found = -1                                 # default when nothing bigger exists
        # Scan strictly to the RIGHT of x looking for the FIRST strictly greater value.
        for j in range(pos + 1, len(nums2)):
            if nums2[j] > x:                       # first element that beats x
                found = nums2[j]                   # that is the next greater element
                break                              # stop here - we want the first, not the largest
        ans.append(found)                          # record the answer (value or -1)
    # Every query restarts its own scan, so shared work between queries is thrown away.
    return ans                                     # same length and order as nums1

complexity.time: O(M * N) — each of the M queries locates its value and then scans up to N elements.
complexity.space: O(1) extra — only the output list is allocated.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: The first thing most people write is the direct reading of the definition: for each value of nums1, find it in nums2, then walk rightwards until something bigger turns up. That is correct, but it is wasteful in a very specific way - neighbouring queries re-read the same stretch of nums2 again and again, so a long run of small numbers gets scanned once per query and the total cost climbs to O(N*M). The observation that unlocks the fast solution is that the answer depends only on nums2, so one single left-to-right sweep can settle it for every value at once. During that sweep, a value that has not yet met anything bigger is simply waiting, and the set of waiting values is always in decreasing order from oldest to newest: if a later value were larger than an earlier waiter, that earlier waiter would already have been answered and would no longer be waiting. Decreasing order with the newest at the end is exactly a stack whose top is the smallest unresolved value, so when a new number arrives it can immediately pay off every waiter it beats by popping from the top until the top is no longer smaller. Each value of nums2 is pushed once and popped at most once, so the sweep costs O(N) for the N elements of nums2, and answering nums1 is then M dictionary lookups, one per query. The price is O(N) memory: the lookup map and the stack each hold at most one entry per element of nums2.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Create an empty dictionary greater_map, which will record for each value of nums2 the first strictly larger value standing to its right, and an empty list stack that holds values still waiting for such a neighbour.
2. Sweep nums2 from left to right with loop variable num. The invariant maintained on every pass is that stack contains exactly the values seen so far that are still unresolved, ordered strictly decreasing from the bottom of the stack to the top.
3. While stack is non-empty and its top stack[-1] is smaller than num, pop that top value and record greater_map[popped] = num, because num is the first value larger than it to appear anywhere to its right.
4. Push num onto stack; it is now the smallest waiter and sits on top, so the decreasing invariant still holds for the next iteration.
5. When the sweep ends, any values still left on stack never met a bigger number, so they were never inserted into greater_map at all - their absence from the map is how the -1 case is encoded.
6. Build the result by mapping every x in nums1 to greater_map.get(x, -1), so a value found in the map yields its next greater element and a value missing from the map yields -1.
approaches.code:
def nextGreaterElement(nums1: List[int], nums2: List[int]) -> List[int]:
    greater_map = {}  # value -> the first greater value standing to its right
    # Values we have seen but not yet answered - each is still waiting for a
    # bigger number to appear on its right. We only ever push a value onto a
    # larger one, so the stack runs large-at-the-bottom, small-at-the-top.
    stack = []
    
    # Find next greater elements in nums2
    for num in nums2:  # a single left-to-right sweep of nums2
        # num beats everything sitting on top, and those are exactly the values
        # whose answer is still unknown, so num answers all of them at once.
        while stack and stack[-1] < num:
            greater_map[stack.pop()] = num
        stack.append(num)  # num now waits for something bigger than itself
        
    # Map values or default to -1
    return [greater_map.get(x, -1) for x in nums1]  # -1 for every value that never found a bigger neighbour

complexity.time: O(N + M) — one left-to-right sweep of the N-element nums2, then one dictionary lookup for each of the M query values in nums1.
complexity.space: O(N) — greater_map holds one entry per value of nums2 and the stack holds at most N values (N = len(nums2)); the returned list of M answers is the output, not extra space.

Next Greater Element.tests:
assert nextGreaterElement([4, 1, 2], [1, 3, 4, 2]) == [-1, 3, -1]
assert nextGreaterElement([2, 4], [1, 2, 3, 4]) == [3, -1]
assert nextGreaterElement([], [1, 2, 3]) == []     # edge: no queries at all
assert nextGreaterElement([1], [1]) == [-1]        # edge: single element has nothing to its right
assert nextGreaterElement([5, 4, 3, 2, 1], [5, 4, 3, 2, 1]) == [-1, -1, -1, -1, -1]
assert nextGreaterElement([1, 3, 5, 2, 4], [6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, 7]) == [7, 7, 7, 7, 7]
prerequisites: The monotonic (strictly decreasing) stack pattern: keep values that are still waiting for a bigger neighbour, and resolve them all at once when a bigger value arrives.
Amortised O(n) reasoning: every element of nums2 is pushed exactly once and popped at most once, so the inner while loop does not make the scan quadratic.
nums1 is guaranteed to be a subset of nums2 with distinct values, which is what lets a plain value-to-answer dictionary work instead of index bookkeeping.
`dict.get(key, -1)` returns the default instead of raising KeyError — perfect for the elements that never found a greater neighbour.
Elements still sitting on the stack when the scan ends have NO next greater element; they are simply never written into the map.
Python lists act as stacks with `append()` and `pop()`, and `stack[-1]` peeks at the top without removing it.

Sort a Stack.title: Sort a Stack
Sort a Stack.problemStatement: You are given a stack of integers, reachable only through its usual operations: push a value onto the top, pop the top value off, and peek at the top. Rearrange its contents so the stack ends up sorted in ascending order from the bottom up, meaning the smallest value rests at the bottom and the largest sits on top. The stack object itself must be left holding the sorted values rather than a new container being returned. The classic form of this exercise adds one restriction — do the sorting with recursion only, using no for or while loop inside the sorting and insertion routines — and the second approach below honours it while the first deliberately ignores it to show the baseline.
edgeCases: Empty stack
Stack already sorted
Stack sorted in reverse order
followUps: Can you solve this without using recursive call stacks? (Using loop with helper stack)

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: Set the recursion restriction aside for a second and ask what sorting a stack even means: smallest value at the bottom, largest on top. A stack hides everything below its top, which is the only reason this is hard at all — so the simplest thing a beginner can do is stop fighting the container. Empty it into a plain list, where indexing and a library sort are both available, then pour it back. Note what happens on the way out: pop() hands you elements top-downwards, so arr receives them in reverse stack order, but that is irrelevant because the very next step sorts arr anyway. Pushing the sorted list back front-to-back means the smallest value goes in first and lands at the bottom, leaving the largest on top, which is exactly the required layout. The cost is O(n log n) time, dominated by arr.sort(), plus O(n) auxiliary space for the helper list. It is a perfectly correct answer, and it is labelled brute force only because it sidesteps the point of the exercise: it never solves anything in terms of stack operations themselves.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Create an empty helper list arr, which will hold the stack's contents outside the stack while they are reordered.
2. While the stack is non-empty, pop its top element and append it to arr. When this loop ends the stack is empty and arr holds every value in top-to-bottom order, which is the reverse of the stack layout — harmless, since the next step reorders everything.
3. Call arr.sort() to put the values into ascending order; this single step does the real work and is what makes the approach O(n log n).
4. Iterate over arr from front to back and push each value x back with stack.append(x). Because the smallest values are pushed first they settle at the bottom, so the invariant after each push is that the stack so far is sorted ascending.
5. Return nothing: the original stack object has been refilled in ascending order with the maximum sitting on top.

complexity.time: O(N log N)
complexity.space: O(N)

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: Read the two complexity badges before anything else, because they say something surprising: this approach is O(N^2), which is SLOWER than the O(N log N) list-and-sort version above. "Optimal" here does not mean fastest - it means best under the rule the problem imposes, which forbids any container other than the stack itself, so the O(N log N) helper list is simply not allowed and this is the best remaining option. If your own problem does allow a helper list, use the first solution. Now the idea. The "no loops" restriction is not there to be annoying — it forces you to find the recursive shape of the problem, and a stack is the one structure where that shape is natural, because the call stack can hold what a temporary variable would. Ask the standard recursion question: if someone handed me a correctly sorted version of everything below the top element, what work would be left? Exactly one thing — drop the saved element into its right place. So pop the top into temp, recursively sort what remains, then insert temp into a stack that is already sorted. Inserting is itself the same shape of problem: if the stack is empty, or temp is greater than the current top, temp belongs on top and a plain push finishes it. Otherwise the top is too large to sit beneath temp, so lift it off, insert temp into the shorter stack below, then push the lifted element back — it lands above temp, preserving order. Each insertion may have to travel the entire depth of the stack, so n insertions give O(n^2) time, and the recursion holds up to n frames, hence O(n) space.
approaches.algorithm:
1. In sortStack(stack), handle the base case first: if the stack is empty there is nothing to order, so return immediately.
2. Otherwise pop the top value into temp, shrinking the problem by exactly one element, and call sortStack(stack) on what is left. When that call returns, the invariant is that everything still in the stack is sorted ascending with its largest value on top.
3. Call sortedInsert(stack, temp) to place the saved element back into that already-sorted stack at the right position, which re-establishes the invariant for a stack one element larger.
4. Inside sortedInsert, check its own base case: if the stack is empty, or element is greater than the current top stack[-1], then element belongs on top, so append it and return.
5. Otherwise the top is larger than element, so pop it into a local temp, call sortedInsert(stack, element) on the now-shorter stack, and once that returns push the saved top back with stack.append(temp) so it settles above the freshly inserted element.
6. When the outermost sortStack call returns, every element has been popped and re-inserted in order, leaving the original stack sorted in place without a single for or while loop.
approaches.code:
# NOT faster than sorting: this is O(N^2), while the list-sort version above is
# O(N log N). It is here because the problem forbids any container other than the
# stack itself, so we must sort using only push/pop and the recursion's own frames.
def sortStack(stack):
    # Base case: if stack is empty, it is already sorted
    if not stack:
        return
    # Pop the top element
    temp = stack.pop()
    # Sort the remaining stack recursively
    sortStack(stack)
    # Insert the popped element back in sorted order
    sortedInsert(stack, temp)

def sortedInsert(stack, element):
    # Base case: if stack is empty or element is greater than top element
    if not stack or element > stack[-1]:
        stack.append(element)
        return
    # Pop the top element if it is greater than the element to insert
    temp = stack.pop()
    # Recursively insert the element in the remaining stack
    sortedInsert(stack, element)
    # Push the popped element back to the stack
    stack.append(temp)

complexity.space: O(N)

Sort a Stack.tests:
s = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5]
sortStack(s)
assert s == [1, 1, 3, 4, 5]
s2 = []
sortStack(s2)
assert s2 == []
s3 = [7]
sortStack(s3)
assert s3 == [7]
s4 = [5, 4, 3, 2, 1]
sortStack(s4)
assert s4 == [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
print("ok")
prerequisites: Loops are banned, so the recursion's own call stack is the temporary storage that holds the popped elements.
Two mutually recursive pieces do the job: sortStack empties the stack one element at a time, and sortedInsert pushes a single element back into the right slot.
sortedInsert's base case is 'stack empty OR element > top', which is what keeps the stack ascending with the largest value on top.
A Python list used as a stack has its TOP at index -1, so stack[-1] peeks while append/pop are push/pop.
Cost analysis: sortStack recurses N deep and each sortedInsert can recurse N deep, giving O(N^2) time and O(N) call-stack space.

Maximum of Minimum for Every Window Size.title: Maximum of Minimum for Every Window Size
Maximum of Minimum for Every Window Size.problemStatement: You are given an integer array of size n. A window is any block of consecutive elements, and its size is how many elements it spans. For a fixed window size k there are n - k + 1 possible windows (one per valid starting index), each of which has a minimum value. Among those minimums, take the largest. Doing that for every window size k from 1 up to n produces n numbers, and you must return them as an array `res` where `res[k-1]` is the answer for window size k -- so the size-1 answer sits at index 0 and the size-n answer at the last index. Note the shape of the two operations: minimum WITHIN each window, then maximum ACROSS all windows of that size. The size-1 entry is therefore just the maximum element of the array, and the size-n entry is the minimum of the whole array, with the values in between decreasing as windows get wider.

examples.explanation: Max of min for size 1 is 70, size 2 is 30, size 3 is 20, sizes 4-7 is 10.

edgeCases: All elements are equal
Sorted array (ascending or descending)
followUps: Can you solve this in O(N) space complexity?

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: Before any cleverness, it is worth writing the definition down as code, because the definition already is an algorithm: for each window size, look at every window of that size, take its minimum, and keep the biggest minimum you saw. Nothing is being inferred here -- we are simply enumerating the entire space the problem describes, which makes this version the correctness reference you can test a faster solution against. The reason it is unsatisfying is the arithmetic of that enumeration. There are n window sizes; for a given size k there are roughly n windows; and computing the minimum of one window by re-scanning it costs another k operations. Multiply those three factors and you land at O(n^3), so an array of 1000 elements already implies on the order of a billion comparisons. The waste is also visible: two neighbouring windows of the same size overlap in k-1 elements, yet the code re-reads all of them, and a window of size k+1 recomputes minimums it effectively already knew from size k. That redundancy is exactly what the optimal monotonic-stack solution eliminates by asking the inverse question -- for each element, what is the widest window in which it is the minimum -- but this triple loop is the honest baseline that makes the speedup meaningful.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Read `n = len(arr)` and allocate the answer array `res = [0] * n`, one slot for each window size 1 through n.
2. Loop over window sizes with `k` running from 1 to n inclusive; each pass of this outer loop is responsible for filling exactly one slot of `res`.
3. At the top of each size, set `max_val = float('-inf')` so that the first real window minimum is guaranteed to replace it; the invariant inside the inner loop is that `max_val` holds the largest window minimum found so far among windows of the current size k.
4. Slide the window with `i` running from 0 to `n - k` (written as `range(n - k + 1)`, since `n - k` is the last starting index at which a full size-k window still fits).
5. For each start `i`, compute `min_val = min(arr[i:i+k])` -- the slice copies and rescans the window, which is the O(k) step responsible for the cubic total -- and update `max_val = max(max_val, min_val)`.
6. Once the sliding loop for size k finishes, store the result with `res[k - 1] = max_val`, minding the off-by-one that maps 1-based window size k onto 0-based index k-1.
7. After all sizes are processed, return `res`.
approaches.code:
def maxOfMin(arr):  # res[k-1] = the largest window minimum over all size-k windows
    n = len(arr)
    res = [0] * n  # one answer slot for each window size 1 through n
    # window sizes are 1-based; results are 0-indexed
    for k in range(1, n + 1):  # k = the window size, from 1 up to the whole array
        max_val = float('-inf')  # starts below any real value, so the first window minimum always replaces it
        # slide a size-k window across the whole array
        for i in range(n - k + 1):  # the last valid start index is n-k, hence the +1
            min_val = min(arr[i:i+k])  # slicing and re-scanning costs O(k) per window
            max_val = max(max_val, min_val)  # track the best (largest) minimum for this window size
        res[k - 1] = max_val  # the off-by-one to watch: size k stores at index k-1
    return res  # O(n^3) overall, correct but far too slow for large n

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: The brute force asks, for each of the n window sizes, every window of that size for its minimum - and it recomputes those minimums from scratch, so the same element is compared as a candidate minimum in hundreds of overlapping windows. The waste is the direction of the question. Turn it around: instead of asking each window which element is smallest, ask each element for the widest window in which IT is the smallest. arr[i] is the minimum of exactly those windows that stay strictly inside the nearest strictly smaller value to its left (index left[i]) and to its right (right[i]), so its widest span has length right[i] - left[i] - 1. In [10, 20, 50, 10], the 50 is fenced in by 20 and 10, so it is the minimum of just one window, of size 1. Those fences come from a monotonic stack - a stack of indices whose stored values only increase from bottom to top, so when a smaller value arrives every larger index on top is popped, because a bar taller than the newcomer can never be the nearest-smaller for anything further right. Why nothing is missed: every window's minimum sits somewhere, and that window fits inside its minimum's span, so the value is already recorded at ans[span]; the final backward pass ans[i] = max(ans[i], ans[i+1]) pushes each winner down to every smaller size, which is valid because shrinking a window around its minimum keeps that element inside. Cost: O(N) time - each index is pushed and popped at most once per sweep, so the inner while loops total n pops - and O(N) space for two boundary arrays, the stack and the answer.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Allocate left[] filled with -1 and right[] filled with n; these sentinels mean 'no smaller element exists on that side', which makes the span formula work at the array edges without special cases.
2. Sweep i from 0 to n-1 with an index stack. While the value at the stack top is >= arr[i], pop it. Whatever survives on top is the nearest strictly smaller element, so set left[i] to that index; then push i.
3. Reset the stack and mirror the sweep, i from n-1 down to 0, popping on the same >= test and setting right[i] from the survivor. Popping on equality (not just >) shortens the span of every element inside a run of equal values EXCEPT the leftmost, which still gets the full span - so the maximum for that size is recorded anyway.
4. Allocate ans = [0] * (n + 1) and index it by window size, leaving slot 0 unused so that ans[k] reads as 'best answer for size k'.
5. For each i, compute length = right[i] - left[i] - 1 and do ans[length] = max(ans[length], arr[i]) - arr[i] competes only at the one size it dominates.
6. Walk i from n-1 down to 1 doing ans[i] = max(ans[i], ans[i+1]), filling in sizes that no element claimed directly.
7. Return ans[1:] to drop the unused slot and shift back to 0-based output.
approaches.code:
def maxOfMin(arr):  # O(n): every element is the minimum of one widest span
    n = len(arr)
    # left[i] and right[i] bound where arr[i] rules as minimum
    left = [-1] * n  # -1 means no smaller element exists to the left at all
    right = [n] * n  # n means no smaller element exists to the right at all
    stack = []  # monotonic stack of indices with increasing values
    # first sweep: previous smaller element for every index
    for i in range(n):  # scan left to right
        while stack and arr[stack[-1]] >= arr[i]:  # pop anything not strictly smaller than arr[i]
            stack.pop()  # a popped bar can never bound an index further right
        if stack:  # whatever survives on top is the nearest smaller value
            left[i] = stack[-1]  # index of the previous strictly smaller element
        stack.append(i)  # i becomes a boundary candidate for later indices
    stack = []  # reset; the mirror sweep needs an empty stack
    # second sweep: next smaller element for every index
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):  # same logic, but scanning right to left
        while stack and arr[stack[-1]] >= arr[i]:  # pop equal values too, which is safe for a minimum
            stack.pop()
        if stack:  # a survivor means a smaller element lies to the right
            right[i] = stack[-1]  # index of the next strictly smaller element
        stack.append(i)  # push i as a boundary candidate for indices on its left
    # indexed by window size, so slot 0 is deliberately unused
    ans = [0] * (n + 1)  # sizes 1..n need n+1 slots when using 1-based indexing
    # each element claims the one window size it dominates
    for i in range(n):  # for every element, compute its span of dominance
        length = right[i] - left[i] - 1  # widest window in which arr[i] is the minimum; -1 for itself
        ans[length] = max(ans[length], arr[i])  # arr[i] is a candidate answer for exactly that size
    # a size-i window fits inside any winning size-(i+1) window
    for i in range(n - 1, 0, -1):  # walk down so each answer inherits from the larger size
        ans[i] = max(ans[i], ans[i + 1])  # fills the sizes no element claimed directly
    # shift back to 0-indexed output for sizes 1..n
    return ans[1:]  # drop the unused slot 0

complexity.time: O(N)
complexity.space: O(N)

Maximum of Minimum for Every Window Size.tests:
assert maxOfMin([10, 20, 30, 50, 10, 70, 30]) == [70, 30, 20, 10, 10, 10, 10]
assert maxOfMin([10, 20, 30]) == [30, 20, 10]
assert maxOfMin([5]) == [5]
assert maxOfMin([7, 7, 7]) == [7, 7, 7]
import random
def brute(arr):
    n=len(arr); res=[]
    for k in range(1,n+1):
        res.append(max(min(arr[i:i+k]) for i in range(n-k+1)))
    return res
random.seed(1)
for _ in range(200):
    a=[random.randint(1,6) for _ in range(random.randint(1,8))]
    assert maxOfMin(a)==brute(a), a
print("ok")
prerequisites: Flip the question: instead of asking 'what is the min of this window?', ask 'for this element, what is the largest window in which it is the minimum?'.
That largest window stretches from the previous strictly-smaller element to the next strictly-smaller element, so length = right[i] - left[i] - 1.
A monotonic stack of indices finds previous-smaller for all i in one O(N) left-to-right pass and next-smaller in one O(N) right-to-left pass.
Sentinels left[i] = -1 and right[i] = n mean 'no smaller element on that side' and make the length formula work at the array edges.

If a value is the minimum of some window of size L, it is also the minimum of some window of every size below L — hence the final right-to-left ans[i] = max(ans[i], ans[i+1]) sweep that fills the gaps.

LRU Cache.title: LRU Cache
LRU Cache.problemStatement: Design a fixed-size cache that discards the least recently used entry whenever it overflows. The constructor is given a positive `capacity`. `get(key)` returns the value stored under that key, or -1 when the key is not present. `put(key, value)` stores or overwrites the value for that key, and if adding a brand-new key would push the number of stored entries above `capacity`, the entry whose last access is furthest in the past must be removed first. Both a successful `get` and any `put` count as using a key and refresh its recency. The target is O(1) average time for both operations, so no scanning of the stored entries.

examples.input: LRUCache(2), put(1, 1), put(2, 2), get(1), put(3, 3), get(2)

constraints: At most 2 * 10^5 calls will be made to get and put
edgeCases: Get of non-existing key
Updating existing key value
Capacity is 1
followUps: Can you write a clean, thread-safe implementation of LRU Cache?

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: The cache has to do two jobs that pull in different directions: looking a key up quickly wants a hash map, while knowing which key is stalest wants an ordering. The natural first attempt is to keep both separately and not think too hard — a dict `self.cache` mapping key to value, plus an ordinary Python list `self.keys` holding the keys arranged least recently used at the front and most recently used at the back. Touching a key means deleting it from wherever it currently sits in the list and re-appending it at the end, and eviction is just popping index 0. This is worth writing because it makes the meaning of LRU completely concrete and it is easy to verify as correct. The problem is the cost hidden in the list: `self.keys.remove(key)` must scan to find the key, and `pop(0)` must shift every remaining element left, so both `get` and `put` are O(n) in the number of cached keys. The ordering is right; only the mechanics are too slow.
approaches.algorithm:
1. In `__init__`, store `self.capacity`, an empty dict `self.cache` mapping key to value, and an empty list `self.keys`. The invariant to maintain everywhere is that `self.keys` holds exactly the keys present in `self.cache`, ordered least recently used first and most recently used last.
2. In `get(key)`, if `key` is not in `self.cache`, return -1 immediately and change nothing.
3. Otherwise refresh the key's recency with `self.keys.remove(key)` followed by `self.keys.append(key)` — this pair is the O(n) step, since `remove` has to search the list — and then return `self.cache[key]`.
4. In `put(key, value)`, first check whether `key` already exists in `self.cache`; if it does, call `self.keys.remove(key)` so it can be re-appended in its new position, and skip eviction entirely because the number of entries is not growing.
5. Otherwise the key is new, so when `len(self.cache) >= self.capacity` evict first: `lru = self.keys.pop(0)` takes the stalest key off the front and `del self.cache[lru]` removes its value, keeping list and dict in sync.
6. Finally run `self.cache[key] = value` and `self.keys.append(key)`. This single tail covers both the update and the insert path and leaves the touched key at the most-recently-used end.
approaches.code:
class LRUCache:
    def __init__(self, capacity: int):
        # Storing capacity
        self.capacity = capacity
        # Storing key-value pairs
        self.cache = {}
        # Track the access order of keys
        self.keys = []

    def get(self, key: int) -> int:
        # Check if key exists in cache
        if key not in self.cache:
            return -1
        # Move key to the end of keys list to mark it as most recently used
        self.keys.remove(key)
        self.keys.append(key)
        # Return key value
        return self.cache[key]

    def put(self, key: int, value: int) -> None:
        # If key is already in cache, remove it from keys list to update position
        if key in self.cache:
            self.keys.remove(key)
        elif len(self.cache) >= self.capacity:
            # Evict least recently used key (first element of keys list)
            lru = self.keys.pop(0)
            del self.cache[lru]
        # Insert key and update access order
        self.cache[key] = value
        self.keys.append(key)

complexity.time: O(N) get and put
complexity.space: O(N)

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: The list-of-keys version is correct but pays O(n) for two distinct things: locating a key inside the ordering, and pulling it out of the middle. Removing from the middle in O(1) is exactly what a doubly linked list gives you, because a node holding both `prev` and `next` can splice itself out without anybody scanning for it. That leaves only the locating problem, which is what the hash map is for: `self.cache` maps a key directly to its `Node`, so a hit jumps straight to the right position with no traversal. Arrange the list so the most recently used node sits just after a dummy `head` and the least recently used sits just before a dummy `tail`, and eviction becomes `self.tail.prev` with no search at all. Those two sentinels are not decoration — they guarantee that every real node always has a neighbour on both sides, which removes every None check from `_remove` and `_add`. Because each `Node` also stores its own `key`, evicting it tells you which dict entry to delete, keeping the two structures consistent. Every operation reduces to a fixed number of pointer writes: O(1) time and O(capacity) space.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Initialize capacity, cache map, dummy head and tail nodes linked to each other.
2. Implement _remove(node) to disconnect a node from DLL.
3. Implement _add(node) to insert node right after head.
4. In get(key), move node to head and return value.
5. In put(key, value), add new node to head and map. If full, evict node before dummy tail.
approaches.code:
class Node:  # doubly linked list node: unlink from anywhere in O(1)
    def __init__(self, key=0, value=0):
        self.key = key  # the key is stored too, so eviction can clean the dict
        self.value = value  # the cached payload returned by get
        self.prev = None  # the back pointer is what makes removal O(1), not O(n)
        self.next = None  # forward pointer toward the least recently used end

class LRUCache:  # dict for lookup plus a list for ordering: both O(1)
    def __init__(self, capacity: int):
        self.capacity = capacity  # hard ceiling on how many keys we retain
        self.cache = {}  # key -> Node, so a hit jumps straight to the list node
        # sentinels remove every None check from the pointer code
        self.head = Node()  # the node just after head is the most recently used
        self.tail = Node()  # the node just before tail is the eviction victim
        self.head.next = self.tail  # start with an empty list between the two sentinels
        self.tail.prev = self.head  # close the loop so both sentinels always have neighbours

    def _remove(self, node: Node) -> None:  # unlink a node without knowing where it sits
        # Disconnect node from its neighbors
        prev_node = node.prev  # both neighbours always exist, thanks to the sentinels
        next_node = node.next  # grab the node on the other side before splicing
        prev_node.next = next_node  # route the previous node past us
        next_node.prev = prev_node  # route the next node back past us; the node is now loose

    def _add(self, node: Node) -> None:  # attach a node at the most-recently-used end
        # Insert node right after the dummy head (most recently used)
        next_node = self.head.next  # the node that was previously newest
        self.head.next = node  # four pointer writes rewire the front of the list
        node.prev = self.head  # head is our new left neighbour
        node.next = next_node  # the old newest becomes our right neighbour
        next_node.prev = node  # close the pair; this node is now most recently used

    def get(self, key: int) -> int:  # lookup that also counts as a use
        if key in self.cache:  # dict hit means the node is somewhere in the list
            node = self.cache[key]  # jump straight to the node, no traversal needed
            # a read refreshes recency, which is the whole point of LRU
            self._remove(node)  # unlink from wherever it currently sits
            self._add(node)  # relink at the front as most recently used
            return node.value  # return the cached payload
        return -1  # miss; -1 is the sentinel the problem specifies

    def put(self, key: int, value: int) -> None:  # insert or update, evicting only when necessary
        if key in self.cache:  # update path: no new node, no eviction
            node = self.cache[key]  # reuse the existing node so its identity stays stable
            # Update value of existing node
            node.value = value  # overwrite the payload in place; the key is unchanged
            # a write counts as a use, same as a read
            self._remove(node)  # unlink from its old position
            self._add(node)  # put it back at the most recently used end
        else:  # insert path: this key is new to the cache
            if len(self.cache) >= self.capacity:  # at capacity, so someone has to be evicted first
                # the oldest node is always the one before the tail sentinel
                lru_node = self.tail.prev  # grab the victim in O(1) without any scanning
                self._remove(lru_node)  # unlink it from the list
                del self.cache[lru_node.key]  # this is exactly why Node stores its own key
            # now there is room for the newcomer
            new_node = Node(key, value)  # wrap the pair in a list node
            self.cache[key] = new_node  # dict and list must stay in sync at all times
            self._add(new_node)  # new entries always start as most recently used

complexity.space: O(C)

LRU Cache.tests:
c = LRUCache(2)
c.put(1, 1); c.put(2, 2)
assert c.get(1) == 1
c.put(3, 3)
assert c.get(2) == -1
c.put(4, 4)
assert c.get(1) == -1
assert c.get(3) == 3
assert c.get(4) == 4
c2 = LRUCache(1)
c2.put(1, 10)
c2.put(2, 20)
assert c2.get(1) == -1
assert c2.get(2) == 20
c2.put(2, 25)
assert c2.get(2) == 25
print("ok")
prerequisites: O(1) get and put needs two structures cooperating: a hash map for lookup and a doubly linked list for recency order.
A doubly linked list can unlink a KNOWN node in O(1) because that node stores both prev and next pointers.
Dummy head and tail sentinel nodes delete every 'is this the first/last node?' special case from _remove and _add.
Fix a convention and stick to it: right after head = most recently used, right before tail = least recently used, i.e. the eviction victim.
The map must store NODES, not raw values — otherwise you cannot reach the node you need to unlink or move.
collections.OrderedDict (move_to_end and popitem(last=False)) is the shortcut, but interviewers want the explicit linked-list version.

Largest Rectangle in Histogram.title: Largest Rectangle in Histogram
Largest Rectangle in Histogram.problemStatement: You are given an array heights, where heights[i] is the height of the i-th bar of a histogram and every bar has a width of exactly 1, with all bars standing side by side on a common baseline. Consider any axis-aligned rectangle that fits entirely inside the shape formed by those bars. Such a rectangle always spans a contiguous range of bars, and its height can be no greater than the shortest bar in that range, so a rectangle covering bars i through j has area equal to (j - i + 1) multiplied by the minimum height over that range. Return the largest area that any such rectangle can achieve. Heights are non-negative, so the answer is never negative, and a single tall bar on its own is a legitimate rectangle of width 1.

examples.explanation: The largest rectangle has heights [5, 6] forming area of 10.

edgeCases: Array of size 1
Strictly increasing heights
Strictly decreasing heights
followUps: Can you solve this problem in one pass without utilizing next smaller arrays?

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: A rectangle inside a histogram is completely described by the range of bars it covers, so the most direct plan is to try every range: choose a left edge i, choose a right edge j at or after it, and evaluate that candidate. The naive way to evaluate is a third loop scanning i..j to find the shortest bar, which makes the whole thing O(N^3) and re-reads the same bars endlessly. The observation that deletes an entire loop is that the minimum is incremental: when the right edge advances from j to j + 1, adding one more bar can only lower the shortest bar or leave it alone, never raise it, so the new minimum is just min(min_h, heights[j+1]). Keeping min_h alive across the inner loop therefore makes every new candidate cost O(1) - its height is min_h and its width is j - i + 1, where the +1 is there because both endpoints are part of the rectangle. Running max_area over all of those candidates gives the correct answer in O(N^2) time and O(1) space. That is perfectly usable on small histograms and is a good correctness reference, but it still asks the same question N^2 times, which is what the stack-based solution replaces.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Initialize max_area = 0.
2. Iterate left boundary i from 0 to N-1.
3. Iterate right boundary j from i to N-1.
4. Find the min height between i and j. Update max_area = max(max_area, min_height * (j - i + 1)).
approaches.code:
def largestRectangleArea(heights):  # try every pair of bars as the rectangle's left/right edge
    max_area = 0  # heights are non-negative, so 0 is a safe starting best
    n = len(heights)  # number of bars in the histogram
    # outer loop fixes the left edge, inner extends the right
    for i in range(n):  # i is the left edge of the candidate rectangle
        min_h = heights[i]  # running minimum height across the span i..j
        for j in range(i, n):  # extend the right edge one bar at a time
            min_h = min(min_h, heights[j])  # the rectangle can only be as tall as the shortest bar
            max_area = max(max_area, min_h * (j - i + 1))  # width counts both endpoints, so the +1 matters
    return max_area  # O(n^2) pairs, each O(1) thanks to the running minimum

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: The quadratic version keeps asking, for each range, which bar is the shortest. Turn the question inside out: for each bar, what is the widest range in which that bar is the shortest one? Every maximal rectangle is capped by some particular bar, so if you compute the best rectangle for each bar acting as the cap and take the maximum, you have covered every possibility. For a given bar, that widest range stretches leftwards until a strictly shorter bar blocks it and rightwards until a strictly shorter bar blocks it, which means each bar needs only its nearest shorter neighbour on each side. A stack of indices kept in non-decreasing height order delivers both boundaries during one sweep. A bar stays on the stack for as long as nothing shorter has appeared to its right; the moment current_height at index i is smaller than the bar on top, that bar's right boundary has just been discovered - it is i - and its left boundary is whatever index now sits below it after the pop, giving width i - stack[-1] - 1, or the full width i when the stack empties because nothing shorter exists anywhere to its left. The loop deliberately runs to i == n with a virtual bar of height 0, which is strictly shorter than everything and therefore forces every remaining bar to be popped and priced. Because the pop test uses a strict >, bars of equal height are left stacked; the earlier one of them gets a width that stops short, but the last one of the run measures the whole span, so the maximum is still found. Each index is pushed once and popped once, so this is O(N) time for O(N) stack space.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Add a dummy 0 height at the end of the heights array.
2. Loop through indices. While heights[i] is smaller than the height of the top of stack, pop from the stack.
3. The width is i if the stack is empty, otherwise i - stack[-1] - 1.
4. Update max_area.
approaches.code:
def largestRectangleArea(heights):  # O(n) using a stack of indices with increasing heights
    stack = []  # holds indices whose bars might still grow to the right
    max_area = 0  # best area seen so far
    n = len(heights)  # bar count; the loop deliberately runs one step past it
    # the virtual final bar flushes everything still stacked
    for i in range(n + 1):  # note the n+1: the extra iteration is the cleanup pass
        current_height = heights[i] if i < n else 0  # past the end, pretend the bar has height 0
        # a taller stacked bar can extend no further right than i
        while stack and heights[stack[-1]] > current_height:  # strict > keeps equal heights stacked, which stays correct
            h = heights[stack.pop()]  # this popped bar's height fixes the rectangle's height
            w = i if not stack else i - stack[-1] - 1  # empty stack means the bar reaches all the way back to 0
            max_area = max(max_area, h * w)  # the core trick: each bar is priced exactly once, when popped
        stack.append(i)  # push after popping, so heights on the stack stay increasing
    return max_area  # every bar was pushed once and popped once, hence O(n)

complexity.time: O(N)
complexity.space: O(N)

Largest Rectangle in Histogram.tests:
# Classic case: bars 5 and 6 give the 2x5 = 10 rectangle.
assert largestRectangleArea([2, 1, 5, 6, 2, 3]) == 10
assert largestRectangleArea([2, 4]) == 4
assert largestRectangleArea([3, 3, 3, 3]) == 12
# Edge case: a single bar -- its own height is the whole answer.
assert largestRectangleArea([5]) == 5
# Edge case: empty histogram and all-zero bars must give area 0.
assert largestRectangleArea([]) == 0
assert largestRectangleArea([0, 0]) == 0
prerequisites: The area of any rectangle in a histogram is decided by ONE bar: the shortest bar inside the chosen range, so area = min_height * width.
Monotonic increasing stack: you keep indices whose heights increase; the moment a shorter bar arrives, every taller bar on the stack has found its right boundary.
Why we store INDICES and not heights: the width of a rectangle needs positions, and `i - stack[-1] - 1` is the distance between the two bars that bound the popped bar.
The sentinel trick: appending a virtual bar of height 0 at index n forces the stack to drain, so you do not need a separate clean-up loop after the main loop.
Python list as a stack: `append` pushes, `pop()` removes from the right, and `stack[-1]` peeks — all O(1).
Amortised analysis: each index is pushed once and popped at most once, which is why a loop containing a while loop is still O(N) overall.

Sliding Window Maximum.title: Sliding Window Maximum
Sliding Window Maximum.problemStatement: You are given an integer array nums together with a window width k. Picture a frame exactly k elements wide laid over the leftmost k entries of the array, then slid one position to the right at a time until its right edge reaches the very end. At each of those positions the frame covers a contiguous block of k values, and you record the largest value inside that block. Return all of those maxima collected in order as a list, from the window that starts at index 0 through to the last legal window. The result contains exactly len(nums) - k + 1 entries, one for every position the frame can occupy.
edgeCases: k = len(nums)
Strictly decreasing array
followUps: Can you solve it in O(N) using double-ended queue?

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: The statement of this problem is already a procedure, and following it literally is the right place to begin when no pattern has occurred to you yet: there is a fixed, small number of window positions, and each one has a maximum you can simply go and compute. So walk a start index `i` across the array and, for each value of `i`, look at the k values sitting in `nums[i:i+k]` and take their maximum with the built-in `max`. Writing it out is what exposes the weakness: two consecutive windows overlap in k-1 elements, yet this version re-examines every one of those shared elements from scratch, so the same large value is compared again and again as the frame crawls past it. That redundancy across neighbouring windows is exactly what a monotonic deque later removes by carrying information forward instead of discarding it. Cost: len(nums)-k+1 windows times O(k) work per window gives O(N*k) time, with nothing allocated beyond the output list and the temporary slice.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Create an empty list `res`, which will collect one maximum per window position in left-to-right order.
2. Loop `i` over `range(len(nums) - k + 1)`, where `i` is the start index of the current window; the `+ 1` is there because the last legal start index is `len(nums) - k`.
3. For the current `i`, take the slice `nums[i:i+k]`, which is exactly the k consecutive elements the window covers at this position, and apply `max` to it — this slice is what costs O(k) each time round.
4. Append that maximum to `res`. Invariant: once the iteration for `i` finishes, `res` holds the correct answers for every window starting at 0 through `i`, in order.
5. When the loop ends, return `res`, which by construction holds exactly `len(nums) - k + 1` values.
approaches.code:
def maxSlidingWindow(nums, k):  # recompute each window's maximum from scratch
    res = []  # one answer per window position
    # slide the window one index at a time
    for i in range(len(nums) - k + 1):  # the last valid start is len-k, hence the +1
        # max over the slice is the answer for this window
        res.append(max(nums[i:i+k]))  # the slice costs O(k), making the whole thing O(n*k)
    return res  # there are exactly len(nums)-k+1 windows

complexity.time: O(N * k)

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition:
Calling `max(nums[i:i+k])` at every start position re-reads the k-1 elements that consecutive windows share, so the same value is compared again and again and the whole thing costs O(N*k). The waste is discarding, at each shift, everything the previous window already learned.

The observation that kills it: if j is to the LEFT of i and nums[j] <= nums[i], then nums[j] can never be a maximum again. Any future window still containing j must also contain i, because windows only slide rightwards, and nums[i] beats it. In [1, 3, 2] with k=2, the moment 3 arrives the 1 is dead forever. So keep only the survivors, in a deque (a double-ended queue, which pushes and pops at both ends in O(1)) holding INDICES whose values decrease from front to back -- a monotonic deque, meaning its values move in one direction only.

Why the true maximum is never thrown away: the back-popping loop removes only indices just proven dead, and `dq[0] < i - k + 1` removes only the one index that has fallen off the left edge -- at most one per step, since `i` advances by one. So the invariant (the property re-established after every step) is: the deque holds exactly the in-window indices not dominated by a later one, in decreasing value order. The window's maximum is never dominated, so it is present, and everything ahead of it in the deque was popped for being smaller -- which is why `dq[0]` is the answer.

Cost: O(N). Each index is appended once and popped at most once, so a single step that pops many is paid for by steps that pop none -- amortised O(1) per step, meaning constant when averaged across the run. Space is O(k) for the deque, traded against re-scanning.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Create an empty deque `dq` of indices and an empty result list.
2. For each index i, first expire the front: if `dq[0] < i - k + 1`, popleft -- only one index can leave the window per step.
3. While the deque is non-empty and nums[dq[-1]] < nums[i], pop from the back: those elements can never be a maximum again.
4. Append i to the back, restoring the front-to-back decreasing order.
5. Once i >= k - 1 the window is fully formed, so append nums[dq[0]] -- the front index -- to the result.
6. Return the result, one maximum per window position.
approaches.code:
from collections import deque  # a deque pops from both ends in O(1), unlike a list

def maxSlidingWindow(nums, k):
    # invariant: values at the stored indices never increase
    dq = deque()  # store indices, not values, so we can test for expiry
    res = []  # collected answers, one per full window
    for i in range(len(nums)):  # each index is pushed once and popped once, so O(n) total
        # the window covers i-k+1 .. i inclusive
        if dq and dq[0] < i - k + 1:  # at most one index expires per step, so if beats while here
            dq.popleft()  # drop the stale front index
        # anything smaller than nums[i] can never be a maximum again
        while dq and nums[dq[-1]] < nums[i]:  # compare values but hold indices; that is the whole trick
            dq.pop()  # pop from the back to restore the descending order
        # i always belongs, since it may dominate later windows
        dq.append(i)  # invariant restored: front is largest, values fall backwards
        # report only once the window is fully formed
        if i >= k - 1:  # the first complete window ends at index k-1
            res.append(nums[dq[0]])  # the front index always holds this window's maximum
    return res  # one entry per window, in left-to-right order

complexity.time: O(N)
complexity.space: O(k)

Sliding Window Maximum.tests:
assert maxSlidingWindow([1, 3, -1, -3, 5, 3, 6, 7], 3) == [3, 3, 5, 5, 6, 7]
assert maxSlidingWindow([9, 8, 7, 6], 2) == [9, 8, 7]
assert maxSlidingWindow([-7, -8, 7, 5, 7, 1, 6, 0], 4) == [7, 7, 7, 7, 7]
# Edge case: k == 1 means every element is its own window maximum.
assert maxSlidingWindow([1, 5, 2], 1) == [1, 5, 2]
# Edge case: k == len(nums) -- exactly one window covering the whole array.
assert maxSlidingWindow([1, 2, 3, 4], 4) == [4]
assert maxSlidingWindow([7], 1) == [7]
prerequisites: Sliding-window pattern: the window always moves right by exactly one index, so at most one element enters and one leaves per step.
`collections.deque` supports O(1) `append`, `pop`, `appendleft` and `popleft` — a plain list's `pop(0)` is O(N) and would ruin the complexity.
Monotonic deque invariant: the deque holds indices whose values are in decreasing order, so `dq[0]` is always the index of the current window's maximum.
Store indices, not values: you need the index to know whether the front element has slid out of the window (`dq[0] < i - k + 1`).
A smaller element sitting behind a larger one can never be a future maximum while the larger one is still in the window — that is why you can pop it forever.
The first answer only exists once the window is full, i.e. from index `i = k - 1` onwards.

Rotten Oranges.title: Rotten Oranges
Rotten Oranges.problemStatement: You are given an m x n grid representing fresh (1), rotten (2), and empty (0) cells. Every minute, any fresh orange that is 4-directionally adjacent to a rotten orange becomes rotten. Return the minimum minutes for all fresh oranges to rot.

examples.explanation: At minute 4, all fresh oranges become rotten.

edgeCases: No fresh oranges initially (returns 0)
Unreachable fresh orange (returns -1)
Empty grid
