Why it is unsatisfying: after a mismatch the algorithm discards everything it just learned and restarts the next offset from scratch, so on input like text 'aaaaaab' with pattern 'aaab' the same characters are re-read again and again, giving O(N*M) worst-case time with O(1) extra space. That discarded knowledge is exactly what KMP's prefix table recovers.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Run a loop i from 0 to n-m.
2. In a nested loop j from 0 to m-1, match text[i+j] with pattern[j].
3. If all characters match, return i.
4. If loop completes without match, return -1.
approaches.code:
def kmpSearch(text: str, pattern: str) -> int:  # naive baseline: try every alignment, O(n*m) worst case
    n, m = len(text), len(pattern)  # n is the text length, m the pattern length
    if m == 0:  # an empty pattern is considered found immediately
        return 0  # by convention the empty match sits at index 0
        
    # The last possible start is n - m, hence the + 1 in range
    for i in range(n - m + 1):  # i is the alignment offset currently being tested
        j = 0  # how many pattern characters have matched at this offset
        # Walk forward while characters agree, bail on first mismatch
        while j < m and text[i + j] == pattern[j]:  # j < m is checked first, keeping text[i + j] in range
            j += 1  # one more character confirmed at this alignment
        # j can only reach m if every character matched
        if j == m:  # the full pattern was consumed
            return i  # leftmost match wins, so return without scanning further
            
    return -1  # no alignment matched anywhere in the text

complexity.time: O(N*M)

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: The brute force tries every offset from 0 to n - m and, on a mismatch, throws away everything it just learned and restarts one character later. Searching 'aaab' inside 'aaaaab', it matches 'aaa' at offset 0, fails, then re-reads those same a's at offset 1, and again at offset 2 - the text cursor keeps walking backwards over characters it has already inspected. The observation that removes this: at the moment of a mismatch we already know the previous j text characters equal pattern[0:j], and that knowledge alone determines the next worthwhile alignment, without touching the text again. The only offsets that can still match are the ones where a proper prefix of the pattern (a prefix that is not the whole pattern) sits on top of a suffix of the part already matched. Such a prefix-that-is-also-a-suffix is called a border, and lps[k] - the longest prefix-suffix table - stores the longest border of pattern[0..k]. For pattern 'ababc' failing on the c after matching 'abab', lps[3] = 2 for 'ab', so the pattern slides until its leading 'ab' covers the text's trailing 'ab' and comparison resumes at j = 2 with i untouched. Nothing is skipped: any offset between the old start and the new one would need a border of pattern[0:j] longer than lps[j-1], and lps[j-1] is by definition the longest one, so no occurrence can hide there. Cost: O(M) to build the table plus O(N) to scan, so O(N + M) time and O(M) space for lps.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Handle the empty pattern first: return 0, since it matches before the scan begins.
2. Build lps of length m, where lps[k] is the length of the longest proper prefix of pattern[0..k] that is also a suffix of it. Start with lps[0] = 0, length = 0, i = 1. If pattern[i] == pattern[length], the current border extends by one, so increment length, write lps[i] = length, and advance i. On a mismatch with length != 0, fall back with length = lps[length - 1] WITHOUT advancing i - the border of the border is the next candidate. With length == 0, write lps[i] = 0 and advance i.
3. Search with i over the text and j over the pattern, both starting at 0. When pattern[j] == text[i], advance both.
4. Immediately after advancing, if j == m the whole pattern has matched, so return i - j, the index where the occurrence began.
5. Otherwise, if i < n and pattern[j] != text[i]: when j != 0 set j = lps[j-1], sliding the pattern forward while i stays put; when j == 0 nothing has matched, so advance i by one.
6. If the loop drains the text without reaching j == m, return -1.
approaches.code:
def kmpSearch(text: str, pattern: str) -> int:  # the text cursor never moves backwards, giving O(n + m)
    m = len(pattern)  # pattern length, which is also the size of the lps table
    n = len(text)  # length of the text being searched
    if m == 0:  # an empty pattern is found before we start
        return 0  # index 0 by convention
        
    # lps[k]: longest prefix of pattern[:k+1] that is also a suffix
    lps = [0] * m  # lps[0] is always 0, since no proper prefix exists there
    length = 0  # length of the border currently being extended
    i = 1  # start at 1; comparing index 0 with itself is pointless
    while i < m:  # one pass over the pattern builds the whole table
        if pattern[i] == pattern[length]:  # the matched border can be extended by one character
            length += 1  # we now have a border one character longer
            lps[i] = length  # record that border length for position i
            i += 1  # move on to the next pattern character
        else:  # mismatch, so the candidate border must shrink
            if length != 0:  # fall back to the border of the current border
                length = lps[length - 1]  # the key recursion; note that i deliberately stays put
            else:  # no shorter border is left to try
                lps[i] = 0  # position i has no matching prefix at all
                i += 1  # only now is it safe to advance the cursor
                
    # Search phase: lps says how far to slide after a mismatch
    i = 0  # text index; it never decreases, which is why this is O(n)
    j = 0  # pattern index; the only pointer allowed to rewind
    while i < n:  # single forward scan across the text
        if pattern[j] == text[i]:  # characters agree, so extend the current partial match
            i += 1  # consume one text character
            j += 1  # and one pattern character
        if j == m:  # the entire pattern has now been matched
            # The match began m characters before the current i
            return i - j  # start index of the occurrence
        elif i < n and pattern[j] != text[i]:  # mismatch, possibly after matching a prefix already
            # Reuse the border instead of restarting at i - j + 1
            if j != 0:  # part of the pattern already matched, so slide smartly
                j = lps[j - 1]  # shift the pattern; i stays exactly where it is
            else:  # nothing matched, so there is no shortcut to take
                i += 1  # just try the next text position
                
    return -1  # text exhausted with no full match found

complexity.time: O(N+M)
complexity.space: O(M)

KMP Algorithm.tests:
assert kmpSearch("sadbutsad", "sad") == 0
assert kmpSearch("leetcode", "leeto") == -1
# Needs the LPS fallback: "abab" matches only at index 3 of "abcabab".
assert kmpSearch("abcabab", "abab") == 3
assert kmpSearch("aaaaa", "aaa") == 0
# Edge case: pattern longer than the text.
assert kmpSearch("ab", "abc") == -1
# Edge case: empty pattern matches at index 0.
assert kmpSearch("aaa", "") == 0
prerequisites: LPS (Longest Prefix Suffix) array: lps[i] is the length of the longest PROPER prefix of pattern[0..i] that is also a suffix of it.
The LPS lets you avoid re-reading the text: after a mismatch at pattern index j, the pattern slides so that j becomes lps[j-1], while the text index never moves backwards.
Building the LPS is itself a self-matching of the pattern with the same fall-back rule — when characters differ and length != 0, you retry with `length = lps[length - 1]` WITHOUT advancing i.
j doubles as a counter of how many characters currently match, so `j == m` means a full occurrence, starting at index `i - j`.
The text pointer i moves forward at most n times and j never exceeds i, giving O(N + M) time and O(M) space for the table.
Edge conventions to agree on with the interviewer: an empty pattern conventionally matches at index 0, and a pattern longer than the text can never match.

Minimum Characters Needed for Palindrome.problemStatement: You are given a string s. You may add characters only at the FRONT of it, as many as you wish, and your goal is to turn it into a palindrome — a string that reads identically forwards and backwards. Return one integer: the smallest number of characters that must be prepended to achieve that. Nothing may be inserted in the middle or appended at the end, and the existing characters of s keep their order and their positions relative to one another. A string that is already a palindrome, including the empty string, needs 0 additions.

examples.explanation: We can make it a palindrome by adding 'AA' at the beginning to get 'AAAACECAAAA'.
We can make it a palindrome by adding 'DCB' at the beginning to get 'DCBABCD'.

edgeCases: Empty string (returns 0)
Already a palindrome (returns 0)
Single character (returns 0)
All characters distinct (e.g. 'abc' -> 2)
followUps: Can you solve this problem if additions were allowed at the end, or both ends?

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: Start by asking what the added characters can possibly be. Whatever you prepend sits at the very front, so it must mirror the tail of s that it faces — and the part of s left untouched by that mirroring, namely some prefix, has to already read the same in both directions on its own. That collapses the whole problem into a single question: how long is the longest prefix of s that is already a palindrome? If it has length i, then the n - i characters after it are the tail, each of which must be copied in reverse onto the front, so the answer is exactly n - i. The straightforward way to find that prefix is to test candidates from longest to shortest, because then the first success is automatically the best answer and the function can return on the spot instead of tracking a maximum. Each test slices out a prefix and compares it against its own reverse, which is O(i) work, and there can be up to n such tests, so this costs O(n^2) time and O(n) space for the slices. The KMP-based solution finds the same longest palindromic prefix in linear time.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Iterate index i from length of s down to 1.
2. Check if the substring s[0:i] is a palindrome.
3. If it is, then the longest palindromic prefix has length i.
4. The characters that need to be added is len(s) - i.
5. Return len(s) - i.
approaches.code:
def minCharForPalindrome(s: str) -> int:  # count characters to prepend so that s becomes a palindrome
    if not s:  # an empty string is already a palindrome
        return 0  # nothing needs to be prepended here
        
    n = len(s)  # total length, used to size the leftover tail
    # The longest palindromic PREFIX decides how little we add
    for i in range(n, 0, -1):  # try the longest prefix first so the first hit is the best
        # prefix is s[0..i-1]; the rest must be mirrored in front
        prefix = s[:i]  # this O(i) slice is what makes the approach O(n^2)
        # Reverse and compare, the naive palindrome test
        if prefix == prefix[::-1]:  # the first match is the longest palindromic prefix
            return n - i  # the characters after it get mirrored onto the front
            
    return 0  # unreachable: a single character is always a palindrome

complexity.space: O(N)

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition:
Scanning prefixes from longest to shortest and testing each for palindromicity gives the right answer -- the first palindromic prefix of length i means n - i characters must be mirrored onto the front -- but each test re-reads up to n characters, so O(n^2) work, and every failed test discards the partial matching it just performed.

The observation: a prefix P of s is a palindrome exactly when P equals reverse(P), and reverse(P) is the suffix of reverse(s) of the same length. So the longest palindromic prefix of s equals the longest prefix of s that is also a suffix of reverse(s). For s = "aacecaaa", reverse(s) = "aaacecaa", and the 7-character prefix "aacecaa" is also its last 7 characters. That is a border question, and KMP's prefix function answers it in one pass: the LPS array (longest proper prefix which is also a suffix), where lps[i] is the length of the longest string that is both a prefix and a suffix of temp[0..i] without being the whole of it.

Why the answer cannot be inflated: the separator '$' between s and reverse(s) must be a character absent from s. Without it a border could straddle the join and report a length above len(s), which corresponds to no real prefix. With it, any border is capped at len(s) and sits wholly inside s at one end and wholly inside reverse(s) at the other -- so lps[-1] is exactly the longest palindromic prefix.

Cost: O(N) time -- `length` rises at most once per character and the fallback `length = lps[length - 1]` can only shrink it, so total fallback work is bounded by total growth. O(N) space for `temp` and `lps` is the trade.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Return 0 for empty input, so that reading lps[-1] later is always safe.
2. Build temp = s + "$" + s[::-1], with '$' chosen as a character that never occurs in s.
3. Allocate lps of len(temp) zeros, set length = 0 and i = 1 (lps[0] is 0 by definition).
4. While i < len(temp): if temp[i] == temp[length], increment length, store lps[i] = length, and advance i.
5. On a mismatch with length != 0, fall back to length = lps[length - 1] WITHOUT advancing i, retrying against a shorter border.
6. On a mismatch with length == 0, write lps[i] = 0 and advance i.
7. Return len(s) - lps[-1]: lps[-1] is the longest palindromic prefix, and every character after it must be mirrored in front.
approaches.code:
def minCharForPalindrome(s: str) -> int:  # the KMP border table turns the O(n^2) scan into O(n)
    # Guard first, so lps[-1] below always has a value to read
    if not s:  # an empty input needs no additions
        return 0  # already a palindrome by definition
        
    # Overlap of s with its reverse is the palindromic prefix
    temp = s + "$" + s[::-1]  # the $ must not occur in s, or borders leak across halves
    n = len(temp)  # length of the combined string
    lps = [0] * n  # border table over that combined string
    length = 0  # length of the border currently matched
    i = 1  # lps[0] is 0 by definition, so the scan starts at 1
    
    # Exactly the KMP lps loop, run on the joined string
    while i < n:  # each step either advances i or shrinks the border
        if temp[i] == temp[length]:  # the border can be extended by one more character
            length += 1  # record the longer border
            lps[i] = length  # store it at the current position
            i += 1  # advance to the next character
        else:  # mismatch, so fall back to a shorter border
            if length != 0:  # try the border of the current border instead
                length = lps[length - 1]  # i intentionally stays put during this fallback
            else:  # no border left at this position
                lps[i] = 0  # explicit zero, written out for clarity
                i += 1  # only advance once the border length is already zero
                
    # lps[-1] is the longest palindromic prefix length of s
    return len(s) - lps[-1]  # every character past that prefix must be mirrored ahead

complexity.time: O(N)
complexity.space: O(N)

Minimum Characters Needed for Palindrome.tests:
# Example from the statement: longest palindromic prefix is "AACECAA" (7 of 9 chars).
assert minCharForPalindrome("AACECAAAA") == 2
# No palindromic prefix beyond the first letter, so 3 chars must be prepended.
assert minCharForPalindrome("ABCD") == 3
# Whole string is already a palindrome -> nothing to add.
assert minCharForPalindrome("aba") == 0
# "aba" is the longest palindromic prefix of "abab", so 1 char is enough.
assert minCharForPalindrome("abab") == 1
# Edge case: single character is trivially a palindrome.
assert minCharForPalindrome("a") == 0
# Edge case: empty string needs nothing added.
assert minCharForPalindrome("") == 0
prerequisites: Reframe the question: adding k characters in FRONT works exactly when the first n-k characters already form a palindrome, so the answer is len(s) minus the length of the longest palindromic PREFIX.
A prefix p of s is a palindrome iff p == p[::-1]; in Python s[::-1] builds the reversed copy in O(n) time and O(n) extra space.
The KMP LPS (Longest Proper Prefix that is also Suffix) array: lps[i] = length of the longest proper prefix of temp[0..i] that is also a suffix of it.

The trick of concatenating s + '$' + reversed(s): a prefix of s that is also a suffix of reversed(s) IS a palindromic prefix, and the '$' separator (a character absent from s) stops any border from spilling across the halves.
Watch the border-reset rule in LPS construction: on a mismatch you set length = lps[length-1] WITHOUT advancing i, which is what keeps the build O(n) overall.

Anagram Check.problemStatement: You are given two strings `s` and `t`, both consisting of lowercase English letters. Return true if `t` is an anagram of `s`, and false otherwise. Two strings are anagrams when one can be turned into the other purely by rearranging its letters -- which means they must use exactly the same letters with exactly the same multiplicity, so "listen" and "silent" are anagrams while "aab" and "abb" are not, because the first has two a's and the second only one. Position does not matter at all; only the counts do. An immediate consequence, and the cheapest possible early rejection, is that two strings of different lengths can never be anagrams. Note that this is a pure yes/no question: you return a boolean, not the rearrangement itself.
constraints: s and t consist of lowercase English letters.
edgeCases: Different lengths (returns false immediately)
Duplicate characters
Single character strings
Empty strings (if allowed, here minimum length is 1)
followUps: What if the inputs contain Unicode characters? How would you adapt your solution?

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: The definition of an anagram says the two strings hold the same multiset of letters, and the trouble is that the order they arrive in hides that fact. So destroy the order deliberately: if you sort the characters of each string, every anagram pair collapses to the exact same canonical string -- "listen" and "silent" both become "eilnst" -- and any pair that is not an anagram must differ at some position of the sorted form, because sorting preserves each letter's count. The comparison then becomes a plain equality check. This is the single easiest correct solution to write and to justify, and it needs no assumption about the alphabet: it works unchanged for Unicode, uppercase, digits, or anything else comparable. What it costs is a full sort of both strings, O(N log N) time, plus O(N) space for the two sorted lists Python builds. That log N factor is pure overhead in hindsight, because sorting computes far more information than the question needs -- it determines the full ordering of the letters when all we ever wanted was how many of each there are. Counting recovers exactly that much and no more, which is why the optimal version drops to O(N).
approaches.algorithm:
1. Compare lengths first: if `len(s) != len(t)`, return False right away, since strings of different lengths cannot contain the same multiset of characters.
2. Call `sorted(s)`, which returns a new list holding every character of `s` in non-decreasing order -- this is the canonical form of `s`.
3. Call `sorted(t)` to build the same canonical form for `t`.
4. Compare the two sorted lists element by element with `==`; they match if and only if the two strings used identical letters with identical counts.
5. Return the result of that comparison directly: True means `t` is an anagram of `s`, False means it is not.

complexity.time: O(N log N)
complexity.space: O(N)

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: Sorting answers a harder question than the one being asked. To decide anagram-hood you never need to know the order of the letters -- you only need, for each of the 26 lowercase letters, whether it appears the same number of times in both strings. Counting gives you exactly that in one pass, with no comparisons between letters at all. The neat refinement is that you do not even need two count arrays. Keep a single array of 26 integers and walk both strings together with one index: add one to the bucket for `s[i]` and subtract one from the bucket for `t[i]`. If the two strings really are anagrams, every letter's additions and subtractions cancel exactly, so the array must be all zeros at the end; if any letter is over-represented in one string it leaves a positive residue and its partner leaves a negative one, so a single non-zero entry is proof of failure. Mapping a character to its bucket is the `ord(c) - ord('a')` trick, which turns 'a' into 0 and 'z' into 25. The result is O(N) time -- one pass to count, then a fixed 26-slot check -- and O(1) space, because the array size is tied to the alphabet rather than to the input. The trade-off is that this assumes a lowercase-only alphabet, whereas the sorting version needs no such assumption.
approaches.algorithm:
1. If lengths of s and t are different, return False.
2. Initialize a frequency array of size 26 with 0.
3. Loop through indices, incrementing for s[i] and decrementing for t[i].
4. If any element in the array is not 0, return False.
5. Return True.
approaches.code:
def isAnagram(s: str, t: str) -> bool:  # counting beats sorting: O(n) instead of O(n log n)
    # A cheap length test rejects most non-anagrams instantly
    if len(s) != len(t):  # different lengths can never be anagrams
        return False  # reject without doing any counting work
        
    # 26 fixed slots, so the space cost is O(1) for any input
    count = [0] * 26  # index 0 stands for a, index 25 for z
    
    # One loop over both strings: add for s, subtract for t
    for i in range(len(s)):  # the lengths are equal, so a single index serves both
        count[ord(s[i]) - ord('a')] += 1  # the ord subtraction maps a letter onto its bucket
        count[ord(t[i]) - ord('a')] -= 1  # same bucket, opposite sign, so equal counts cancel out
        
    # Perfect cancellation is the invariant we now verify
    for val in count:  # 26 checks, constant work no matter how long the strings
        if val != 0:  # some letter appeared a different number of times
            return False  # a leftover count proves they are not anagrams
            
    return True  # every bucket cancelled, so the strings are anagrams

complexity.time: O(N)

Anagram Check.tests:
# Classic anagram pair.
assert isAnagram("anagram", "nagaram") == True
# Same length, different multiset of letters.
assert isAnagram("rat", "car") == False
# Edge case: single-character strings.
assert isAnagram("a", "a") == True
# Edge case: different lengths must short-circuit to False.
assert isAnagram("ab", "abc") == False
# Same character SET but different counts -> not an anagram.
assert isAnagram("aacc", "ccac") == False
# Repeated letters handled correctly.
assert isAnagram("aabbcc", "bacabc") == True
prerequisites: Two strings are anagrams iff they have identical character multisets — the same letters with the same counts, order irrelevant.
The very first check is len(s) != len(t): different lengths can never be anagrams, and it lets the counting loop safely index both strings with one index.
Frequency counting with a fixed 26-slot list: ord(c) - ord('a') maps 'a'..'z' to 0..25, giving O(1) bucket access with no hashing overhead.
The one-pass +1/-1 trick: increment for s and decrement for t in the same loop, then the strings are anagrams iff every bucket ends at 0.
sorted(s) in Python returns a list of characters and costs O(n log n) — fine as a brute force, but counting is O(n).
Know the limitation of the 26-slot array: it assumes lowercase English letters, so Unicode or mixed-case input needs collections.Counter instead.

Count and Say.problemStatement: The count-and-say sequence is a sequence of digit strings defined by the recursive formula: countAndSay(1) = '1', countAndSay(n) is the run-length encoding of countAndSay(n-1). Given an integer n, return the n-th term of the count-and-say sequence.

examples.explanation: This is the base case.
countAndSay(1) = "1", countAndSay(2) = RLE of "1" = "11", countAndSay(3) = RLE of "11" = "21", countAndSay(4) = RLE of "21" = "1211".

edgeCases: n = 1 (returns '1' immediately)
n = 30 (limits of recursion/iteration length)
followUps: Can you write a generator to yield this sequence indefinitely without memory constraints?

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: The sequence is defined by pointing at itself: term n is what you get by reading term n-1 aloud as runs of identical digits, saying three ones for the string 111 and writing that down as 31. A definition shaped like that converts into recursion almost mechanically — if n is 1 you already know the answer is the seed 1, and otherwise you ask the same function for term n-1 and run-length encode whatever comes back. That is what makes recursion the natural first attempt here: you never have to reason about how the terms accumulate, only about a single rewrite step, and the code ends up reading almost exactly like the English definition. The price is the sequence's own growth. Each term is roughly 1.3 times longer than the one before, so the strings blow up exponentially in n, and all n nested calls stay alive on the stack at once, each holding its own string. The encoding pass itself is only linear in the term it reads — the expense comes entirely from how long those terms become.
approaches.algorithm:
1. If n == 1, return '1'.
2. Call countAndSay(n-1) to get the previous term.
3. Loop through the previous term to count consecutive characters and build the next string.
4. Return the new string.
approaches.code:
def countAndSay(n: int) -> str:  # each term is read aloud from the digit runs of the previous
    # Base case: term 1 is the seed the whole chain grows from
    if n == 1:  # the recursion bottoms out here
        return "1"  # the first term, fixed by the problem statement
        
    # Term n is literally a description of term n-1
    prev = countAndSay(n - 1)  # one recursive call per term, so depth is n
    res = []  # collect pieces in a list; one join beats repeated +=
    i = 0  # index of the first character of the current run
    
    # Run-length encode prev: the count, then the digit counted
    while i < len(prev):  # i jumps forward to the start of each new run
        count = 1  # a run always contains at least prev[i] itself
        while i + 1 < len(prev) and prev[i] == prev[i+1]:  # peek ahead only after the bound check, or it crashes
            count += 1  # another copy of the same digit joins the run
            i += 1  # i ends up on the LAST character of the run
        res.append(str(count))  # emit the run length as a digit
        res.append(prev[i])  # then emit the digit that was repeated
        i += 1  # step past the run onto the next one
        
    # One join at the end keeps this linear, not quadratic
    return "".join(res)  # the n-th term, returned as a string

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: Look at what the recursive version actually does in time order: it computes term 1, then term 2 from it, then term 3, and so on, merely arranging that sequence by unwinding a call stack. Once term k has been produced, term k-1 is never needed again, so nothing about the problem requires keeping n stack frames alive. Flip the direction and the stack disappears: start with `curr = "1"` and rewrite it n-1 times, each rewrite scanning `curr` for runs of identical digits and appending the count then the digit into `next_str`, then setting `curr` to the joined result. The output is identical, but the recursion depth is now constant, so a large n can never trip Python's recursion limit and there is no per-call overhead. The asymptotic cost is unchanged — the terms still grow exponentially in length, which is a property of the sequence rather than of the method — but at any instant you are only holding the current term and the one being built, instead of every term simultaneously.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Initialize curr = '1'.
2. Loop from 2 to n. In each iteration, construct the next string by traversing curr.
3. Maintain index i, count duplicate characters, append count + character to string builder list.
4. Update curr = join(list).
5. Return curr.
approaches.code:
def countAndSay(n: int) -> str:  # iterative version, so there is no recursion depth to blow
    # Guard non-positive n before the generation loop starts
    if n <= 0:  # terms are numbered starting from one
        return ""  # nothing sensible exists to return
    
    curr = "1"  # term 1, the seed every later term is read from
    # n-1 rewrites carry us from term 1 up to term n
    for _ in range(1, n):  # the loop variable is unused; only the repeat count matters
        next_str = []  # pieces of the term currently being built
        i = 0  # index of the first character of the current run
        # Scan curr as a sequence of runs of identical characters
        while i < len(curr):  # each pass of this loop consumes one whole run
            count = 1  # the run holds at least curr[i] itself
            # Bound check comes first, or curr[i+1] would go out of range
            while i + 1 < len(curr) and curr[i] == curr[i+1]:  # extend the run while the next character repeats
                count += 1  # one more copy of the same digit
                i += 1  # i lands on the run's last character, not past it
            # Say the count first, then the digit being counted
            next_str.append(str(count))  # how many characters this run contained
            next_str.append(curr[i])  # which digit the run was made of
            i += 1  # move past the run to start the next one
        # curr becomes the term that the next iteration reads
        curr = "".join(next_str)  # a single join per term keeps each rewrite linear
        
    # After n-1 rewrites curr holds the requested term
    return curr  # curr is the n-th term of the sequence

Count and Say.tests:
# Edge case: the seed term of the sequence.
assert countAndSay(1) == "1"
# "1" is read as "one 1" -> "11".
assert countAndSay(2) == "11"
# 1 -> 11 -> 21 -> 1211
assert countAndSay(4) == "1211"
assert countAndSay(5) == "111221"
assert countAndSay(6) == "312211"
# Each term must be the run-length encoding of the previous one.
prev = countAndSay(7)
decoded = "".join(prev[k + 1] * int(prev[k]) for k in range(0, len(prev), 2))
assert decoded == countAndSay(6)
prerequisites: The sequence is defined recursively: term 1 is '1', and every later term is the run-length encoding (say-what-you-see) of the previous term.
Run-length encoding a string means scanning maximal runs of identical characters and emitting count followed by the character, e.g. '1211' -> '111221'.
Building strings with += inside a loop is O(n^2) because Python strings are immutable; collect pieces in a list and use ''.join(...) once instead.
The two-pointer run scan: an outer while over i, and an inner while that advances i while curr[i] == curr[i+1] — the i+1 < len(curr) guard must come FIRST to avoid an index error.
The iterative version replaces recursion so that n up to 30 never risks a deep call stack, and it only ever keeps two terms in memory.

Compare Version Numbers.problemStatement: Given two version strings version1 and version2, compare them. If version1 < version2 return -1, if version1 > version2 return 1, otherwise return 0. The comparisons should ignore leading zeros and treat missing components as 0.

examples.explanation: Ignoring leading zeroes, both '01' and '001' represent the same integer 1.
version1 has less components, treat missing components as 0.
version1's first revision is 0, version2's first revision is 1. 0 < 1.

constraints: version1 and version2 consist of digits and dots.
version1 and version2 are valid version numbers.
edgeCases: Unequal length of segments ('1.0.1' vs '1')
Trailing zeros ('1.0' vs '1.0.0')
Single version segment ('1' vs '2')
followUps: How would you handle versions with non-numeric suffixes like alpha, beta (e.g. '1.0-alpha' vs '1.0-beta')?

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: A version string is not a number and it is not a word, which is where the naive attempts fail: comparing '1.10' against '1.9' character by character declares 1.9 the newer one, and reading them as floats is even worse once a third dot appears. The correct unit of comparison is the dot-separated segment, read as an integer. The tempting shortcut is split('.'), but that allocates two lists covering the entire input when the comparison only ever needs one segment from each side at any moment. The observation that keeps memory constant is that a segment can be accumulated on the fly with Horner's method - num = num * 10 + digit - while a cursor walks digits until it meets a '.' or runs off the end, so nothing is ever stored. Two independent cursors i and j march through the two strings in lock step, one segment per outer pass. The outer condition is i < n1 or j < n2, deliberately 'or' rather than 'and', so a string that has run out still takes part with its num reset to 0 each round - that is exactly what makes '1.0' compare equal to '1'. The first segment where num1 and num2 differ decides the whole comparison and returns immediately, because later segments are less significant, and the digit accumulation drops leading zeros for free so '01' equals '1'. O(N+M) time and O(1) extra space.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Initialize pointer i = 0, j = 0.
2. In a loop, extract the number from version1 starting at i until dot or end, convert to int.
3. Similarly extract from version2 starting at j.
4. Compare numbers. If not equal, return -1 or 1.
5. Advance pointers past dots. Continue until both strings are fully read.
6. If loop completes, return 0.
approaches.code:
def compareVersion(version1: str, version2: str) -> int:  # two-pointer parse: no split(), so no extra lists allocated
    i, j = 0, 0  # independent read cursors, one walking each version string
    n1, n2 = len(version1), len(version2)  # cache lengths once; the loop tests them on every pass
    
    while i < n1 or j < n2:  # 'or' not 'and': "1.0" vs "1" must still be judged equal
        num1, num2 = 0, 0  # reset each round; a missing segment therefore counts as 0
        # walk digits of version1 until the dot that ends this segment
        while i < n1 and version1[i] != '.':  # stop at '.' or at the end of the string, whichever comes first
            num1 = num1 * 10 + int(version1[i])  # Horner accumulation: value*10 + digit builds the number left to right
            i += 1  # consume the digit we just folded into num1
        # identical digit scan on version2, kept in lock step
        while j < n2 and version2[j] != '.':  # j is version2's own cursor; the two never share an index
            num2 = num2 * 10 + int(version2[j])  # leading zeros vanish for free, so "01" equals "1"
            j += 1  # advance j past this digit
            
        # the first differing segment decides the entire comparison
        if num1 < num2:  # version1's segment is smaller, so version1 is the older one
            return -1  # early exit: later segments cannot change this verdict
        elif num1 > num2:  # mirror case, version1 is the newer release
            return 1  # caller convention: 1 means the first argument is greater
            
        # both cursors now sit on a '.' (or just past the end)
        i += 1  # step over the dot; if i == n1 the while condition ends the loop
        j += 1  # same for j, harmless when j is already past the string end
        
    return 0  # every segment matched pairwise, so the versions are equal

complexity.time: O(N+M)

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: The manual two-pointer parse is correct, but it braids three separate concerns - locating segment boundaries, converting digit characters into numbers, and comparing the results - inside one nested loop, and that braid is where off-by-one bugs live. The observation here is that the language already implements the first two concerns perfectly: split('.') hands back the segment list, and int() converts a segment while silently discarding leading zeros, so '01' and '1' become the same value with no special case written anywhere. What is left is the mismatch in segment counts, and the trick for that is to iterate range(max(n1, n2)) rather than the shorter of the two lists. An index beyond the end of a list means that segment is simply absent, and an absent segment is worth 0, which is what the if i < n1 else 0 guard expresses - zero-padding both lists conceptually without physically building padded lists. That is why '1.0.0' and '1' come out equal, and why looping only the shorter list would silently get '1' versus '1.0.1' wrong. The first index where the two values differ returns -1 or 1 straight away, and falling off the end of the loop means every segment matched, so 0 is returned. The gain in readability costs O(N+M) space for the two lists, which the manual scan avoided.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Split version1 and version2 by '.' into v1_parts and v2_parts.
2. Iterate through index range of max length of both lists.
3. For each index, fetch integer value at index, or 0 if index is out of bounds.
4. Compare values and return -1 or 1 if different.
5. Return 0 if loop ends without differences.
approaches.code:
def compareVersion(version1: str, version2: str) -> int:  # split-based version: shorter and easier to read than manual parsing
    # split turns "1.20.3" into the segment list ["1","20","3"]
    v1_parts = version1.split('.')  # still strings at this point; int() conversion happens lazily below
    v2_parts = version2.split('.')  # the two lists may well have different lengths
    n1, n2 = len(v1_parts), len(v2_parts)  # segment counts differ often, e.g. "1.0" vs "1.0.0.0"
    
    # loop the LONGER list so no trailing segment is ever skipped
    for i in range(max(n1, n2)):  # max() is the zero-padding trick without building padded lists
        # out-of-range index means the segment is absent, which reads as 0
        num1 = int(v1_parts[i]) if i < n1 else 0  # int() also strips leading zeros, so "01" == "1"
        num2 = int(v2_parts[i]) if i < n2 else 0  # the 'else 0' is why "1.0.0" and "1" compare equal
        
        # first mismatch wins; nothing after it can change the answer
        if num1 < num2:  # version1 lags behind at this segment
            return -1  # return immediately, skipping the remaining segments
        elif num1 > num2:  # symmetric case: version1 is ahead
            return 1  # positive result means the first argument is the greater version
            
    # fell off the end with no mismatch found
    return 0  # 0 is the 'same version' signal expected by callers

complexity.time: O(N+M)
complexity.space: O(N+M)

Compare Version Numbers.tests:
# Leading zeros are ignored: 01 == 001.
assert compareVersion("1.01", "1.001") == 0
# Missing trailing components count as 0.
assert compareVersion("1.0", "1.0.0.0") == 0
# 0 < 1 on the very first component.
assert compareVersion("0.1", "1.1") == -1
# Numeric (not lexicographic) comparison: 2 < 10.
assert compareVersion("1.2", "1.10") == -1
# Extra non-zero component makes the longer version bigger.
assert compareVersion("1.0.1", "1") == 1
# Edge case: single-segment versions.
assert compareVersion("7", "7") == 0
assert compareVersion("2", "10") == -1
prerequisites: A version string is a list of numeric revisions separated by dots; comparison is component-by-component from left to right, and the first difference decides the answer.
Compare components as INTEGERS, never as strings: '01' and '1' are different strings but equal numbers, and '2' > '10' lexicographically while 2 < 10 numerically.
Missing trailing components are treated as 0, so '1.0' and '1.0.0.0' are equal — pad the shorter version conceptually instead of returning early on length.
Python idioms that carry the solution: 'a.b.c'.split('.') gives ['a','b','c'], int('007') is 7, and range(max(n1, n2)) walks the longer list.
Return values are -1 / 0 / 1, not booleans, so remember which side each sign belongs to (-1 means version1 is smaller).

Longest Palindromic Prefix.problemStatement: You are given a string s. A prefix of s is any run of characters taken from the very beginning of the string, and a palindrome is a string that reads identically forwards and backwards. Among all of the prefixes of s that happen to be palindromes, return the longest one — the actual string, not merely its length. Every non-empty input has at least one qualifying prefix, because its first character on its own reads the same in both directions, so the answer is only ever the empty string when s itself is empty.

examples.explanation: The prefix 'aacecaa' is a palindrome and is the longest possible.
Only 'a' is a palindrome prefix.

constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters.
edgeCases: Empty string (returns '')
Single character string (returns s)
Whole string is a palindrome (returns s)
All distinct characters (returns s[0])
followUps: Can you solve this using rolling hashes?

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: There is no obvious shortcut the first time you meet this problem, so start from the definition and test candidates head-on. The candidate set is small and trivially enumerable: a string of length n has exactly n non-empty prefixes, one per length, and checking whether a given string is a palindrome is a single comparison against its own reverse. The one idea worth holding onto is the direction of the loop. Iterate the lengths downwards, from len(s) to 1, rather than upwards, because then the very first prefix that passes the palindrome test is automatically the longest one and you can return it immediately with no best-so-far variable to maintain. What makes this unsatisfying is the cost buried in two innocent-looking slices: `s[:i]` copies i characters and `prefix[::-1]` copies them all again, so the work per candidate is proportional to its length. Summed over all candidates that is O(N^2) time, plus O(N) space for the temporary copies. The empty input is handled up front so no slicing happens on it.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Loop index i from len(s) down to 1.
2. Slice prefix s[:i].
3. If prefix == prefix[::-1], return prefix.
4. Return s[0] (or '' if empty).
approaches.code:
def longestPalindromicPrefix(s: str) -> str:  # try every prefix, longest first, and test each one directly
    if not s:  # guard the empty string before any slicing happens
        return ""  # no prefix exists, so the empty answer is correct
        
    # descending length means the FIRST palindrome found is the longest
    for i in range(len(s), 0, -1):  # range stops at 1, since a 0-length prefix needs no testing
        prefix = s[:i]  # s[:i] copies i characters, which is what makes this O(n^2)
        # reversed-slice equality is the simplest palindrome test there is
        if prefix == prefix[::-1]:  # prefix[::-1] is the reverse; equal means it reads the same both ways
            return prefix  # longest-first ordering makes the first hit automatically optimal
            
    return ""  # unreachable for non-empty s: a single character is always a palindrome

complexity.space: O(N)

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: The quadratic version keeps re-reading the same leading characters, so the question becomes whether one linear pass can measure how far s agrees with its own reverse. Here is the specific insight: a prefix of s is a palindrome exactly when that same block of characters also appears at the tail end of the reversed string — in other words, a palindromic prefix of s is simultaneously a prefix of s and a suffix of reverse(s). "Longest thing that is both a prefix and a suffix" is precisely what KMP's LPS array (longest proper prefix that is also a suffix) computes for you. So build `temp = s + "$" + s[::-1]`; the sentinel character appears in neither half, and that is what prevents a matched border from straddling the middle and reporting a length larger than len(s). Run the standard LPS scan, where a mismatch falls back to `lps[length - 1]` rather than restarting from zero, so `i` never moves backwards and every position is settled in bounded amortised work. Then `lps[-1]`, the border of the whole combined string, is the answer's length and `s[:max_len]` is the prefix. Cost: O(N) time and O(N) space.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Construct temp = s + '$' + s[::-1].
2. Compute the LPS array for temp using KMP precomputation.
3. The value at lps[-1] represents the length of the longest palindromic prefix.
4. Return the prefix s[:lps[-1]].
approaches.code:
def longestPalindromicPrefix(s: str) -> str:  # KMP's LPS array finds the answer in one linear pass
    if not s:  # nothing to scan, so bail out before building the combined string
        return ""  # empty input has an empty palindromic prefix
        
    # trick: a prefix of s that is a palindrome is a suffix of reversed s
    temp = s + "$" + s[::-1]  # '$' is a sentinel that matches nothing, blocking overlap across halves
    n = len(temp)  # combined length is 2*len(s) + 1
    lps = [0] * n  # lps[k] = longest proper prefix of temp[:k+1] that is also a suffix
    length = 0  # length of the border matched so far; doubles as a compare index
    i = 1  # lps[0] is always 0 by definition, so the scan starts at index 1
    
    # single left-to-right pass; i never moves backwards
    while i < n:  # loop over every position of the combined string exactly once
        if temp[i] == temp[length]:  # characters agree, so the current border can grow by one
            length += 1  # extend the matched border length
            lps[i] = length  # record the border length that ends exactly at index i
            i += 1  # only now may i advance to the next character
        else:  # mismatch: the border must shrink instead of resetting to zero
            if length != 0:  # a shorter border may still match, so try that one first
                length = lps[length - 1]  # this fallback is the core trick that keeps the whole scan linear
            else:  # already at zero, there is nothing shorter to fall back to
                lps[i] = 0  # no border ends at this position
                i += 1  # advance only in this branch, otherwise we retry the same char
                
    # the last entry spans the whole combined string
    max_len = lps[-1]  # border of s+rev(s) = longest prefix of s that is also its own reverse
    return s[:max_len]  # the sentinel guarantees max_len can never exceed len(s)

complexity.time: O(N)
complexity.space: O(N)

Longest Palindromic Prefix.tests:
# "aacecaa" is a palindrome, "aacecaaa" is not.
assert longestPalindromicPrefix("aacecaaa") == "aacecaa"
# Nothing beyond the first letter is a palindrome.
assert longestPalindromicPrefix("abcd") == "a"
# The whole string is a palindrome.
assert longestPalindromicPrefix("aaaa") == "aaaa"
assert longestPalindromicPrefix("abab") == "aba"
# Edge case: single character.
assert longestPalindromicPrefix("a") == "a"
# Edge case: empty string.
assert longestPalindromicPrefix("") == ""
prerequisites: You must return a prefix (starting at index 0) that reads the same forwards and backwards — the answer is always at least s[0] for a non-empty string.
Checking one prefix costs O(n) via prefix == prefix[::-1], so scanning all prefixes is O(n^2) — acceptable as a brute force, too slow for n = 10^5.
KMP's LPS array: lps[i] is the length of the longest proper prefix of the string ending at i that is also a suffix ending at i.
The core trick: on temp = s + '$' + s[::-1], the value lps[-1] equals the length of the longest prefix of s that is also a suffix of reversed(s), which is exactly the longest palindromic prefix.
The '$' separator must be a character that cannot appear in s; without it the border could run past the midpoint and report a length larger than len(s).
Python slicing detail: s[:k] returns the first k characters and s[:0] is '' — which is what makes the empty-string edge case fall out naturally.

Implement strstr().problemStatement: You are given two strings, haystack and needle, and must report where the needle first appears inside the haystack. Return the index of the first character of the leftmost occurrence — that is, the smallest i for which haystack[i .. i+m-1] equals needle, where m is the needle's length — and return -1 if the needle does not occur at all. The match must be contiguous and in order, so the needle's characters have to sit next to each other in the haystack. One convention matters here: an empty needle is considered to occur at the very beginning, so the function returns 0 in that case rather than -1. This is the classic substring-search primitive that C calls strstr and Python spells str.find.

examples.explanation: 'sad' occurs at index 0 and 6. The first occurrence is at index 0.
'leeto' did not occur in 'leetcode'.

constraints: haystack and needle consist of lowercase English characters.
edgeCases: Needle is empty (returns 0)
Needle is longer than haystack (returns -1)
Needle matches start, end, or middle
Multiple partial matches
followUps: Can you implement the Boyer-Moore or Rabin-Karp algorithms to solve this problem?

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: Strip away all pattern-matching theory and the problem reduces to a question you can answer by hand: for each place the needle could begin, does it actually begin there? A window of length m only fits at offsets 0 through n - m, so those are the only candidates, and testing each one in increasing order means the first success is automatically the leftmost occurrence. This is the version worth writing first because it is obviously correct and needs no extra memory. What makes it unsatisfying is that the innocent-looking line haystack[i:i+m] == needle is not a single step — it copies m characters and compares them, so the real cost is O(n*m). Worse, it is deeply forgetful: if the first four characters of a five-character needle matched at offset i and then failed, the loop restarts from scratch at offset i+1 and re-reads those same characters, even though what it already saw was enough to rule out several offsets at once. Recovering that discarded knowledge is exactly what KMP is for.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Handle empty needle case.
2. Iterate i from 0 to len(haystack) - len(needle).
3. If haystack[i:i+len(needle)] == needle, return i.
4. If loop completes, return -1.
approaches.code:
def strStr(haystack: str, needle: str) -> int:  # naive scan: compare the needle at every possible start offset
    # convention required by the problem statement
    if not needle:  # an empty needle is considered found at position 0
        return 0  # return the leftmost index, which is 0 here
        
    n, m = len(haystack), len(needle)  # m is both the window width and the success length
    # each window is a fresh O(m) comparison, hence O(n*m) worst case
    for i in range(n - m + 1):  # the +1 matters: the last legal start offset is exactly n-m
        if haystack[i:i+m] == needle:  # slicing copies m chars before comparing; that is the naive cost
            return i  # i only grows, so the first hit is the leftmost occurrence
            
    return -1  # no starting offset produced a full match

complexity.time: O(N*M)

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: Look closely at what the naive scan throws away. When the needle matches j characters and then hits a mismatch, those j characters are not unknown text — they are, by definition, the first j characters of the needle itself. So before ever touching the haystack you can work out, for each prefix length, how far the needle may safely slide when a mismatch happens there: you need the longest proper prefix of needle[0..j-1] that is also a suffix of it, since only such a border can still line up with the text you just consumed. That table is the LPS array, and the code builds it in O(m) with the length pointer retreating through lps[length-1] whenever an extension fails. Armed with it, the search pointer i over the haystack never moves backwards even once: on a mismatch the code sets j = lps[j-1], which slides the needle forward while keeping i frozen, and on the rare case j == 0 it simply advances i. Each haystack character is therefore consumed at most once and each mismatch strictly decreases j, giving O(n + m) time in total, at the cost of O(m) space for the table. The match is reported as i - j the moment j reaches m, because the occurrence began exactly j characters before the current position.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Compute LPS table for the needle.
2. Perform matching. If characters match, increment both pointers.
3. If full needle is matched, return start index.
4. If mismatch and needle pointer j > 0, fallback j to LPS[j-1]. Else, increment haystack pointer i.
5. Return -1 if no match.
approaches.code:
def strStr(haystack: str, needle: str) -> int:  # KMP: each haystack character is read at most once, so O(n+m)
    if not needle:  # same empty-needle convention as the naive version
        return 0  # match at index 0 with nothing to compare
        
    n = len(haystack)  # text length, scanned by the single forward pointer i
    m = len(needle)  # pattern length; j reaching m is the success condition
    lps = [0] * m  # lps[k] = longest proper prefix of needle[:k+1] that is also a suffix
    length = 0  # border length built so far during the preprocessing pass
    i = 1  # lps[0] is trivially 0, so table construction begins at index 1
    
    # the table depends only on the needle, never on the haystack
    while i < m:  # build pass: i moves forward, length may bounce backwards
        if needle[i] == needle[length]:  # the current border extends by one character
            length += 1  # grow the matched border by one
            lps[i] = length  # store the border length ending at index i
            i += 1  # advance to the next needle position
        else:  # characters disagree while building the table
            if length != 0:  # do not restart at 0; retreat to the next shorter border
                length = lps[length - 1]  # i is deliberately NOT advanced, so this char is retried
            else:  # length is already 0, so no shorter border exists
                lps[i] = 0  # no prefix-suffix overlap ends here
                i += 1  # only now is it safe to move to the next position
                
    # now walk the haystack using the table just built
    i = 0  # haystack index; it never moves backwards, hence O(n) scanning
    j = 0  # needle index: how many characters currently match ending at i-1
    while i < n:  # one pass over the text, no backtracking on i
        if needle[j] == haystack[i]:  # characters agree, so extend the partial match
            i += 1  # consume this haystack character
            j += 1  # and the matching needle character
        if j == m:  # j hit the needle length, meaning a full match just completed
            # the match started j characters before the current position
            return i - j  # i - j is the start index, so no second pointer is needed
        elif i < n and needle[j] != haystack[i]:  # mismatch after j characters already matched
            # the LPS entry says how far the needle can slide safely
            if j != 0:  # some prefix already matched, so reuse it instead of rescanning
                j = lps[j - 1]  # the core KMP move: shift the pattern, keep i frozen
            else:  # j is 0, so there is nothing matched to reuse
                i += 1  # no partial match, so simply try the next haystack character
                
    return -1  # the text ran out before the needle was ever completed

complexity.time: O(N+M)
complexity.space: O(M)

Implement strstr().tests:
# Match at index 0.
assert strStr("sadbutsad", "sad") == 0
# No occurrence at all.
assert strStr("leetcode", "leeto") == -1
# Match in the middle after partial matches.
assert strStr("mississippi", "issip") == 4
# Heavy partial-overlap case where naive shifting would redo work.
assert strStr("aabaaabaaac", "aabaaac") == 4
# Edge case: empty needle is found at index 0 by convention.
assert strStr("aaa", "") == 0
# Edge case: needle longer than haystack.
assert strStr("a", "aaa") == -1
prerequisites: The task is exact substring search: return the smallest index i with haystack[i:i+m] == needle, or -1; by convention an empty needle returns 0.
The naive method compares the needle against every window of the haystack, costing O(n*m) in the worst case (think 'aaaaab' searched for 'aaab').
KMP's insight: after a mismatch, the characters already matched are known, so the haystack pointer i never moves backwards — only the needle pointer j retreats.
The LPS/failure table lps[j] = length of the longest proper prefix of needle[0..j] that is also a suffix; on a mismatch, j = lps[j-1] reuses that overlap.
Total work is O(n + m) because i only increases and j decreases at most as many times as it increased — an amortized counting argument worth being able to state.
Edge cases to keep in mind: empty needle, needle longer than haystack, and a match that ends exactly at the last character of the haystack.

Postorder Traversal.problemStatement: You are given the root of a binary tree, where every node holds a value and may have a left child, a right child, both, or neither. Return a list of all node values arranged in postorder. Postorder is defined recursively: for any node, you first list every value in its entire left subtree, then every value in its entire right subtree, and only then the node's own value. Applying that rule from the root downwards means each parent always appears after both of its children, so the root ends up last in the output. If the tree is empty, the returned list is empty. Every node contributes its value exactly once.

examples.explanation: Node 3 is visited first, then Node 2, then Node 1.

constraints: The number of the nodes in the tree is in the range [0, 100].
edgeCases: Empty tree (returns [])
Single node tree (returns [val])
Skewed tree (only left or only right children)
followUps: Can you implement the solution iteratively without recursion?

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: Beginners often try to write this iteratively with an explicit stack first, and it goes badly, because postorder needs you to know whether you are on the way down into a node or on the way back up from it. A node has to be pushed to the output only after you have returned from both of its children, so a naive stack loop keeps emitting parents too early and you end up bolting on visited flags or reversing a modified preorder. The observation that makes the recursive version almost trivial is that the language's own call stack already tracks the descend-versus-return state for you. The definition of postorder is itself recursive, so writing it as three lines in the correct order literally is the definition: recurse left, recurse right, and only then append this node's value. The placement of the append after both recursive calls is the entire difference between post-, in- and preorder; move it above `dfs(node.left)` and you have preorder instead. The `if not node: return` guard handles missing children so no caller has to check. Every node is entered exactly once, giving O(N) time, with O(H) call-stack space that degrades to O(N) on a completely skewed tree, plus the O(N) output list.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Initialize an empty list res.
2. Define a helper function dfs(node). If node is None, return.
3. Call dfs(node.left).
4. Call dfs(node.right).
5. Append node.val to res.
6. Call dfs(root) and return res.
approaches.code:
# Definition for a binary tree node.
# class TreeNode:
#     def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
#         self.val = val
#         self.left = left
#         self.right = right

def postorderTraversal(root) -> list[int]:
    res = []
    
    # Helper function to perform recursive postorder traversal
    def dfs(node):
        if not node:
            return
        # Traverse left child
        dfs(node.left)
        # Traverse right child
        dfs(node.right)
        # Append current node value
        res.append(node.val)
        
    dfs(root)
    return res

complexity.time: O(N)
complexity.space: O(N)

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: Recursion is correct here and costs almost nothing to write - what it costs is control. Every node on the current descent path holds a full interpreter frame, and on a skewed tree of a hundred thousand nodes that hits Python's recursion limit and raises rather than answering. All those frames exist to preserve a single bit per node: have I already come back from this node's right child? That bit does not need a frame. It can be reconstructed from one variable, `last_visited`, holding the most recently emitted node. Peek at the stack top; if its right child *is* `last_visited`, you have just returned from the right subtree and the node is finished. This test is complete, not a heuristic, because postorder emits every node of a subtree before anything above it, so the very last value emitted out of a right subtree is that subtree's own root - the right child itself. Nothing else can be sitting in `last_visited` at that moment. Nodes with no right child, and nodes whose right subtree is already drained, both fall to the same branch and are emitted immediately. Cost: O(N) time, since each node is pushed once and popped once; the stack holds one root-to-leaf path, O(H), which is the stated O(N) on a degenerate tree. You trade three lines of recursion for explicit state you can step through and that cannot overflow.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Return `[]` at once if `root` is None; otherwise set `res = []`, `stack = []`, `curr = root`, `last_visited = None`.
2. Loop while `curr` is not None or `stack` is non-empty.
3. If `curr` is not None, push it and descend with `curr = curr.left`, driving to the leftmost node.
4. Otherwise peek at `peek_node = stack[-1]` without popping.
5. If `peek_node.right` exists and is not `last_visited`, its right subtree is unexplored - set `curr = peek_node.right` and go back to step 2.
6. Else the node is finished: append `peek_node.val` to `res`, pop it, and set `last_visited` to the popped node.
7. Return `res` when both `curr` and `stack` are exhausted.
approaches.code:
# Definition for a binary tree node.
# class TreeNode:
#     def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
#         self.val = val
#         self.left = left
#         self.right = right

def postorderTraversal(root) -> list[int]:
    res = []
    if not root:
        return res
        
    stack = []
    curr = root
    last_visited = None
    
    # Iterate while there are nodes to process
    while stack or curr:
        # Reach the leftmost node of current node
        if curr:
            stack.append(curr)
            curr = curr.left
        else:
            peek_node = stack[-1]
            # If right child exists and is not yet processed, move right
            if peek_node.right and last_visited != peek_node.right:
                curr = peek_node.right
            else:
                # Process current node and pop it from stack
                res.append(peek_node.val)
                last_visited = stack.pop()
                
    return res

complexity.time: O(N)
complexity.space: O(N)
