assert verticalTraversal(build_tree([3, 9, 20, None, None, 15, 7])) == [[9], [3, 15], [20], [7]]
# EDGE: two nodes share (row=2, col=0) -> tie broken by smaller value first (5 before 6)
assert verticalTraversal(build_tree([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7])) == [[4], [2], [1, 5, 6], [3], [7]]
assert verticalTraversal(build_tree([1])) == [[1]]
# EDGE: empty tree
assert verticalTraversal(None) == []
prerequisites: Assign every node a coordinate: the root is (row 0, col 0), a left child is (row+1, col-1) and a right child is (row+1, col+1).
The required ordering is column ascending, then row ascending, then node VALUE ascending — the value tie-break is what makes this harder than Top/Bottom View.
collections.defaultdict(list) lets you append to col_map[col] without checking whether the key exists yet.
Python sorts tuples lexicographically, so sorting (col, row, val) triples in one call implements the whole ordering rule.
BFS visits rows in increasing order, but two nodes can still land on the SAME (row, col) cell, so an explicit sort by value inside a column is still required.
Columns can be negative, so you either sort the dictionary keys or track min_col/max_col.

Top View of Binary Tree.problemStatement: You are given the root of a binary tree and must report what an observer looking straight down at it from above would see. Give the root the horizontal position 0; a left child sits one position to the left of its parent and a right child one position to the right, so the nodes group themselves into vertical columns. Within each column only the node closest to the top — the one at the smallest depth — is visible, because it blocks the view of everything beneath it. Return the values of those visible nodes ordered by column, from the leftmost column to the rightmost.
constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [1, 10^5].
edgeCases: Single node tree (returns [root.val]).
Skewed tree.
Nodes that overlap horizontally but one is lower (BFS will naturally process higher node first).
followUps: Can you solve this in O(N) time without sorting the keys at the end?

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: The mental picture is a stack of nodes in each column with only the highest one visible, and that picture dictates the data structure: a dictionary keyed by column, holding the best candidate found so far for that column. Getting the coordinates is easy — carry (row, col) down the recursion, adding 1 to row on every step downwards and subtracting or adding 1 to col for a left or right move. The trap is deciding who wins a column, and it is exactly where a naive DFS goes wrong if it simply keeps the first arrival: depth-first search dives all the way down the left spine before it ever touches the right subtree, so a deep left-side node can claim a column that a much shallower right-side node also occupies, and the reported view would be wrong. Storing the row alongside the value fixes it — a new node replaces the stored one only when row is strictly smaller than the stored row — and with that comparison in place the traversal order stops mattering. Finally a dictionary has no order of its own, so the keys must be sorted before output, which is why this costs O(n log n) time rather than O(n), with O(n) space for the map.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Create an empty dictionary col_map that will map a column index to a (row, value) pair recording the shallowest node found in that column so far.
2. Define dfs(node, row, col) and return immediately when node is None, since a missing child claims no column.
3. Let this node claim its column only if it deserves to: if col is not yet a key of col_map, or if row is strictly less than the stored col_map[col][0], overwrite col_map[col] with (row, node.val). Keeping the row is what maintains the invariant "col_map[col] holds the shallowest node yet seen in column col" regardless of the order the branches happen to be explored in.
4. Recurse into the children with updated coordinates: dfs(node.left, row + 1, col - 1) for the left child and dfs(node.right, row + 1, col + 1) for the right child, so depth always grows by one and the horizontal offset moves one step in the matching direction.
5. Launch the traversal with dfs(root, 0, 0), which anchors the root at row 0 and column 0 and makes every other coordinate relative to it.
6. Sort the keys of col_map — this puts the negative columns first, then 0, then the positive ones — and return the list of the values stored under them, which is the view read from left to right.
approaches.code:
def topView(root):  # top view = the first node met in each column, looking from above
    col_map = {}  # column -> (depth, value) of the shallowest node found so far
    # DFS carrying both the depth and the horizontal offset
    def dfs(node, row, col):  # row is depth from the root, col is the horizontal distance
        if not node:  # recursion base case for a missing child
            return  # a missing child claims no column
        # a shallower node in the same column hides the deeper one
        if col not in col_map or row < col_map[col][0]:  # the row comparison is what makes DFS safe here, not just BFS
            col_map[col] = (row, node.val)  # store depth alongside value so later nodes can be rejected
        dfs(node.left, row + 1, col - 1)  # left child: one row deeper, one column to the left
        dfs(node.right, row + 1, col + 1)  # right child: one row deeper, one column to the right
        
    dfs(root, 0, 0)  # root anchors the grid at row 0, column 0
    # columns must be emitted left to right, so sort the keys
    return [col_map[c][1] for c in sorted(col_map.keys())]  # sorted() orders the negative columns first, then 0, then positive

complexity.time: O(N log N)
complexity.space: O(N)

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition:
A depth-first walk carrying (row, col) dives down the left spine before touching anything right, so the first node it reaches in a column is often not the highest. It must store a depth beside each candidate and compare on every visit, then sort the columns.

The observation: breadth-first search - a queue that drains one level before starting the next - dequeues nodes in nondecreasing depth. The first node popped for a column is therefore the shallowest there, so the depth field and its comparison vanish and the test becomes "is this column absent from the map?".

Why the sort vanishes too: a column shifts by exactly one per edge, so the path from the root to a node at column c passes through every integer between 0 and c. Occupied columns form a contiguous run, which is what makes min_col/max_col tracking safe: every key in `range(min_col, max_col + 1)` exists, and walking it emits them left to right.

Cost: each node enters and leaves the queue once - O(N) time, O(N) for map plus queue. The trade against DFS is memory: the queue holds a whole level where recursion needed O(H).
approaches.algorithm:
1. If `root` is None, return [].
2. Create `col_map` = {} (column -> first value seen there), a queue seeded with (root, 0), and `min_col = max_col = 0`.
3. While the queue is non-empty, pop (node, col) from the FRONT - popping the front is what keeps the depths nondecreasing.
4. If `col` is not already a key in `col_map`, record `col_map[col] = node.val`; an existing key means a shallower node already claimed this column.
5. Update `min_col = min(min_col, col)` and `max_col = max(max_col, col)`.
6. Push (node.left, col - 1) and (node.right, col + 1) for whichever children exist.
7. Return [col_map[c] for c in range(min_col, max_col + 1)].
approaches.code:
from collections import deque

def topView(root):
    # Return empty list if root is null
    if not root:
        return []
    # Map to store the first node value seen at each column
    col_map = {}
    # Queue containing tuples of (node, col)
    queue = deque([(root, 0)])
    # Keep track of minimum and maximum column encountered
    min_col, max_col = 0, 0
    # Process BFS queue
    while queue:
        # Pop front element from queue
        node, col = queue.popleft()
        # If column is visited for the first time, record it
        if col not in col_map:
            col_map[col] = node.val
        # Update min and max columns to avoid sorting keys later
        min_col = min(min_col, col)
        max_col = max(max_col, col)
        # Add left child with col - 1
        if node.left:
            queue.append((node.left, col - 1))
        # Add right child with col + 1
        if node.right:
            queue.append((node.right, col + 1))
    # Build result list using range from min_col to max_col
    return [col_map[col] for col in range(min_col, max_col + 1)]

complexity.time: O(N)
complexity.space: O(N)

Top View of Binary Tree.tests:
assert topView(build_tree([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7])) == [4, 2, 1, 3, 7]
# EDGE: node 4 sits in column 0 but deeper than root, so root 1 stays visible
assert topView(build_tree([1, 2, None, None, 4])) == [2, 1]
assert topView(build_tree([1])) == [1]
# EDGE: empty tree
assert topView(None) == []
prerequisites: Horizontal distance (column) is the key idea: root = 0, left child = col - 1, right child = col + 1.
The top view keeps the FIRST node encountered in each column when scanning the tree level by level, so only write to the map when the column is unseen.
BFS is the natural fit because it guarantees shallower nodes are processed before deeper ones; a DFS needs an explicit row comparison to be correct.
The set of occupied columns is always a contiguous range, so tracking min_col/max_col lets you build the answer without sorting the dictionary keys.
Dict membership testing with 'col not in col_map' is O(1) on average.
Answer order is left to right by column, not by tree structure, so the output can look nothing like a level order.

Bottom View of Binary Tree.problemStatement: You are given the root of a binary tree and must return its bottom view: the list of node values you would see if you stood underneath the tree and looked straight up. To make that precise, assign every node a horizontal distance (a column). The root sits in column 0, a left child sits one column to the left of its parent, and a right child sits one column to the right, so two nodes in different branches can share a column. Within each occupied column, exactly one node is visible from below -- the one at the greatest depth -- and when two nodes in the same column sit at the same depth, the one encountered later in the traversal (the rightmost one) is the one reported. Return those visible values ordered by column from leftmost to rightmost. An empty tree produces an empty list.
constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [1, 10^5].
edgeCases: Single node tree (returns [root.val]).
Left or right skewed tree.
Two nodes sharing the same horizontal col (BFS processes nodes level-by-level, and for the same level from left to right, so the rightmost node at that level/col overwrites and is correct).
followUps: Can you solve this in O(N) time and O(N) space without sorting the columns?

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: The phrase "viewed from the bottom" sounds geometric and vague until you notice it is really a grouping problem in disguise. Give every node a pair of coordinates -- a row for how far down it sits and a column for its horizontal offset from the root -- and the bottom view is simply: bucket the nodes by column, and inside each bucket keep the one with the largest row. That reframing means you no longer have to reason about geometry at all, only about a dictionary keyed by column. The naive alternative would be to collect every node with its coordinates into a big list and then sort or group it afterwards, but you can fold the selection into the traversal itself: a plain DFS that carries `(row, col)` down each branch, writing `col_map[col] = (row, node.val)` whenever the current node is at least as deep as whatever that column already holds. The `>=` rather than `>` is deliberate and encodes the tie rule -- because the DFS visits the left child before the right, a later same-depth visit is the more rightward node, and it correctly overwrites. The reason this is filed as the brute force is the ending: a dictionary has no order, so the columns must be sorted before output, which pushes the total to O(N log N) time and O(N) space, whereas a level-order BFS makes depth increase automatically and lets you track just the minimum and maximum column to emit the answer without sorting.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Create an empty dictionary `col_map` that will map each column index to a tuple `(row, value)` describing the deepest node seen in that column so far -- that pairing is the invariant the traversal maintains.
2. Define a recursive `dfs(node, row, col)` and return immediately when `node` is None, so a missing child contributes nothing.
3. Inside `dfs`, record the current node if either `col` is not yet a key of `col_map` or the current `row` is greater than or equal to the stored row; the `>=` lets a later same-depth visit win, which is what makes the rightmost node the visible one.
4. Recurse into the left child with `dfs(node.left, row + 1, col - 1)` -- one row deeper, one column further left.
5. Recurse into the right child with `dfs(node.right, row + 1, col + 1)` -- one row deeper, one column further right; doing this after the left call is what establishes the tie-breaking order.
6. Kick the traversal off with `dfs(root, 0, 0)`, anchoring the root at the origin of the coordinate grid.
7. Finally, sort the keys of `col_map` and return the stored value from each column in that left-to-right order.
approaches.code:
def bottomView(root):                                       # bottom view = lowest node sitting in each column
    col_map = {}                                            # column -> (row, value) of the deepest node seen there
    # DFS carries (row, col) coordinates down every branch
    def dfs(node, row, col):                                # row grows downward, col grows rightward from the root
        if not node:                                        # missing child: this branch records nothing
            return                                          # unwind and let the caller try the other side
        # ties on depth go to the later (rightmost) visit
        if col not in col_map or row >= col_map[col][0]:    # deeper node in this column overwrites the old one
            col_map[col] = (row, node.val)                  # keep the row too, so future nodes can compare depth
        dfs(node.left, row + 1, col - 1)                    # left child: one row down, one column to the left
        dfs(node.right, row + 1, col + 1)                   # right child: one row down, one column to the right
        
    dfs(root, 0, 0)                                         # root anchors the coordinate grid at (0, 0)
    return [col_map[c][1] for c in sorted(col_map.keys())]  # sorting the columns puts the view in left-to-right order

complexity.time: O(N log N)
complexity.space: O(N)

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition:
Collecting every node as a (row, column, value) triple and then sorting or grouping by column costs O(N log N) and stores a full coordinate table, when one winner per column is all that is ever read.

BFS already picks that winner. Breadth-first order - dequeue at the front, enqueue children at the back - retires every node at depth d before touching depth d + 1, so nodes arrive in non-decreasing depth, and `col_map[col] = node.val` written unconditionally on every visit leaves the deepest node of each column as its last writer.

Overwriting cannot lose the answer: any write that clobbers an earlier one comes from a node dequeued later, so at the same depth or deeper, and the survivor is never shallower. At equal depth the queue hands nodes over left to right, so the rightmost wins - the standard tie rule. `range(min_col, max_col + 1)` never hits a missing key, since each step down shifts the column by exactly 1, making the occupied columns contiguous.

O(N) time, O(N) space for queue and map. Tracking min and max during the sweep removes the final sort, but leans on that contiguity.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Return [] immediately when root is None.
2. Create an empty dict `col_map`, a deque seeded with the pair (root, 0), and set `min_col = 0`, `max_col = 0`.
3. While the queue is non-empty, popleft a (node, col) pair.
4. Overwrite `col_map[col] = node.val` without checking whether the column already has an entry - the later write is always the deeper node.
5. Update `min_col = min(min_col, col)` and `max_col = max(max_col, col)` so no key sort is needed at the end.
6. Append the left child as (node.left, col - 1) and the right child as (node.right, col + 1), skipping absent children.
7. Return `[col_map[col] for col in range(min_col, max_col + 1)]`.
approaches.code:
from collections import deque

def bottomView(root):
    # Return empty list if root is null
    if not root:
        return []
    # Map to store the last node value seen at each column
    col_map = {}
    # Queue containing tuples of (node, col)
    queue = deque([(root, 0)])
    # Keep track of minimum and maximum column encountered
    min_col, max_col = 0, 0
    # Process BFS queue
    while queue:
        # Pop front element from queue
        node, col = queue.popleft()
        # Overwrite column map entry with current node value
        col_map[col] = node.val
        # Update min and max columns to avoid sorting keys later
        min_col = min(min_col, col)
        max_col = max(max_col, col)
        # Add left child with col - 1
        if node.left:
            queue.append((node.left, col - 1))
        # Add right child with col + 1
        if node.right:
            queue.append((node.right, col + 1))
    # Build result list using range from min_col to max_col
    return [col_map[col] for col in range(min_col, max_col + 1)]

complexity.time: O(N)
complexity.space: O(N)

Right View of Binary Tree.problemStatement: You are given the root of a binary tree. Picture standing to the right of the tree and looking straight at it: at every depth exactly one node blocks your view, namely the rightmost node on that level. Return the list of those visible values, ordered from the top of the tree downward. Note that this is not the same as repeatedly following right children — if a node has only a left child, that left child is the rightmost thing at its depth and so it is visible. An empty tree produces an empty list, and a tree that is one long left-leaning chain makes every node visible.
constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [0, 100].
edgeCases: Empty tree (returns []).
Left-skewed tree (the left nodes will be visible once right branches terminate).
Single node tree.
followUps: Can you solve this both iteratively (BFS) and recursively (DFS)?

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: The name of the problem tempts you into walking down the right spine, taking `root.right` over and over. That breaks as soon as a node has no right child but does have a left one, because then the left child is the only node at its depth and is therefore what you see. So the thing to reason about is not the shape of a path but the levels themselves: exactly one node per depth is visible, and it is the last node of that depth in left-to-right order. Breadth-first search is the traversal that hands you the tree one complete level at a time, so the plan is to drain the tree level by level and record only the final node of each level. The detail that makes it work is freezing `level_size = len(queue)` before the inner loop runs, because children are appended to the very same queue while the level is being consumed; without that snapshot there would be no way to tell where the current level ends and the next begins, and the visible node is at index `level_size - 1`, not `level_size`. Each node is enqueued and dequeued exactly once, though note that `pop(0)` on a Python list shifts the remaining elements, so swapping in a deque is what makes the dequeue genuinely constant time -- and until you make that swap the traversal is not really O(N): draining a level of width W costs O(W^2), which on a complete tree adds up to O(N^2).
approaches.algorithm:
1. If root is None, return [].
2. Initialize queue = [root].
3. Loop while queue is not empty.
4. Take the level size, and pop elements. If the element is the last in the level, add to result.
5. Push non-null left and right children to queue.
6. Return result.
approaches.code:
def rightSideView(root):                 # level-order walk, keeping the last node of each level
    if not root:                         # no tree means nothing is visible from the right
        return []
    queue = [root]                       # queue always holds exactly one full level of nodes
    result = []                          # one value per depth, collected top to bottom
    while queue:                         # each outer pass drains one entire level
        level_size = len(queue)          # freeze the count BEFORE children get appended below
        for i in range(level_size):      # i is the position inside THIS level, not the whole tree
            curr = queue.pop(0)          # pop(0) is O(n) on a list; a deque would make it O(1)
            # the last index of a level is its rightmost node
            if i == level_size - 1:      # off-by-one trap: it is size - 1, not size
                result.append(curr.val)  # exactly what a viewer standing on the right can see
            if curr.left:                # enqueue left first to keep each level left-to-right
                queue.append(curr.left)
            if curr.right:               # right child goes last, so it ends the next level
                queue.append(curr.right)
    return result                        # one visible node per depth, ordered top to bottom

complexity.time: O(N * W) worst case, where W is the widest level - every node is handled exactly once, but `queue.pop(0)` on a Python list shifts every remaining element, so draining a level of width W costs O(W^2). On a complete tree the bottom level alone holds about N/2 nodes, which makes the whole traversal O(N^2). Swap the list for collections.deque and popleft() (O(1) per removal) to get a genuine O(N).
complexity.space: O(W)

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: The level-order brute force is already O(N) in time, but it pays for the answer with memory: a queue that holds an entire level at once, which on the bottom level of a balanced tree is about N/2 nodes, all buffered so the last one can be read. The waste is buffering a whole level just to identify one node in it. The observation: you never need to see the level to know its rightmost node - you only need to ARRIVE there first. Visit node, then right subtree, then left subtree, and at any depth the very first node reached is the rightmost at that depth, so it can be recorded on sight and everything else at that depth ignored. The test depth == len(result) is the whole mechanism: result holds one value per depth already seen, so its length is the count of recorded depths, and equality means this depth is brand new and this node is its first arrival. Why this cannot pick the wrong node: within a depth, root-right-left visits every node of a right subtree before any node of the corresponding left subtree, and that holds recursively at every level of nesting, so arrival order at a fixed depth is strictly right to left. Depths are also recorded densely - you cannot reach depth d without passing through d-1 - so len(result) never runs ahead and no depth is skipped. Cost: O(N) time and O(H) stack, which on a balanced tree is O(log N) instead of the queue's O(N); on a skewed tree recursion depth is O(N) again.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Create result = [], which will end up holding exactly one value per depth, top to bottom.
2. Define solve(node, depth) and return immediately when node is None.
3. Test depth == len(result). If it holds, no node at this depth has been seen yet, so append node.val - this node is the rightmost one at its depth.
4. Recurse into node.right with depth + 1 BEFORE node.left, which is what makes the first arrival at each depth the rightmost node; swapping these two lines silently produces the left view.
5. Recurse into node.left with depth + 1, so subtrees with no right sibling still get their nodes counted at depths not yet reached.
6. Call solve(root, 0) and return result; an empty tree exits at step 2 and yields [].
approaches.code:
def rightSideView(root):
    # Result list to store the right side view
    result = []
    
    # Helper function for recursive DFS traversal (Root-Right-Left)
    def solve(node, depth):
        # Base case: if node is null, return
        if not node:
            return
        # If current depth equals length of result, add node val
        if depth == len(result):
            result.append(node.val)
        # Recurse on right subtree first to prioritize rightmost nodes
        solve(node.right, depth + 1)
        # Recurse on left subtree
        solve(node.left, depth + 1)
        
    # Start recursion from root at depth 0
    solve(root, 0)
    # Return right side view list
    return result

complexity.time: O(N)
complexity.space: O(H)

Left View of Binary Tree.problemStatement: You are given the root of a binary tree. Picture yourself standing to the left of the drawn tree and looking at it horizontally: at every depth, the leftmost node stands in front of and hides every other node on that same level. Return the list of node values you would see, ordered from the top of the tree downwards - that is, exactly one value per level, being the value of the first node encountered at that depth when the level is read from left to right. A level contributes its visible node regardless of whether that node happens to be a left child or a right child, so a node with no left sibling at its depth is still visible. If the tree is empty, return an empty list.
constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [0, 100].
edgeCases: Empty tree (returns []).
Right-skewed tree.
Single node tree.
followUps: Can you solve this both iteratively (BFS) and recursively (DFS)?

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: The phrase 'leftmost node of each level' is the entire problem, and the difficulty is that a tree's natural traversals do not hand you levels. A depth-first walk visits deep nodes on one side before shallow nodes on the other, so you would have to carry a depth counter and separately remember which depths you had already recorded. Breadth-first traversal produces the nodes in level order, but only helps if you can tell where one level ends and the next begins, and a plain queue blurs that boundary because children of level d are appended right next to the nodes of level d that are still being popped. The observation that makes it clean is a loop invariant: if the queue holds exactly one complete level at the top of each outer pass, then level_size = len(queue) freezes that level's node count before any children are appended, so popping exactly level_size times drains precisely this level and leaves the queue holding precisely the next one, re-establishing the invariant. Inside that inner loop the counter i is the node's rank within its own level, so i == 0 identifies the leftmost node and is the only case that appends to result. Because each node's left child is always enqueued before its right child, the ranks stay in genuine left-to-right order. Space is O(W) for the widest level. Time is the part worth being careful about: each node is handled once, but pop(0) on a Python list shifts every element behind it, so draining a level of width W costs O(W^2) and the traversal as a whole can reach O(N^2) -- on a complete tree the bottom level alone holds about N/2 nodes. Swapping the list for collections.deque makes popleft() O(1) and the traversal genuinely O(N).
approaches.algorithm:
1. If root is None, return [].
2. Initialize queue = [root].
3. Loop while queue is not empty.
4. Take the level size, and pop elements. If the element is the first in the level, add to result.
5. Push non-null left and right children to queue.
6. Return result.
approaches.code:
def leftSideView(root):                  # level-order walk, keeping the first node of each level
    if not root:                         # no tree means nothing is visible from the left
        return []
    queue = [root]                       # queue always holds exactly one full level of nodes
    result = []                          # one value per depth, collected top to bottom
    while queue:                         # each outer pass drains one entire level
        level_size = len(queue)          # freeze the count BEFORE children get appended below
        for i in range(level_size):      # i is the position inside THIS level, not the whole tree
            curr = queue.pop(0)          # pop(0) is O(n) on a list; a deque would make it O(1)
            # index 0 of a level is its leftmost node
            if i == 0:                   # only the very first pop of each level qualifies
                result.append(curr.val)  # exactly what a viewer standing on the left can see
            if curr.left:                # left child first keeps the next level in the same order
                queue.append(curr.left)
            if curr.right:               # right child trails behind every left one at this depth
                queue.append(curr.right)
    return result                        # one visible node per depth, ordered top to bottom

complexity.time: O(N * W) worst case, where W is the widest level - every node is handled exactly once, but `queue.pop(0)` on a Python list shifts every remaining element, so draining a level of width W costs O(W^2). On a complete tree the bottom level alone holds about N/2 nodes, which makes the whole traversal O(N^2). Swap the list for collections.deque and popleft() (O(1) per removal) to get a genuine O(N).
complexity.space: O(W)

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition:
Breadth-first traversal reaches levels in order, but a plain queue blurs where one level ends, so the fix is to record the queue length at the start of each level and consume exactly that many nodes. It works, and it holds an entire level in memory -- up to about N/2 nodes at the widest row -- in order to use one node from it.

The observation: identifying the leftmost node of a level does not require having the level. It requires knowing who arrived FIRST. Walk Root -> Left -> Right carrying a depth counter; because the left subtree is fully explored before the right one, every node at depth d in the left subtree is visited before any node at depth d in the right subtree, so visit order within a depth IS left-to-right order. The first node ever seen at a depth is that depth's answer.

Why `depth == len(result)` is a correct first-visit test, with no set or dictionary: depths are recorded strictly in increasing order, because a node at depth d is only reached through its parent at depth d-1, which was visited earlier. So `result` always holds one entry for depths 0 through len(result)-1 and nothing beyond, making `len(result)` exactly the next unrecorded depth. No level can be skipped, and no later node at an already-recorded depth can overwrite the first.

Cost: O(N) time, one visit per node. Space is O(H) for the recursion stack, H the height -- a clear win over the level-order queue on wide trees, and the trade is that a left-leaning chain of N nodes pushes N frames where the queue would have held one node.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Start with an empty `result` list.
2. Define solve(node, depth) and call it as solve(root, 0).
3. If node is None, return -- nothing at this position.
4. If depth == len(result), this is the first node reached at this depth, so append node.val.
5. Recurse left with solve(node.left, depth + 1) BEFORE recursing right, so the leftmost node of each depth arrives first.
6. Recurse right with solve(node.right, depth + 1).
7. Return `result`, one value per depth, top to bottom.
approaches.code:
def leftSideView(root):
    # Result list to store the left side view
    result = []
    
    # Helper function for recursive DFS traversal (Root-Left-Right)
    def solve(node, depth):
        # Base case: if node is null, return
        if not node:
            return
        # If current depth equals length of result, add node val
        if depth == len(result):
            result.append(node.val)
        # Recurse on left subtree first to prioritize leftmost nodes
        solve(node.left, depth + 1)
        # Recurse on right subtree
        solve(node.right, depth + 1)
        
    # Start recursion from root at depth 0
    solve(root, 0)
    # Return left side view list
    return result

complexity.time: O(N)
complexity.space: O(H)

Symmetric Binary Tree.problemStatement: You are given the root of a binary tree and must decide whether the tree is a mirror image of itself about a vertical line drawn through the root. Concretely, reflecting the whole tree left-to-right has to reproduce exactly the same tree: the root's left subtree must be the mirror of its right subtree, which means the paired nodes hold equal values and the outermost child on one side corresponds to the outermost child on the other, all the way down. Return True when the tree has this property and False when it does not. An empty tree counts as symmetric, and so does a tree consisting of the root alone.
constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [1, 1000].
edgeCases: Single node tree (symmetric).
Left and right subtrees have identical values but mirror shapes mismatch.
Asymmetric structure but matching node values.
followUps: Could you solve it both recursively and iteratively?

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: "Symmetric" is defined as "looks the same when reflected", and the most literal way to check a definition is to carry it out. So actually construct the reflection: `cloneAndMirror` walks the tree and builds a brand-new node for every original one, but cross-wires the children, making the new node's left the mirror of the original's right and the new node's right the mirror of the original's left. Once that reflected copy exists, symmetry collapses into a question you already know how to answer — "are these two trees identical?" — handled by `isIdentical`, which walks both trees in lockstep and fails the moment one side runs out while the other has not, or two paired values disagree. The approach is correct and easy to trust, which is its real merit. What makes it brute force is the copy: you allocate an entire second tree, O(N) extra memory, purely to compare it against the original, when the mirrored comparison could have been made directly on the original pointers without building anything at all. Cost: O(N) time and O(N) space.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Define `cloneAndMirror(node)`, which returns None when `node` is falsy — a missing subtree mirrors into nothing — and otherwise creates a fresh `new_node = TreeNode(node.val)`.
2. Still inside `cloneAndMirror`, set `new_node.left = cloneAndMirror(node.right)` and `new_node.right = cloneAndMirror(node.left)`, then return `new_node`. The deliberate crossing of left and right is what performs the reflection, and because only new nodes are written, the original tree is never mutated.
3. Define `isIdentical(p, q)`: return True when both `p` and `q` are None (the two walks ran out together), return False when exactly one is None (the shapes disagree at this spot), otherwise return `p.val == q.val` combined with `isIdentical(p.left, q.left)` and `isIdentical(p.right, q.right)` — note these pairings are straight, not crossed, because the mirroring already happened during the clone.
4. In the main function, if `root` is None return True immediately, since an empty tree is trivially symmetric and there is nothing to reflect.
5. Otherwise build `mirrored_root = cloneAndMirror(root)`, which is the O(N) allocation this approach is judged on.
6. Return `isIdentical(root, mirrored_root)`: the tree is symmetric exactly when it is equal to its own reflection.
approaches.code:
def isSymmetric(root):                                        # symmetric = the tree reads the same reflected left<->right
    # Brute force: build a mirrored copy, then compare the two
    def cloneAndMirror(node):                                 # returns a fresh tree; the original is never modified
        if not node:                                          # a missing subtree mirrors into nothing
            return None
        new_node = TreeNode(node.val)                         # copy the value, then cross-wire the two children
        new_node.left = cloneAndMirror(node.right)            # the mirror trick: the right child becomes the left one
        new_node.right = cloneAndMirror(node.left)            # and symmetrically, the left child becomes the right one
        return new_node                                       # hand the finished mirrored subtree back to the parent
        
    # Structural equality: same shape AND same values throughout
    def isIdentical(p, q):                                    # walks both trees in lockstep, one node per side
        if not p and not q:                                   # both ran out together, so the shapes agree here
            return True
        if not p or not q:                                    # only one ran out: shapes differ, fail fast
            return False
        return p.val == q.val and isIdentical(p.left, q.left) and isIdentical(p.right, q.right)  # value must match and both child pairs must match too
        
    if not root:                                              # an empty tree is trivially symmetric
        return True
    mirrored_root = cloneAndMirror(root)                      # costs O(n) extra memory -- that is why this is brute force
    return isIdentical(root, mirrored_root)                   # symmetric exactly when the tree equals its own mirror

complexity.time: O(N)
complexity.space: O(N)

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: Building the reflection and then comparing it answers the question by re-enacting the definition, and it pays twice for that literalism: `cloneAndMirror` allocates a second tree of N nodes, and no comparison can begin until the last of them exists. A tree whose two root children already disagree is still cloned in full before the mismatch is noticed. The observation is that the copy is never consulted for anything except its shape, and its shape is fully determined by the original - the mirror's left child at any position is the original's right child at the matching position. So cross the arguments in the recursion instead of crossing the pointers in memory: `isMirror(t1.left, t2.right)` and `isMirror(t1.right, t2.left)`, outer child against outer child, inner against inner. Correctness is an induction on that pairing. The first call hands over `root.left` and `root.right`, which are mirrored positions by definition, and each crossed recursive call preserves the property, so every call really is comparing two nodes that reflection maps onto each other. Two Nones are mirrors; one None facing a node never is; anything else needs equal values plus both crossed pairs holding. Because `and` short-circuits, the first disagreement stops the descent instead of finishing the walk. Cost: O(N) in the worst case, O(H) for the recursion stack, and not one node allocated.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Define the helper `isMirror(t1, t2)`, which answers whether subtree `t1` is the reflection of subtree `t2`. Every call receives two nodes occupying mirrored positions, which is what makes comparing them directly meaningful.
2. Inside `isMirror`, return True when both `t1` and `t2` are None - two absent subtrees reflect each other, and this ends the recursion successfully.
3. Return False when exactly one of them is None: one side has a node where the other has a gap, and no reflection reconciles that.
4. Otherwise return `t1.val == t2.val and isMirror(t1.left, t2.right) and isMirror(t1.right, t2.left)`. The crossed pairings are the heart of it, and Python's `and` short-circuits on the first failure.
5. Back in `isSymmetric`, return True immediately when `root` is None, since an empty tree is symmetric.
6. Otherwise return `isMirror(root.left, root.right)`, comparing the two halves in place so that no copy of the tree is ever built and only the O(H) recursion stack is spent.

complexity.time: O(N)
complexity.space: O(H)

assert isSymmetric(build_tree([1, 2, 2, None, 3, 3, None])) == True

The mirror check compares nodes in crossed pairs: t1.left with t2.right, and t1.right with t2.left.
Both-null is True, exactly-one-null is False, and only then do you compare values — getting this null ordering right avoids AttributeError.
Structure counts as much as values: [1,2,2,null,3,null,3] has matching values but mismatched shape, so it is not symmetric.
An empty tree is symmetric by convention, and a single node is too.
The iterative version pushes pairs of nodes onto a queue/stack and pops two at a time; it is the same logic without recursion.

Root to Node Path.problemStatement: You are given the root of a binary tree and a target value, and you must report how to walk from the root down to the node holding that value. Return a list of integers containing the values of every node on that route, beginning with the root's value and ending with the target itself, with each step moving to a left or right child. Because there is exactly one route from the root to any node in a tree, the answer is unique when it exists. If no node in the tree holds the target value, return an empty list. Node values are assumed to be distinct, so the target identifies at most one node.
constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [1, 10^5].
edgeCases: Target node is the root itself.
Target node is not present in the tree (returns []).
Tree has duplicate values (returns first found path).
followUps: Can you write a variation of this to find the path between any two nodes in a binary tree?

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: The hard part for a newcomer is not finding the node — it is carrying the route back out of the recursion, because a plain DFS knows where it is but not how it got there. The blunt way around that is to stop trying to return anything and instead push the route downward: hand every recursive call the list of ancestor values collected so far, extend it with the current node, and record that as a complete candidate path. Copying the list with path + [node.val] at each node rather than mutating one shared list is what keeps the left and right branches from corrupting each other. Do that everywhere and you end up with all_paths, holding one root-to-node path for every node in the tree, after which answering the question is a trivial linear scan for the path whose last element equals the target. It is easy to trust, but it is wasteful twice over: there are N paths and each can be up to N long, so both the time and the memory are O(N^2), and it keeps exploring the whole tree even after walking straight past the target. The optimised version instead lets the recursion return true upward and pops nodes off a single shared list on the way back, which is O(N) time and O(H) space.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Run DFS starting from root.
2. Accumulate current path list, creating copies along the way.
3. Store all paths in a global list.
4. Search the global list for the path ending with target and return it. If none, return [].
approaches.code:
def solve(root, target):               # returns the chain of values from root down to target
    all_paths = []                     # brute force: collect EVERY root-to-node path first
    # DFS drags the path built so far down each branch
    def dfs(node, path):               # path holds the ancestors' values, root first
        if not node:                   # dead end, there is nothing to record here
            return
        curr_path = path + [node.val]  # copy on purpose, so siblings never share one list
        all_paths.append(curr_path)    # every node contributes exactly one candidate path
        dfs(node.left, curr_path)      # left branch extends this prefix independently
        dfs(node.right, curr_path)     # right branch extends the identical prefix
        
    dfs(root, [])                      # start at the root with an empty prefix above it
    # Now scan the collected paths for the one ending at target
    for p in all_paths:                # O(n) paths, each up to O(n) long -- the wasteful part
        if p[-1] == target:            # the last element is the node this path terminates at
            return p                   # first match wins; node values are assumed unique
    return []                          # target never appeared anywhere in the tree

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition:
Pushing `path + [node.val]` downward copies the ancestor list at every node, and keeps exploring after the target is found, since nothing stops it.

There is exactly one route from the root to any node, and the recursion's call stack is that route. One shared list, appended on the way in and popped on the way out, tracks it with no copies, and a boolean return propagates discovery straight up: the moment a child returns True, its parent does too, without popping.

The asymmetry is the whole proof. `path.pop()` sits only on the failure path, so a value left by a successful subtree stays; once the recursion unwinds, `result` holds exactly the nodes whose calls returned True -- root to target, in order. A failing call removes its own value first, restoring the list its caller handed over, so a sibling never inherits a dead branch. At every call entry, `path` holds the ancestors of `node` and nothing else.

O(N) worst case (an absent target visits everything), O(H) space for stack and path. `result` is returned unchecked, safe only because failures clean up after themselves.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Create `result = []`, the single list every recursive call will share.
2. Define `get_path(node, target_val, path)` returning a boolean meaning 'target found below here'.
3. If `node` is None, return False without touching `path`.
4. Append `node.val` to `path`.
5. If `node.val == target_val`, return True immediately, leaving the value on `path`.
6. Recurse left; if it returns True, return True at once and do not pop.
7. Recurse right; if it returns True, return True at once and do not pop.
8. Both failed: pop `node.val` back off `path` and return False.
9. Call `get_path(root, target, result)` and return `result`, which is empty when the target is absent.
approaches.code:
def solve(root, target):
    # Helper function to find path using backtracking
    def get_path(node, target_val, path):
        # Base case: if node is null, path does not exist
        if not node:
            return False
        # Add current node val to path list
        path.append(node.val)
        # If target node is found, return True
        if node.val == target_val:
            return True
        # Recurse on left subtree; if path found, return True
        if get_path(node.left, target_val, path):
            return True
        # Recurse on right subtree; if path found, return True
        if get_path(node.right, target_val, path):
            return True
        # Backtrack: remove current node val from path if not found in subtrees
        path.pop()
        # Return False indicating target is not in this path
        return False

    # List to store root to node path
    result = []
    # Call helper starting from root
    get_path(root, target, result)
    # Return path or empty list if target not found
    return result

complexity.time: O(N)
complexity.space: O(H)

Root to Node Path.tests:
assert solve(build_tree([1, 2, 3, None, None, 4, 5]), 4) == [1, 3, 4]
assert solve(build_tree([1, 2, 3, 4, 5]), 5) == [1, 2, 5]
# EDGE: target absent -> empty path, and backtracking must leave nothing behind
assert solve(build_tree([1, 2, 3]), 99) == []
# EDGE: empty tree
assert solve(None, 1) == []
assert solve(build_tree([1]), 1) == [1]
prerequisites: This is classic backtracking: append the node to the path on the way down, and pop it on the way back up if the target was not found below.
The recursive helper returns a boolean 'found' flag so the search can stop the moment the target is located.
Because a binary tree has exactly one path from the root to any node, the first successful path is THE answer.
Forgetting the path.pop() is the classic bug: the returned list then contains dead-end nodes from failed branches.
Passing one shared list (instead of copying path + [val] at every call) keeps the space at O(h) instead of O(n * h).
If the target does not exist, the recursion unwinds completely and the shared list ends up empty, which is exactly the required output.

Lowest Common Ancestor in Binary Tree.problemStatement: Given a binary tree, find the lowest common ancestor (LCA) of two given nodes in the tree. According to the definition of LCA on Wikipedia: The lowest common ancestor is defined between two nodes p and q as the lowest node in T that has both p and q as descendants (where we allow a node to be a descendant of itself).

examples.explanation: The LCA of nodes 5 and 1 is 3.
The LCA of nodes 5 and 4 is 5, since a node can be a descendant of itself.

constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [2, 10^5].
p and q will exist in the tree.
edgeCases: p or q is the root itself.
p is the parent of q (LCA should be p).
p and q are at the opposite extreme bottom ends of the tree.
followUps: Can you solve this if the binary tree nodes have parent pointers?

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: The definition suggests an obvious but wasteful plan: for every node in the tree, search its subtree for p and search it again for q, and among all the nodes where both searches succeed keep the deepest one. That is a full subtree scan per node, so it lands at O(N^2). The observation that keeps things linear is to stop thinking downwards and think upwards instead. The ancestors of any node form a single chain running from the root down to it, and two such chains must both start at the root, agree for a while, and then split apart at the point where p and q live in different subtrees. The last node they still agree on is by definition the deepest node with both p and q beneath it, which is exactly the LCA. So the job becomes: produce the root-to-p chain and the root-to-q chain explicitly, then compare them position by position. Building a chain needs backtracking, since you append a node optimistically and pop it again when neither subtree turns out to contain the target. This costs two O(N) traversals plus O(H) for the recursion and the stored paths. It is still linear, but it is unsatisfying next to the single-pass version because it walks the tree twice and materialises both paths in memory purely to compare their shared prefix.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Define the helper `get_path(node, target, path)` which returns True when target lies in this subtree and, when it does, leaves `path` holding the full root-to-target chain. If `node` is None, return False immediately.
2. Append `node` to `path`, optimistically assuming target sits somewhere inside this subtree, and return True at once if `node == target`.
3. Otherwise recurse with `get_path(node.left, target, path) or get_path(node.right, target, path)`; the `or` short-circuits on the first hit, and returning True here keeps `node` on the path as a genuine ancestor.
4. If neither child found the target, `path.pop()` to undo the optimistic append and return False. The invariant is that whenever the helper returns False, `path` is left exactly as the caller handed it over.
5. Create two empty lists `path_p` and `path_q` and fill them with `get_path(root, p, path_p)` and `get_path(root, q, path_q)`, two independent O(N) walks both beginning at the root.
6. Set `lca = None`, then iterate `zip(path_p, path_q)`, which automatically stops at the shorter chain.
7. While the paired nodes are equal you are still inside the shared prefix, so overwrite `lca = node_p`; the moment they differ, `break`, because the chains have split.
8. Return `lca`, the deepest node common to both chains, or None if either target was never found.
approaches.code:
def lowestCommonAncestor(root, p, q):                         # LCA = deepest node that has both p and q beneath it
    # Step 1: record the exact root-to-target chain for each
    def get_path(node, target, path):                         # path is filled in place; True means target lies below
        if not node:                                          # ran off the tree, so this branch cannot hold target
            return False
        path.append(node)                                     # tentatively assume target sits inside this subtree
        if node == target:                                    # found it: path now holds root..target inclusive
            return True
        if get_path(node.left, target, path) or get_path(node.right, target, path):  # try left, then right; short-circuits on the first hit
            return True                                       # a child found it, so this node stays on the path
        path.pop()                                            # backtrack: wrong turn, undo the tentative append
        return False                                          # tell the caller this subtree does not contain target
        
    path_p, path_q = [], []                                   # two independent chains, both beginning at the root
    get_path(root, p, path_p)                                 # one O(n) walk to fill p's ancestor chain
    get_path(root, q, path_q)                                 # a second O(n) walk for q's chain
    
    # Step 2: walk both chains while they still agree
    lca = None                                                # deepest common node found so far
    for node_p, node_q in zip(path_p, path_q):                # zip stops automatically at the shorter chain
        if node_p == node_q:                                  # still inside the shared prefix from the root
            lca = node_p                                      # keep overwriting; the final match is the deepest one
        else:
            break                                             # first divergence: the two paths split here, stop
    return lca                                                # the deepest shared ancestor, or None if a target is absent

complexity.time: O(N)
complexity.space: O(H)

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition:
Read literally, the definition gives: for every node, search its subtree for p, search again for q, keep the deepest where both succeed. That is a full subtree scan per node - O(N^2), re-examining each node once per ancestor.

The observation: one post-order pass - children resolved before the parent acts - reports upward instead. Each call returns whichever target it found below, and a node hearing back from BOTH children has p on one side, q on the other. No node below holds both, so it is the LCA.

Why the wrong ancestor is never returned: a call returns "p, q, or their LCA - whichever exists in this subtree", so with one target below it sends that target up as a marker. Children finish before the parent inspects them, so the deepest node seeing both markers reports `root`, and ancestors above pass that value through untouched. The `root == p` early return handles p being an ancestor of q, which the definition allows: a node is its own descendant.

Cost: one traversal, O(N) time, O(H) stack. The trade is a precondition: both p and q must be present, or it returns the one it found.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Base case: if `root` is None, return None; if `root` is p or q, return `root` - a found target propagates upward as a marker, and searching below it is unnecessary.
2. Recurse into the left subtree: `left = lowestCommonAncestor(root.left, p, q)`.
3. Recurse into the right subtree: `right = lowestCommonAncestor(root.right, p, q)`.
4. If both `left` and `right` are non-null, the two targets sit on opposite sides of this node, so return `root` as the lowest common ancestor.
5. Otherwise return whichever of `left` or `right` is non-null (or None if neither is), forwarding the single marker up to the caller.
6. The value the top-level call returns is the LCA.
approaches.code:
def lowestCommonAncestor(root, p, q):
    # Base case: if root is null or matches either target node p or q
    if not root or root == p or root == q:
        # Return current node (propagates match upwards)
        return root
    # Recurse on left subtree
    left = lowestCommonAncestor(root.left, p, q)
    # Recurse on right subtree
    right = lowestCommonAncestor(root.right, p, q)
    # If both left and right are non-null, current node is LCA
    if left and right:
        return root
    # Otherwise return whichever subtree search returned non-null
    return left if left else right

complexity.time: O(N)
complexity.space: O(H)

Lowest Common Ancestor in Binary Tree.tests:
def _find(node, v):
    if not node:
        return None
    if node.val == v:
        return node
    return _find(node.left, v) or _find(node.right, v)

root = build_tree([3, 5, 1, 6, 2, 0, 8, None, None, 7, 4])
assert lowestCommonAncestor(root, _find(root, 5), _find(root, 1)).val == 3
# EDGE: a node can be its own ancestor -> LCA(5, 4) is 5
assert lowestCommonAncestor(root, _find(root, 5), _find(root, 4)).val == 5
assert lowestCommonAncestor(root, _find(root, 7), _find(root, 4)).val == 2
# EDGE: single-node tree where p == q == root
one = build_tree([1])
assert lowestCommonAncestor(one, one, one).val == 1
prerequisites: There is no BST ordering to exploit here, so you cannot compare values to choose a side — you must search both subtrees.
The recursion is post-order: it asks each side 'did you find p or q?' and combines the two answers at the current node.
Base case: a null node returns None, and a node equal to p or q returns itself, which encodes 'a node can be its own ancestor'.
If both recursive calls come back non-null, the current node is the split point and therefore the LCA; otherwise you propagate the single non-null result upward.
p and q are NODE references, so comparisons use object identity, not values — this matters when values repeat.
The algorithm assumes both nodes actually exist in the tree; otherwise it returns the one node it found, which is a good follow-up discussion.

Maximum Width of Binary Tree.title: Maximum Width of Binary Tree
Maximum Width of Binary Tree.problemStatement:
Given the root of a binary tree, return the maximum width of the given tree.

The maximum width of a tree is the maximum width among all levels.

The width of one level is defined as the length between the end-nodes (the leftmost and rightmost non-null nodes in the level, where the null nodes between the end-nodes that would be present in a complete binary tree extending down to that level are also counted into the width calculation).

It is guaranteed that the answer will fit in a 32-bit signed integer.

examples.explanation: The maximum width exists in the third level with width 4 (5, 3, null, 9).
The maximum width exists in the fourth level with width 7 (6, null, null, null, null, null, 7).

constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [1, 3000].
edgeCases: Empty tree (returns 0).
Single node tree (returns 1).
Skewed tree (width remains 1 at each level).
followUps: Can you solve this without using a queue?
How would you handle integer overflow if the tree depth is very large (e.g. depth > 64)?

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: Perform a level order traversal (BFS) where we keep all nodes, including None, in the level list. For each level, we strip the None nodes from both ends and the length of the remaining list is the width of that level. We stop when the list contains only None nodes.
approaches.algorithm:
1. If root is None, return 0.
2. Store the nodes of the current level in a list, starting with root.
3. Loop while there is at least one non-None node in the current level list.
4. Find the first non-None node from the left and the first non-None node from the right.
5. Calculate the width as right_idx - left_idx + 1 and update max_width.
6. Generate the next level list by appending left and right children (including None) of all nodes between left_idx and right_idx.
7. Repeat until no more non-None nodes are left.
8. Return max_width.
approaches.code:
def widthOfBinaryTree(root):
    # If root is None, width is 0
    if not root:
        return 0
    # Store the nodes of the current level, starting with root
    current_level = [root]
    # Keep track of the maximum width
    max_width = 0
    # Continue as long as there are nodes to process
    while any(node is not None for node in current_level):
        # Find the first non-None node index from left
        left = 0
        while left < len(current_level) and current_level[left] is None:
            left += 1
        # Find the first non-None node index from right
        right = len(current_level) - 1
        while right >= 0 and current_level[right] is None:
            right -= 1
        # Calculate width of current level
        level_width = right - left + 1
        # Update maximum width
        max_width = max(max_width, level_width)
        # Generate next level including None nodes
        next_level = []
        for i in range(left, right + 1):
            node = current_level[i]
            if node:
                next_level.append(node.left)
                next_level.append(node.right)
            else:
                next_level.append(None)
                next_level.append(None)
        # Update current level
        current_level = next_level
    # Return the maximum width found
    return max_width

complexity.time: O(2^H) in the worst case where H is tree height
complexity.space: O(2^H) to store the level nodes

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition:
Keeping the None placeholders in each level list allocates a slot for every position a complete tree would hold: a level with two real nodes at its edges still materialises 2^d entries, memory exponential in depth while the tree is tiny.

A position can be named without being stored. Number nodes as a binary heap does - root 0, children of i at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2 - and the gaps acquire numbers for free: a level whose nodes carry indices 3 and 6 has width 6 - 3 + 1 = 4, the phantom slots never allocated.

Heap numbering is exactly what 'as if the tree were complete down to this level' means, so the gap counts real nodes plus the nulls between them. `cur_id = idx - min_idx` subtracts one constant from every node on a level, leaving within-level differences untouched, and children are numbered off the normalised parent - width identical, 2^d blowup blocked. The queue holds each level left to right, so i == 0 and i == size - 1 are the end nodes.

Space falls from exponential to O(W). Each node is enqueued and dequeued once, though `queue.pop(0)` on a list shifts the rest - `collections.deque` makes the stated O(N) literal.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Return 0 when root is None; otherwise set `max_width = 0` and seed the queue with (root, 0).
2. While the queue is non-empty, record `size = len(queue)` (the node count on this level) and `min_idx = queue[0][1]` (the index of its leftmost node).
3. Loop i from 0 to size - 1, popping (node, idx) off the front and computing the normalised index `cur_id = idx - min_idx`.
4. Store `first = cur_id` when i == 0 and `last = cur_id` when i == size - 1, capturing the level's two end nodes.
5. Append the left child as (node.left, 2 * cur_id + 1) and the right child as (node.right, 2 * cur_id + 2), numbering from the normalised parent so indices cannot blow up.
6. After the level is drained, set `max_width = max(max_width, last - first + 1)`.
7. Return `max_width` once the queue empties.
approaches.code:
def widthOfBinaryTree(root):
    # If root is None, width is 0
    if not root:
        return 0
    # Initialize maximum width to 0
    max_width = 0
    # Queue stores pairs of (node, index)
    queue = [(root, 0)]
    # Loop until queue is empty
    while queue:
        # Number of nodes at current level
        size = len(queue)
        # Index of first node in current level
        min_idx = queue[0][1]
        # Variables to track first and last index of level
        first, last = 0, 0
        # Iterate over all nodes in the current level
        for i in range(size):
            # Pop node and index from queue
            node, idx = queue.pop(0)
            # Normalize index to prevent overflow
            cur_id = idx - min_idx
            # If it is the first node of the level
            if i == 0:
                first = cur_id
            # If it is the last node of the level
            if i == size - 1:
                last = cur_id
            # If left child exists, push with index 2 * cur_id + 1
            if node.left:
                queue.append((node.left, 2 * cur_id + 1))
            # If right child exists, push with index 2 * cur_id + 2
            if node.right:
                queue.append((node.right, 2 * cur_id + 2))
        # Update maximum width
        max_width = max(max_width, last - first + 1)
    # Return the maximum width found
    return max_width

complexity.time: O(N) where N is the total number of nodes
complexity.space: O(W) where W is the maximum width of the tree

Maximum Width of Binary Tree.tests:
assert widthOfBinaryTree(build_tree([1, 3, 2, 5, 3, None, 9])) == 4
# EDGE: nulls between the end nodes still count -> width 7 on the last level
assert widthOfBinaryTree(build_tree([1, 3, 2, 5, None, None, 9, 6, None, 7])) == 7
assert widthOfBinaryTree(build_tree([1])) == 1
# EDGE: empty tree has width 0
assert widthOfBinaryTree(None) == 0
prerequisites: Give every node an array-style heap index: root = 0, left child = 2*i + 1, right child = 2*i + 2, as if the tree were stored in a complete array.
The width of a level is last_index - first_index + 1, which automatically counts the nulls sitting between the two end nodes.
Indices double every level, so on deep trees you must subtract the level's minimum index (rebasing) to keep the numbers small.
BFS with (node, index) pairs, processing exactly len(queue) nodes per level, is the standard shape of this solution.
Only non-null children are pushed; the missing ones are represented purely by the gaps in the index numbering.
An empty tree has width 0, and a single node has width 1.

Children Sum Property.title: Children Sum Property
Children Sum Property.problemStatement:
Given a binary tree, write a program to convert it so that it satisfies the Children Sum Property.

The property is: for every node, the data value must be equal to sum of data values in left and right children. If both left and right children are NULL, then the node value can be anything. You can only increment node values (cannot decrement).
edgeCases: Leaf node (no changes needed).
Already satisfying children sum property.
Root value is already much larger than children sum.
followUps: How can you check if a binary tree satisfies the children sum property in O(N) time and O(1) space?

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: Forget clever ordering for a moment and just be stubborn about it. Walk over every node of the tree and repair whatever is wrong right there: if a parent is smaller than the sum of its children, raise the parent to that sum; if the parent is larger, we are not allowed to shrink it, so we raise the children up to the parent's value instead. One repair can easily break a node we already looked at, because changing a child changes its parent's required sum. So we simply do the whole sweep again, and again, until a complete pass over the tree finds nothing left to fix. That 'repeat until nothing changes' idea is called reaching a fixed point, and it is the honest beginner solution: obviously correct, but wasteful, because most nodes are re-checked many times for nothing.
approaches.algorithm:
1. If the tree is empty, there is nothing to convert, so return immediately.
2. Collect every node of the tree once into a list using an iterative pre-order walk, so each later sweep is just a for-loop over that list.
3. Start a sweep: for every non-leaf node, compute child_sum, the total of the children that actually exist (a missing child contributes 0). Leaves are skipped because a leaf may hold any value.
4. If node.val is less than child_sum, raise node.val to child_sum; if node.val is greater than child_sum, copy node.val down into every existing child. Either way, remember that something changed.
5. If the sweep changed anything at all, run another full sweep, because a repair at one node may have broken its parent or its children.
6. When a whole sweep passes with no change, every non-leaf equals its children sum, no value was ever decreased, and the tree is done.
approaches.code:
def changeTree(root):
    # BRUTE FORCE IDEA: keep sweeping the whole tree and repair every violation
    # we meet, until one complete sweep finds nothing left to repair.
    if not root:
        return  # empty tree: nothing to convert, mutating helpers return None
    # ---- Step 1: list every node once so each sweep is a simple for-loop ----
    nodes = []          # will hold every node of the tree in preorder
    stack = [root]      # explicit stack keeps us safe on very deep trees
    while stack:        # classic iterative preorder walk
        node = stack.pop()          # take the next node to visit
        nodes.append(node)          # remember it for the repair sweeps below
        if node.right:              # push right first ...
            stack.append(node.right)
        if node.left:               # ... so the left child is popped first
            stack.append(node.left)
    # ---- Step 2: sweep again and again until the tree stops changing ----
    changed = True      # force at least one sweep to happen
    while changed:      # a "fixed point" loop: repeat until stable
        changed = False             # assume this sweep will find nothing
        for node in nodes:          # re-check EVERY node on EVERY sweep
            if not node.left and not node.right:
                continue            # leaves are free: any value is allowed
            child_sum = 0           # sum of the children that actually exist
            if node.left:
                child_sum += node.left.val      # left child contributes
            if node.right:
                child_sum += node.right.val     # right child contributes
            if node.val < child_sum:
                # parent is too small: raising the parent is a legal increment
                node.val = child_sum
                changed = True      # tree changed -> we must sweep again
            elif node.val > child_sum:
                # parent is too big: we may not shrink it, so raise the children
                if node.left:
                    node.left.val = node.val    # copy parent value down-left
                if node.right:
                    node.right.val = node.val   # copy parent value down-right
                changed = True      # tree changed -> we must sweep again
    # the tree was fixed in place, so there is nothing to return

complexity.time: O(N * H) in practice — every sweep touches all N nodes, and a change has to ripple at most one level per sweep, so the number of sweeps grows with the height H (worst case O(N^2) on a skewed tree)
complexity.space: O(N) — we materialise a list holding every node plus the explicit traversal stack

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: The brute force sweeps the whole tree fixing whatever is broken, then sweeps again because each fix breaks the node above it, and keeps going until a full pass changes nothing - O(N) per pass with the number of passes growing with the tree's height. The waste is re-visiting settled nodes to propagate a change that could have been anticipated. The observation is that the two repairs belong at two different moments of a SINGLE traversal. On the way down (pre-order), if a parent exceeds its children's sum, push the parent's value into both children - that raises them, and raising is the only legal move. On the way back up (post-order), overwrite the parent with the sum its children actually finished with. Pushing the parent's full value into both children deliberately overshoots, giving a child sum of 2 x parent, and the post-order write then lifts the parent to that larger figure, which is still an increase. Why one pass suffices: after the downward push, each child is already at least as large as its parent needs, and recursion can only grow it further, so the post-order write records a sum that nothing above will disturb - no ancestor touches a subtree after that subtree has returned. Cost: O(N) time, one visit per node, and O(H) recursion stack. One assumption is load-bearing: node values are non-negative, otherwise a child could sit above the children-sum and the downward push would decrease it.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Return immediately if root is None. Return also if root is a leaf (no left and no right child) - the property places no constraint on leaves, and a leaf is the value the whole subtree is anchored to.
2. Compute child_sum by adding root.left.val and root.right.val, guarding each with an existence check so a missing child contributes 0.
3. If root.val > child_sum, the parent is too big and may not be shrunk, so assign root.val into EVERY child that exists. This raises the children (the legal direction) and intentionally overshoots when both children exist.
4. If root.val <= child_sum, change nothing on the way down - the post-order step will raise the parent instead.
5. Recurse into root.left and then root.right, so both subtrees are fully repaired before the parent is finalised.
6. Post-order, recompute tot_sum from the children's FINAL values (they may have grown during the recursion) and assign root.val = tot_sum, which makes this node satisfy the property permanently.
approaches.code:
def changeTree(root):  # convert the tree in place so every parent = sum of children
    # Base case: if root is None, return
    if not root:  # nothing to fix in an empty subtree
        return  # this function mutates the tree, so it returns None
    # Base case: if it is a leaf node, return
    if not root.left and not root.right:  # a leaf may keep any value it likes
        return  # so there is nothing to enforce here
    # Calculate sum of children
    child_sum = 0  # running total of the children that actually exist
    if root.left:  # a missing child simply contributes nothing
        child_sum += root.left.val  # add the left child value
    if root.right:  # same check on the right side
        child_sum += root.right.val  # add the right child value
    # If parent's value is greater than sum of children
    if root.val > child_sum:  # we may not shrink the parent, so lift the children
        if root.left:  # push the parent value down-left ...
            root.left.val = root.val  # ... which is always an increment
        if root.right:  # push the parent value down-right ...
            root.right.val = root.val  # ... also an increment
    # Recurse on left and right subtrees
    changeTree(root.left)  # fix the whole left subtree first
    changeTree(root.right)  # then the whole right subtree
    # Post-order update of parent value
    tot_sum = 0  # recompute the children sum AFTER they were fixed
    if root.left:  # left child may have grown during the recursion
        tot_sum += root.left.val  # so read its final value now
    if root.right:  # same for the right child
        tot_sum += root.right.val  # read its final value too
    # Update parent value
    root.val = tot_sum  # parent now equals the true children sum

complexity.time: O(N)
complexity.space: O(H) recursion stack space

Children Sum Property.tests:
def _holds(node):
    # every non-leaf must equal the sum of its existing children
    if not node or (not node.left and not node.right):
        return True
    s = (node.left.val if node.left else 0) + (node.right.val if node.right else 0)
    return node.val == s and _holds(node.left) and _holds(node.right)

def _vals(node, out):
    if node:
        out.append(node.val)
        _vals(node.left, out)
        _vals(node.right, out)
    return out

root = build_tree([50, 7, 2, 3, 5, 1, 30])
before = _vals(root, [])
changeTree(root)
after = _vals(root, [])
assert _holds(root) is True
# only increments are allowed: no node may have shrunk
assert all(a >= b for a, b in zip(after, before))
# a tree that already satisfies the property must stay valid and keep its root value
ok = build_tree([10, 4, 6])
changeTree(ok)
assert _holds(ok) is True and ok.val == 10
# EDGE: single leaf keeps its value; empty tree must not crash
leaf = build_tree([5])
changeTree(leaf)
assert leaf.val == 5
assert changeTree(None) is None
prerequisites: The property: for every non-leaf node, node.val must equal the sum of the values of its existing children; leaves may hold any value.
The hard constraint is that you may only INCREASE values, never decrease them, which rules out simply writing the smaller number down.
Two directions are needed: if the parent is bigger, push the parent's value down into the children; if it is smaller, pull the children's sum up into the parent.
The clean solution is a single traversal with a pre-order push-down and a post-order sum-up, so each node is repaired exactly once.
The post-order step must read the children AFTER their subtrees were fixed, which is why the parent update comes after both recursive calls.
The function mutates the tree in place and returns None, so tests must inspect the tree afterwards rather than a return value.

Nodes at Distance K.title: Nodes at Distance K
Nodes at Distance K.problemStatement: Given the root of a binary tree, the value of a target node target, and an integer k, return an array of the values of all nodes that have a distance k from the target node. You can return the answer in any order.

examples.explanation: The nodes that are a distance 2 from the target node (with value 5) have values 7, 4, and 1.

constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [1, 500].
All the values Node.val are unique.
target is the value of one of the nodes in the tree.
edgeCases: k = 0 (returns [target]).
target is the root.
No nodes at distance k (returns []).
followUps: Can you solve this using a single DFS traversal without building parent pointers?

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: Convert the binary tree to an undirected graph (adjacency list representation). Then, perform a Breadth-First Search (BFS) or Depth-First Search (DFS) on this graph starting from the target node up to depth k.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Build an adjacency list of the graph by traversing the tree recursively.
2. Start BFS from target node with distance 0.
3. Track visited nodes to avoid visiting parents again.
4. When distance equals k, collect all values in the queue and return.
approaches.code:
def distanceK(root, target, k):                  # all nodes exactly k edges from target, in any direction
