    def inorder(node):  # nested so it can append into vals directly
        if not node:  # a missing child contributes nothing to the list
            return  # unwind back to the parent call
        inorder(node.left)  # every left value is smaller, so visit those first
        vals.append(node.val)  # the node sits between its two subtrees when sorted
        inorder(node.right)  # the right subtree holds all the larger values
    # O(n) work; this ignores the BST search shortcut
    inorder(root)  # after this line vals is sorted ascending
    # scan the sorted list for the last value <= key
    floor_val = -1  # -1 is the sentinel for 'no value <= key exists'
    for val in vals:  # ascending order means a later hit is always better
        if val <= key:  # still a valid candidate for the floor
            floor_val = val  # overwrite: this one is closer to key than the last
        else:  # first value above key, so nothing after can qualify
            break  # this early exit only works because vals is sorted
    # the sentinel survives if every value exceeded key
    return floor_val  # largest value that did not go past key

complexity.time: O(N)
complexity.space: O(N) to store tree nodes

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition:
The traversal attempt flattens the tree with a full inorder walk, then scans the list for the last value not exceeding the key. It visits all N nodes and allocates N values, even when the answer sits two steps below the root.

The observation: at a node holding v, one comparison with `key` disqualifies a whole subtree. If key < v, then v and its entire right subtree exceed the key, so the answer lies left. If v <= key, v is a candidate beating everything on its left, all smaller - record it and go right for something closer. For key = 14 at node 10: 10 qualifies, but a 12 may wait right.

Why the discarded subtree never held the answer: a move drops a subtree only after proving nothing inside beats what is recorded - the right because every value there exceeds the key, the left because the current node beats all of it while staying under the key. `floor` is only ever overwritten by a larger value still at most the key.

Cost: one root-to-leaf path: O(H) time (O(log N) balanced, O(N) degenerate), O(1) space. The trade is the -1 sentinel, indistinguishable from a real -1 in the tree.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Set `floor = -1` (the "no valid value found" sentinel) and `curr = root`.
2. While `curr` is not None, compare `curr.val` with `key`.
3. If `curr.val == key`, the key is present and is itself the greatest value not exceeding it: return `curr.val`.
4. If `key < curr.val`, this node and its whole right subtree are too large, so move left with `curr = curr.left`, leaving `floor` unchanged.
5. Otherwise `curr.val < key`, making it a valid candidate better than anything on its left: set `floor = curr.val` and move right with `curr = curr.right`.
6. When the walk falls off the tree, return `floor`.
approaches.code:
def findFloor(root, key):
    # Initialize floor value to -1
    floor = -1
    # Pointer to traverse the BST
    curr = root
    # Loop until we reach a leaf node
    while curr:
        # If node value equals key, it is the floor
        if curr.val == key:
            return curr.val
        # If key is smaller, floor must be in left subtree
        elif key < curr.val:
            curr = curr.left
        # If key is larger, current node is a candidate floor
        else:
            floor = curr.val
            # Move to right subtree to search for a larger candidate
            curr = curr.right
    # Return the floor value
    return floor

complexity.time: O(H) where H is the height of the BST
complexity.space: O(1) auxiliary space

Floor in BST.tests:
#            8
#          /   \
#         4     12
#        / \   /  \
#       2   6 10   14
root = build_tree([8, 4, 12, 2, 6, 10, 14])
# 5 is absent: the greatest value <= 5 is 4.
assert findFloor(root, 5) == 4
# An exact match returns the key itself.
assert findFloor(root, 12) == 12
# A key above everything returns the maximum of the tree.
assert findFloor(root, 100) == 14
# EDGE: nothing is <= 1, so there is no floor -> -1.
assert findFloor(root, 1) == -1
# EDGE: an empty tree has no floor either.
assert findFloor(None, 5) == -1
prerequisites: BST ordering invariant: every value in the left subtree is smaller than the node and every value in the right subtree is larger — this is what lets you discard half the tree at each step.
Floor(key) = the largest value <= key. When you stand on a node smaller than the key it is a VALID candidate, so record it before moving right to look for a bigger one.
When the node is larger than the key it can never be the floor, so move left without recording anything.
An exact match is the best possible answer and lets you return immediately.
Keep a `floor` answer variable initialised to -1 (the 'not found' sentinel) — the loop may end without ever finding a candidate, e.g. when the key is below the minimum.
The iterative walk is O(h) time and O(1) space: O(log n) on a balanced BST but O(n) on a fully skewed one.

Ceil in BST.title: Ceil in BST
Ceil in BST.problemStatement:
Given a Binary Search Tree (BST) and a key, find the ceil of the key in BST.

The ceil value is the smallest value in the BST that is greater than or equal to the key. If no such value exists, return -1.

examples.explanation: The smallest value in BST which is >= 5 is 8.

edgeCases: Key is larger than the largest element in BST (returns -1).
Key exists in BST (returns key).
Empty BST.
followUps: How would you perform ceil if the keys in the BST are floating-point numbers?

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: When you are not yet comfortable exploiting the BST property, the safe move is to stop treating the structure as special and just look at every value. That is what this does, with one helpful twist: an inorder traversal of a binary search tree, visiting left subtree then node then right subtree, emits the values already sorted ascending. So the recursion turns the whole tree into a sorted list `vals` without you having to call sort at all. Once the data is ascending, the ceil is easy to characterise: the first value you meet that is greater than or equal to key is automatically the smallest such value, because everything after it in the list is at least as large. That is why the loop records the hit and breaks immediately rather than continuing to overwrite, which is exactly the opposite of how a floor search behaves. If the scan finishes with no value reaching key, the sentinel `ceil_val = -1` survives and is returned, covering the case where key is larger than every element. The reason this is unsatisfying is that it visits all N nodes and stores all N values, throwing away the very ordering property that would let a comparison at each node discard an entire half of the tree and reach the answer in O(H) steps with O(1) memory. Cost here is O(N) time and O(N) space.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Do inorder traversal, saving node values to a list `vals`.
2. Initialize ceil_val = -1.
3. Loop through `vals`. If val >= key, update ceil_val = val and break.
4. Return ceil_val.
approaches.code:
def findCeil(root, key):  # ceil = the smallest value in the tree that is >= key
    # inorder traversal of a BST comes out sorted ascending
    vals = []  # collect the values so we can scan them in order
    # left, node, right is the sorted visiting order
    def inorder(node):  # closure appends into vals from the outer scope
        if not node:  # an empty subtree ends this branch of the recursion
            return  # hand control back to the parent call
        inorder(node.left)  # smaller values must be recorded before this node
        vals.append(node.val)  # the node's value belongs between its two subtrees
        inorder(node.right)  # larger values get appended after this node
    # O(n) pass; BST ordering is only used for sorting here
    inorder(root)  # vals is now sorted ascending and ready to scan
    # the first value >= key in a sorted list is the ceil
    ceil_val = -1  # sentinel meaning 'no value >= key was found'
    for val in vals:  # ascending scan, so the first hit is the smallest one
        if val >= key:  # the earliest qualifying value is already the answer
            ceil_val = val  # record it; nothing later can be any smaller
            break  # stop at once, unlike floor which keeps overwriting
    # -1 survives when key is bigger than everything
    return ceil_val  # smallest value that was not below key

complexity.time: O(N)
complexity.space: O(N)

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition:
Flattening the tree with an inorder traversal and scanning for the first value at or above key reads all N nodes and stores all N values, though the tree was already arranged so most could be dismissed unseen.

One comparison disqualifies a whole subtree. If v < key then v and its entire left subtree are below key, so all of it goes in a single test - move right. If v > key then v is a legal answer, and anything better must be smaller than v yet still at or above key, which by the ordering lives only in v's left subtree - record v and move left. With root 8 and key 6, 8 is banked and everything above it is dropped at once.

Overwriting `ceil` never loses the answer: it is assigned only where `curr.val > key`, so it always holds a qualifying value, and its replacement always comes from the previous candidate's left subtree - strictly smaller, still at or above key. Every skipped subtree is provably below key or above a candidate already banked.

O(H) time - O(log N) balanced, O(N) on a chain - and O(1) space, being a loop with no recursion stack. Ending with ceil still -1 means every value was below key.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Set `ceil = -1` as the answer-so-far and `curr = root`.
2. While `curr` is not None, compare `curr.val` with key.
3. If `curr.val == key`, return `curr.val` at once - no value can beat an exact match.
4. If `key > curr.val`, the node and its whole left subtree are below key, so move right with `curr = curr.right` and leave `ceil` untouched.
5. Otherwise `curr.val > key`, making it a valid candidate: set `ceil = curr.val`, then move left with `curr = curr.left` to look for a smaller value that still clears key.
6. When the walk falls off the tree, return `ceil`, which stays -1 if no node ever cleared key.
approaches.code:
def findCeil(root, key):
    # Initialize ceil value to -1
    ceil = -1
    # Pointer to traverse the BST
    curr = root
    # Loop until we reach a leaf node
    while curr:
        # If node value equals key, it is the ceil
        if curr.val == key:
            return curr.val
        # If key is larger, ceil must be in right subtree
        elif key > curr.val:
            curr = curr.right
        # If key is smaller, current node is a candidate ceil
        else:
            ceil = curr.val
            # Move to left subtree to search for a smaller candidate
            curr = curr.left
    # Return the ceil value
    return ceil

complexity.time: O(H) where H is BST height
complexity.space: O(1) auxiliary space

Ceil in BST.tests:
#            8
#          /   \
#         4     12
#        / \   /  \
#       2   6 10   14
root = build_tree([8, 4, 12, 2, 6, 10, 14])
# 5 is absent: the smallest value >= 5 is 6.
assert findCeil(root, 5) == 6
# An exact match returns the key itself.
assert findCeil(root, 4) == 4
# A key below everything returns the minimum of the tree.
assert findCeil(root, 0) == 2
# EDGE: nothing is >= 15, so there is no ceil -> -1.
assert findCeil(root, 15) == -1
# EDGE: an empty tree has no ceil either.
assert findCeil(None, 5) == -1
prerequisites: Ceil(key) = the smallest value >= key. It is the exact mirror of Floor, so the only differences are the comparison direction and which child you walk to.
When the current node is >= key it is a valid candidate: record it, then move LEFT to try to find something even smaller that still qualifies.
When the current node is < key it can never be the ceil, so move right without recording.
Initialise the answer to -1 so that a key larger than every value in the tree correctly reports 'no ceil'.
An exact hit (`curr.val == key`) is optimal and can return immediately — nothing smaller can still be >= key.
Time is O(h) with O(1) extra space; collecting a full inorder list first would cost O(n) time and O(n) space.

Insert Node in BST.title: Insert Node in BST
Insert Node in BST.problemStatement: Given the root of a binary search tree and a value to insert, insert the value into the BST and return the root of the modified BST. It is guaranteed that the new value does not exist in the original BST.
constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [0, 10^4].
val does not exist in the BST.
edgeCases: Empty BST (returns TreeNode(val)).
Inserting as a left child of a leaf node.
Inserting as a right child of a leaf node.
followUps: Can you insert a node into BST recursively in O(H) space?
Can we keep the BST balanced after insertions?

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: The first question is where a new value is even allowed to go, and in a BST that is not a choice. Every node's left subtree holds only smaller keys and its right subtree only larger ones, so comparing val with root.val eliminates one entire subtree in a single step, and repeating that comparison walks one root-to-leaf path ending at the unique empty slot where val preserves the ordering. That is why the code ever recurses into only one child. The neat part is how the new node gets attached. Rather than tracking a parent pointer, the recursion returns the possibly-new subtree root and the caller writes it straight back with root.left = insertIntoBST(root.left, val). When the walk runs off the bottom of the tree, `if not root` fires and returns TreeNode(val), and that return value lands in exactly the child slot that was None, so the link is made with no special-case code. Every untouched node just returns itself, leaving the rest of the tree unchanged. The cost is O(H) comparisons, which is O(log N) on a balanced tree and O(N) on a degenerate one. It is labelled brute force here only because the recursion holds O(H) frames on the call stack, which an iterative walk with a running pointer avoids at O(1) space.
approaches.algorithm:
1. If root is None, return a new TreeNode with val.
2. If val < root.val, recursively set root.left = insertIntoBST(root.left, val).
3. Else, recursively set root.right = insertIntoBST(root.right, val).
4. Return root.
approaches.code:
def insertIntoBST(root, val):  # insert val as a new leaf while keeping BST order
    # an empty slot is exactly where the new node belongs
    if not root:  # we fell off the tree, so this is the insertion point
        return TreeNode(val)  # the parent's pointer picks up this leaf on unwind
    # the BST rule picks a side; only one subtree is walked
    if val < root.val:  # smaller keys always live in the left subtree
        root.left = insertIntoBST(root.left, val)  # reassigning the child handles the None case for free
    else:  # equal or larger keys go right by this convention
        root.right = insertIntoBST(root.right, val)  # same trick: the child link is rebuilt from the return
    # untouched nodes still return themselves up the chain
    return root  # caller keeps the same root unless the tree was empty

complexity.time: O(H)
complexity.space: O(H) recursion stack space

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: The recursive version is correct, but look at what it spends: a stack frame for every node on the root-to-leaf path, and on the way back up it reassigns node.left or node.right at each level - writes that store the pointer each node already held. The waste is unwinding a path when nothing along it actually changed. The observation is that inserting alters exactly ONE pointer in the entire tree, the empty child slot where the new node lands, so there is no reason to come back. Walk down with a single cursor, and the moment the direction you want to move is None you are standing on the parent of the new node and can attach it in place. Why the descent can never miss the right spot: the BST rule says every key in a node's left subtree is smaller than it and every key in its right subtree is larger, so one comparison eliminates an entire subtree - if val < curr.val then val cannot legally sit anywhere in curr's right subtree. The path taken is therefore the only path val could occupy, and the empty slot at its end is the unique position that keeps the ordering intact, because the comparison at each ancestor is precisely what sent the new node to the correct side of it. Cost: O(H) time, meaning O(log N) on a balanced tree and O(N) on a degenerate chain, with O(1) extra space - one pointer instead of H frames. Nothing rebalances, so inserting already-sorted values still degrades the tree into a list.
approaches.algorithm:
1. If root is None the tree is empty, so return TreeNode(val) as the new root - this is the only case where the returned root differs from the one passed in.
2. Set curr = root, a single cursor that will walk one root-to-leaf path.
3. Loop forever. If val < curr.val, the value belongs somewhere in the left subtree: move curr = curr.left when that child exists, otherwise set curr.left = TreeNode(val) and break.
4. Otherwise val is larger (the problem guarantees no duplicates), so it belongs in the right subtree: move curr = curr.right when that child exists, otherwise set curr.right = TreeNode(val) and break.
5. Each iteration discards one whole subtree, so the loop runs at most H times and always terminates at an absent child.
6. Return root - unchanged as an object, since only one interior pointer was written.

complexity.time: O(H) where H is the height of BST
complexity.space: O(1) auxiliary space

Insert Node in BST.tests:
def inorder_vals(node):
    return inorder_vals(node.left) + [node.val] + inorder_vals(node.right) if node else []

#        4
#      /   \
#     2     7
#    / \
#   1   3
root = build_tree([4, 2, 7, 1, 3])
root = insertIntoBST(root, 5)
# 5 belongs as the left child of 7; inorder stays sorted.
assert inorder_vals(root) == [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7]
assert root.right.left is not None and root.right.left.val == 5
# Inserting a new minimum walks all the way left.
root = insertIntoBST(root, 0)
assert inorder_vals(root) == [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7]
# EDGE: inserting into an empty tree returns a brand-new single-node root.
newRoot = insertIntoBST(None, 9)
assert newRoot is not None and newRoot.val == 9 and inorder_vals(newRoot) == [9]
prerequisites: A new value in a BST always becomes a LEAF: you never restructure existing nodes, you only find the empty slot where the search for that value would fail.
Use the BST ordering rule at every node — go left when val < curr.val, otherwise go right — and stop as soon as that child pointer is None.
The iterative version needs no recursion stack: keep a `curr` pointer, attach the new TreeNode, then break.
Always return the root: when the original tree is empty the answer is a brand-new node, so callers must reassign (`root = insertIntoBST(root, v)`).
Inserting is O(h): O(log n) on a balanced tree, but O(n) if repeated inserts of sorted values turn the tree into a linked list.

Delete Node in BST.title: Delete Node in BST
Delete Node in BST.problemStatement:
Given a root node reference of a BST and a key, delete the node with the given key in the BST. Return the root node reference (possibly updated) of the BST.

Basically, the deletion can be divided into two stages:
1. Search for a node to remove.
2. If the node is found, delete the node.
constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [0, 10^4].
Each node has a unique value.
edgeCases: Key not present in BST.
Node to delete has 0 children (leaf).
Node to delete has 1 child.
Node to delete has 2 children.
Deleting the root node.
followUps: Can you implement this by replacing the node with its inorder predecessor instead of successor?

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: Reconstruct the BST without the deleted node. For example, convert the BST to a sorted array, remove the target value, and rebuild a balanced BST from the sorted array. This takes O(N) time and space.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Traverse tree inorder to build sorted array.
2. Filter out key from array.
3. Recursively build BST from subarray: root is mid element, left is left subarray, right is right subarray.
4. Return root.
approaches.code:
def deleteNode(root, key):  # brute force: rebuild the entire tree without key
    # inorder exposes the sorted values hiding in the BST
    vals = []  # a sorted array is easy to delete from and rebuild
    def inorder(node):  # the standard left, node, right recursive walk
        if not node:  # an empty subtree adds nothing to vals
            return  # base case simply unwinds to the parent
        inorder(node.left)  # smaller values are recorded before this node
        vals.append(node.val)  # appending here is what keeps vals sorted ascending
        inorder(node.right)  # larger values are recorded after this node
    inorder(root)  # one O(n) pass; vals is now sorted ascending
    # removing the key from a sorted list keeps it sorted
    vals = [v for v in vals if v != key]  # drops every copy of key, and is a no-op if absent
    # rebuild a balanced BST from the sorted values
    def build(start, end):  # start and end are inclusive index bounds
        if start > end:  # an empty range means there is no node here
            return None  # None becomes the parent's missing child link
        mid = (start + end) // 2  # middle element as root is what keeps it balanced
        node = TreeNode(vals[mid])  # everything left of mid is smaller, by sortedness
        node.left = build(start, mid - 1)  # mid - 1 excludes mid so it is never reused
        node.right = build(mid + 1, end)  # mid + 1 avoids recursing forever on one element
        return node  # this subtree's root travels up to its parent
    return build(0, len(vals) - 1)  # empty vals gives 0 > -1, correctly returning None

complexity.time: O(N) to traverse and rebuild
complexity.space: O(N) for array storage and recursion stack

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition:
Flattening the BST to a sorted array, dropping the key and rebuilding costs O(N) time and O(N) space, and it destroys and reconstructs every node in the tree. The number of pointers that genuinely have to change is at most a couple.

The observation: the ordering property (every value in a node's left subtree is smaller than the node, every value in its right subtree is larger) means only the search path matters -- each comparison of `key` against `root.val` eliminates a whole subtree. Reattachment needs no parent pointers either, because the recursion returns the new subtree and the caller writes it back with `root.left = deleteNode(root.left, key)`. At the target: with zero or one child, return the surviving child and that assignment splices it into place. With two children the node cannot be removed at all, so replace its VALUE with the inorder successor -- the smallest value in the right subtree, found by going right once then left as far as possible -- then delete that successor from the right subtree.

Why the successor is the only safe replacement: it exceeds every value on the left (it lives in the right subtree) and is the minimum of the right subtree, so it is below everything remaining there. Both ordering conditions survive. And the follow-up deletion cannot recurse forever: a subtree's minimum has no left child by definition, so it always falls into the zero-or-one-child case.

Cost: O(H) time, H the height -- one descent to the key plus one to the successor -- and O(H) recursion stack. About log N when balanced, N in a degenerate chain. The trade against rebuilding is that nothing rebalances, so repeated deletions can leave the tree more skewed than it started.
approaches.algorithm:
1. If root is None, the key is absent: return None.
2. If key < root.val, recurse left and write the result back: root.left = deleteNode(root.left, key).
3. If key > root.val, recurse right and write the result back: root.right = deleteNode(root.right, key).
4. Otherwise this is the target. If it has no left child, return root.right; if it has no right child, return root.left -- the caller's assignment splices the survivor in.
5. With two children, walk temp = root.right then temp = temp.left until temp.left is None: temp is the inorder successor.
6. Copy root.val = temp.val, then remove the duplicate with root.right = deleteNode(root.right, temp.val), which lands in the easy case since a minimum has no left child.
7. Return root, the (possibly rewritten) subtree root.
approaches.code:
def deleteNode(root, key):
    # Base case: if root is None, key not found
    if not root:
        return None
    # Search for the node to delete
    if key < root.val:
        root.left = deleteNode(root.left, key)
    elif key > root.val:
        root.right = deleteNode(root.right, key)
    # Target node found
    else:
        # Case 1 & 2: Node has 0 or 1 child
        if not root.left:
            return root.right
        elif not root.right:
            return root.left
        # Case 3: Node has 2 children
        # Find inorder successor (minimum in right subtree)
        temp = root.right
        while temp.left:
            temp = temp.left
        # Copy successor's value to current node
        root.val = temp.val
        # Delete successor node
        root.right = deleteNode(root.right, temp.val)
    # Return root
    return root

complexity.time: O(H) where H is the height of BST
complexity.space: O(H) for recursive call stack

Delete Node in BST.tests:
def inorder_vals(node):
    return inorder_vals(node.left) + [node.val] + inorder_vals(node.right) if node else []

def is_bst(node, lo=float('-inf'), hi=float('inf')):
    if not node:
        return True
    if not (lo < node.val < hi):
        return False
    return is_bst(node.left, lo, node.val) and is_bst(node.right, node.val, hi)

#          5
#        /   \
#       3     6
#      / \     \
#     2   4     7
# Delete 3 (two children) -> must stay a valid BST without the value 3.
r = deleteNode(build_tree([5, 3, 6, 2, 4, None, 7]), 3)
assert inorder_vals(r) == [2, 4, 5, 6, 7] and is_bst(r)
# Delete a leaf.
r2 = deleteNode(build_tree([5, 3, 6, 2, 4, None, 7]), 2)
assert inorder_vals(r2) == [3, 4, 5, 6, 7] and is_bst(r2)
# Delete a key that is not present -> tree unchanged.
r3 = deleteNode(build_tree([5, 3, 6]), 10)
assert inorder_vals(r3) == [3, 5, 6] and is_bst(r3)
# EDGE: deleting the only node leaves an empty tree.
assert deleteNode(build_tree([1]), 1) is None
# EDGE: deleting from an empty tree is a no-op.
assert deleteNode(None, 1) is None
prerequisites: Deletion splits into three cases: a leaf (just drop it), one child (splice the child up into the node's place), and two children (replace the value, then delete a simpler node).
For two children, use the inorder SUCCESSOR — the leftmost node of the right subtree — because it is the smallest value still bigger than everything on the left, so the BST order survives.
The successor has at most a right child by construction, so deleting it recursively always hits one of the easy cases; the recursion never spirals.
The 'return the (possibly new) subtree root and let the parent reassign' pattern (`root.left = deleteNode(root.left, key)`) is what rewires pointers without tracking parents manually.
Deleting an absent key must be a harmless no-op: the search simply falls off the tree and the base case returns None to a leaf's child slot.
Time is O(h) and space is O(h) for the recursion stack — O(log n) balanced, O(n) skewed.

Coin Change II.problemStatement: You are given an integer array coins representing coins of different denominations and an integer amount representing a total amount of money. Return the number of combinations that make up that amount. If that amount of money cannot be made up by any combination of the coins, return 0. You may assume that you have an infinite number of each kind of coin.

examples.explanation:
There are four ways to make up the amount:
5=5
5=2+2+1
5=2+1+1+1
5=1+1+1+1+1
The amount of 3 cannot be made up just with coins of 2.

constraints: All the values of coins are unique.
edgeCases: amount = 0: there is 1 way (empty combination)
No coins available: 0 ways
No combination is possible: return 0
followUps: Can you optimize the space complexity to O(amount)?

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: Try all possible combinations of coins to sum up to the target amount. For each coin, we can either choose to include it and stay at the same index (since we have infinite coins) or exclude it and move to the next coin index.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Define a recursive helper function solve(index, current_amount).
2. If current_amount is 0, return 1 (found a valid combination).
3. If current_amount < 0 or index >= len(coins), return 0 (invalid state).
4. Try two choices: pick the coin (solve(index, current_amount - coins[index])) and skip the coin (solve(index + 1, current_amount)).
5. Return the sum of both choices.
approaches.code:
def change(amount: int, coins: list[int]) -> int:
    # Define helper function for recursion
    def helper(idx, rem):
        # Base Case: if remainder is 0, we found a valid combination
        if rem == 0:
            return 1
        # Base Case: if remainder is negative or no coins left, invalid
        if rem < 0 or idx == len(coins):
            return 0
        # Choice 1: Take current coin and stay at the same index
        take = helper(idx, rem - coins[idx])
        # Choice 2: Skip current coin and move to next index
        skip = helper(idx + 1, rem)
        # Sum up both decisions
        return take + skip
    # Call helper starting at coin index 0 and full amount
    return helper(0, amount)

complexity.time: O(2^(N + amount))
complexity.space: O(N + amount)

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: The take/stay recursion re-derives the same situation over and over. Reaching a remaining amount of 5 with coins [1,2,5] after picking 1 then 2, and after picking 2 then 1, are two separate branch tips that expand into identical subtrees, and the count of ways below them is recomputed both times - exponentially many times across the whole search. The observation is that the number of ways depends only on which coins are still allowed and how much is left, never on the order they were picked. So hold one array where `dp[i]` is the number of combinations making amount `i` using only the coins folded in so far, seeded with `dp[0] = 1` because there is exactly one way to make nothing: take nothing. Two details carry the correctness. The coin loop is on the outside, and that is what counts combinations rather than orderings - each combination is tallied once, at the moment its last-processed coin is folded in; swap the loops and 1+2 and 2+1 become two separate answers. The inner loop runs upward from `coin`, so `dp[i - coin]` on the right-hand side has already been updated in this same pass, which is intentional: it means combinations that use `coin` again are included, giving unlimited reuse for free. Cost: O(N * amount) time and O(amount) space, one reused row instead of a full N-by-amount table.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Allocate `dp = [0] * (amount + 1)`, where `dp[i]` will hold the number of combinations summing to `i`.
2. Set the base case `dp[0] = 1`: the empty selection is the one way to reach 0.
3. Loop over each `coin` in `coins` on the OUTER loop - this ordering is what makes the count combinations rather than ordered sequences.
4. For each coin, loop `i` from `coin` up to `amount` in ascending order.
5. Apply `dp[i] += dp[i - coin]`; because the inner loop ascends, `dp[i - coin]` already accounts for this coin, which is what permits using it repeatedly.
6. Return `dp[amount]`, which is 0 if no combination reaches the target.
approaches.code:
def change(amount: int, coins: list[int]) -> int:
    # Initialize dp table with zeros of size amount + 1
    dp = [0] * (amount + 1)
    # Base case: 1 way to make amount 0 (using no coins)
    dp[0] = 1
    # Loop through each coin denomination
    for coin in coins:
        # Update dp array for all amounts greater than or equal to current coin
        for i in range(coin, amount + 1):
            # Add combinations using the current coin
            dp[i] += dp[i - coin]
    # Return the total ways to make the target amount
    return dp[amount]

complexity.time: O(N * amount)
complexity.space: O(amount)

Coin Change II.tests:
# {1,1,1,1,1}, {1,1,1,2}, {1,2,2}, {5} -> 4 combinations.
assert change(5, [1, 2, 5]) == 4
# 3 can never be built from 2-coins only.
assert change(3, [2]) == 0
# Exactly one way: a single 10-coin.
assert change(10, [10]) == 1
# EDGE: amount 0 always has exactly one combination - take nothing.
assert change(0, [7]) == 1
# EDGE: no coins at all and a positive amount -> impossible.
assert change(5, []) == 0
prerequisites: This counts COMBINATIONS, not permutations: {1,2} and {2,1} are the same answer, which is what makes the loop order matter.
Unbounded knapsack pattern: after taking a coin you stay on the same coin index, because each denomination has unlimited supply.
dp[a] = number of combinations that sum to a; dp[0] = 1 because there is exactly one way to make 0 — pick nothing.
Put the COIN loop outside and the amount loop inside: each coin is fully absorbed before the next one appears, so every combination is counted once in non-decreasing coin order.
The inner loop runs forward from `coin` to `amount` (not backwards), which is exactly what allows reusing the same coin many times.
The 1-D array is a space-squeezed version of a 2-D dp[coin][amount] table, since each row only ever reads the row above at the same or smaller amount.

0/1 Knapsack.problemStatement: You are given weights and values of N items, put these items in a knapsack of capacity W to get the maximum total value in the knapsack. Note that we have only one quantity of each item. In other words, given two integer arrays val[0..N-1] and wt[0..N-1] which represent values and weights associated with N items respectively. Also given an integer W which represents knapsack capacity, find out the maximum value subset of val[] such that sum of the weights of this subset is smaller than or equal to W.

examples.explanation: The maximum value is obtained by choosing items with weights 20 and 30.

edgeCases: W = 0: maximum value is 0
All items heavier than W: maximum value is 0
Total weight of all items is <= W: select all items
followUps: Can you optimize the space complexity to O(W) using a single 1D array?

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: For each item, we have two choices: either include it in the knapsack (if its weight is less than or equal to the remaining capacity) or exclude it. We recursively try both and return the maximum value.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Define helper(idx, W).
2. If idx == N or W == 0, return 0.
3. If weight of current item > W, we must skip it: helper(idx + 1, W).
4. Otherwise, return max of picking item (values[idx] + helper(idx + 1, W - weights[idx])) or skipping item (helper(idx + 1, W)).

complexity.space: O(N)

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition:
Take-or-skip recursion branches twice per item, 2^N paths, most landing on a state already solved: reaching item i with 4 capacity left is the same subproblem however you got there.

The answer depends only on (item index, remaining capacity), not the route, so each deserves computing once. Collapse it into one row: dp[w] is the best value within capacity w using the items processed so far, and item i updates it with dp[w] = max(dp[w], val[i] + dp[w - wt[i]]) -- skip it, or take it and add the best packing of what is left.

Correctness rests entirely on the loop running backwards: dp[w - wt[i]] must still hold the value from before item i was considered, or the item gets counted twice, and descending w from W to wt[i] keeps that smaller index untouched. Ascending breaks it: with W = 10 and one item of weight 5, value 3, going up sets dp[5] = 3, then dp[10] reads it and returns 6 -- the item used twice, which is unbounded knapsack instead. Backwards, dp[10] reads dp[5] = 0 and gives 3.

O(N*W) time, O(W) space. One row remembers the best value only, not which items produced it.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Allocate `dp` of size W + 1 filled with 0s: with no items processed, every capacity is worth nothing.
2. Loop over item indices i from 0 to N-1, folding one item into `dp` per pass.
3. For each item, loop w downwards from W to wt[i], so `dp[w - wt[i]]` is still the pre-item value.
4. Set `dp[w] = max(dp[w], val[i] + dp[w - wt[i]])`: keep the skip value or take the item.
5. Leave capacities below wt[i] alone, since the item cannot fit there.
6. Return `dp[W]` after all items have been folded in.
approaches.code:
def knapsack(W: int, wt: list[int], val: list[int]) -> int:
    n = len(wt)
    # dp[w] will store the maximum value for capacity w
    dp = [0] * (W + 1)
    # Iterate through all given items
    for i in range(n):
        # Iterate backwards from capacity W down to current item's weight
        for w in range(W, wt[i] - 1, -1):
            # Update capacity w with max of picking or skipping item i
            dp[w] = max(dp[w], val[i] + dp[w - wt[i]])
    # Return the maximum value for full capacity W
    return dp[W]

complexity.time: O(N * W)
complexity.space: O(W)

0/1 Knapsack.tests:
# Basic case: only the light high-value item fits.
assert knapsack(4, [4, 5, 1], [1, 2, 3]) == 3
# Classic case: pick items 0,2,3 (weights 1+4+5=10) for value 5+8+6=19.
assert knapsack(10, [1, 2, 4, 5], [5, 4, 8, 6]) == 19
# Edge case: capacity 0 means nothing can be taken.
assert knapsack(0, [1, 2], [10, 20]) == 0
# Edge case: every item is heavier than the knapsack.
assert knapsack(3, [4, 5, 6], [1, 2, 3]) == 0
prerequisites: The pick-or-skip recursion pattern: at every item you branch into 'take it' (spend its weight, collect its value) and 'skip it', and the answer is the max of the two branches.
Why memoisation collapses this: the recursion only ever depends on (item index, remaining capacity), so there are at most N x (W+1) distinct states no matter how many branches exist.
How a 2D dp[i][w] table folds into a single 1D array of size W+1: row i only ever reads row i-1, so one row can be updated in place.

The critical 1D detail: you must iterate capacity DOWNWARD (range(W, wt[i]-1, -1)) so dp[w - wt[i]] still holds the previous item's value — sweeping upward would let one item be reused and silently turn this into unbounded knapsack.
Python range with a negative step: range(W, wt[i] - 1, -1) stops just above wt[i] - 1, which is exactly the smallest capacity the item still fits in.
0/1 knapsack is pseudo-polynomial: O(N*W) is fast for small W but blows up when W is huge, which is why the capacity bound matters in interviews.

Unbounded Knapsack.problemStatement: Given a set of N items, each with a weight and a value, represented by the arrays wt[] and val[] respectively. Also, a knapsack with weight limit W. Find the maximum value that can be put into the knapsack. You are allowed to use an item multiple times (unbounded times).

examples.explanation: Choose item 1 (weight 3, val 40) once and item 3 (weight 5, val 70) once. Total weight = 8, value = 110.

edgeCases: W = 0: max value is 0
No item weighs <= W: max value is 0
followUps: Can you implement this with time complexity O(N*W) and space complexity O(W)?

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: The word "unbounded" is the whole difference from the classic 0/1 knapsack, and it changes the recursion in exactly one place. In 0/1 you walk the items and decide take-or-leave for each, then move on to item i+1 permanently, because that item can never be used again — the index has to be part of the state. Here an item may be reused any number of times, so moving on is simply wrong; after taking an item you are allowed to consider the entire item list all over again. That is why the state collapses to a single number, the remaining capacity rem_w: how you arrived at that capacity places no restriction on what you may buy next. So the recursion asks, for a given rem_w, which item goes in next — try every item i whose wt[i] fits, spend that much capacity, collect val[i], and add helper(rem_w - wt[i]) for the best value obtainable from what is left. Take the maximum over all such choices, and return 0 once the capacity is exhausted. It is correct, but wildly wasteful: the same rem_w gets re-solved along countless different paths, so the runtime is exponential until a memo or a DP table over capacity is added.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Define helper(rem_w).
2. If rem_w is 0, return 0.
3. Initialize max_val = 0.
4. Loop through all items: if wt[i] <= rem_w, max_val = max(max_val, val[i] + helper(rem_w - wt[i])).
5. Return max_val.

complexity.time: O(N^W)
complexity.space: O(W)

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition:
The recursion carries one piece of state, the remaining capacity, because a taken item stays available. Correct, but it re-solves the same capacity once per order of picks: capacity 7 reached as 3 then 4, and as 4 then 3, spawns identical subtrees, compounding exponentially.

The observation: the best value at capacity w depends on nothing but w. Sweep w upward from 1, setting dp[w] = max over items i with wt[i] <= w of dp[w - wt[i]] + val[i]. The lookback reads the SAME array being filled, not a previous row, which is what lets an item repeat: with wt = [3], val = [5], dp[6] reads dp[3] + 5 = 10 - the item used twice, no repeat loop.

Why every packing is covered: an optimal packing of w has some last item i; removing it leaves an optimal packing of w - wt[i], or substituting a better one beats the optimum. Maximising over the last item enumerates every packing. And wt[i] >= 1 gives w - wt[i] < w, so every value read was final earlier in the sweep; a zero-weight item breaks that.

Cost: O(N * W) time, O(W) space - pseudo-polynomial in W, and the table gives the value, not the items.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Create `dp` of length W + 1 filled with 0s, where dp[w] is the best value reachable when capacity w is available.
2. Sweep capacity `w` from 1 up to W in increasing order, so every smaller capacity is final before it is read.
3. For each `w`, loop over all N items.
4. Skip item i when `wt[i] > w`; it cannot fit.
5. Otherwise set `dp[w] = max(dp[w], dp[w - wt[i]] + val[i])`, treating i as the last item placed - reading the same dp array is what allows i to be chosen again.
6. Return `dp[W]`.

complexity.time: O(N * W)
complexity.space: O(W)

Unbounded Knapsack.tests:
# Item of weight 2 (value 3) plus item of weight 3 (value 5) fills capacity 5.
assert unboundedKnapsack(5, [2, 3], [3, 5]) == 8
# Repetition allowed: use weight-1 item eight times.
assert unboundedKnapsack(8, [1, 4], [2, 7]) == 16
# Edge case: capacity 0 -> nothing can be picked.
assert unboundedKnapsack(0, [1, 2], [10, 20]) == 0
# Edge case: the only item is heavier than the knapsack.
assert unboundedKnapsack(2, [5], [10]) == 0
prerequisites: The one-line difference from 0/1 knapsack: after taking an item you stay on the SAME item instead of moving to the next, because unlimited copies are allowed.
In the 1D table that translates into sweeping capacity UPWARD, so dp[w - wt[i]] may already include the current item — that self-reference is exactly what permits repetition.
The state is just the remaining capacity: dp[w] = best value packable into capacity w, so the table has W+1 entries regardless of item count.
This is the same skeleton as Coin Change / Rod Cutting — recognising the family lets you reuse one template for all three.
Watch for items of weight 0 with positive value: they make the answer unbounded, so real inputs must exclude them (or you must special-case them).

Rod Cutting Problem.problemStatement: Given a rod of length N inches and an array of prices, price[] that contains prices of all pieces of size smaller than N. Determine the maximum value obtainable by cutting up the rod and selling the pieces.

examples.explanation: The maximum value is obtained by cutting the rod into two pieces of lengths 2 and 6, price is 5 + 17 = 22.

edgeCases: N = 1: return price[0]
Single cut gives max value vs multiple cuts
followUps: How does this relate to the Unbounded Knapsack problem?

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: The paralysing part of this problem is that a cut anywhere changes what is left over, so it feels like you must consider all cutting patterns at once. Recursion escapes that by committing to only ONE decision at a time: whatever the optimal solution looks like, it has some FIRST piece, and that first piece has a length i somewhere between 1 and the remaining length. You do not know which i is right, so try them all. For each choice you collect `price[i - 1]` for the piece you just cut off, and the rest of the rod, of length `rem_len - i`, is an identical but smaller instance of the same problem -- so `helper` calls itself on it. Take the maximum over all i and you have the answer, with `rem_len == 0` returning 0 as the base case where nothing is left to sell. This is worth writing because it makes the recurrence visible, and the recurrence is the thing you actually have to understand before any table makes sense. What it costs is enormous: the branching factor is the remaining length itself, so the call tree grows like 2^N, and the same subproblem is solved over and over -- a rod of length 3 left over is recomputed from scratch along every path that happens to reach it. Recursion depth adds O(N) stack space. That repeated recomputation, and nothing else, is what memoisation or a bottom-up table removes.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Define helper(n).
2. If n == 0, return 0.
3. Initialize max_val = 0.
4. Loop i from 1 to n: max_val = max(max_val, price[i-1] + helper(n - i)).
5. Return max_val.

complexity.space: O(N)

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: The recursion is not wrong, it is just forgetful: the maximum value obtainable from a rod of length 4 depends only on the number 4, yet the brute force recalculates it every single time a leftover of length 4 appears anywhere in the call tree. Once you see that a subproblem is identified by one small integer, the fix writes itself -- give each length its own slot and solve the lengths in increasing order, so that whenever you need a smaller answer it is already sitting in the table. Let `dp[i]` be the best total price obtainable from a rod of length i, with `dp[0] = 0` because a rod of length zero earns nothing. To fill `dp[i]`, reuse the same decision the recursion made: try every first cut of length j from 1 to i, collect `price[j - 1]` for that piece, and add `dp[i - j]`, which is already final because i - j is strictly smaller than i and was computed on an earlier iteration. Taking the maximum over all j gives `dp[i]`, and the invariant that every entry below i is already correct is exactly what makes a single left-to-right sweep sufficient. Two nested loops over lengths and cuts give O(N^2) time -- a colossal improvement on 2^N -- with O(N) space for the table and no recursion stack at all. The answer for the full rod is `dp[n]`.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Initialize dp array of size N + 1 with 0s.
2. Iterate length i from 1 to N.
3. For each i, find max price by trying all possible first cuts of size j (from 1 to i).
4. dp[i] = max(price[j-1] + dp[i-j]) for all j.
5. Return dp[N].
approaches.code:
def cutRod(price: list[int], n: int) -> int:
    # Initialize dp table with size n + 1
    dp = [0] * (n + 1)
    # Build DP values for each length up to n
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        max_val = -1
        # Look at every cut length j from 1 to i
        for j in range(1, i + 1):
            # Keep track of the maximum obtainable value
            max_val = max(max_val, price[j - 1] + dp[i - j])
        # Store the maximum value for length i
        dp[i] = max_val
    # Return the maximum value for length n
    return dp[n]

complexity.space: O(N)

Rod Cutting Problem.tests:
# Classic rod-cutting table: best for length 8 is 2+6 -> 5 + 17 = 22.
assert cutRod([1, 5, 8, 9, 10, 17, 17, 20], 8) == 22
# Length 4 with prices [2,5,7,8]: two pieces of length 2 give 5 + 5 = 10.
assert cutRod([2, 5, 7, 8], 4) == 10
# Edge case: rod of length 0 yields no money.
assert cutRod([3, 5], 0) == 0
# Edge case: rod of length 1 can only be sold whole.
assert cutRod([3, 5, 9], 1) == 3
prerequisites: Rod cutting IS unbounded knapsack in disguise: a piece of length i is an item of weight i and value price[i-1], and you may cut as many pieces of a length as you like.
1-indexing trap: price[j - 1] is the price of a piece of LENGTH j, so the off-by-one between length and array index must be kept straight everywhere.
The recurrence dp[i] = max over j in 1..i of price[j-1] + dp[i-j] works by fixing the FIRST piece's length j and delegating the rest to an already-solved subproblem.
Because dp[i] only reads strictly smaller dp values, filling lengths in increasing order guarantees every dependency is final by the time it is read.
dp[0] = 0 is the real base case: a rod of length 0 sells for nothing, and it is what terminates every chain of cuts.

Longest Common Subsequence.problemStatement: You are given two strings, text1 and text2. A subsequence is what remains after deleting zero or more characters from a string while keeping the surviving characters in their original relative order — 'ace' is a subsequence of 'abcde', but 'aec' is not, because the order changed. A common subsequence is a string that is a subsequence of both inputs at once. Return a single integer: the length of the longest common subsequence of text1 and text2. Only the length is returned, never the characters themselves, and if the two strings share nothing the answer is 0.

examples.explanation: The longest common subsequence is "ace" and its length is 3.

constraints: text1 and text2 consist of only lowercase English characters.
edgeCases: No characters match: return 0
Identical strings: return length of strings
Single character strings
followUps: Can you print the actual longest common subsequence, not just its length?

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: Think of two cursors, one in each string. If the characters under the cursors are the same, that pair can safely join the common subsequence, so count it and move both cursors forward. If they differ, at least one of those two characters can never be matched in this alignment, but we cannot tell which one, so we branch: try skipping the character in text1, try skipping the character in text2, and keep whichever branch produces the longer result. The recursion bottoms out as soon as either cursor runs off the end, since an empty remainder can contribute nothing. This is a faithful translation of the definition and it is completely correct, but the two-way branching on every mismatch makes the call tree exponential.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Define solve(i, j) = the LCS length of text1[i:] and text2[j:].
2. Base case: if i has reached len(text1) or j has reached len(text2), return 0.
3. If text1[i] == text2[j], return 1 + solve(i + 1, j + 1) — matching pairs are always worth taking.
4. Otherwise return max(solve(i + 1, j), solve(i, j + 1)), covering both ways of discarding one character.
5. Call solve(0, 0) to answer for the full strings.

complexity.time: O(2^(M+N)) — every mismatch splits into two recursive calls with no memory of past work.
complexity.space: O(M + N) — the recursion depth is bounded by the total length of both strings.

approaches.name: Better (Memoization / Top-Down DP)
approaches.intuition: Trace the brute force by hand on 'abcde' and 'ace' and you will see solve(2, 1) evaluated over and over from different branches. That is the whole inefficiency: the recursion depends only on the pair (i, j), yet it recomputes each pair many times. There are only (m + 1) * (n + 1) distinct pairs, so if we store each answer the first time we compute it and return the stored value afterwards, the total work collapses from exponential to the number of states. functools.lru_cache does exactly that with one decorator line, and the code is otherwise character-for-character the brute force. This is the classic bridge from 'correct but exponential' to real dynamic programming, and it is often the fastest route to a working solution in an interview.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Write the same solve(i, j) recursion as the brute force.
2. Decorate it with @lru_cache(maxsize=None) so every (i, j) result is stored the first time it is computed.
3. Keep the base case: return 0 when either cursor reaches the end of its string.
4. Keep the match rule (1 + solve(i + 1, j + 1)) and the mismatch rule (max of the two skips).
5. Call solve(0, 0), then clear the cache so the memo table does not outlive the call, and return the stored answer.
approaches.code:
from functools import lru_cache                   # ready-made memo table decorator

def longestCommonSubsequence(text1: str, text2: str) -> int:
    # Better: identical recursion, but every (i, j) pair is solved ONCE and cached.
    # There are only (m+1) * (n+1) distinct states, so the exponential blow-up disappears.
    @lru_cache(maxsize=None)                        # unlimited cache keyed by (i, j)
    def solve(i: int, j: int) -> int:
        if i == len(text1) or j == len(text2):      # ran off the end of a string
            return 0                                # nothing left to match
        if text1[i] == text2[j]:                    # characters agree
            return 1 + solve(i + 1, j + 1)          # take the match, advance both cursors
        # No match: drop one character from either side and keep the better result.
        return max(solve(i + 1, j), solve(i, j + 1))

    ans = solve(0, 0)                               # answer for the two full strings
    solve.cache_clear()                             # free the memo table before returning
    return ans

complexity.time: O(M * N) — each of the (M+1)*(N+1) states is computed once and reused thereafter.
complexity.space: O(M * N) — the memo table, plus O(M + N) recursion depth.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: Generating every subsequence of text1 and testing each one against text2 means 2^m candidates, which is hopeless past about twenty characters. The escape is to stop reasoning about whole strings and instead ask a smaller, repeatable question: what is the answer for the first i characters of text1 against the first j characters of text2? Look only at the last character of each of those prefixes. If text1[i-1] == text2[j-1], that pair can always be used — matching two equal characters never costs you a better answer elsewhere — so the result is 1 plus the answer for both prefixes with those characters removed, which is the diagonal neighbour dp[i-1][j-1]. If they differ, at least one of the two characters cannot participate, so you discard one of them and keep whichever gives more, max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]). Every cell now depends only on cells above and to the left, so filling the table in plain row-major order always finds its dependencies already computed. Each of the m*n cells costs O(1), giving O(m*n) time and O(m*n) space for the table.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Let m = len(text1) and n = len(text2), and allocate dp as an (m+1) x (n+1) grid of zeros. Row 0 and column 0 stand for an empty prefix, whose common subsequence with anything has length 0, so they are ready-made base cases that need no special handling inside the loops.
2. Loop i from 1 to m and, nested inside, j from 1 to n. This order guarantees that when dp[i][j] is computed its three dependencies dp[i-1][j-1], dp[i-1][j] and dp[i][j-1] are already final. The loop invariant is that dp[i][j] holds the LCS length of text1's first i characters and text2's first j characters.
3. Compare text1[i-1] with text2[j-1] — the minus one is needed because dp is one-based while the strings are zero-based. If the characters are equal, set dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1, extending the diagonal answer by this newly matched pair.
4. If the characters differ, set dp[i][j] = max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]), which drops either the last character of text1 or the last character of text2, keeping whichever choice leaves the longer common subsequence.
5. Once both loops finish, return dp[m][n], the single cell that corresponds to both strings taken in full.
approaches.code:
def longestCommonSubsequence(text1: str, text2: str) -> int:
    m, n = len(text1), len(text2)  # the table dimensions come from the two string lengths
    dp = [[0] * (n + 1) for _ in range(m + 1)]  # row 0 and column 0 stay 0: an empty prefix matches nothing
    
    # Populate DP matrix
    for i in range(1, m + 1):  # i = how many characters of text1 we are considering
        for j in range(1, n + 1):  # j = how many characters of text2 we are considering
            if text1[i - 1] == text2[j - 1]:  # careful: dp is 1-based while the strings are 0-based
                # Characters match -> add diagonal
                dp[i][j] = dp[i - 1][j - 1] + 1
            else:
                # Discrepancy -> take best fallback
                dp[i][j] = max(dp[i - 1][j], dp[i][j - 1])
                
    return dp[m][n]  # the cell for the two FULL strings is the answer

complexity.time: O(M * N)
complexity.space: O(M * N) table size

Longest Common Subsequence.tests:
assert longestCommonSubsequence("abcde", "ace") == 3
assert longestCommonSubsequence("abc", "abc") == 3
assert longestCommonSubsequence("abc", "def") == 0
assert longestCommonSubsequence("", "abc") == 0    # edge: empty string shares nothing
assert longestCommonSubsequence("a", "") == 0      # edge: the other side empty too
assert longestCommonSubsequence("bsbininm", "jmjkbkjkv") == 1
prerequisites: A SUBSEQUENCE keeps the original relative order but may skip characters; a SUBSTRING must be contiguous — LCS is about the former.
The recurrence: if the current characters match, the answer is 1 + LCS of both remainders; if not, it is the max of dropping one character from either side.
The 1-based dp table with an extra zero row and column removes every i-1 / j-1 boundary check, but remember dp[i][j] then refers to text1[i-1] and text2[j-1].
Row 0 and column 0 stay 0 forever: an empty string has no common subsequence with anything.
The table is filled row by row and each cell only reads dp[i-1][j-1], dp[i-1][j] and dp[i][j-1] — all already computed, which is why the loop order works.
Because each row depends only on the previous row, the O(m*n) space can be squeezed to O(min(m, n)) with two rolling rows.

Longest Common Substring.problemStatement: You are given two strings S1 and S2. Return the length of the longest string that appears as a contiguous block of characters inside both of them. Contiguity is the crucial word: unlike the longest common subsequence, the matched characters must sit next to each other and in the same order in both strings, so for abcde and abfce the answer is 2 for ab, not 3. If the two strings have no character in common at all, the answer is 0. Only the length has to be reported, not the substring itself, and there may well be several different substrings that all tie at that maximum length.

examples.explanation: The longest common substring is "CDGH" of length 4.

edgeCases: No common substring: return 0
Whole string matches: return len(S1)
followUps: Can you reduce space complexity to O(min(M, N))?

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: With no insight whatsoever, the definition itself already gives you a plan: a common substring is some contiguous slice of S1 that also happens to occur somewhere in S2, so enumerate every slice of S1 and test each one. Two nested loops produce the slice boundaries — `i` for where the slice starts and `j` for where it ends — and Python's `in` operator answers the membership question without you writing a single line of matching logic. Whenever a slice turns out to be present in S2, its length competes for `max_len`. It is worth writing this once, because it makes the definition concrete and gives you a reference implementation to check a faster solution against. The cost is brutal though: there are about n^2/2 slices, materialising each one copies up to n characters, and the `in` check scans S2 as well. Nothing is carried from one slice to the next — knowing that S1[i:j] matched tells the following iteration absolutely nothing — and eliminating exactly that redundancy is what the dynamic programming solution does.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Initialize max_len = 0.
2. Iterate through all starting positions i and ending positions j of S1.
3. For each substring S1[i:j], check if S1[i:j] is in S2.
4. If it is, update max_len with the maximum length.

complexity.space: O(N)

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition:
Enumerating every slice of S1 and asking whether it occurs in S2 tests O(N^2) slices, each membership check rescanning S2 from the start - S1[i:j+1] and S1[i:j] differ by one character, yet the second search matches from scratch.

Change the question: instead of the longest common block anywhere, ask for the longest common SUFFIX of two prefixes, which grows one character at a time. dp[i][j] is the length of the longest block ending exactly at S1[i-1] and S2[j-1]; if those characters match it is dp[i-1][j-1] + 1, and if they differ no block can end at that pair, so dp[i][j] = 0. That reset is the one line enforcing contiguity - the only difference from longest common subsequence.

The maximum over the table is exact both ways: every common substring ends at some pair (i, j) and the loops visit all N*M pairs, so none can hide, while dp[i][j] cannot overstate, since it counts an unbroken run of matching pairs back to the last zero, each step advancing both indices by exactly one.

O(N*M) time and space. Traded: the table holds lengths only, so `max_len` says how long, not where.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Set n = len(S1) and m = len(S2), build `dp` as an (n+1) x (m+1) grid of zeros, and set `max_len = 0`. Row 0 and column 0 stay zero as the empty-prefix base case.
2. Loop i from 1 to n and, inside it, j from 1 to m, so the diagonal predecessor is always computed before it is read.
3. If `S1[i-1] == S2[j-1]`, set `dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1` and raise `max_len = max(max_len, dp[i][j])`.
4. Otherwise set `dp[i][j] = 0`, since no common block can end at a mismatched pair - this reset is what keeps the match contiguous.
5. After both loops finish, return `max_len`.
approaches.code:
def longestCommonSubstring(S1: str, S2: str) -> int:
    n, m = len(S1), len(S2)
    # dp[i][j] stores longest common suffix length of S1[0..i-1] and S2[0..j-1]
    dp = [[0] * (m + 1) for _ in range(n + 1)]
    max_len = 0
    # Loop through characters of S1
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        # Loop through characters of S2
        for j in range(1, m + 1):
            # If characters at current positions match
            if S1[i - 1] == S2[j - 1]:
                # Extend the common substring length from previous diagonal
                dp[i][j] = dp[i - 1][j - 1] + 1
                # Update the maximum length found so far
                max_len = max(max_len, dp[i][j])
            else:
                # If they do not match, common suffix length at this point becomes 0
                dp[i][j] = 0
    # Return the maximum common substring length
    return max_len

complexity.time: O(N * M)
complexity.space: O(N * M)

Longest Common Substring.tests:
# "cjk" is the longest contiguous block shared by both strings.
assert longestCommonSubstring("abcjklp", "acjkp") == 3
# "aba" (or "bab") is the longest common substring here.
assert longestCommonSubstring("abab", "baba") == 3
# Edge case: no character is shared at all.
assert longestCommonSubstring("abc", "def") == 0
# Edge case: an empty string shares nothing.
assert longestCommonSubstring("", "abc") == 0
prerequisites: Substring means CONTIGUOUS, unlike subsequence — that single word changes the whole recurrence and is the most common source of confusion here.
The DP state is a common SUFFIX length: dp[i][j] = length of the longest common suffix of S1[0..i-1] and S2[0..j-1], not the answer for those prefixes.
On a mismatch you reset dp[i][j] to 0 (never carry a max across), because contiguity is broken; on a match you extend the diagonal dp[i-1][j-1] by 1.
Since dp[i][j] is not itself the answer, you must keep a separate running max_len variable updated on every match.
The extra row 0 and column 0 of zeros represent the empty prefix and let you write dp[i-1][j-1] without bounds checks.
Space can be cut to two rows (or one row scanned right-to-left) because each cell only reads the row above.

Longest Palindromic Subsequence.problemStatement: Given a string s, find the longest palindromic subsequence's length in s. A subsequence is a sequence that can be derived from another sequence by deleting some or no elements without changing the order of the remaining elements.

examples.explanation: One possible longest palindromic subsequence is "bbbb".

constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters.
edgeCases: Single character: return 1
Already a palindrome: return len(s)
All unique characters: return 1
followUps: Can you solve this by finding the LCS between s and its reverse?

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: A subsequence is formed by deleting characters and keeping the rest in order, so the first plan that comes to mind is to enumerate all 2^N subsets of positions and test each one for being a palindrome. That is correct but hopeless for any real string, and it is unsatisfying for a deeper reason: it spends most of its effort on candidates that were never going to be palindromic, testing them only at the very end. The observation that turns the search into a series of small decisions is to look only at the two ends of a window s[i..j]. If s[i] == s[j], that pair can always serve as the outermost layer of the palindrome - there is never any advantage in throwing away a free matching pair - so the best answer is 2 + helper(i+1, j-1), the best answer for the shrunken window inside them. If the two characters differ, they cannot both be the endpoints of one palindrome, so at least one of them is useless in this window, and since we do not know which, we try both: helper(i+1, j) discards the left character, helper(i, j-1) discards the right, and the larger of the two wins. The recursion bottoms out on windows that are empty, i > j giving 0, or a single character, i == j giving 1 because one character is trivially a palindrome. The cost is O(2^N) time, because the mismatch case branches in two and the very same (i, j) window is re-solved along many different paths, with O(N) recursion depth - and it is exactly that overlap that memoising on (i, j) collapses into an O(N^2) dynamic program.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Define helper(i, j) where i and j are start and end pointers.
2. If i > j, return 0. If i == j, return 1.
3. If s[i] == s[j], return 2 + helper(i+1, j-1).
4. Else, return max(helper(i+1, j), helper(i, j-1)).

complexity.space: O(N)

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: Enumerating all 2^N subsets of positions spends nearly all of its effort building candidates that were never going to read the same both ways, and only discovers this at the very end, after the whole subsequence has been assembled. The waste is testing whole candidates instead of making one decision at a time. The observation: only the two ends of a window s[i..j] matter. If s[i] == s[j], that pair can serve as the outermost layer and the rest of the question is the identical question on the shorter window s[i+1..j-1], so dp[i][j] = dp[i+1][j-1] + 2. If they differ, both endpoints cannot appear in the same palindrome - the first and last characters of a palindrome must be equal - so at least one is excluded, giving max(dp[i+1][j], dp[i][j-1]). The subtle claim is the matching case: taking BOTH endpoints is always safe. Given any optimal palindrome inside s[i..j] that omits s[i], wrapping it in s[i] and s[j] makes it 2 longer, contradicting optimality; and if it uses s[i] but ends at some other copy of that character before j, moving that endpoint to index j keeps the same length. So an optimal solution using both ends always exists and nothing is lost. Windows are filled by increasing length because dp[i][j] reads only windows shorter by one or two, all already final. Cost: O(N^2) windows at O(1) each, so O(N^2) time and O(N^2) space for the table.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Let n = len(s) and allocate an n x n table dp filled with 0, where dp[i][j] will hold the answer for the window s[i..j] and only the cells with i <= j are ever meaningful.
2. Seed the diagonal: dp[i][i] = 1 for every i, since a single character is a palindrome of length 1.
3. Loop length from 2 up to n, so every window is computed only after all shorter windows are final - this ordering is what makes the reads in steps 5 and 6 safe.
4. For each length, loop the start index i from 0 to n - length, and set j = i + length - 1 as the window's end.
5. If s[i] == s[j], set dp[i][j] = dp[i+1][j-1] + 2. For length 2 this reads dp[i+1][i], a cell below the diagonal that was never written and is still 0, giving the correct answer of 2.
6. Otherwise set dp[i][j] = max(dp[i+1][j], dp[i][j-1]), dropping whichever endpoint helps less.
7. Return dp[0][n-1], the answer for the full string.
approaches.code:
def longestPalindromeSubseq(s: str) -> int:
    n = len(s)
    # dp[i][j] will store the LPS length for substring s[i..j]
    dp = [[0] * n for _ in range(n)]
    # Every single character is a palindrome of length 1
    for i in range(n):
        dp[i][i] = 1
    # Loop over substring lengths from 2 to n
    for length in range(2, n + 1):
        # Loop over all possible start indices
        for i in range(n - length + 1):
            j = i + length - 1
            # If boundary characters match
            if s[i] == s[j]:
                # Value is 2 + inner substring's LPS
                dp[i][j] = dp[i + 1][j - 1] + 2
            else:
                # Else, max of excluding left or excluding right
                dp[i][j] = max(dp[i + 1][j], dp[i][j - 1])
    # Return the answer for the full string
    return dp[0][n - 1]

Longest Palindromic Subsequence.tests:
# "bbbb" is the longest palindromic subsequence of "bbbab".
assert longestPalindromeSubseq("bbbab") == 4
# Only "bb" survives in "cbbd".
assert longestPalindromeSubseq("cbbd") == 2
# Edge case: a single character is a palindrome of length 1.
assert longestPalindromeSubseq("a") == 1
# Edge case: all characters distinct -> best is any single character.
assert longestPalindromeSubseq("abcde") == 1
prerequisites: The core insight: LPS(s) equals LCS(s, reverse(s)) — knowing that gives you a second, fully independent way to solve and to sanity-check the answer.
Interval DP: the state is a range dp[i][j] over s[i..j], and the table must be filled by increasing substring LENGTH (or by decreasing i) so the inner ranges are ready.
Matching ends give dp[i][j] = 2 + dp[i+1][j-1]; mismatching ends give max(dp[i+1][j], dp[i][j-1]) — you drop exactly one of the two offending characters.
Base case: every single character is a palindrome of length 1, so the entire main diagonal is initialised to 1.
Only the upper triangle (i <= j) is ever meaningful; cells with i > j stay 0 and conveniently supply the '2 + 0' answer for two adjacent matching characters.
Subsequence (delete, keep order) is not substring (contiguous) — the answer for 'bbab' is 3, not 2.

Edit Distance.problemStatement:
Given two strings word1 and word2, return the minimum number of operations required to convert word1 to word2. You have the following three operations permitted on a word:
1. Insert a character
2. Delete a character
3. Replace a character

examples.explanation:
horse -> rorse (replace 'h' with 'r')
rorse -> rose (remove 'r')
rose -> ros (remove 'e')

constraints: word1 and word2 consist of lowercase English letters.
edgeCases: One string is empty: return the length of the other string
Identical strings: return 0
followUps: Can you optimize the space complexity to O(min(M, N))?

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: Start with the only decision that is actually forced. Compare the last characters of the two remaining pieces: if `word1[i-1]` equals `word2[j-1]`, there is nothing sensible to do with that pair, since you would never pay an operation to turn a character into itself. Both strings shrink by one for free and the cost is simply whatever `helper(i-1, j-1)` returns. When they differ, no single move is obviously right, so the honest thing is to try all three permitted operations and let the cheapest one win: insert the character word2 wants, consuming one character of word2 via `helper(i, j-1)`; delete the offending character of word1 via `helper(i-1, j)`; or replace it, consuming one of each via `helper(i-1, j-1)`. Each of those costs 1 plus its sub-answer. The base cases drop out of the same reasoning: with `i == 0` nothing is left of word1 so only j insertions remain, and with `j == 0` only i deletions remain. What makes it unsatisfying is that the same `(i, j)` pair is reached along many different chains of operations and recomputed every single time, giving roughly O(3^(M+N)) time for only O(M+N) stack depth.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Define helper(i, j) where i and j are indices in word1 and word2.
2. If i == 0, return j (need to insert all remaining characters of word2).
3. If j == 0, return i (need to delete all remaining characters of word1).
4. If word1[i-1] == word2[j-1], return helper(i-1, j-1).
5. Else, return 1 + min(helper(i, j-1) [insert], helper(i-1, j) [delete], helper(i-1, j-1) [replace]).

complexity.space: O(M+N)

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: The recursion is not wrong, it is merely forgetful: `helper(3, 4)` is arrived at by many different sequences of operations and re-derives the identical answer each time. Notice how small the state actually is — a subproblem is described entirely by the pair `(i, j)`, meaning how much of word1 and how much of word2 is still left — so the whole problem contains only `(m+1) * (n+1)` distinct sub-answers. That count is the insight: there are few enough of them to store, so store them instead of recomputing them. Let `dp[i][j]` be the edit distance between the first i characters of word1 and the first j of word2. The base row and column are filled directly, `dp[i][0] = i` for the deletions and `dp[0][j] = j` for the insertions. Every other cell depends only on the three neighbours above, to the left, and diagonally up-left, so filling row by row with i and j both increasing guarantees those three are already final when they are read — that ordering is the loop invariant that lets an iterative table replace the recursion entirely. Cost: O(M*N) time and O(M*N) space, and `dp[m][n]` is the answer.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Initialize dp matrix of size (m+1) x (n+1).
2. Set dp[i][0] = i and dp[0][j] = j.
3. Loop i from 1 to m, and j from 1 to n.
4. If word1[i-1] == word2[j-1], dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1].
5. Else, dp[i][j] = 1 + min(dp[i][j-1], dp[i-1][j], dp[i-1][j-1]).
6. Return dp[m][n].

complexity.time: O(M * N)
complexity.space: O(M * N)

Edit Distance.tests:
# horse -> rorse -> rose -> ros costs 3 operations.
assert minDistance("horse", "ros") == 3
# sunday -> saturday needs 3 operations (2 inserts + 1 replace).
assert minDistance("sunday", "saturday") == 3
# Edge case: identical strings need no operations.
assert minDistance("abc", "abc") == 0
# Edge case: empty source means we insert every character of the target.
assert minDistance("", "abc") == 3
prerequisites: The three operations map onto three neighbouring cells: insert = dp[i][j-1], delete = dp[i-1][j], replace = dp[i-1][j-1] — memorising which is which prevents the classic off-by-one.
The state dp[i][j] is the distance between PREFIXES: the first i characters of word1 and the first j characters of word2.
Base row and column are not zeros: dp[i][0] = i (delete everything) and dp[0][j] = j (insert everything), and getting these wrong quietly breaks the whole table.
When the current characters match, the cost carries straight down the diagonal with no +1 — that free move is what makes long shared runs cheap.
This is the Levenshtein distance; the answer is symmetric (minDistance(a,b) == minDistance(b,a)) because insert and delete are mirror operations.
Space can be reduced to two rows of length n+1, since row i only reads row i-1 and the cell immediately to its left.

Distinct Subsequences.problemStatement: You are given two strings s and t, and you must count how many distinct subsequences of s are equal to t. A subsequence is what remains after deleting zero or more characters from s without reordering the ones you keep, so the chosen characters must appear in s in the same relative order as in t but need not be adjacent. Two subsequences count as different when the sets of positions chosen from s differ, even though the resulting strings are identical — that is why s = "rabbbit" and t = "rabbit" gives 3, one answer for each of the three b's that can be skipped. Return that count as an integer. If t cannot be formed at all the answer is 0, and the empty string t can always be formed in exactly one way.

examples.explanation: There are 3 ways to form 'rabbit' from 'rabbbit'.

constraints: s and t consist of English letters.
edgeCases: t is empty: return 1 (empty string is always a subsequence)
s is shorter than t: return 0
followUps: Can you solve this in O(N) space where N is the length of t?

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: The first idea most people have is to enumerate every subsequence of s and count the ones that spell t, but s of length n has 2^n subsequences and almost all of them are the wrong length, so nearly all that work is thrown away. The improvement is to build the match incrementally instead of generating candidates: keep a pointer i into s and a pointer j into t, and ask only 'in how many ways can s[i:] produce t[j:]?' Now the character s[i] presents a genuine fork, and seeing why both branches are needed is the heart of the problem. If s[i] != t[j] there is nothing to decide — s[i] can never be used here, so skip it. But if s[i] == t[j] you must count both worlds: the one where this occurrence is consumed to satisfy t[j], moving to helper(i+1, j+1), and the one where it is deliberately left out so that some later duplicate of the same character satisfies t[j] instead, moving to helper(i+1, j). Adding those two totals is precisely what makes the three b's of "rabbbit" count as three separate answers. The base cases anchor it: j == len(t) means all of t has been matched, which is one valid way, and running off the end of s with t unfinished contributes zero. Because both branches fire on every matching character, the recursion tree is exponential — O(2^n) time with O(n) recursion depth — and the identical (i, j) pairs it recomputes are exactly what memoisation later eliminates.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Define helper(i, j) where i is index in s and j is index in t.
2. If j == len(t), return 1.
3. If i == len(s), return 0.
4. If s[i] == t[j], return helper(i+1, j+1) + helper(i+1, j).
5. Else, return helper(i+1, j).
