complexity.space: O(M)

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition:
Generating all 2^n subsequences of s and keeping those spelling t throws away nearly every candidate on length alone. The pointer recurrence in the brute force fixes the generation but not the repetition: the same pair of positions in s and t is reached along exponentially many paths and recounted each time.

This code memoises that recurrence forwards, over PREFIXES. dp[j] holds the number of ways the characters of s consumed so far can spell t[0..j-1]. Processing one character `char` of s, the new dp[j] is the ways that ignore `char`, which is the old dp[j], plus the ways that spend `char` on t[j-1], which is the old dp[j-1] -- and only when char == t[j-1]. Both terms predate this character, so a single row of size len(t)+1 is enough.

Why the backwards loop is load-bearing, not a micro-optimisation: `dp[j] += dp[j-1]` must read dp[j-1] as it stood BEFORE this character. Running j from len(t) down to 1 updates each cell after its left neighbour has been read and before that neighbour is touched. Going forwards, an updated dp[j-1] would feed dp[j], letting one character of s match two positions of t at once and inflating the count. dp[0] = 1 anchors it: the empty prefix of t is spelled by exactly one subsequence, the empty one. Every valid subsequence is pinned by the s-position it uses for each character of t, each s-position is processed in exactly one outer iteration, so each is counted once.

Cost: O(M*N) time with M = len(s), N = len(t), and O(N) space -- one row instead of the full (M+1) x (N+1) table. The trade is that only counts survive, so which positions were chosen can no longer be reconstructed.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Allocate dp of len(t) + 1 zeros; dp[j] will count the ways to spell the prefix t[0..j-1].
2. Set dp[0] = 1: the empty prefix of t is spelled one way, by the empty subsequence.
3. For each character `char` of s, in order.
4. Loop j from len(t) down to 1, so dp[j-1] is still the value from before this character.
5. If char == t[j-1], do dp[j] += dp[j-1], adding the subsequences that end by matching t[j-1] with this occurrence.
6. Leave dp[j] untouched when the characters differ -- those counts already include the option of skipping `char`.
7. After all of s is consumed, return dp[len(t)].
approaches.code:
def numDistinct(s: str, t: str) -> int:
    m, n = len(s), len(t)
    # dp[j] will store ways to match prefix t[0..j-1]
    dp = [0] * (n + 1)
    # Empty prefix t[0..-1] is matched by 1 way (empty string)
    dp[0] = 1
    # Loop through each character of s
    for char in s:
        # Loop backwards through t to use values from previous state
        for j in range(n, 0, -1):
            # If characters match
            if char == t[j - 1]:
                # Add number of ways to form t[0..j-2]
                dp[j] += dp[j - 1]
    # Return the answer for matching entire t
    return dp[n]

complexity.time: O(M * N)
complexity.space: O(N)

Distinct Subsequences.tests:
# "rabbit" can be carved out of "rabbbit" in 3 distinct ways.
assert numDistinct("rabbbit", "rabbit") == 3
# "bag" appears as a subsequence of "babgbag" 5 times.
assert numDistinct("babgbag", "bag") == 5
# Edge case: target longer than source -> impossible.
assert numDistinct("a", "aa") == 0
# Edge case: the empty target is always matched exactly once.
assert numDistinct("abc", "") == 1
prerequisites: This is a COUNTING dp, not an optimisation one: you add the branches together instead of taking a max or a min.
When s[i] == t[j] you have two independent choices — use this character to match t[j], or deliberately skip it — and both counts must be summed.
The empty target is matched exactly one way (pick nothing), so dp[0] = 1; this base case is what seeds every other count.
Rolling the 2D table into 1D requires iterating j from n down to 1, so dp[j-1] still holds the count from BEFORE the current character of s was folded in.
Only the target index needs a dp slot — the source string is consumed one character at a time by the outer loop, which is why the array has n+1 entries.
Counts can grow very large; Python's arbitrary-precision ints handle this for free, but a fixed-width language would need a modulus.

Wildcard Matching.problemStatement:
Given an input string (s) and a pattern (p), implement wildcard pattern matching with support for '?' and '*' where:
- '?' Matches any single character.
- '*' Matches any sequence of characters (including the empty sequence).

examples.explanation: '*' matches any sequence.
'?' matches 'c', but 'a' does not match 'b'.

constraints: s contains only lowercase English letters.
p contains only lowercase English letters, '?' or '*'.
edgeCases: Both s and p empty: true
p is '*' only: true
p is all '*': true
followUps: Can you solve this with O(1) extra space using two pointers and backtracking?

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: A single left-to-right scan is the first thing anyone tries, and '*' is what breaks it. When you reach a '*' you simply cannot decide locally how many characters it ought to swallow, because the correct amount depends on what the rest of the pattern will demand later; matching greedily works on many inputs and then fails on something like s = 'aab', p = '*b', where the greedy star eats everything and leaves 'b' unmatched. The observation that rescues correctness is to refuse to guess: make the choice explicit and try both branches. At a '*', either it absorbs the current character s[i], which means advancing i while keeping j parked on the star so it can absorb more, or it stops absorbing right here, which means advancing j past the star and leaving i alone. Everything else is forced, with no decision to make: '?' or an exact character match consumes one symbol on each side, and any other character mismatch kills the branch. Two base cases close it off, one for the pattern running out (only an equally exhausted string matches) and one for the string running out (only remaining stars can still succeed). It is correct but explores every possible way to split the string among the stars, giving O(2^(M+N)) time and O(M+N) recursion depth. Notice that the same pair (i, j) is reached over and over along different branches, and that repetition is the direct hint that memoisation or a DP table comes next.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Define helper(i, j).
2. If j == len(p), return i == len(s).
3. If i == len(s), return p[j] == '*' and helper(i, j+1).
4. If p[j] == '*', return helper(i+1, j) or helper(i, j+1).
5. If p[j] == '?' or p[j] == s[i], return helper(i+1, j+1).
6. Else return false.
approaches.code:
def isMatch(s: str, p: str) -> bool:  # '?' matches one char, '*' matches any run of chars
    # the helper explores every way '*' can split s
    def helper(i, j):  # i is the read head into s, j the read head into p
        # pattern exhausted: only a used-up string can match
        if j == len(p):  # no pattern symbols are left to consume
            return i == len(s)  # leftover string characters mean this branch fails
        # string exhausted: only '*' can still match nothing
        if i == len(s):  # s is used up but the pattern still has symbols
            return p[j] == '*' and helper(i, j + 1)  # each trailing '*' may absorb the empty string
        # the branching line: '*' either eats a char or ends
        if p[j] == '*':  # this single choice is the whole exponential blowup
            return helper(i + 1, j) or helper(i, j + 1)  # eat s[i] and keep '*', or drop '*' and move on
        # '?' matches any single char, so treat it as equal
        if p[j] == '?' or s[i] == p[j]:  # exactly one character is consumed on both sides
            return helper(i + 1, j + 1)  # advance both heads; there is no choice to make here
        return False  # plain characters differ, so this branch dies
    return helper(0, 0)  # kick things off with both read heads at the front

complexity.space: O(M+N)

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: Branching at each '*' - try absorbing this character, else try matching empty - is correct and pays for every guess forever, re-exploring the same (position in s, position in p) pair down many different branches; with k stars the work explodes exponentially. What that search never notices is that the stars do not need to be remembered independently. Only the newest one matters. If a mismatch happens after some '*', there is no reason to go back and stretch an older star: the newest star lies between that older one and the mismatch, so any character an older star would have swallowed can be swallowed by the newest one instead, reaching the same outcome. That collapses the whole search tree into four integers - `star_idx` for the most recent '*', `match_idx` for how much of s it currently absorbs, plus the two read heads. On a mismatch, rewind `p_idx = star_idx + 1`, let the star eat one more character with `match_idx += 1`, and restart at `s_idx = match_idx`. Nothing is skipped, because the star begins absorbing zero characters and grows by exactly one per failure, so every possible length is tried in increasing order and the shortest workable one is found; the literal and '?' symbols between stars can only sit in one place, so growing the newest star never invalidates a prefix already matched. Cost, per the stated bounds: O(N * M) worst case and O(N + M) typical, in O(1) extra memory rather than the DP table's O(N * M).
approaches.algorithm:
1. Cache `s_len, p_len = len(s), len(p)`, then initialise the read heads `s_idx = 0` and `p_idx = 0`, plus `star_idx = -1` (no '*' seen yet) and `match_idx = 0` (how much of s the current '*' is absorbing).
2. Loop `while s_idx < s_len`, so the walk ends only once every character of s has been accounted for.
3. Case 1, a direct hit: if `p_idx < p_len and (p[p_idx] == '?' or p[p_idx] == s[s_idx])`, advance both `s_idx += 1` and `p_idx += 1`. The `p_idx < p_len` guard comes first so the indexing never overruns the pattern.
4. Case 2, meeting a star: else if `p_idx < p_len and p[p_idx] == '*'`, do not branch. Record `star_idx = p_idx` and `match_idx = s_idx`, then `p_idx += 1`, tentatively assuming the star matches zero characters.
5. Case 3, mismatch with a star to fall back on: else if `star_idx != -1`, rewind by setting `p_idx = star_idx + 1`, incrementing `match_idx += 1` so the star swallows one more character, and restarting with `s_idx = match_idx`. `star_idx` is always the most recent '*' and `match_idx` marks the boundary of what it absorbs - that pair is what lets the backtrack cost O(1) instead of a recursive call.
6. Case 4, mismatch with nothing to fall back on: else return False, since no earlier '*' exists to stretch.
7. After the loop, s is fully consumed, so skip any trailing stars with `while p_idx < p_len and p[p_idx] == '*': p_idx += 1`, because each of them matches the empty string.
8. Return `p_idx == p_len`, which is True only if the pattern was entirely consumed as well.
approaches.code:
def isMatch(s: str, p: str) -> bool:  # greedy two pointers that backtrack to the last '*'
    s_len, p_len = len(s), len(p)  # cached lengths keep the loop conditions cheap
    s_idx, p_idx = 0, 0  # read heads walking s and p respectively
    star_idx = -1  # position of the newest '*'; -1 means none seen yet
    match_idx = 0  # how much of s that '*' is currently absorbing
    # walk s left to right; p moves only when it matches
    while s_idx < s_len:  # ends once every character of s is accounted for
        # case 1: characters line up, or '?' accepts anything
        if p_idx < p_len and (p[p_idx] == '?' or p[p_idx] == s[s_idx]):  # check p_idx first or the indexing would overrun p
            s_idx += 1  # consume one character from the string
            p_idx += 1  # and one symbol from the pattern
        # case 2: a '*' tentatively matches zero characters
        elif p_idx < p_len and p[p_idx] == '*':  # do not branch; just remember where to come back to
            star_idx = p_idx  # save the '*' so we can retry it with a longer match
            match_idx = s_idx  # the s position where this '*' began absorbing
            p_idx += 1  # step past '*' assuming it matched nothing so far
        # case 3: mismatch, but an earlier '*' can stretch
        elif star_idx != -1:  # the core trick: rewind cheaply instead of recursing
            p_idx = star_idx + 1  # resume the pattern right after that saved '*'
            match_idx += 1  # let the '*' swallow one more character of s
            s_idx = match_idx  # restart the string scan from the new boundary
        # case 4: mismatch with no '*' to fall back on
        else:  # there is nothing left to backtrack to
            return False  # this pattern can never match this string
    # s is done; only trailing '*' may remain in p
    while p_idx < p_len and p[p_idx] == '*':  # each trailing '*' happily matches the empty string
        p_idx += 1  # skip it and inspect the next pattern symbol
    return p_idx == p_len  # true only if the pattern was fully consumed

complexity.time: O(N * M) worst case, O(N + M) average

Wildcard Matching.tests:
# '*' can absorb any run of characters, so "*a*b" matches "adceb".
assert isMatch("adceb", "*a*b") is True
# No wildcard can rescue a plain length mismatch.
assert isMatch("aa", "a") is False
# '?' matches exactly one character, so "?a" cannot match "cb".
assert isMatch("cb", "?a") is False
# Edge case: an empty string is matched by a pattern of only stars.
assert isMatch("", "**") is True
# Edge case: an empty pattern matches only the empty string.
assert isMatch("abc", "") is False
prerequisites: The two wildcards behave very differently: '?' consumes exactly one character, while '*' can consume zero or more, and only '*' creates branching.
The DP formulation: dp[i][j] = does s[0..i-1] match p[0..j-1], with dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j] or dp[i][j-1] when p[j-1] == '*' (star eats one more character, or eats nothing).
The greedy two-pointer alternative works because you only ever need to reconsider the MOST RECENT '*': remembering star_idx and match_idx is enough to retry with the star eating one more character.
star_idx = -1 is the sentinel for 'no star seen yet' — in that state a mismatch is immediately fatal and you return False.
After the string is exhausted the pattern may still have trailing '*' characters, which match the empty string, so a final cleanup loop must skip them before comparing p_idx to p_len.
Empty inputs are legal: an empty pattern matches only the empty string, and a pattern of only stars matches everything including ''.

Longest Increasing Subsequence.problemStatement: You are given an integer array `nums`. A subsequence is any sequence you can obtain by deleting zero or more elements from `nums` without reordering the ones you keep -- so the kept elements must stay in their original left-to-right order, but they need not be adjacent. A subsequence is strictly increasing when every element is strictly greater than the one before it; equal neighbours are not allowed. Return the LENGTH of the longest strictly increasing subsequence that `nums` contains -- just the number, not the subsequence itself. For example, in [10,9,2,5,3,7,101,18] one longest choice is [2,3,7,101], so the answer is 4. An empty input yields 0, and an array that never rises has answer 1 because any single element counts as an increasing subsequence of length one.

examples.explanation: The longest increasing subsequence is [2, 3, 7, 101], therefore the length is 4.

edgeCases: Empty list (handled by constraints)
All elements sorted descending: return 1
All identical elements: return 1
followUps: Can you solve it in O(N log N) time complexity?

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: Every subsequence is the result of a take-or-skip decision at each index, so the most direct plan is to explore both decisions everywhere. The only thing that constrains a future 'take' is the value we most recently took, so that single number is all the state we need to carry: solve(i, prev) answers 'what is the best I can still build from index i onward, given that the last chosen value was prev'. Skipping is always allowed; taking is allowed only when nums[i] > prev, and then nums[i] becomes the new prev. Starting with prev = negative infinity makes the very first element always takeable. Correct and easy to believe, but the two branches per index give 2^n calls.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Define solve(i, prev) = the LIS length obtainable from index i onward when the previously taken value was prev.
2. Base case: when i reaches n, return 0 because there is nothing left to decide.
3. Always compute option A, skipping nums[i]: solve(i + 1, prev).
4. If nums[i] > prev, also compute option B, taking it: 1 + solve(i + 1, nums[i]).
5. Return the maximum of the available options.
6. Kick the recursion off with solve(0, float('-inf')) so no element is blocked at the start.
approaches.code:
def lengthOfLIS(nums: List[int]) -> int:
    n = len(nums)                                   # how many numbers we must decide about
    # Brute force: at every index make a TAKE / SKIP decision, remembering only the
    # value we most recently took, because that is the sole constraint on the next take.
    def solve(i: int, prev: int) -> int:
        if i == n:                                  # every index has been decided
            return 0                                # an empty tail adds nothing
        best = solve(i + 1, prev)                   # option A: SKIP nums[i] entirely
        # Option B is legal only if nums[i] keeps the subsequence strictly increasing.
        if nums[i] > prev:
            best = max(best, 1 + solve(i + 1, nums[i]))   # TAKE it and become the new 'prev'
        return best                                 # the better of the two decisions
    # -infinity as the starting 'prev' means the very first element is always takeable.
    return solve(0, float('-inf'))

complexity.time: O(2^N) — two branches at every index with nothing memoized.
complexity.space: O(N) — the recursion stack is at most N frames deep.

approaches.name: Better (O(N^2) Dynamic Programming)
approaches.intuition: The recursion keeps re-deriving the same sub-answers, so flip it into a table. Define dp[i] as the length of the longest increasing subsequence whose LAST element is nums[i]. Anchoring the definition at the ending index is the key move, because then dp[i] depends only on earlier indices: look back at every j < i, and if nums[j] < nums[i] then the chain ending at j can be extended by nums[i], giving a candidate of dp[j] + 1. Every element alone is a valid chain, so dp starts at 1 everywhere. The final answer is the maximum over the whole table rather than the last cell, because the best subsequence may end at any position. This is quadratic instead of exponential and is the version most interviewers want to see before the binary-search trick.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Handle the empty array up front by returning 0.
2. Create dp = [1] * n, since a single element is always an increasing subsequence of length 1.
3. For each index i from 0 to n - 1, scan every earlier index j < i.
4. Whenever nums[j] < nums[i], update dp[i] = max(dp[i], dp[j] + 1).
5. After both loops, return max(dp) because the longest chain can end at any index.
approaches.code:
def lengthOfLIS(nums: List[int]) -> int:
    n = len(nums)                                   # number of elements
    if n == 0:                                      # no elements means no subsequence
        return 0                                    # so the answer is 0
    # Better: define dp[i] = length of the longest increasing subsequence that ENDS at i.
    dp = [1] * n                                    # every element alone is a valid LIS of 1
    for i in range(n):                              # decide dp[i] using only earlier indices
        for j in range(i):                          # look back at every j before i
            # nums[i] can extend the chain ending at j only if it is strictly larger.
            if nums[j] < nums[i]:
                dp[i] = max(dp[i], dp[j] + 1)       # hang i behind the best such j
    # The LIS may finish at ANY index, so the answer is the maximum over the whole table.
    return max(dp)

complexity.time: O(N^2) — every pair (j, i) with j < i is examined once.
complexity.space: O(N) — a single dp array of length N.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: The natural first solution is the O(N^2) dynamic program: for every index i, look back at every earlier index j and extend the best chain ending at a smaller value. It is easy to reason about, but that backward scan re-examines the entire prefix for each element, and at N = 100000 the quadratic cost is fatal. The unlock is to stop tracking a best answer per index and instead track, for each possible chain LENGTH, the smallest value that can sit at the end of a chain of that length. Call that list `tails`, so `tails[k]` is the smallest possible final element of an increasing subsequence of length k+1. Why is that the right thing to store? Because when you are deciding whether a future number can extend a chain, the only fact about the chain that matters is its last value -- and a smaller last value is never worse, since anything that could extend a chain ending in 9 can also extend one ending in 3. Two properties follow. First, `tails` is automatically sorted in increasing order, because a longer chain must end at a value at least as large as the best ending of a shorter one. Second, since it is sorted, a binary search places each new value x in O(log N): if x is greater than every tail it extends the longest chain and gets appended, growing the answer by one; otherwise it replaces the first tail that is greater than or equal to it, quietly making some length cheaper to achieve later. One pass, a binary search per element, O(N log N) time and O(N) space. Be honest about the trade: the contents of `tails` are not necessarily a real subsequence of `nums`, so only its LENGTH is meaningful -- which is exactly what the problem asks for.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Create an empty list `tails`; the invariant carried through the whole loop is that `tails[k]` holds the smallest possible last value among all increasing subsequences of length k+1 seen so far, and that `tails` is therefore always sorted ascending.
2. Iterate over the input once, taking each value `x` in `nums` in order.
3. Call `bisect.bisect_left(tails, x)` to binary search the sorted `tails` for the leftmost position `idx` where `x` could be inserted -- that is, the index of the first tail value that is greater than or equal to `x`.
4. If `idx == len(tails)`, then `x` is strictly larger than every existing tail, so append `x` to `tails`: the longest achievable chain just grew by one.
5. Otherwise overwrite `tails[idx] = x`, replacing an equal-or-larger tail with this smaller one; the length represented by that slot is unchanged but is now easier to extend later.
6. After the pass finishes, return `len(tails)`, which is the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence.
approaches.code:
import bisect  # binary search over the always-sorted tails list

def lengthOfLIS(nums: List[int]) -> int:
    tails = []  # tails[k] = smallest possible last value of a length-(k+1) chain
    
    for x in nums:  # a single left-to-right pass over the input
        # Binary search to find candidate slot
        idx = bisect.bisect_left(tails, x)
        # If it is larger than all elements in tails, append it
        if idx == len(tails):  # x beats every tail, so the longest chain can grow
            tails.append(x)  # the answer length increases by one
        else:  # otherwise x fits somewhere inside the existing tails
            # Replace tails value with smaller candidate
            tails[idx] = x
            
    return len(tails)  # only the LENGTH is guaranteed; tails may not be a real LIS

complexity.time: O(N log N)
complexity.space: O(N) tails capacity

Longest Increasing Subsequence.tests:
assert lengthOfLIS([10, 9, 2, 5, 3, 7, 101, 18]) == 4
assert lengthOfLIS([0, 1, 0, 3, 2, 3]) == 4
assert lengthOfLIS([7, 7, 7, 7, 7, 7, 7]) == 1     # edge: equal values are NOT increasing
assert lengthOfLIS([]) == 0                        # edge: empty input has length 0
assert lengthOfLIS([5]) == 1
assert lengthOfLIS([5, 4, 3, 2, 1]) == 1           # edge: strictly decreasing input
prerequisites: "Strictly increasing" means equal values cannot both be used, so [7,7,7] has an LIS of length 1 — this decides whether you use bisect_left or bisect_right.
The O(n^2) DP defines dp[i] as the LIS length ENDING at index i; the answer is max(dp), not dp[-1], because the best chain may finish anywhere.
The patience-sorting idea: tails[k] is the SMALLEST possible last value among all increasing subsequences of length k+1 — keeping it small leaves the most room to extend later.
`tails` is always sorted, which is exactly why binary search applies; `bisect.bisect_left(tails, x)` returns the first index whose value is >= x.
Overwriting tails[idx] never shortens the answer, it only improves a future option — so len(tails) never decreases and ends up equal to the LIS length.
Important caveat: the final `tails` list is NOT necessarily an actual increasing subsequence of the input; only its LENGTH is guaranteed correct.

Largest Divisible Subset.problemStatement:
Given a set of distinct positive integers nums, return the largest subset answer such that every pair (answer[i], answer[j]) of elements in this subset satisfies:
- answer[i] % answer[j] == 0, or
- answer[j] % answer[i] == 0
If there are multiple solutions, return any of them.

examples.explanation: [1, 3] is also accepted.

constraints: All the integers in nums are unique.
edgeCases: Single element: return itself
No elements are divisible: return any single element
followUps: Can you solve it without sorting first?

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: The condition looks awkward at first, since every pair inside the answer must divide one way or the other, and verifying all pairs of an arbitrary subset is expensive. Sorting the numbers ascending is what tames it: in sorted order, if you build the subset left to right and each new number is divisible by the one added immediately before it, then divisibility against every earlier member comes for free, because divisibility is transitive, so c % b == 0 and b % a == 0 together force c % a == 0. The whole pairwise requirement therefore collapses into a single check against last_val, the most recently taken element. With that, the problem becomes a plain include-or-exclude search: at index idx you either skip nums[idx] and keep last_val unchanged, or, when nums[idx] % last_val == 0, take it and continue with last_val set to nums[idx]. The sentinel last_val = 1 for the very first pick works because every positive integer is divisible by 1, so nothing is wrongly excluded at the start. Each call returns the longer of its two branches, and the base case at idx == len(nums) returns the empty list. It is easy to trust but it explores two branches per element, so it is O(2^N) time with O(N) recursion depth, which is why a DP that tabulates the longest chain ending at each index replaces it.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Sort nums.
2. Define helper(idx, last_val).
3. If idx == len(nums), return [].
4. Option 1: skip = helper(idx+1, last_val).
5. Option 2: if nums[idx] % last_val == 0, take = [nums[idx]] + helper(idx+1, nums[idx]).
6. Return the longer of skip and take.
approaches.code:
def largestDivisibleSubset(nums: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    # Sort numbers first to facilitate divisibility check
    nums.sort()
    # Recursive helper
    def helper(idx, last_val):
        # Base Case: no numbers left
        if idx == len(nums):
            return []
        # Skip current number
        skip = helper(idx + 1, last_val)
        take = []
        # Take current number if it's divisible by the last value
        if last_val == 1 or nums[idx] % last_val == 0:
            take = [nums[idx]] + helper(idx + 1, nums[idx])
        # Return the larger subset
        return take if len(take) > len(skip) else skip
    return helper(0, 1)

complexity.space: O(N)

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition:
Enumerating subsets and pair-checking each is exponential; sorting makes each check cheap but still rebuilds chains sharing long prefixes from scratch.

Once sorted, a valid subset is a chain in which each element is divisible by the one before it -- the shape of longest increasing subsequence, with divisibility as the ordering. Let dp[i] be the length of the best chain ending at nums[i]: every j < i with nums[i] % nums[j] == 0 offers to extend its chain, the longest offer wins, and each prefix is solved once and reused.

Testing the immediate predecessor alone suffices because divisibility is transitive and the array ascends: every earlier member of j's chain divides nums[j], which divides nums[i]. Nothing valid is lost, since the inner loop offers every j < i. dp yields a length only, so parent[i] records which j was used; walking parent back from max_idx to -1 (the chain-start marker) rebuilds the members, reversed into ascending order.

O(N^2) pair tests plus an O(N log N) sort, O(N) space. The input is reordered, and one longest subset comes back when several tie.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Sort `nums` ascending so divisibility only ever needs testing from a smaller index to a larger one.
2. Initialise `dp = [1] * n` (every element is a chain of one) and `parent = [-1] * n`, with `max_idx = 0`.
3. For each i from 1 to n-1, scan every j < i.
4. If `nums[i] % nums[j] == 0` and `dp[j] + 1 > dp[i]`, set `dp[i] = dp[j] + 1` and `parent[i] = j`.
5. After finishing i's inner loop, if `dp[i] > dp[max_idx]`, update `max_idx = i`.
6. Reconstruct: start `curr = max_idx`, append `nums[curr]`, and follow `curr = parent[curr]` until it is -1.
7. Reverse the collected list and return it.
approaches.code:
def largestDivisibleSubset(nums: list[int]) -> list[int]:  # every pair in the answer must divide one another
    # sorting makes divisibility one-directional here
    nums.sort()  # after sorting we only test nums[i] % nums[j], j < i
    n = len(nums)  # cached length used by both dp loops below
    # dp[i] = size of the best subset ending at nums[i]
    dp = [1] * n  # every element on its own is already a valid subset
    # parent[i] remembers who came before i in that subset
    parent = [-1] * n  # -1 marks a chain start and stops the walk-back
    max_idx = 0  # index where the globally longest chain ends
    # LIS-shaped O(n^2) scan, with divisibility as the order
    for i in range(1, n):  # index 0 keeps dp = 1 since nothing precedes it
        for j in range(i):  # consider every smaller element as a predecessor
            # divisible by the smaller one and a strictly longer chain
            if nums[i] % nums[j] == 0 and dp[i] < dp[j] + 1:  # sortedness makes this one check enough for the whole set
                dp[i] = dp[j] + 1  # extend j's best chain by this element
                parent[i] = j  # record the link so we can walk backwards later
        # track the winner as we go, avoiding a second pass
        if dp[i] > dp[max_idx]:  # strict > keeps the earliest of the longest chains
            max_idx = i  # new best endpoint to reconstruct from
    # walk the parent chain back from the best endpoint
    res = []  # collects the subset in reverse order
    curr = max_idx  # start at the tail of the longest chain
    while curr != -1:  # a -1 parent means we reached the chain's first element
        res.append(nums[curr])  # append values by following links, not positions
        curr = parent[curr]  # hop to the predecessor recorded during the dp
    # we collected from tail back to head, so reverse it
    return res[::-1]  # ascending order, matching the sorted input

complexity.space: O(N)

Largest Divisible Subset.tests:
def _check(nums, expected_len):
    original = list(nums)
    res = largestDivisibleSubset(list(nums))
    # the answer must be a real sub-multiset of the input
    assert sorted(res) == sorted(set(res)), "no duplicates allowed"
    assert all(v in original for v in res), "returned values must come from nums"
    # every pair must divide one another (sorting makes it a chain check)
    chain = sorted(res)
    for a, b in zip(chain, chain[1:]):
        assert b % a == 0, "pair is not divisible"
    assert len(res) == expected_len
    return res

# [1,2,4,8] is a full divisibility chain.
_check([1, 2, 4, 8], 4)
# Only chains of size 2 exist here (e.g. [1,2] or [1,3]).
_check([1, 2, 3], 2)
# Unsorted input with a chain 1 -> 3 -> 9 -> 18.
_check([9, 18, 54, 90, 108, 180, 360, 540, 720], 6)
# Edge case: a single element is trivially its own largest subset.
assert largestDivisibleSubset([7]) == [7]
prerequisites: Divisibility is transitive on a sorted list: if a divides b and b divides c then a divides c, so checking each new element only against its chosen predecessor is enough for the whole set to be pairwise divisible.
Sorting ascending is mandatory — it turns 'every pair divides' into 'each element divides the next', which is exactly a Longest Increasing Subsequence shape.
This is LIS with the comparison nums[i] > nums[j] replaced by nums[i] % nums[j] == 0; recognising the template gives you the O(n^2) solution immediately.
Returning the actual subset (not just its size) requires a parent[] array recording which index each element chained onto, plus the index where the best chain ends.
Reconstruction walks parent pointers backwards from max_idx until it hits the -1 sentinel, so the collected list must be reversed before returning.
Unlike plain LIS, this problem has no O(n log n) trick — the divisibility relation is not a total order, so the O(n^2) scan is the intended solution.

Longest String Chain.problemStatement: You are given an array of words where each word consists of lowercase English letters. wordA is a predecessor of wordB if and only if we can insert exactly one letter anywhere in wordA without changing the order of the other characters to make it equal to wordB. Return the length of the longest possible word chain.

examples.explanation: One of the longest word chains is ["a","ba","bda","bdca"] which has length 4.

constraints: words[i] consists of only lowercase English letters.
edgeCases: Single word: return 1
All words same length: return 1
followUps: Can you solve this using a Trie to match predecessors?

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: A chain is built by repeatedly inserting exactly one letter, so every step raises the word length by exactly 1 — which means a chain, listed in order, has strictly increasing lengths. Sorting words by length makes that structure visible and is the key enabler here: any successor of a word must live later in the sorted array, so the search only ever moves rightwards and can never revisit or loop. The other half of the problem is checking a single step cheaply. "w1 becomes w2 by inserting one letter" sounds like it requires trying every insertion position, but once you know the lengths differ by exactly one it is simply asking whether w1 is a subsequence of w2 — so walk both with two pointers, advancing j through w2 on every character and advancing i through w1 only on a match, and w1 qualifies when i reaches its end. What makes this the brute-force version is helper(idx): it explores every chain starting at idx from scratch, and since many different chains pass through the same word, the identical subtree of work is recomputed over and over, which is where the exponential blow-up comes from. Memoising on idx removes exactly that repetition.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Sort words by length.
2. Define isPredecessor(w1, w2).
3. Define helper(idx).
4. Loop i from idx+1 to N: if isPredecessor(words[idx], words[i]), count = 1 + helper(i).
5. Return max count.
approaches.code:
def longestStrChain(words: list[str]) -> int:  # chain: each word made by inserting one letter
    # predecessor test: w1 becomes w2 by adding one char
    def isPredecessor(w1, w2):  # order matters, w1 must be the shorter word
        if len(w2) != len(w1) + 1:  # exactly one insertion, so lengths differ by one
            return False  # any other length gap can never be a chain step
        i, j = 0, 0  # i walks w1, j walks w2 as a subsequence check
        while i < len(w1) and j < len(w2):  # stop as soon as either word runs out of letters
            if w1[i] == w2[j]:  # matched character, so consume it from w1 as well
                i += 1  # i advances only on a match; j advances every time
            j += 1  # j is the read head that skips the inserted letter
        return i == len(w1)  # true when all of w1 was found in order inside w2
    
    # sorting by length puts every predecessor first
    words.sort(key=len)  # after this, a chain can only ever move rightwards
    n = len(words)  # cached count used by both loops below
    # longest chain that starts at index idx
    def helper(idx):  # recomputed from scratch, no memo, hence exponential
        max_len = 1  # the word itself is always a chain of length one
        for i in range(idx + 1, n):  # only later words can be longer, thanks to the sort
            if isPredecessor(words[idx], words[i]):  # words[i] extends the chain by exactly one letter
                max_len = max(max_len, 1 + helper(i))  # count this word, then the best chain onward from i
        return max_len  # best chain length that starts right here
        
    ans = 0  # global best across every possible starting word
    for i in range(n):  # any word could be the head of the longest chain
        ans = max(ans, helper(i))  # the repeated work here is why this is brute force
    return ans  # length of the longest chain we managed to build

complexity.space: O(N)

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition:
Sorting by length exposes the structure, but the natural follow-up wastes it: for each word, scan every earlier word to test whether it is a predecessor. That is O(N^2) pair tests, nearly all failing.

The observation: reverse the question. Instead of asking which of the N earlier words is a predecessor, generate the predecessors outright. A predecessor is the word with one character deleted, so there are only L - "bcad" yields "cad", "bad", "bcd", "bca" - each a hash-map lookup.

Why no chain is missed: deleting one character is the complete definition of a predecessor, so those L strings are all of them. Sorting by length means every word one character shorter already holds its final dp value, so dp[word] = 1 + best predecessor is built from finished numbers. Equal-length words never link, since a chain step changes length by exactly 1, so order inside a length group is irrelevant.

Cost: O(N log N) sorting, then N words times L deletions times O(L) per candidate - O(N * L^2) time, O(N) space. The trade is L strings allocated per word, and a result that is a length, not the chain.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Sort `words` in place by length ascending, so every candidate predecessor is processed before the word that could extend it.
2. Create an empty dict `dp` mapping a word to the longest chain ending at that word, and set `max_chain = 0`.
3. For each `word` in the sorted order, start `current_max = 1` - the word alone is a chain of length 1.
4. For each position i in the word, build `predecessor = word[:i] + word[i+1:]`, the word with character i deleted.
5. If that predecessor is a key in `dp`, set `current_max = max(current_max, dp[predecessor] + 1)`.
6. Store `dp[word] = current_max` and update `max_chain = max(max_chain, current_max)`.
7. Return `max_chain`.
approaches.code:
def longestStrChain(words: list[str]) -> int:
    # Sort words by their length
    words.sort(key=len)
    # dp map to store word -> longest chain length
    dp = {}
    max_chain = 0
    # Iterate through sorted words
    for word in words:
        current_max = 1
        # Generate all possible predecessor words by deleting one character
        for i in range(len(word)):
            predecessor = word[:i] + word[i+1:]
            # If predecessor was seen, update current word's chain length
            if predecessor in dp:
                current_max = max(current_max, dp[predecessor] + 1)
        # Store the max chain length for current word
        dp[word] = current_max
        # Update global max chain length
        max_chain = max(max_chain, current_max)
    # Return the longest string chain found
    return max_chain

complexity.time: O(N * L^2) where L is max word length
complexity.space: O(N)

Longest String Chain.tests:
# a -> ba -> bda -> bdca is a chain of length 4.
assert longestStrChain(["a", "b", "ba", "bca", "bda", "bdca"]) == 4
# xb -> xbc -> cxbc -> pcxbc -> pcxbcf is a chain of length 5.
assert longestStrChain(["xbc", "pcxbcf", "xb", "cxbc", "pcxbc"]) == 5
# Edge case: no word is a predecessor of another -> chain of 1.
assert longestStrChain(["abcd", "dbqca"]) == 1
# Edge case: a single word is a chain of length 1.
assert longestStrChain(["a"]) == 1
prerequisites: A predecessor is always exactly one character shorter, so sorting the words by length guarantees every predecessor is processed before the word that extends it.
The clever inversion: instead of testing every pair (O(n^2) comparisons), generate each word's <=16 possible predecessors by deleting one character and look them up in a hash map.
Python string slicing makes the deletion a one-liner: word[:i] + word[i+1:] removes the character at index i.
dp[word] means 'longest chain ENDING at this word', which starts at 1 (the word alone) and improves to dp[predecessor] + 1 whenever a predecessor exists.
Dict lookups are O(1) on average, which is what turns the whole algorithm into O(n * L^2) — L for the deletions, another L for building each sliced string.
The chain does not need contiguous words from the input, and words of equal length can never chain to each other.

Bitonic Subsequence.problemStatement: Given an array of positive integers nums, find the maximum length of a Bitonic Subsequence. A subsequence is bitonic if it is first strictly increasing and then strictly decreasing. Note that a strictly increasing or strictly decreasing sequence is also bitonic.

examples.explanation: The longest bitonic subsequence is [1, 2, 4, 5, 2, 1] of length 6.

edgeCases: Strictly increasing: return length of LIS
Strictly decreasing: return length of LDS
Identical elements: return 1
followUps: Can you solve this in O(N log N) time using binary search LIS technique twice?

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: A bitonic subsequence rises and then falls, and the difficulty is that those two halves interact: making the rising part longer might force the falling part to start from an awkward value. Trying to build both at once is where beginners stall. The decoupling observation is that every bitonic sequence has a single highest element -- its PEAK -- and once you fix which index is the peak, the two halves stop interfering. To the left of the peak you just want the longest increasing subsequence, to the right you just want the longest decreasing subsequence, and neither choice constrains the other beyond the peak itself. So loop over every index i, let it be the peak, and add the two answers together, subtracting 1 because the peak gets counted once by each half. What makes this the brute force is how each half is computed: rather than a table, `get_lis` and `get_lds` are plain take-or-skip recursions. At each index they branch twice -- skip this element, or take it if it respects the ordering relative to `prev_idx`, the last element already chosen -- and return the better of the two. Note that `get_lis` walks LEFTWARD from the peak, which is why its ordering test reads `nums[idx] < nums[prev_idx]`: scanning backwards, each newly taken element must be smaller than the one to its right for the sequence to be increasing when read forwards. `get_lds` is the mirror image walking rightward. The branching costs O(2^N) per call and it runs for all n peaks, so it is purely a way to make the structure of the answer obvious before memoising the two halves into O(N^2) DP tables.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Record `n = len(nums)` and initialise `max_len = 0`, which will hold the best bitonic length found over all candidate peaks.
2. Define `get_lis(idx, prev_idx)`, which explores the array leftwards from `idx`: return 0 when `idx < 0`, otherwise compute `skip = get_lis(idx - 1, prev_idx)` for the branch that ignores `nums[idx]`.
3. Inside `get_lis`, allow the take branch only when `prev_idx == -1` (nothing chosen yet) or `nums[idx] < nums[prev_idx]`, setting `take = 1 + get_lis(idx - 1, idx)` so `idx` becomes the new `prev_idx`; return `max(skip, take)`. The invariant is that the chosen elements always increase when read left to right.
4. Define the mirror helper `get_lds(idx, prev_idx)`, which walks rightwards: return 0 when `idx == n`, compute `skip = get_lds(idx + 1, prev_idx)`, and allow `take = 1 + get_lds(idx + 1, idx)` under the same `prev_idx == -1 or nums[idx] < nums[prev_idx]` test, so the kept elements strictly descend; return `max(skip, take)`.
5. Loop `i` from 0 to n-1, treating each index as the peak of the mountain.
6. For each peak, evaluate `get_lis(i, -1) + get_lds(i, -1) - 1`, where `-1` seeds `prev_idx` as "nothing chosen yet" and the `- 1` cancels the double count of the peak, then fold it into `max_len` with `max`.
7. After every peak has been tried, return `max_len`.
approaches.code:
def LongestBitonicSequence(nums: list[int]) -> int:  # bitonic = strictly rising, then strictly falling
    n = len(nums)  # shared by both recursive helpers below
    # longest rising run over the prefix up to idx
    def get_lis(idx, prev_idx):  # prev_idx is the element already chosen to the right
        if idx < 0:  # we walked off the left end of the array
            return 0  # an empty stretch contributes no elements
        skip = get_lis(idx - 1, prev_idx)  # option A: ignore nums[idx] and keep scanning left
        take = 0  # stays 0 when taking it would break the ordering
        if prev_idx == -1 or nums[idx] < nums[prev_idx]:  # we scan leftwards, so smaller keeps it increasing
            take = 1 + get_lis(idx - 1, idx)  # option B: take it and make it the new previous
        return max(skip, take)  # best of the two choices available at this index
        
    # longest falling run over the suffix from idx
    def get_lds(idx, prev_idx):  # mirror of get_lis, walking the other direction
        if idx == n:  # we ran past the right end of the array
            return 0  # nothing further can be appended here
        skip = get_lds(idx + 1, prev_idx)  # option A: skip nums[idx] and move one step right
        take = 0  # remains 0 when nums[idx] would break the descent
        if prev_idx == -1 or nums[idx] < nums[prev_idx]:  # each kept element must sit below the previous one
            take = 1 + get_lds(idx + 1, idx)  # option B: take it as the new previous element
        return max(skip, take)  # best of skipping versus taking at this index
        
    max_len = 0  # best bitonic length seen over all candidate peaks
    # every index gets a turn as the peak of the mountain
    for i in range(n):  # O(n) peaks, each costing an exponential recursion
        # rise over nums[:i+1] and fall over nums[i:] meet at i
        # the peak is counted in both halves, so subtract one
        max_len = max(max_len, get_lis(i, -1) + get_lds(i, -1) - 1)  # -1 seeds prev_idx as 'nothing chosen yet'
    return max_len  # longest bitonic subsequence length found

complexity.space: O(N)

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition:
Fixing a peak and re-running a longest-increasing pass over the prefix and a longest-decreasing pass over the suffix repeats work N times: the rise ending at index 4 is recomputed for every later peak.

That independence is the observation. lis[i] - the longest strictly increasing subsequence ending at i - and lds[i] - the longest strictly decreasing one starting at i - depend on the index alone, not on which peak you are testing, so build each table once: the best sequence peaking at i is `lis[i] + lds[i] - 1`, the -1 because i sits in both halves. For [1, 3, 5, 4, 2] at i = 2 both are 3, giving 5.

Nothing is missed: every bitonic sequence has exactly one highest element, so sweeping i as the peak covers each candidate once, and the halves cannot interfere - the left uses values below nums[i] before i, the right those after it. Fill order guarantees finished reads: lis[i] reads lis[j] for j < i as i ascends, lds[i] reads lds[j] for j > i as i descends. Strict `>` bars equal values.

O(N^2) time and O(N) space, down from O(N^3); the surviving N^2 is the pairwise scan inherent to this LIS formulation.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Set n = len(nums) and return 0 immediately when n is 0, since the peak sweep assumes at least one index.
2. Create `lis` as n copies of 1 (every element alone is a rise of length one). For i from 1 to n-1 and j from 0 to i-1, if `nums[i] > nums[j]` set `lis[i] = max(lis[i], lis[j] + 1)`.
3. Create `lds` as n copies of 1. For i from n-2 down to 0 and j from n-1 down to i+1, if `nums[i] > nums[j]` set `lds[i] = max(lds[i], lds[j] + 1)` - filling right to left so `lds[j]` is already final.
4. Set `max_len = 0` and sweep i from 0 to n-1, treating i as the shared peak: `max_len = max(max_len, lis[i] + lds[i] - 1)`, subtracting 1 because i is counted in both tables.
5. Return `max_len`.
approaches.code:
def LongestBitonicSequence(nums: list[int]) -> int:  # rise to a peak then fall, both sides strict
    n = len(nums)  # both dp tables are sized to the input
    if n == 0:  # guard: the peak sweep below assumes at least one index
        return 0  # an empty array has no bitonic subsequence
    # lis[i] = longest rise ending exactly at index i
    lis = [1] * n  # each element alone is already a rise of length one
    for i in range(1, n):  # lis[0] stays 1 because nothing sits to its left
        for j in range(i):  # every earlier index is a candidate predecessor
            if nums[i] > nums[j]:  # strict > forbids equal values inside the rise
                lis[i] = max(lis[i], lis[j] + 1)  # lis[j] is final already, so reading it here is safe
                
    # lds[i] = longest fall starting exactly at index i
    lds = [1] * n  # mirror table, this one filled from the right
    for i in range(n - 2, -1, -1):  # go backwards so lds[j] is ready when we need it
        for j in range(n - 1, i, -1):  # only indices strictly right of i may follow it
            if nums[i] > nums[j]:  # nums[i] must sit above its successor to keep falling
                lds[i] = max(lds[i], lds[j] + 1)  # extend the best fall that begins at index j
                
    # combine: index i is the shared peak of both halves
    max_len = 0  # running best over every candidate peak
    for i in range(n):  # a single O(n) sweep now that both tables are built
        max_len = max(max_len, lis[i] + lds[i] - 1)  # subtract 1 because i is counted in both tables
    # an i with no rise or no fall still yields length 1
    return max_len  # longest bitonic subsequence length overall

complexity.space: O(N)

Bitonic Subsequence.tests:
# 1,2,5,3,2 is already bitonic (up then down) -> length 5.
assert LongestBitonicSequence([1, 2, 5, 3, 2]) == 5
# 1,2,10,4,2,1 is the longest bitonic subsequence -> length 6.
assert LongestBitonicSequence([1, 11, 2, 10, 4, 5, 2, 1]) == 6
# Edge case: a purely increasing array is itself bitonic.
assert LongestBitonicSequence([10, 20, 30]) == 3
# Edge case: a single element.
assert LongestBitonicSequence([1]) == 1
prerequisites: A bitonic subsequence is two LIS problems glued at a peak: the longest increasing run ENDING at i, and the longest decreasing run STARTING at i.
The decreasing half is just an LIS computed right-to-left, so one template written twice (once forwards, once backwards) solves the whole problem.
The peak element belongs to both halves, so the combined length is lis[i] + lds[i] - 1 — forgetting the -1 is the classic off-by-one here.
Under this problem's definition a purely increasing or purely decreasing sequence still counts as bitonic, which the formula handles automatically since the other side contributes 1.
Both halves must be STRICTLY monotonic, so the comparisons are > and not >=; equal neighbouring values cannot both be kept.
The O(n^2) double loop is the standard answer; an O(n log n) version exists using patience sorting on both directions if the interviewer pushes.

Matrix Chain Multiplication.problemStatement: Given a sequence of matrices, find the most efficient way to multiply these matrices together. The problem is not actually to perform the multiplications, but merely to decide in which order to perform the multiplications. You are given an array arr[] which represents the chain of matrix dimensions such that the ith matrix has dimensions arr[i-1] x arr[i].
edgeCases: Only two matrices (length of arr = 3): single way to multiply
Identical dimensions
followUps: Can you print the optimal parenthesis arrangement for matrix multiplication?

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: To find the minimum cost to multiply matrices from index i to j, try placing parentheses at every partition point k (from i to j-1) and recursively calculate the cost of multiplying the two split chains, adding the cost of multiplying the resulting two matrices.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Define helper(i, j) where i and j are the matrix boundary indices.
2. If i == j, return 0 (only one matrix, cost is 0).
3. Initialize min_cost = infinity.
4. Loop k from i to j-1: cost = helper(i, k) + helper(k+1, j) + arr[i-1]*arr[k]*arr[j]. Update min_cost.
5. Return min_cost.

complexity.space: O(N)

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: Matrix multiplication is associative, so every way of parenthesising the chain produces the same product — but not the same amount of work. Multiplying an a x b matrix by a b x c matrix costs a*b*c scalar multiplications, and reordering can change the total by orders of magnitude. Trying every parenthesisation is hopeless, since there are Catalan-many of them. The observation that cracks the problem is this: whatever the optimal order turns out to be, some single multiplication happens last, and that final multiply splits the chain into a left block i..k and a right block k+1..j, each of which must itself have been computed optimally and independently. That yields a recurrence over intervals, dp[i][j] = min over k of dp[i][k] + dp[k+1][j] + arr[i-1]*arr[k]*arr[j], where the last term is the cost of the final multiply because the left block has arr[i-1] rows, the shared inner dimension is arr[k], and the right block has arr[j] columns. Since an interval only ever depends on strictly shorter intervals, the table can be filled bottom-up by increasing chain `length` rather than by recursing. Filling O(n^2) intervals and testing up to n split points in each gives O(n^3) time and O(n^2) space.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Let n = len(arr) - 1 (number of matrices).
2. Initialize dp table of size (n+1) x (n+1) with 0s.
3. Loop length l from 2 to n.
4. Loop start index i from 1 to n - l + 1. Let j = i + l - 1.
5. Initialize dp[i][j] = infinity.
6. Loop k from i to j-1: cost = dp[i][k] + dp[k+1][j] + arr[i-1]*arr[k]*arr[j]. Update dp[i][j] = min(dp[i][j], cost).
7. Return dp[1][n].
approaches.code:
def matrixMultiplication(arr: list[int]) -> int:
    n = len(arr) - 1
    # dp[i][j] will store the minimum cost to multiply matrices from index i to j
    dp = [[0] * (n + 1) for _ in range(n + 1)]
    # Loop over chain lengths from 2 to n
    for length in range(2, n + 1):
        for i in range(1, n - length + 2):
            j = i + length - 1
            dp[i][j] = float('inf')
            # Test all possible partition points k
            for k in range(i, j):
                # Sum of left cost, right cost, and current multiplication cost
                cost = dp[i][k] + dp[k + 1][j] + arr[i - 1] * arr[k] * arr[j]
                dp[i][j] = min(dp[i][j], cost)
    # Return the minimum cost for the entire chain of matrices
    return dp[1][n]

Matrix Chain Multiplication.tests:
# Dimensions 40x20, 20x30, 30x10, 10x30 -> 26000 scalar multiplications.
assert matrixMultiplication([40, 20, 30, 10, 30]) == 26000
# Two matrices 10x20 and 20x30 -> exactly one product of cost 6000.
assert matrixMultiplication([10, 20, 30]) == 6000
# Edge case: a single matrix needs no multiplication at all.
assert matrixMultiplication([10, 20]) == 0
# Larger chain check.
assert matrixMultiplication([1, 2, 3, 4, 3]) == 30
prerequisites: Matrix dimensions are encoded implicitly: matrix A_i has shape arr[i-1] x arr[i], so an array of length n+1 describes n matrices.
Multiplying a p x q matrix by a q x r matrix costs exactly p*q*r scalar multiplications, and the result is p x r — that formula is the whole cost model.
This is interval DP with a SPLIT point: dp[i][j] = min over k in i..j-1 of dp[i][k] + dp[k+1][j] + arr[i-1]*arr[k]*arr[j], where k is where the final multiplication happens.
Fill the table by increasing chain LENGTH, because dp[i][j] depends on strictly shorter intervals that must already be final.
dp[i][i] = 0 is the base case: a single matrix needs no multiplication at all, which is why the diagonal stays zero.
Initialising each cell to float('inf') before the k loop is what makes the running min work; the three nested loops give O(n^3) time and O(n^2) space.

Buy and Sell Stock.title: Buy and Sell Stock
Buy and Sell Stock.problemStatement: You are given an array prices where prices[i] is the price of a stock on day i. You may buy the stock on exactly one day and sell it on exactly one LATER day (you cannot sell before you buy, and you cannot short-sell). Return the maximum profit you can achieve from this single buy-sell transaction. If no profitable transaction exists — for example, prices only go down — you should not trade at all and must return 0. Nothing is modified in place; you just return one integer.

examples.explanation: Walk through the days: buying at 7 (day 0) is bad because every later price is lower than 7 except none give a big gap. The cheapest day is day 1 (price 1). From day 1 you could sell at 5 (profit 4), at 3 (profit 2), at 6 (profit 5) or at 4 (profit 3). The best is buy at 1, sell at 6, profit 6 - 1 = 5. Note we cannot 'buy at 1 and sell at 7' because 7 happened BEFORE 1 — order matters.
Prices strictly fall every day, so every buy-then-sell pair loses money. The best strategy is to not trade at all, so the answer is 0.

edgeCases: A single day ([5]) — you can never sell after buying, so the answer must be 0, and code that assumes at least 2 days may crash or return garbage.
Strictly decreasing prices ([9,7,4,1]) — every trade loses money, so the answer is 0, which trips up code that initializes best profit to a negative or to prices[1]-prices[0].
The minimum price appearing on the LAST day ([5,3,1]) — a new minimum that can never be sold; the code must not 'sell' on the same day it buys.
All prices equal ([3,3,3]) — profit is exactly 0, testing that the comparison uses strict '>' and does not do a useless 0-profit 'trade'.
The best sell coming BEFORE an even lower later minimum ([2,10,1]) — answer is 8; code must not throw away the earlier profit when min_price later drops.
followUps: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock II: what changes if you may make unlimited transactions (buy/sell many times)? (Greedy: sum every upward step.)
What if you may make at most k transactions? (DP with states day x transactions x holding — LeetCode 188.)
What if prices arrive as a live stream and you must report the best profit so far after each tick in O(1) per tick? (This one-pass solution already does exactly that.)
What if every sale is charged a fixed transaction fee, or you must wait one cooldown day after selling? (State-machine DP variants.)
prerequisites: Single-pass 'running extreme' pattern: keeping a running minimum/maximum while scanning lets you answer pair questions without nested loops.
Why order matters here: profit = prices[sell] - prices[buy] is only valid when buy index < sell index, so a plain max(prices) - min(prices) is WRONG.
float('inf') in Python is a safe 'plus infinity' initial value: every real number compares smaller than it.
Big-O basics: nested loops over n days is O(n^2) (~10^10 steps at n = 10^5 — too slow); one pass is O(n).

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: The most literal reading of the problem: a transaction is a pair of days (buy, sell) with buy before sell. There are only n*(n-1)/2 such pairs, so try them all, compute each profit, and remember the biggest. Nothing clever is needed — this is the answer-checking definition itself turned into code. It is correct by construction, but at n = 10^5 that is about 5 * 10^9 pairs, far too slow; it exists to make the optimized version's insight obvious.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Initialize best = 0 (not trading is always allowed).
2. Loop buy over every index 0..n-1.
3. For each buy, loop sell over every later index buy+1..n-1.
4. Compute profit = prices[sell] - prices[buy].
5. If profit > best, update best.
6. After all pairs are tried, return best.

complexity.time: O(n^2) — every one of the ~n^2/2 buy/sell pairs is checked.
complexity.space: O(1) — only two loop indices and two integers are stored.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: The brute force wastes work: when we stand on a potential sell day, the ONLY buy day worth pairing with it is the cheapest day seen so far — pairing with any more expensive earlier day can only shrink the profit. So instead of re-scanning the past for every sell day, carry the past along as a single number: min_price, the cheapest price so far. On each day, either today is a new cheapest (better future buy), or we pretend to sell today against min_price and see if that beats our best. One pass, two variables, and every pair the brute force checked is implicitly covered because min_price summarizes all earlier days.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Set min_price = +infinity (no day seen yet) and best = 0.
2. Walk the days left to right; let price be today's price.
3. If price < min_price, record price as the new min_price (today becomes the best buy candidate) and move on — selling today at a new minimum can't profit.
4. Otherwise compute price - min_price (sell today, having bought at the cheapest earlier day); if it beats best, update best.
5. After the single pass, return best (it stays 0 when prices never rise).
approaches.code:
def maxProfit(prices: List[int]) -> int:
    # Track the cheapest price seen so far (the best day to buy)
    min_price = float('inf')
    # Track the best profit found so far (0 = never trade)
    best = 0
    # Scan each day's price exactly once, left to right
    for price in prices:
        # A new lowest price is an even better future buy day
        if price < min_price:
            min_price = price
        # Otherwise, see if selling today beats our best profit
        elif price - min_price > best:
            best = price - min_price
    # best holds the maximum achievable profit (0 if prices only fall)
    return best

complexity.time: O(n) — one pass with O(1) work per day.
complexity.space: O(1) — just min_price and best, regardless of input size.

Buy and Sell Stock.tests:
assert maxProfit([7,1,5,3,6,4]) == 5      # classic: buy at 1, sell at 6
assert maxProfit([7,6,4,3,1]) == 0        # falling prices: never trade
assert maxProfit([5]) == 0                # single day edge case: cannot sell
assert maxProfit([3,3,3]) == 0            # flat prices: zero profit
assert maxProfit([2,10,1]) == 8           # best sell happens before a later, lower min
assert maxProfit([1,2]) == 1              # minimal profitable case

Rotate Matrix.title: Rotate Matrix
Rotate Matrix.problemStatement: You are given an n x n square matrix of integers (think of it as an image made of pixels). Rotate the matrix by 90 degrees clockwise, IN PLACE: you must modify the given matrix directly and are not allowed to allocate a second n x n matrix for the answer. After rotation, what was the first ROW (read left to right) becomes the last COLUMN (read top to bottom). The function returns nothing; the caller sees the change through the mutated input.

examples.explanation: Picture turning the page 90 degrees clockwise. The top row [1,2,3] must end up as the RIGHT column read top-to-bottom: 1 goes to position (0,2), 2 to (1,2), 3 to (2,2). Similarly the left column [1,4,7] becomes the new top row reversed: [7,4,1]. Check cell by cell: new row 0 is [7,4,1] (the old first column bottom-to-top), new row 1 is [8,5,2], new row 2 is [9,6,3].
The old first column [5,2,13,15] read bottom-to-top gives the new first row [15,13,2,5], and the same rule maps every other column.

constraints: n == matrix.length == matrix[i].length (the matrix is square)
edgeCases: A 1x1 matrix ([[7]]) — rotation must leave it unchanged, and loops with empty ranges must not crash.
A 2x2 matrix — the smallest case where the transpose actually swaps something; off-by-one errors in the inner loop bound show up here.
Transposing with the inner loop starting at j = 0 instead of j = i+1 — every pair swaps TWICE, silently restoring the original matrix (a classic bug this case exposes).
Even vs odd n — odd n has a center cell that must stay fixed; code that special-cases the center often breaks one of the two parities.
Duplicated values in the matrix — a test that only checks the multiset of values would pass a wrong rotation; positions must be asserted exactly.
followUps: Rotate 90 degrees COUNTER-clockwise in place — which two operations compose now? (Transpose then reverse each COLUMN, or reverse rows then transpose.)
Rotate by 180 degrees in place — can you do it with two reversals and no transpose?
The matrix is m x n (not square). Why is a true in-place 90-degree rotation impossible in the same buffer, and what would you do instead?
Rotate the matrix layer by layer in a single pass (four-way cyclic swap) — same O(1) space, different cell choreography; can you code it without off-by-one errors?
prerequisites: Transpose of a matrix: mirroring across the main diagonal means cell (i,j) swaps with cell (j,i); rows become columns.
The key composition fact: clockwise 90-degree rotation = transpose, then reverse each row. Try it on paper with a 2x2 before coding.
Python tuple swap a, b = b, a evaluates the right side first, so matrix[i][j], matrix[j][i] = matrix[j][i], matrix[i][j] is a safe in-place swap.
list.reverse() reverses a Python list in place in O(n) with O(1) extra space (unlike reversed() or slicing, which create new objects).
In-place means the caller's object is mutated: the function returns None and tests must inspect the original variable after the call.

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: Forget the in-place restriction for a moment and just ask: where does each cell GO? Watching the top row become the last column shows the rule — the value at (i, j) lands at (j, n-1-i): its row index becomes the column counted from the right, and its column index becomes the row. So build a brand-new n x n matrix, place every value with that formula, then copy the result back into the original so the caller still sees an in-place change. Correct and easy to reason about, but it uses O(n^2) extra memory, which is exactly what the interviewer asked us to avoid.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Read n = len(matrix).
2. Allocate a new n x n matrix 'rotated' filled with zeros.
3. For every cell (i, j) of the original, write matrix[i][j] into rotated[j][n-1-i].
4. Copy every cell of 'rotated' back into 'matrix' so the input object itself is modified.
5. Return nothing — the mutation is the result.

complexity.time: O(n^2) — every cell is placed once and copied back once.
complexity.space: O(n^2) — a full second matrix is allocated.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: The extra matrix exists only because moving a value to its new home overwrites a value we still need. The trick: a 90-degree clockwise rotation is exactly two simple mirror operations composed — first TRANSPOSE (swap (i,j) with (j,i), turning rows into columns), then REVERSE EACH ROW (flip left-right). Both mirrors are just swaps of two cells at a time, and a swap never loses information — so no scratch matrix is needed. Verify on the top-left cell of a 3x3: 1 at (0,0) transposes to (0,0), then row-reversal sends it to (0,2) — precisely where a clockwise turn puts it. The inner transpose loop starts at j = i+1 so each symmetric pair swaps exactly once (swapping twice would undo everything).
approaches.algorithm:
1. Read n = len(matrix).
2. Transpose in place: for every i, for every j > i, swap matrix[i][j] with matrix[j][i]. The j > i bound guarantees each pair is swapped exactly once and diagonal cells stay put.
3. Reverse each row in place with row.reverse(), flipping the matrix left-right.
4. Done — the matrix now holds the 90-degree clockwise rotation; return nothing.

complexity.time: O(n^2) — transpose touches each off-diagonal pair once, reversal touches each cell once.
complexity.space: O(1) — only loop indices and the implicit swap temporary.

Merge Overlapping Intervals.title: Merge Overlapping Intervals
Merge Overlapping Intervals.problemStatement: You are given a list of intervals, where each interval is a pair [start, end] with start <= end. Two intervals overlap when they share at least one point — note that touching endpoints like [1,4] and [4,5] count as overlapping. Your job is to merge every group of overlapping intervals into one single interval that covers the whole group, and return the resulting list of non-overlapping intervals. The input list is NOT guaranteed to be sorted, and the output should cover exactly the same set of points as the input. You return a new list; the order of the answer should be by increasing start.

examples.explanation: Draw the intervals on a number line. [1,3] and [2,6] overlap because 2 (the second start) is <= 3 (the first end) — they share the points 2 and 3 — so they fuse into [1,6] (smallest start, largest end). [8,10] starts at 8, which is past 6, so it cannot join the first block. [15,18] starts past 10, so it stays alone too. Final answer: [[1,6],[8,10],[15,18]].
The intervals touch at the single point 4. Touching counts as overlapping here, so they merge into [1,5].

edgeCases: Touching endpoints like [1,4] and [4,5] — the overlap test must use <= (not <) or these wrongly stay separate.
One interval completely swallowing another, e.g. [1,10] and [2,3] — the merge must take max(end, new end), not just the newer end, or the block wrongly shrinks to [1,3].
A single interval — the answer is the input itself; empty-answer initialization must still work when the loop runs once.
Unsorted input like [[4,7],[1,4]] — code that skips the sort merges wrong pairs or misses overlaps entirely.
A chain where each interval overlaps only the next one ([[1,3],[2,4],[3,6]]) — all three must collapse into one block [1,6], which tests that merging extends the SAME block repeatedly.
followUps: Insert Interval (LeetCode 57): a new interval arrives into an already-merged sorted list — can you insert and re-merge in O(n) without re-sorting?
Meeting Rooms II: instead of merging, return the maximum number of intervals that overlap at any single point (min-heap of end times or a sweep line of +1/-1 events).
Streaming version: intervals arrive one by one and you must be able to report the merged set at any moment — what balanced structure (sorted map / interval tree) keeps each insert at O(log n)?
Total covered length: return the sum of lengths of the merged intervals instead of the list — can you compute it in the same single sweep?
prerequisites: The sort-then-sweep pattern: after sorting by start, any interval can only overlap the block that is currently 'open' — earlier blocks are sealed forever.
The overlap test for sorted intervals: current.start <= last.end (with <= to treat touching endpoints as overlap).
Python's list.sort(key=lambda it: it[0]) sorts in place by start in O(n log n); merged[-1] reads the last appended block in O(1).
Why max() is needed when absorbing: the new interval may end EARLIER than the block ([1,10] absorbing [2,3]), so the block keeps the larger end.
Lists are mutable references: merged[-1][1] = ... edits the block already inside the answer, which is what lets one block grow repeatedly.

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: Even a brute solution benefits from sorting first, so sort by start. Then, for each interval that isn't already covered by an answer block, treat it as the seed [start, end] of a new block and re-scan every LATER interval: any interval whose start is <= our current end overlaps (or touches), so absorb it by extending end. Because we restart this inner scan for every seed, later intervals get re-examined again and again — that repeated re-scanning is the wasted work (O(n^2)) that the optimal single sweep removes. A previously merged interval is recognized because its end already fits inside the last sealed block.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Sort the intervals by start value.
2. Walk each index i from left to right; let [start, end] = intervals[i].
3. If the answer list is non-empty and end <= last answer's end, interval i was already absorbed by an earlier seed — skip it.
4. Otherwise scan every j > i: if intervals[j].start <= end, absorb it with end = max(end, intervals[j].end).
5. Append the finished block [start, end] to the answer.
6. Return the answer list after all seeds are processed.

complexity.time: O(n^2) — after the O(n log n) sort, each seed re-scans all later intervals.
complexity.space: O(n) — the sorted copy and the answer list.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: The brute force re-scans the future for every seed, but sorting already did the hard part: once intervals are ordered by start, every interval can only interact with the block IMMEDIATELY before it. So sweep once, keeping just the last block of the answer 'open'. For each interval: if its start is <= the open block's end, it overlaps (or touches), and we absorb it by raising the block's end to max(both ends) — max matters because a nested interval like [2,3] must not shrink an open [1,10]. If its start is beyond the open end, there is a genuine gap, the open block can never grow again (all later starts are even bigger), so we seal it and open a new block. One pass, each interval touched once.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Sort intervals in place by start (O(n log n)).
2. Create an empty answer list 'merged'.
3. For each [start, end] in sorted order: if merged is non-empty and start <= merged[-1][1], absorb it: merged[-1][1] = max(merged[-1][1], end).
4. Otherwise append [start, end] as a brand-new block.
5. After the sweep, 'merged' holds disjoint intervals in start order — return it.
approaches.code:
def merge(intervals: List[List[int]]) -> List[List[int]]:
    # Sort by start so intervals that can overlap become neighbours
    intervals.sort(key=lambda it: it[0])
    merged = []  # output list of disjoint, merged intervals
    # Sweep the sorted intervals left to right
    for start, end in intervals:
        # Overlap test: this start falls inside (or touches) the last merged block
        if merged and start <= merged[-1][1]:
            # Absorb: stretch the last block's right edge if this one reaches further
            merged[-1][1] = max(merged[-1][1], end)
        else:
            # No overlap: this interval starts a fresh block
            merged.append([start, end])
    # Every overlapping group is now collapsed into a single interval
    return merged

complexity.time: O(n log n) — the sort dominates; the sweep itself is O(n).
complexity.space: O(n) — for the answer list (O(1) extra beyond the output; Python's sort uses O(n) internally).

Merge Overlapping Intervals.tests:
assert merge([[1,3],[2,6],[8,10],[15,18]]) == [[1,6],[8,10],[15,18]]
assert merge([[1,4],[4,5]]) == [[1,5]]            # touching endpoints must merge
assert merge([[5,7]]) == [[5,7]]                  # single interval edge case
assert merge([[4,7],[1,4]]) == [[1,7]]            # unsorted input
assert merge([[1,10],[2,3],[4,5]]) == [[1,10]]    # nested intervals must not shrink the block
assert merge([[1,3],[2,4],[3,6]]) == [[1,6]]      # chain merges into one block

Merge Two Sorted Arrays Without Extra Sp.title: Merge Two Sorted Arrays Without Extra Space
Merge Two Sorted Arrays Without Extra Sp.problemStatement: You are given two sorted (non-decreasing) integer arrays. nums1 has length m + n: its first m entries are real sorted values and its last n entries are 0-placeholders reserved for the merge. nums2 has exactly n sorted values. Merge nums2 into nums1 IN PLACE so that nums1 ends up holding all m + n values in sorted order. The function returns nothing — the answer must appear inside nums1 itself, and the challenge is to do it without allocating a third array (O(1) extra space).

examples.explanation: The real values are [1,2,3] and [2,5,6]; the three 0s are just empty slots. A correct merge interleaves them in sorted order: 1, then the two 2s, then 3, 5, 6. Watch how the in-place version does it BACKWARDS: compare the tails 3 and 6 — 6 is bigger, so 6 goes into the last slot; then 3 vs 5 puts 5; then 3 vs 2 puts 3; then 2 vs 2 puts nums2's 2; then j is exhausted and the remaining [1,2] of nums1 are already in place.
nums1 has no real elements at all (m = 0), so the merge simply copies nums2's single value into the placeholder slot.

constraints: Both arrays are sorted in non-decreasing order
edgeCases: n = 0 (nums2 empty) — nothing must change; a loop keyed on j >= 0 handles this by doing zero iterations, while a loop keyed on k can walk off and corrupt nums1.

m = 0 (nums1 has only placeholders) — every write comes from nums2; the i >= 0 guard is what stops the code from reading nums1[-1] (which in Python silently reads the LAST element instead of crashing!).
All of nums2 smaller than all of nums1 ([4,5,6] and [1,2,3]) — the merge must keep copying nums2 after i is exhausted, exercising the else branch repeatedly.
Duplicate values across both arrays ([1,2,3] and [2,2]) — ties must be handled by either branch consistently or elements get lost/duplicated.
Front-to-back merging attempt — writing at index 0 first overwrites nums1's unread values; this problem is specifically designed to punish that, which is WHY we merge from the back.
followUps: The Striver/GfG variant: two separate full arrays a (size m) and b (size n), no placeholder slots at all — how does the gap method (shell-sort style) achieve O((m+n) log(m+n)) time with true O(1) space?
Merge k sorted arrays into one — why does a min-heap of k head elements give O(N log k), and where does the in-place trick break down?
What if nums1's spare space were at the FRONT instead of the back? Which direction would you merge then?
Count the cross-pairs (i, j) with nums1[i] > nums2[j] during the merge — connection to counting inversions between two sorted lists.
prerequisites: Two-pointer merging: the merge step of merge sort — repeatedly take the smaller (or larger) of two front (or tail) elements.
The key in-place insight: nums1's free space is at its END, so writing from the back (largest values first) never overwrites values that still need to be read.
