v = StockSpanner()
assert [v.next(p) for p in [10, 9, 8, 7]] == [1, 1, 1, 1]   # edge: strictly falling market

Power Set.title: Power Set
Power Set.problemStatement: You are given a string s. A subsequence is any string you can build by walking through s from left to right and choosing, independently for each character, whether to keep it or drop it — the kept characters stay in their original relative order, and you never rearrange them. Your task is to return every NON-EMPTY subsequence of s, and the list must come back in lexicographic (dictionary) order. The collection of all these choices is called the power set of s: with n characters there are 2^n possible keep/drop combinations, one of which is the empty string, so you return 2^n - 1 strings. Duplicated characters in s produce duplicated strings, and that is fine — positions are what differ, so both copies are reported. Since the output itself is exponential, no algorithm can beat O(2^n) work; the goal is to generate the set cleanly, without recursion bugs or missed cases.

examples.explanation: Each character has two options, keep or drop, so there are 2^3 = 8 combinations. Writing the choices as bits (bit 0 = 'a', bit 1 = 'b', bit 2 = 'c'), mask 000 gives the empty string which we skip; 001 gives 'a'; 010 gives 'b'; 011 gives 'ab'; 100 gives 'c'; 101 gives 'ac'; 110 gives 'bc'; 111 gives 'abc'. That is the raw list ['a', 'b', 'ab', 'c', 'ac', 'bc', 'abc'], which contains 7 = 2^3 - 1 strings. Sorting it alphabetically — comparing character by character, and a shorter string first when it is a prefix of a longer one — gives ['a', 'ab', 'abc', 'ac', 'b', 'bc', 'c']. Note that 'ab' comes before 'ac' (b < c) and 'abc' comes before 'ac' because after the shared 'a' we compare 'b' against 'c'.
One character gives 2^1 = 2 combinations: the empty string, which is excluded, and 'a' itself.
The two 'a's sit at different positions, so keeping only the first and keeping only the second are two distinct choices even though they print identically; both are reported, followed by 'aa'.

constraints: 1 <= len(s) <= 20 on the original judge (2^20 ≈ 10^6 subsequences is already a large output)
s consists of lowercase (or generally printable) characters and may contain repeats
The returned list must be in lexicographically sorted order and must exclude the empty subsequence
edgeCases: An empty string — 1 << 0 is 1, so range(1, 1) is empty and the answer is [] rather than [''], which is exactly right.
A single character — there is only one non-empty subsequence, and off-by-one bugs (starting mask at 0) would wrongly add the empty string.
Repeated characters like 'aa' — the output legitimately contains duplicates, so 'deduplicating to be safe' would give a wrong answer here.
n around 20 — the output holds about a million strings, so building each string with ''.join instead of repeated string concatenation matters for memory and speed.
Sorting is by string, not by length — 'abc' sorts before 'ac', which surprises people who expect shorter strings to always come first.
followUps: How would you return only the DISTINCT subsequences when s has repeats? (Sort the characters first and, at each recursion level, skip a character equal to the previous one you already tried — or collect into a set.)

Can you produce the subsequences in lexicographic order WITHOUT a final sort? (Recurse over the sorted characters choosing 'take' before 'skip' — the generation order then already matches dictionary order.)
The output no longer fits in memory for n = 30 — what changes? (Turn the function into a generator that yields one subsequence at a time, so space drops to O(n) and the caller streams the results.)

How would you return the k-th subsequence directly, without generating the others? (The bitmask IS an index: decode k's bits, though you must map it through the sorted order if lexicographic ranking is required.)

What about subsets of an array of numbers, where the answer must contain lists instead of strings, and sums are needed? (Same masks; and 'sum of all subset sums' has a closed form, since each element appears in exactly 2^(n-1) subsets.)
prerequisites: Subsequence vs substring: a subsequence keeps relative order but may skip characters, while a substring must be contiguous — this problem is about subsequences.
The bit trick: with n items, integers 0 .. 2^n - 1 enumerate all keep/drop patterns exactly once; 1 << n is 2^n and mask & (1 << i) tests whether item i is kept.
The recursive 'pick / not-pick' template, which is the same idea expressed with a call stack instead of bits.
Python string handling: ''.join(list_of_chars) builds a string in one pass, whereas repeated += inside a loop creates a new string every time.
Python's sort on strings is lexicographic and compares character by character, treating a prefix as smaller than the longer string.

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: Think of building a subsequence as walking through the string and making one yes/no decision per character. That is exactly a binary recursion tree: at index i we branch twice, once taking s[i] into the string we are carrying and once leaving it out, and when i reaches the end of the string the carried value is one complete subsequence. Every root-to-leaf path in this tree is a distinct combination of choices, so all 2^n of them are produced with no duplicates and none missed. We drop the single path that took nothing, since the empty subsequence is excluded, and finally sort. It is correct and it is the classic teaching form of the pattern, but every recursive call copies the string built so far (current + s[i] creates a new string), so it uses O(n) call-stack depth and does extra copying work at every node of the tree.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Record n = len(s) and create an empty list result.
2. Define build(i, current) where i is the index being decided and current is the string built so far.
3. Base case: if i == n, append current to result when it is non-empty, then return.
4. Recursive case 1: call build(i + 1, current + s[i]) — this branch TAKES s[i].
5. Recursive case 2: call build(i + 1, current) — this branch SKIPS s[i].
6. Kick the recursion off with build(0, ""), then sort result and return it.
approaches.code:
def power_set(s):
    n = len(s)                                 # number of characters we must decide on
    result = []                                # every non-empty subsequence lands here

    def build(i, current):
        # i = the index we are deciding right now, current = characters picked so far.
        if i == n:                             # no characters left to decide
            if current:                        # skip the empty subsequence
                result.append(current)         # a completed choice is recorded
            return                             # backtrack to the caller
        build(i + 1, current + s[i])           # BRANCH 1: take s[i]
        build(i + 1, current)                  # BRANCH 2: leave s[i] out

    build(0, "")                               # start with nothing decided, nothing picked
    result.sort()                              # the problem wants lexicographic order
    return result

complexity.time: O(2^n * n) to generate plus O(2^n * n log(2^n)) to sort — one leaf per subset, each costing O(n) to copy
complexity.space: O(2^n * n) for the output, plus O(n) recursion depth

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: The recursion is really just counting in binary, so let us count directly. Give character s[i] the bit i of an integer mask: if that bit is 1 the character is taken, if it is 0 it is dropped. Then the integers 0, 1, 2, ..., 2^n - 1 enumerate every possible choice exactly once — no recursion tree, no call stack, no risk of a missed branch. Skipping mask = 0 removes the empty subsequence, so we loop from 1. For each mask we read its bits left to right over the string, collect the chosen characters into a small list and join them, which builds each result string in one pass instead of concatenating repeatedly. The asymptotic cost is the same O(2^n * n) — it has to be, since that is the size of the output — but the constants are much better, the memory is O(1) beyond the answer, and the code has no stack-depth limit to worry about.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Let n = len(s) and create an empty list result.
2. Loop mask from 1 to (1 << n) - 1 inclusive; mask 0 is skipped because it means 'take nothing'.
3. For each mask start a fresh empty list pick.
4. For each index i from 0 to n-1, test mask & (1 << i); if that bit is set, append s[i] to pick.
5. Join pick into a string and append it to result — the characters are appended in increasing i, so their original relative order is preserved automatically.
6. After all masks, sort result lexicographically and return it.
approaches.code:
def power_set(s):
    n = len(s)                                 # a string of n characters
    result = []                                # collects every non-empty subsequence
    # Every subset matches an n-bit number: bit i of mask set means "take s[i]".
    # mask 0 encodes the empty subsequence, so we start counting from 1.
    for mask in range(1, 1 << n):              # 1 .. 2^n - 1 = all non-empty subsets
        pick = []                              # characters chosen by THIS mask
        for i in range(n):                     # test every position exactly once
            if mask & (1 << i):                # is bit i of mask switched on?
                pick.append(s[i])              # then s[i] belongs to this subsequence
        result.append(''.join(pick))           # glue the chosen characters into a string
    result.sort()                              # lexicographic order, as the problem asks
    return result                              # 2^n - 1 subsequences in sorted order

complexity.time: O(2^n * n) to build every subsequence plus O(2^n * n * log(2^n)) for the final sort
complexity.space: O(2^n * n) for the output list; only O(n) auxiliary space for the pick buffer

Power Set.tests:
assert power_set("abc") == ['a', 'ab', 'abc', 'ac', 'b', 'bc', 'c']
assert power_set("a") == ['a']
assert power_set("") == []                    # edge: no characters -> no subsequences
assert len(power_set("abcde")) == 31          # 2^5 - 1 non-empty subsets
assert power_set("aa") == ['a', 'a', 'aa']    # edge: duplicate characters are kept

Maximum XOR Subarray.title: Maximum XOR Subarray
Maximum XOR Subarray.problemStatement: You are given an array of non-negative integers. A subarray is any block of CONSECUTIVE elements, for example arr[2], arr[3], arr[4]. XOR all the elements of a subarray together (Python's ^ operator: a bit of the result is 1 exactly when an odd number of the inputs have that bit set) and you get that subarray's value. Your job is to return the maximum value over every non-empty subarray. You do not have to report the indices, and the array must not be modified. Because a subarray must be contiguous, you cannot simply pick the two most 'opposite' numbers — but a prefix-XOR reformulation turns the problem into exactly that kind of pair search, which a binary trie can answer in about 30 steps per element instead of scanning all O(n^2) subarrays.

examples.explanation: List every subarray: [1]=1, [1,2]=3, [1,2,3]=0, [1,2,3,4]=4, [2]=2, [2,3]=1, [2,3,4]=5, [3]=3, [3,4]=7, [4]=4. The largest is 7, produced by [3, 4] because 3 = 011 and 4 = 100 have no bits in common, so their XOR turns on all three bits. The prefix view explains the same answer: the prefix XORs are pre = [0, 1, 3, 0, 4], and the XOR of arr[i..j] equals pre[j+1] ^ pre[i]. Here pre[4] ^ pre[2] = 4 ^ 3 = 7, and those two prefixes bound exactly the subarray [3, 4]. So finding the best subarray is the same as finding the two prefix values with the largest XOR.

The prefix XORs are 0, 8, 9, 11, 7, 0, 6. The best pair among them is 8 ^ 7 = 15, and those two prefixes sit just before index 1 and just after index 3, which marks the subarray [1, 2, 12] — indeed 1 ^ 2 ^ 12 = 15.
The only subarray is [5] itself; the trie already holds the seeded prefix 0, and 5 ^ 0 = 5.

constraints: 0 <= len(arr) <= 10^5 (an empty array has no subarray, so the answer is 0)
0 <= arr[i] <= 10^9, so around 30 bit positions are enough
Subarrays must be contiguous and non-empty
edgeCases: Forgetting to insert the prefix value 0 before the sweep — then no subarray may start at index 0, and an input like [5] wrongly answers 0.
An array of all zeros — every prefix is 0, so the greedy walk never finds an opposite branch and correctly returns 0.
A single element — the answer is that element itself, which only works because the seeded prefix 0 is available as its partner.
Repeated prefix values (as in [1, 2, 3], where prefix returns to 0) — inserting the same value twice must reuse existing nodes instead of corrupting the links.
Sizing the trie from the wrong value — prefixes are XORs of the elements, so max(arr).bit_length() is the right depth, but hardcoding a smaller depth silently drops high bits.
An empty array — max() would raise ValueError, so the early return is not optional.
followUps: How would you also return the START and END indices of the best subarray? (Store, at every trie node, the index of one prefix that passes through it, then read it off at the end of the winning walk.)
What about the MINIMUM XOR subarray instead of the maximum? (Same trie, but at each level prefer the branch that MATCHES your bit; note the answer is usually 0 whenever any prefix repeats.)
Can you count subarrays whose XOR equals a given value k? (Drop the trie and use a hash map of prefix counts — for each prefix p, add the count of p ^ k seen so far.)

How do you find the maximum XOR subarray within a query range [l, r], for many queries? (Persistent trie over prefixes, so the version at r minus the version at l-1 restricts the search to that window.)

Does the algorithm still work with negative numbers or 64-bit values? (Yes, but fix the bit width explicitly — for negatives use a two's-complement width and handle the sign bit's greedy direction deliberately.)
prerequisites: Prefix XOR: define pre[0] = 0 and pre[k+1] = pre[k] ^ arr[k]; then the XOR of arr[i..j] is pre[j+1] ^ pre[i], because every element before i is XOR-ed twice and cancels (x ^ x = 0).
That identity converts 'best subarray' into 'best PAIR of prefix values', which is the classic maximum-XOR-of-two-numbers problem.
Binary trie over bits, MSB first: the greedy walk takes the branch opposite to your own bit whenever it exists, because a 1 in a higher bit beats every combination of lower bits.
Order matters: for each new prefix you must QUERY the trie before INSERTING it, otherwise a prefix can pair with itself and report a bogus 0-length subarray.
Python bit idioms: (x >> b) & 1 reads bit b, (1 << b) is its value, and int.bit_length() sizes the trie instead of hardcoding 32 levels.

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: Enumerate every subarray, but do it smartly enough not to be O(n^3): fix the left end i, then let the right end j slide rightwards while keeping a running XOR. Since XOR is associative, extending the subarray by one element is a single operation cur ^= arr[j] — no need to recompute the whole block. That gives every one of the ~n^2/2 subarrays in constant time each. This is the definition-driven baseline you should always be able to write, and it doubles as the reference implementation for testing the fast version on random inputs. The problem is scale: with n = 10^5 there are about 5*10^9 subarrays, which is far beyond an interview time limit.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Set best = 0, which is safe because all values are non-negative.
2. Loop i from 0 to n-1 to fix the left end of the subarray.
3. Reset cur = 0 for this left end — cur will hold the XOR of arr[i..j].
4. Loop j from i to n-1, updating cur ^= arr[j] so the subarray grows by exactly one element.
5. If cur > best, update best.
6. Return best after both loops.
approaches.code:
def max_xor_subarray(arr):
    best = 0                          # every value is non-negative, so 0 is a safe floor
    n = len(arr)                      # nothing to do when the array is empty
    for i in range(n):                # i = left end of the subarray
        cur = 0                       # XOR of arr[i..j], grown one element at a time
        for j in range(i, n):         # j = right end, extending to the right
            cur ^= arr[j]             # reuse the previous XOR instead of recomputing it
            if cur > best:            # is this subarray the best so far?
                best = cur            # remember the new maximum
    return best                       # 0 for an empty array

complexity.time: O(n^2) — one constant-time update per subarray
complexity.space: O(1) — only the running XOR and the maximum

approaches.name: Better (Prefix XOR Pairs)
approaches.intuition: Build the prefix-XOR table pre, where pre[k] is the XOR of the first k elements and pre[0] = 0. The crucial identity is that the XOR of arr[i..j] equals pre[j+1] ^ pre[i]: every element before index i appears in both prefixes and cancels out, because x ^ x = 0. So the problem is no longer about contiguous blocks at all — it is 'pick two entries of the pre array and maximise their XOR'. This reformulation is the real insight of the problem, and it is worth writing out explicitly even though checking all pairs of prefixes is still quadratic. Once you see it, the last step is easy: 'maximum XOR of two numbers from a set' is exactly what a binary trie solves in linear time.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Let n = len(arr) and allocate pre of length n+1 with pre[0] = 0.
2. For k from 0 to n-1, set pre[k+1] = pre[k] ^ arr[k].
3. Set best = 0.
4. For every pair of indices i < j in 0..n, compute cand = pre[i] ^ pre[j], which is the XOR of the subarray arr[i..j-1].
5. Keep the maximum of those candidates in best.
6. Return best — the pair (i, j) that wins identifies the winning subarray.
approaches.code:
def max_xor_subarray(arr):
    # Prefix XOR: pre[k] = arr[0] ^ arr[1] ^ ... ^ arr[k-1], with pre[0] = 0.
    # Because x ^ x = 0, the XOR of arr[i..j] equals pre[j+1] ^ pre[i].
    n = len(arr)                      # size of the input
    pre = [0] * (n + 1)               # pre[0] = 0 represents the empty prefix
    for k in range(n):                # build the prefix table in one pass
        pre[k + 1] = pre[k] ^ arr[k]  # extend the previous prefix by one element
    best = 0                          # answer so far
    for i in range(n + 1):            # choose the earlier prefix
        for j in range(i + 1, n + 1): # and a later one; they bound a real subarray
            cand = pre[i] ^ pre[j]    # XOR of the subarray strictly between them
            if cand > best:           # track the maximum
                best = cand
    return best                       # the subarray problem is now a PAIR problem

complexity.time: O(n^2) — the prefix table is linear, but all pairs of prefixes are still examined
complexity.space: O(n) — the prefix-XOR table

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: Combine the prefix identity with a binary trie. Sweep the array once, maintaining the running prefix. At each step we want the earlier prefix that maximises prefix ^ earlier — and a trie of the earlier prefixes answers that in about 30 steps: read our prefix MSB-first and always try to descend into the branch holding the OPPOSITE bit, because a 1 in a high bit is worth more than everything below it; if that branch is missing, every stored prefix agrees with us there, that XOR bit is unavoidably 0, and we follow the only branch available. Two details make it correct. First, seed the trie with the value 0, the empty prefix, so subarrays starting at index 0 are allowed. Second, QUERY before you INSERT the current prefix, so the partner is always a strictly earlier prefix and the reported subarray is non-empty. Total work is O(n * 30).
approaches.algorithm:
1. Return 0 immediately for an empty array, then set BITS = max(arr).bit_length() (at least 1) and create the trie root children = [[-1, -1]].
2. Insert the value 0 into the trie — it represents the empty prefix and lets a subarray begin at index 0.
3. Set prefix = 0 and best = 0, then loop over every num in arr.
4. Update prefix ^= num so prefix is the XOR of everything seen so far.
5. QUERY: walk from the root with cur = 0; for b from BITS-1 down to 0 let bit = (prefix >> b) & 1 and want = 1 - bit; if children[node][want] exists, set cur |= (1 << b) and go there, else follow children[node][bit].
6. cur is now prefix ^ (best earlier prefix), which is the XOR of the subarray between them, so update best if cur is larger.
7. INSERT the current prefix into the trie, creating nodes only where a branch is missing, so future positions can pair with it.
8. After the sweep, return best.
approaches.code:
def max_xor_subarray(arr):
    if not arr:                                # an empty array has no subarray
        return 0
    BITS = max(max(arr).bit_length(), 1)       # enough bit levels for any prefix XOR
    children = [[-1, -1]]                      # children[node][bit], -1 = branch missing
    # Insert the prefix value 0 first: it stands for the empty prefix before index 0,
    # and it is what allows the best subarray to start at index 0.
    node = 0                                   # start at the root
    for b in range(BITS - 1, -1, -1):          # the trie is empty, so every level is new
        children.append([-1, -1])              # allocate the next node of the 0-path
        children[node][0] = len(children) - 1  # every bit of the value 0 is 0
        node = children[node][0]               # descend
    prefix = 0                                 # running XOR of arr[0..i]
    best = 0                                   # largest subarray XOR found so far
    for num in arr:                            # single sweep over the array
        prefix ^= num                          # prefix now covers arr[0..i]
        node = 0                               # QUERY: which stored prefix pairs best?
        cur = 0                                # XOR value being assembled, MSB first
        for b in range(BITS - 1, -1, -1):      # greedy, most significant bit first
            bit = (prefix >> b) & 1            # our bit at position b
            want = 1 - bit                     # the opposite bit makes this XOR bit 1
            if children[node][want] != -1:     # some earlier prefix has that bit
                cur |= (1 << b)                # so this bit of the answer can be 1
                node = children[node][want]    # follow the greedy branch
            else:                              # forced: all earlier prefixes match us
                node = children[node][bit]     # this XOR bit stays 0
        if cur > best:                         # cur = prefix ^ some earlier prefix
            best = cur                         # = XOR of the subarray between them
        node = 0                               # INSERT: make this prefix usable later
        for b in range(BITS - 1, -1, -1):      # store prefix as a path of bits
            bit = (prefix >> b) & 1            # bit of prefix at position b
            if children[node][bit] == -1:      # create the branch only when missing
                children.append([-1, -1])      # a fresh empty node
                children[node][bit] = len(children) - 1   # link parent -> child
            node = children[node][bit]         # descend one level
    return best                                # best XOR over all subarrays

complexity.time: O(n * B) with B ≈ 30 — each element triggers one query walk and one insertion walk
complexity.space: O(n * B) — worst case one trie node per bit of every inserted prefix

Maximum XOR Subarray.tests:
assert max_xor_subarray([1, 2, 3, 4]) == 7            # subarray [3, 4]
assert max_xor_subarray([8, 1, 2, 12, 7, 6]) == 15    # subarray [1, 2, 12]
assert max_xor_subarray([5]) == 5                     # edge: single element
assert max_xor_subarray([0, 0, 0]) == 0               # edge: all zeros
assert max_xor_subarray([]) == 0                      # edge: empty array

# Cross-check against an independent O(n^2) reference on random data.
import random
random.seed(7)
for _ in range(30):
    a = [random.randint(0, 63) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 12))]
    ref = 0
    for i in range(len(a)):
        c = 0
        for j in range(i, len(a)):
            c ^= a[j]
            ref = max(ref, c)
    assert max_xor_subarray(a) == ref

Coin Change.title: Coin Change
Coin Change.problemStatement: You are given a list of coin denominations (for example [1, 2, 5]) and a target amount of money. You own an UNLIMITED number of coins of each denomination, and you may use the same coin type as many times as you like. Your job is to return the smallest number of coins whose values add up to exactly the target amount. If the amount simply cannot be assembled from the given denominations, return -1. You are not asked for the actual coins, only how many, and nothing is modified in place. Be careful: the obvious greedy idea of always grabbing the biggest coin that fits is WRONG for general denominations (with coins [1, 3, 4] and amount 6, greedy takes 4 + 1 + 1 = 3 coins while the true best is 3 + 3 = 2 coins), which is exactly why this is a dynamic-programming problem and not a greedy one.

examples.explanation: Build the answer for every amount from 1 upward. Amount 1 needs one coin (1). Amount 2 needs one coin (2) because the single coin 2 beats 1 + 1. Amount 3 needs two coins (2 + 1). Amount 4 needs two coins (2 + 2). Amount 5 needs one coin (5). Amount 6 = 5 + 1 needs two, amount 7 = 5 + 2 needs two, amount 10 = 5 + 5 needs two, and finally amount 11 = 5 + 5 + 1 needs three coins. No arrangement uses fewer than three, so the answer is 3.
Every sum of 2s is even, so an odd target such as 3 can never be reached. The DP table keeps dp[3] at infinity, and we translate that into -1.
Zero money needs zero coins - this is the base case the whole table stands on.

constraints: 1 <= coins[i] <= 2^31 - 1 (a denomination may be larger than the amount)
Coin supply is unlimited for every denomination
edgeCases: amount = 0 - the answer is 0, not -1; if your base case is missing you will wrongly report the target as unreachable.

A denomination larger than the amount (coins = [5, 10], amount = 3) - the `c <= a` guard must skip it, otherwise dp[a - c] indexes with a negative number and Python silently wraps to the end of the list.
Unreachable amounts such as coins = [2], amount = 3 - the cell stays at infinity and must be converted to -1 at the very end, never treated as a real count.
Denominations that make greedy fail, like coins = [1, 3, 4], amount = 6 - greedy answers 3 coins while the DP answers 2, which is the whole reason we cannot sort and grab.
Duplicate denominations such as coins = [2, 2, 5] - harmless for correctness (the same relaxation just runs twice) but it doubles wasted work, so dedupe if you care about constants.
followUps: Coin Change II: instead of the minimum number of coins, count how many distinct combinations sum to the amount - why must the coin loop become the OUTER loop there to avoid counting permutations?
Return the actual multiset of coins used, not just the count, while keeping O(amount * len(coins)) time (hint: store the coin that produced each cell and walk backwards).
What if every denomination may be used at most once (0/1 knapsack flavour)? How does the loop direction over `amount` have to change?
Amount up to 10^9 with tiny coin values - the table no longer fits in memory; discuss the coin-problem / Frobenius structure or BFS on residues modulo the smallest coin.
prerequisites: The unbounded-knapsack pattern: because coins can repeat, the recursion stays on the same index after taking a coin instead of moving to i + 1.
Why greedy fails here: taking the largest fitting coin is only optimal for 'canonical' coin systems like real currency, not for arbitrary denominations.
Bottom-up tabulation over the amount axis: dp[a] depends only on strictly smaller amounts, so a single increasing loop fills the table with no recursion at all.
Using float('inf') as an 'impossible' sentinel and translating it to -1 at the end, so min() comparisons stay clean without special cases inside the loop.
Python detail: dp[a - c] with a negative index silently wraps to the tail of the list, so the `c <= a` bounds check is mandatory, not decorative.

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: Forget clever tricks and just ask the only question the problem really contains: for each coin denomination, do I use it or not, and if I use it how many times? We turn that into a recursion over (index, remaining amount). At coin type i we either skip the type entirely and recurse on i + 1 with the same remainder, or we pay one coin of type i and recurse on the SAME index i (because supply is unlimited) with a smaller remainder. Every possible multiset of coins is enumerated exactly once by this pair of choices, so the answer is certainly correct. The problem is repetition: the state (i = 1, rem = 7) can be reached through dozens of different coin orders, and each time we redo the entire subtree of work below it.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Define solve(i, rem) = the fewest coins needed to pay exactly `rem` using only coin types i and later.
2. Base case A: rem == 0 -> return 0, the bill is settled.
3. Base case B: i == len(coins) while rem > 0 -> return infinity, this branch failed.
4. Branch 'not take': solve(i + 1, rem), abandoning denomination i forever.
5. Branch 'take': if coins[i] <= rem, 1 + solve(i, rem - coins[i]); index stays because coins repeat.
6. Return min(take, not_take); at the top level convert an infinite result to -1.

complexity.time: O(2^(amount/min_coin)) - every coin can be taken many times, so the recursion tree branches exponentially with no memo to stop it
complexity.space: O(amount / min_coin) - depth of the recursion stack when we keep taking the smallest coin

approaches.name: Better (Memoization)
approaches.intuition: Look at what the brute force actually recomputes. The state of the recursion is fully described by two numbers: which coin index we are allowed to start from, and how much money is still owed. There are at most len(coins) * (amount + 1) such states, yet the naive tree visits them exponentially many times because paying 5 then 2 lands on the same state as paying 2 then 5. Caching the answer for each (i, rem) pair collapses the whole tree into that small grid of states: the first visit computes, every later visit reads. The logic is copied verbatim from the brute force - the only new thing is the cache - which is exactly how you should present this step in an interview.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Keep the identical solve(i, rem) recursion from the brute force.
2. Wrap it in an lru_cache (or a dict/2-D memo array) keyed by the pair (i, rem).
3. On entry, the cache returns instantly for a state that was already solved.
4. Otherwise compute min(not_take, take) exactly as before and let the cache store it.
5. Call solve(0, amount), clear the cache, and map an infinite result to -1.
approaches.code:
from functools import lru_cache

def coinChange(coins: List[int], amount: int) -> int:
    INF = float('inf')              # "impossible" marker

    # SAME recursion as brute force, but every (i, rem) pair is solved only once
    @lru_cache(maxsize=None)
    def solve(i: int, rem: int):
        if rem == 0:                # exact change: nothing more to pay
            return 0
        if i == len(coins):         # no coin types left but money still owed
            return INF
        not_take = solve(i + 1, rem)            # skip this denomination entirely
        take = INF                              # assume the coin does not fit
        if coins[i] <= rem:                     # it fits -> pay one and stay on i
            take = 1 + solve(i, rem - coins[i])
        return min(take, not_take)              # cheapest of the two branches

    ans = solve(0, amount)          # kick off with all denominations available
    solve.cache_clear()             # free the memo table before returning
    return -1 if ans == INF else int(ans)

complexity.time: O(n * amount) - each of the n * (amount + 1) states is computed once and then reused from the cache
complexity.space: O(n * amount) for the memo table plus O(amount) recursion stack depth

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: The memoised recursion already visits only O(n * amount) states, but it pays for a call stack and a hash table. Notice the dependency direction: the answer for amount a only ever looks at strictly smaller amounts (a - c). That means we can drop the index dimension entirely and fill one flat array from amount 1 upward, and by the time we reach a, every value it needs is already final. dp[a] = 1 + min over all coins c that fit of dp[a - c]. Because we allow ourselves to reuse dp[a - c] which itself may already contain coin c, repetition of coins is handled for free - that is the signature of unbounded knapsack. The result is an iterative O(n * amount) solution with a single array, no recursion limit worries and excellent cache behaviour.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Create dp of length amount + 1 filled with infinity, meaning 'not reachable yet'.
2. Set dp[0] = 0: paying nothing costs no coins.
3. Loop a from 1 to amount, in increasing order, so every smaller cell is already final.
4. For each denomination c with c <= a, relax dp[a] = min(dp[a], dp[a - c] + 1).
5. Skip any coin larger than a - it cannot be part of a payment of size a.
6. After the loops, return -1 if dp[amount] is still infinity, otherwise dp[amount].
approaches.code:
def coinChange(coins: List[int], amount: int) -> int:
    # INF marks "this amount is impossible to build with the given coins"
    INF = float('inf')
    # dp[a] = fewest coins that add up to exactly a
    dp = [INF] * (amount + 1)
    # amount 0 needs zero coins - the anchor every other cell is built from
    dp[0] = 0
    # solve small amounts first so dp[a - c] is always ready when we need it
    for a in range(1, amount + 1):
        # try finishing amount a with one coin of each denomination
        for c in coins:
            # the coin must fit, and using it must beat the best plan found so far
            if c <= a and dp[a - c] + 1 < dp[a]:
                # one coin c placed on top of the best way to make (a - c)
                dp[a] = dp[a - c] + 1
    # a cell still holding INF means no combination reaches that amount
    return -1 if dp[amount] == INF else int(dp[amount])

complexity.time: O(amount * n) - one pass over every amount, trying each of the n denominations
complexity.space: O(amount) - a single 1-D table, no recursion stack

Coin Change.tests:
assert coinChange([1, 2, 5], 11) == 3          # 5 + 5 + 1 is optimal
assert coinChange([1, 2, 5], 6) == 2            # 5 + 1 beats 2 + 2 + 2
assert coinChange([2], 3) == -1                 # odd target, even-only coin -> impossible
assert coinChange([1], 0) == 0                  # edge case: amount 0 needs no coins
assert coinChange([5, 7], 12) == 2              # 5 + 7, greedy on 7 alone would fail
assert coinChange([5, 7], 13) == -1             # no combination of 5s and 7s reaches 13

Minimum Cost to Cut a Stick.title: Minimum Cost to Cut a Stick
Minimum Cost to Cut a Stick.problemStatement: You are given a wooden stick of length n lying on a number line from 0 to n, and a list `cuts` holding the positions where the stick must be cut. You may perform the cuts in ANY order you like. The cost of a single cut equals the length of the piece of wood you are currently cutting - not the length of the whole original stick. After a cut, that piece splits into two smaller pieces, and any later cut only pays for the smaller piece it lands in. Return the minimum total cost to perform all the required cuts. The order you choose genuinely changes the bill: cutting near the middle first makes the remaining pieces short and therefore cheap, while cutting near an end first leaves a long expensive piece behind. Nothing is modified in place; you return one integer.

examples.explanation: First sort the cuts and add the stick ends as sentinels: positions become [0, 1, 3, 4, 5, 7]. A cheapest order is: cut at 3 (the whole stick of length 7 costs 7, leaving pieces [0,3] and [3,7]); then cut at 5 inside the piece [3,7] of length 4 (cost 4, leaving [3,5] and [5,7]); then cut at 1 inside the piece [0,3] of length 3 (cost 3); finally cut at 4 inside the piece [3,5] of length 2 (cost 2). Total 7 + 4 + 3 + 2 = 16. A naive left-to-right order 1, 3, 4, 5 would cost 7 + 6 + 4 + 3 = 20, which shows why the order must be searched, not guessed.

Sorted positions with sentinels are [0, 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 9]. An optimal schedule is 4, 2, 1, 6, 5: cutting at 4 splits the whole stick of length 9, so it costs 9; cutting at 2 happens inside the piece [0, 4], so it costs 4; cutting at 1 happens inside [0, 2], so it costs 2; cutting at 6 happens inside [4, 9], so it costs 5; cutting at 5 happens inside [4, 6], so it costs 2. Total 9 + 4 + 2 + 5 + 2 = 22, and no ordering does better. Order really is what you are paying for: the same five cuts taken as 4, 2, 5, 1, 6 come to 9 + 4 + 5 + 2 + 4 = 24, because cutting 5 first leaves the cut at 6 sitting in a piece of length 4 rather than 2.
With only one cut there is no ordering choice at all: it happens on the full stick, so the cost is the full length 4.

constraints: 1 <= cuts[i] <= n - 1 and all cut positions are distinct
`cuts` is NOT given in sorted order
edgeCases: A single cut - there is no ordering decision, and the answer is exactly n; a solution that forgets the i > j base case can loop forever or return infinity here.
Unsorted input such as cuts = [5, 1, 3] - if you skip the sort, a cut no longer separates the remaining cuts into independent left/right groups and the DP recurrence silently becomes wrong.
Forgetting the sentinels 0 and n - without them the piece length c[j+1] - c[i-1] cannot be expressed, and the first and last pieces get mispriced.

Cuts crowded at one end, for example n = 10^6 with cuts = [1, 2, 3] - the answer is dominated by the first expensive cut, a good sanity check that cost uses the CURRENT piece length, not the original stick.
Maximum cuts (100) with a huge n - the table is only 102 x 102, so the answer is still instant; students who index the DP by stick position instead of by cut index blow up to a 10^6 x 10^6 table.
followUps: Also return one optimal ORDER of cuts, not just the cost - how do you store the chosen k for each window and rebuild the schedule?

Knuth / Yao's optimal-splitting speedup: this recurrence satisfies the quadrangle inequality, so the k-loop can be narrowed to bring O(m^3) down to O(m^2). Can you argue why the optimal split index is monotone?
What if each cut had its own fixed fee added on top of the piece length - does the interval DP still work unchanged?
Streaming variant: new cut positions keep arriving; can you update the answer incrementally, or must the whole table be rebuilt?
prerequisites: Interval / partition DP (the Matrix Chain Multiplication family): solve a range by trying every split point inside it and combining the two sub-ranges.
Why sorting the cuts is what makes the problem decomposable: once sorted, performing cut k means the cuts left of k and right of k live on physically separate pieces and never influence each other.
The sentinel trick: prepending 0 and appending n turns 'the length of the current piece' into the clean expression c[j+1] - c[i-1].
Bottom-up filling order for interval DP: the answer for a window depends on strictly SHORTER windows, so iterate i downward and j upward (or by increasing window length).
Recognising that the last thing to decide is the FIRST cut here (in Burst Balloons it is the LAST balloon) - choosing the right 'pivot event' is the heart of every partition DP.

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: The only freedom we have is the order of the cuts, so let us just try all of them. Sort the cut positions and pad them with the stick ends 0 and n; then a piece of wood is fully described by a window of pending cuts c[i..j], because that piece physically spans from c[i-1] to c[j+1]. Pick any pending cut k in the window as the FIRST cut we perform: we immediately pay the whole current piece length, and afterwards the cuts left of k live only on the left piece and the cuts right of k live only on the right piece - they can never interfere again. Recursing on both sides and taking the best k over all choices explores every possible schedule. It is correct but explosive, since the number of distinct orders grows like a Catalan number.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Sort `cuts` and build c = [0] + sorted(cuts) + [n], so index i-1 and j+1 always exist.
2. Define solve(i, j) = minimum cost for the pending cuts c[i..j] on the piece (c[i-1], c[j+1]).
3. Base case: if i > j the window is empty, so the cost is 0.
4. Compute length = c[j+1] - c[i-1]: the price of any single cut performed on this piece.
5. For every k in i..j, try cost = length + solve(i, k-1) + solve(k+1, j) and keep the minimum.
6. The answer is solve(1, m-2), the whole stick with every cut still to do.
approaches.code:
def minCost(n: int, cuts: List[int]) -> int:
    # Sorting is the key preparation: only on a sorted list does one cut split the
    # remaining cuts into a clean LEFT group and RIGHT group that never interact.
    c = [0] + sorted(cuts) + [n]
    m = len(c)                      # positions incl. the two stick ends (sentinels)

    # solve(i, j) = cheapest way to perform cuts c[i..j] on the piece (c[i-1], c[j+1])
    def solve(i: int, j: int) -> int:
        # empty window: no cut is pending on this piece, so it costs nothing
        if i > j:
            return 0
        # the piece we hold spans c[i-1] .. c[j+1]; its length is the price of ANY cut in it
        length = c[j + 1] - c[i - 1]
        best = float('inf')
        # try every pending cut as the FIRST one performed on this piece
        for k in range(i, j + 1):
            # pay the whole length once, then recurse on the two pieces it creates
            cost = length + solve(i, k - 1) + solve(k + 1, j)
            if cost < best:         # remember the cheapest first cut
                best = cost
        return best

    # the outermost call: the full stick with every cut still pending
    return solve(1, m - 2)

complexity.time: O(Catalan(m)) ~ exponential - every ordering of the cuts is explored and identical windows are recomputed again and again
complexity.space: O(m) recursion depth, where m = len(cuts) + 2

approaches.name: Better (Memoization)
approaches.intuition: Count the truly distinct questions the brute force asks. A recursive call is completely identified by the window (i, j) of pending cuts - the history of how we arrived there is irrelevant, because the physical piece is always c[i-1] .. c[j+1]. There are only about m^2 / 2 such windows, yet the naive recursion revisits them an exponential number of times: the window (2, 4) is reached by every schedule that happens to isolate that stretch. Storing each window's answer the first time we compute it turns the exponential tree into a small triangular table of states, each solved once with an O(m) loop inside. This is the same code as before plus one decorator, which is exactly how you should evolve it on a whiteboard.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Prepare c = [0] + sorted(cuts) + [n] exactly as in the brute force.
2. Memoise solve(i, j) with lru_cache (or a 2-D array of -1 sentinels).
3. Return 0 immediately for the empty window i > j.
4. Otherwise loop k from i to j, combining length + solve(i, k-1) + solve(k+1, j).
5. Cache and return the minimum; the first call computes, later calls just read.
6. Answer = solve(1, m-2).
approaches.code:
from functools import lru_cache

def minCost(n: int, cuts: List[int]) -> int:
    c = [0] + sorted(cuts) + [n]    # sentinels + sorted cut positions
    m = len(c)                      # total number of positions

    # exactly the brute-force recursion, but each (i, j) window is solved only once
    @lru_cache(maxsize=None)
    def solve(i: int, j: int) -> int:
        if i > j:                   # nothing left to cut in this window
            return 0
        length = c[j + 1] - c[i - 1]        # price of one cut on the current piece
        best = float('inf')
        for k in range(i, j + 1):           # k = the cut we make first
            cost = length + solve(i, k - 1) + solve(k + 1, j)
            if cost < best:                 # keep the cheapest opening move
                best = cost
        return best

    ans = solve(1, m - 2)           # solve the whole stick
    solve.cache_clear()             # drop the memo table before returning
    return ans

complexity.time: O(m^3) - about m^2 windows, each scanning up to m split points once
complexity.space: O(m^2) memo table plus O(m) recursion stack

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: The memoised version already reaches O(m^3), so the remaining win is structural: remove the recursion and fill the same triangular table directly. The dependency is clear - the window (i, j) reads only windows that are strictly SHORTER, namely (i, k-1) and (k+1, j). If we let i run downward from m-2 to 1 and j run upward from i, then dp[i][k-1] (same row, smaller column) and dp[k+1][j] (bigger row) are guaranteed to be computed already. The zero-initialised cells with j < i conveniently represent empty windows that cost nothing, so no special case is needed inside the loop. The result is a tight triple loop with no call stack, no hashing and perfect predictability - the version you want to write in an interview once you have explained the recursion.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Build c = [0] + sorted(cuts) + [n] and let m = len(c).
2. Allocate dp as an m x m table of zeros; a cell with j < i means an empty window costing 0.
3. Loop i from m-2 down to 1 (backwards) and, inside it, j from i up to m-2 (forwards).
4. Set length = c[j+1] - c[i-1], the price of one cut on the piece this window sits on.
5. For every split k in i..j compute length + dp[i][k-1] + dp[k+1][j] and keep the minimum in dp[i][j].
6. Return dp[1][m-2], the cost of cutting the entire stick.
approaches.code:
def minCost(n: int, cuts: List[int]) -> int:
    # sort first: only then does a cut split its piece into two independent halves
    c = [0] + sorted(cuts) + [n]
    # m = number of positions including the two stick ends we added as sentinels
    m = len(c)
    # dp[i][j] = cheapest cost to perform cuts c[i..j] on the piece (c[i-1], c[j+1])
    dp = [[0] * m for _ in range(m)]
    # i walks BACKWARDS so dp[k + 1][j] (a larger first index) is already filled
    for i in range(m - 2, 0, -1):
        # j walks forwards so dp[i][k - 1] (a smaller second index) is already filled
        for j in range(i, m - 1):
            # length of the piece currently held - the price of any single cut inside it
            length = c[j + 1] - c[i - 1]
            best = float('inf')     # cheapest plan for this window so far
            # try every pending cut in the window as the FIRST cut on this piece
            for k in range(i, j + 1):
                # pay the length now, then reuse the answers of the two smaller windows
                cost = length + dp[i][k - 1] + dp[k + 1][j]
                if cost < best:     # keep the cheapest opening cut
                    best = cost
            # this window is solved; bigger windows may now reuse it
            dp[i][j] = best
    # the full stick, with every cut still pending
    return dp[1][m - 2]

complexity.time: O(m^3) where m = len(cuts) + 2 - each of the ~m^2/2 windows scans up to m split points (about 10^6 operations at the limit of 100 cuts)
complexity.space: O(m^2) for the DP table, and no recursion stack at all

Minimum Cost to Cut a Stick.tests:
assert minCost(7, [1, 3, 4, 5]) == 16          # classic example: order matters a lot
assert minCost(9, [5, 6, 1, 4, 2]) == 22
assert minCost(5, [1, 3]) == 8                  # cut at 3 first (5), then at 1 (3)
assert minCost(4, [2]) == 4                     # edge case: a single cut costs the whole length
assert minCost(10, [3]) == 10
assert minCost(6, [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]) == 16        # every position cut

Burst Balloons.title: Burst Balloons
Burst Balloons.problemStatement: You are given n balloons in a row, each painted with a number. You must burst all of them, one at a time, in whatever order you prefer. When you burst the balloon at position i you earn left * nums[i] * right coins, where left and right are the values of the balloons that are CURRENTLY its immediate neighbours - not its original neighbours, because burst balloons disappear and the row closes up. If a neighbour does not exist (you are at the edge of the row) treat it as an imaginary balloon holding the value 1. Return the maximum number of coins you can collect after every balloon has been burst. The difficulty is that the row keeps changing shape as you pop, so the coins earned by a balloon depend on the order chosen for all the others.

examples.explanation: Pad the row with imaginary 1s: [1, 3, 1, 5, 8, 1]. Burst the balloon 1 first: its neighbours are 3 and 5, so we earn 3 * 1 * 5 = 15 and the row becomes [3, 5, 8]. Burst 5 next: neighbours 3 and 8 give 3 * 5 * 8 = 120, leaving [3, 8]. Burst 3: its left neighbour is missing (counts as 1) so we earn 1 * 3 * 8 = 24, leaving [8]. Finally burst 8 with both neighbours missing: 1 * 8 * 1 = 8. The total is 15 + 120 + 24 + 8 = 167, and no other order beats it - notice the strategy of keeping the big balloons alive as long as possible so they can multiply their neighbours.
Bursting 1 first earns 1 * 1 * 5 = 5 and then 5 earns 1 * 5 * 1 = 5, total 10. The reverse order earns 1 * 5 * 1 = 5 then 1 * 1 * 1 = 1, only 6. So 10 is the maximum.
One balloon with both neighbours imaginary: 1 * 7 * 1 = 7.

constraints: Out-of-range neighbours count as balloons with value 1 (they are never actually burst)
Every balloon must eventually be burst
edgeCases: A single balloon - both neighbours are imaginary, so the answer is 1 * nums[0] * 1; code that assumes real neighbours exist will index out of range.
Balloons with value 0 - they contribute nothing when burst but still block their neighbours from multiplying, so they cannot simply be deleted from the array.
Two balloons only - the order still matters (see [1, 5] giving 10 versus 6), which is a compact proof that greedy 'burst the smallest first' is not a valid rule.
All values equal, like [1, 1, 1] - useful sanity check that the padding is right, since the answer 3 comes from three products of 1 * 1 * 1.

Thinking in terms of the FIRST balloon burst instead of the LAST - the sub-arrays then stop being independent (the pieces can still influence each other through the gap), which is the single most common wrong start on this problem.
followUps: Reconstruct the actual burst order that achieves the maximum, not just the coin total (store the winning k for each window and recurse).
What if bursting a balloon only earned left + nums[i] + right coins instead of a product - does the same 'last balloon' decomposition still hold?
n up to 5000 would make O(n^3) too slow; discuss why no sub-cubic algorithm is known here and what pruning (e.g. removing zeros, Knuth-style split narrowing) is still valid.

Compare this with Matrix Chain Multiplication and Minimum Cost to Cut a Stick: all three are interval DP, but the pivot event differs (last balloon vs first cut) - can you state the rule for choosing the pivot?
prerequisites: Interval DP over a window i..j, where the answer to a window is built from strictly shorter windows.
The 'think about the LAST operation' trick: choosing the last balloon in a window fixes its neighbours to the window walls and makes the left and right halves independent.
Why the naive 'first balloon' split is wrong: after bursting a balloon in the middle, the two sides become adjacent and can affect each other's coins.
Padding with sentinel 1s at both ends so the expression a[i-1] * a[k] * a[j+1] never needs a boundary special case.
Bottom-up fill order for triangular tables: loop i downward and j upward so both dp[i][k-1] and dp[k+1][j] are already final when read.

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: The problem statement is already an algorithm if we are willing to be slow: at every moment we may burst any surviving balloon, so simply try each of them, collect the coins that popping it earns right now, physically remove it from the row (which makes its neighbours adjacent) and recurse on what is left. Taking the maximum over all first choices explores every possible burst order and therefore must find the best one. The catch is that with n balloons there are n! orders, and rebuilding the shortened list at every step costs extra time on top. Even n = 10 is already millions of calls, so this version exists to prove correctness and to expose the real difficulty: after a middle balloon pops, the two sides are no longer independent, so we cannot memoise on 'the sub-array' in any obvious way.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Represent the surviving balloons as a tuple `cur`.
2. Base case: an empty tuple earns 0 coins.
3. For each index i in cur, read its current neighbours, treating a missing side as the value 1.
4. Earn left * cur[i] * right, remove index i to form the shorter tuple `rest`, and recurse on it.
5. Keep the maximum over all choices of i and return it.
6. Start the recursion with the full tuple of balloons.
approaches.code:
def maxCoins(nums: List[int]) -> int:
    # best(cur) = most coins obtainable from the balloons still on the table
    def best(cur: Tuple[int, ...]) -> int:
        # no balloons left -> no more coins can be earned
        if not cur:
            return 0
        top = 0
        # try bursting EVERY remaining balloon next and keep the best total
        for i in range(len(cur)):
            # a missing neighbour counts as an imaginary balloon of value 1
            left = cur[i - 1] if i > 0 else 1
            right = cur[i + 1] if i + 1 < len(cur) else 1
            # coins earned right now by popping balloon i
            gain = left * cur[i] * right
            # the remaining balloons close the gap - neighbours change!
            rest = cur[:i] + cur[i + 1:]
            total = gain + best(rest)
            if total > top:         # keep the most profitable first pop
                top = total
        return top

    # start with every balloon present (tuple so it could be hashed/memoised)
    return best(tuple(nums))

complexity.time: O(n! * n) - every burst order is enumerated and each step rebuilds a list of length n
complexity.space: O(n^2) - recursion depth n, each frame holding a copy of the shrinking row

approaches.name: Better (Memoization)
approaches.intuition: The reason the brute force cannot be memoised is that it thinks about the FIRST balloon burst: once you pop something in the middle, the left and right pieces become neighbours and keep influencing each other, so a piece is not an independent subproblem. Flip the question and ask instead which balloon in the window i..j is burst LAST. That single change fixes everything: if k is last, then at the moment k pops, every other balloon of the window is already gone, so its neighbours are exactly the walls a[i-1] and a[j+1], earning a[i-1] * a[k] * a[j+1]. Everything left of k must be fully burst inside the window (i, k-1) and everything right inside (k+1, j), and those two halves genuinely never touch each other because k separates them until the very end. Now the state is just the window, so we can cache it.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Build a = [1] + nums + [1] so that indices i-1 and j+1 always exist.
2. Define solve(i, j) = best coins from bursting every balloon in the window i..j, with i, j over real balloons.
3. Base case: i > j means an empty window worth 0 coins.
4. For each k in i..j, treat k as the LAST balloon burst: coins = a[i-1] * a[k] * a[j+1].
5. Add solve(i, k-1) + solve(k+1, j), the independent left and right sub-windows.
6. Cache the maximum over all k, and return solve(1, m-2) for the whole row.
approaches.code:
from functools import lru_cache

def maxCoins(nums: List[int]) -> int:
    # Pad with imaginary 1-balloons so every real balloon always has two neighbours.
    a = [1] + list(nums) + [1]
    m = len(a)

    # KEY INSIGHT: think about which balloon in the window is burst LAST.
    # solve(i, j) = best coins from bursting all balloons in the window i..j
    @lru_cache(maxsize=None)
    def solve(i: int, j: int) -> int:
        if i > j:                   # empty window earns nothing
            return 0
        top = 0
        for k in range(i, j + 1):   # k = the balloon burst LAST inside the window
            # because k is last, its surviving neighbours are exactly the walls a[i-1], a[j+1]
            coins = a[i - 1] * a[k] * a[j + 1]
            # everything left of k and right of k is burst BEFORE k, independently
            coins += solve(i, k - 1) + solve(k + 1, j)
            if coins > top:         # keep the most profitable "last balloon"
                top = coins
        return top

    ans = solve(1, m - 2)           # the window of all real balloons
    solve.cache_clear()             # release the memo table
    return ans

complexity.time: O(n^3) - about n^2 windows, each trying up to n candidates for the last balloon, computed once thanks to the cache
complexity.space: O(n^2) memo table plus O(n) recursion stack

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: The last-balloon recurrence is already optimal in complexity, so the final step is to write it as a plain table and remove the recursion entirely. Every window (i, j) reads only dp[i][k-1] and dp[k+1][j], both of which describe strictly SHORTER windows. Filling the table with i going from m-2 down to 1 and j going from i up to m-2 guarantees those two cells are already final when we read them: dp[i][k-1] sits in the same row further left, and dp[k+1][j] sits in a row we processed earlier. Cells with j < i are never written and keep their initial 0, which is exactly the correct value for an empty window - so the base case needs no code at all. The result is a clean triple loop, O(n^3) time with tiny constants and no risk of hitting Python's recursion limit on n = 300 balloons.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Pad the row: a = [1] + nums + [1], m = len(a); real balloons are at indices 1 .. m-2.
2. Allocate an m x m table dp of zeros; cells with j < i stay 0 and stand for empty windows.
3. Loop i from m-2 down to 1, and inside it loop j from i up to m-2.
4. For each window, try every k in i..j as the LAST balloon: coins = a[i-1]*a[k]*a[j+1] + dp[i][k-1] + dp[k+1][j].
5. Store the maximum of those candidates in dp[i][j].
6. Return dp[1][m-2], the best total for the window containing every real balloon.
approaches.code:
def maxCoins(nums: List[int]) -> int:
    # pad with imaginary 1-balloons so every real balloon always has two neighbours
    a = [1] + list(nums) + [1]
    # m = padded length; the real balloons occupy indices 1 .. m - 2
    m = len(a)
    # dp[i][j] = most coins obtainable by bursting EVERY balloon in the window i..j
    dp = [[0] * m for _ in range(m)]
    # i decreases so dp[k + 1][j] (a window starting further right) is already known
    for i in range(m - 2, 0, -1):
        # j increases so dp[i][k - 1] (a window ending further left) is already known
        for j in range(i, m - 1):
            best = 0                # best coins found for this window so far
            # k = the balloon we choose to burst LAST inside this window
            for k in range(i, j + 1):
                # k is last, so at that moment its neighbours are the walls a[i-1] and a[j+1]
                coins = a[i - 1] * a[k] * a[j + 1] + dp[i][k - 1] + dp[k + 1][j]
                if coins > best:    # keep the most profitable choice of last balloon
                    best = coins
            # window i..j is fully solved and safe to reuse
            dp[i][j] = best
    # the window covering every real balloon
    return dp[1][m - 2]

complexity.time: O(n^3) - n^2/2 windows times up to n choices of the last balloon (about 2.7 * 10^7 steps at n = 300)
complexity.space: O(n^2) for the DP table, with no recursion stack

Burst Balloons.tests:
assert maxCoins([3, 1, 5, 8]) == 167           # the classic LeetCode example
assert maxCoins([1, 5]) == 10                   # burst 1 first, then 5
assert maxCoins([3, 1, 5]) == 35
assert maxCoins([7]) == 7                       # edge case: single balloon -> 1 * 7 * 1
assert maxCoins([1, 1, 1]) == 3

Palindrome Partitioning II.title: Palindrome Partitioning II
Palindrome Partitioning II.problemStatement: You are given a string s. You must split it into consecutive pieces so that EVERY piece is a palindrome - a string that reads the same forwards and backwards, like 'aa' or 'noon'. A single character is always a palindrome, so such a split always exists (in the worst case you cut between every pair of characters). Your task is to return the MINIMUM number of cuts needed, not the pieces themselves. Note the difference between cuts and pieces: producing k pieces requires k - 1 cuts, so a string that is already a palindrome needs 0 cuts. For example 'aab' can be split as 'aa' | 'b', which uses one cut, and no split uses zero cuts because 'aab' itself is not a palindrome. The string is not modified; you return a single integer.

examples.explanation: First work out which substrings are palindromes: 'a' (index 0), 'a' (index 1), 'b' (index 2) and 'aa' (indices 0..1) are palindromes, while 'ab' (1..2) and 'aab' (0..2) are not. Now build the answer prefix by prefix. Prefix 'a' is a palindrome, so dp[0] = 0 cuts. Prefix 'aa' is also a palindrome, so dp[1] = 0 cuts. Prefix 'aab' is NOT a palindrome, so the last piece must start somewhere after index 0: the only palindromic last piece is 'b' (index 2..2), which costs one cut placed before it plus dp[1] = 0 cuts for 'aa'. Therefore dp[2] = 1, and the split is 'aa' | 'b'.
No two neighbouring characters are equal, so the only palindromic pieces are the single letters. Five pieces means four cuts, the worst possible answer for a string of length 5.
The whole string reads the same both ways, so it is already one valid palindromic piece and no cut is required.

constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters only
The answer is always between 0 and len(s) - 1
edgeCases: A string that is already a palindrome, such as 'aabbaa' - the answer must be 0, so the code has to test the whole prefix before ever entering the cut loop.
A single character or an empty string - there is nothing to cut, and an unguarded dp[n-1] would index an empty list and crash.
No repeated characters, like 'abcde' - the answer is n - 1, which is exactly the initial value of `best`, so a missing initialisation would leave the value at infinity.
Even-length palindromes such as 'abba' - the check j - i < 2 must handle the length-2 case ('bb') before consulting pal[i+1][j-1], which would otherwise read a nonsense window where i + 1 > j - 1.
Long strings of identical characters like 'a' * 2000 - every substring is a palindrome, so the O(n^3) approaches degenerate to their worst case while the O(n^2) version stays instant.
followUps: Palindrome Partitioning I: return every possible palindromic partition instead of the minimum cut count - why does that problem become exponential output and require backtracking?
Also return one optimal partition, not just the number of cuts (store, for each j, the start index of the winning last piece and walk backwards).
Can you drop the O(n^2) palindrome table to O(n) extra space by expanding around every centre and relaxing dp on the fly? Sketch the two-pointer expansion version.
What if you were allowed at most k cuts and had to maximise the length of the shortest piece - how does the DP state change?
prerequisites: Palindrome DP: s[i..j] is a palindrome exactly when s[i] == s[j] and the inner window s[i+1..j-1] is a palindrome, with lengths 1 and 2 as base cases.
Prefix DP for partitioning: dp[j] answers a question about the prefix s[0..j], built by choosing where the LAST piece starts.
The cuts-versus-pieces distinction: k pieces need k - 1 cuts, which is why a whole-prefix palindrome scores 0 and not 1.
Fill-order reasoning for a 2-D boolean table: iterating i downward and j upward guarantees pal[i+1][j-1] is already computed when it is read.
Why precomputing all palindromes first turns an O(n^3) solution into O(n^2): the inner cut loop then only performs O(1) lookups instead of re-scanning substrings.

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: Read the problem literally: the first piece of the string must be some palindromic prefix s[0..j], and once we commit to it the rest of the job is the very same problem on the suffix s[j+1..]. So we recurse: for every end index j, check whether s[i..j] is a palindrome with a two-pointer scan, and if it is, pay one piece and recurse on j + 1. Counting pieces is easier than counting cuts, so the base case returns -1 when we reach the end of the string, which cancels the extra +1 charged by the final piece and turns the piece count into a cut count. Every valid partition is enumerated, so the result is right, but the same suffix is re-solved through many different prefixes and each visit re-scans substrings character by character.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Handle the trivial case: a string of length 0 or 1 needs 0 cuts.
2. Write is_pal(i, j) as a two-pointer scan comparing s[i] with s[j] while walking inward.
3. Define solve(i) = minimum number of pieces for the suffix s[i..], offset by -1 at the base case.
4. Base case: solve(n) = -1 so the final piece's +1 is cancelled and we end up counting cuts.
5. For every j from i to n-1, if s[i..j] is a palindrome try 1 + solve(j + 1) and keep the minimum.
6. Return solve(0).
approaches.code:
def minCut(s: str) -> int:
    n = len(s)                      # how many characters we must cover
    # an empty string or a single character needs no cut at all
    if n <= 1:
        return 0

    # straightforward two-pointer palindrome check for the slice s[i..j]
    def is_pal(i: int, j: int) -> bool:
        while i < j:                # walk the two ends towards each other
            if s[i] != s[j]:        # mismatch anywhere -> not a palindrome
                return False
            i += 1                  # move the left pointer inward
            j -= 1                  # move the right pointer inward
        return True                 # the pointers met, so every pair matched

    # solve(i) = minimum number of PIECES needed for the suffix s[i..], minus 1 at the end
    def solve(i: int):
        # consumed the whole string: -1 cancels the extra +1 counted by the last piece
        if i == n:
            return -1
        best = float('inf')         # no legal partition found for this suffix yet
        # try every possible end for the first piece of this suffix
        for j in range(i, n):
            # the piece s[i..j] must itself be a palindrome to be allowed
            if is_pal(i, j):
                # one piece for s[i..j] plus the best answer for the rest
                cost = 1 + solve(j + 1)
                if cost < best:     # fewest pieces wins
                    best = cost
        return best                 # cheapest partition of this suffix

    return int(solve(0))            # pieces - 1 == number of cuts

complexity.time: O(2^n * n) - every one of the 2^(n-1) cut placements can be explored, and each palindrome check costs O(n)
complexity.space: O(n) recursion stack depth

approaches.name: Better (Memoization)
approaches.intuition: Notice that solve(i) depends on nothing but the starting index i - the cuts already placed to the left of i are irrelevant to how cheaply the rest can be partitioned. That means there are only n distinct states, yet the brute force reaches solve(5) once for every palindromic way of covering the first five characters. Adding a cache collapses the exponential tree into n states, each doing an O(n) loop with an O(n) palindrome test inside, giving O(n^2) states-work and O(n^3) total. That already runs for moderate inputs, and it isolates the one remaining inefficiency: we keep re-checking whether the same substring is a palindrome, which the optimal solution fixes with a precomputed table.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Keep the same recursion solve(i) over suffix start indices.
2. Decorate it with lru_cache so each i is computed only once.
3. Base case solve(n) = -1 keeps converting the piece count into a cut count.
4. Loop j from i to n-1 and test is_pal(i, j) before recursing on j + 1.
5. Take the minimum of 1 + solve(j + 1) over all palindromic first pieces.
6. Call solve(0), clear the cache and return the result.
approaches.code:
from functools import lru_cache

def minCut(s: str) -> int:
    n = len(s)
    if n <= 1:                      # nothing to cut
        return 0

    def is_pal(i: int, j: int) -> bool:
        # expand from both ends; O(n) per call, and that is the remaining weakness
        while i < j:
            if s[i] != s[j]:
                return False
            i += 1
            j -= 1
        return True

    # the SAME recursion as the brute force, but each starting index is solved once
    @lru_cache(maxsize=None)
    def solve(i: int) -> int:
        if i == n:                  # whole string consumed
            return -1               # cancels the +1 charged by the final piece
        best = float('inf')
        for j in range(i, n):       # first piece is s[i..j]
            if is_pal(i, j):        # only palindromic pieces are legal
                cost = 1 + solve(j + 1)
                if cost < best:     # fewest pieces wins
                    best = cost
        return best

    ans = int(solve(0))
    solve.cache_clear()             # drop the cache before returning
    return ans

complexity.time: O(n^3) - n cached states, each looping over n end points with an O(n) palindrome check
complexity.space: O(n) for the cache plus O(n) recursion depth

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: Two separate wastes remain: re-checking palindromes, and recursion. Kill both. First build a boolean table pal[i][j] in O(n^2) using the rule 'a window is a palindrome when its two ends match and the window strictly inside it is a palindrome' - filling i downward guarantees the inner window pal[i+1][j-1] is already known, and windows of length 1 or 2 need no inner check at all. Second, replace the suffix recursion with a forward prefix scan: dp[j] = fewest cuts for s[0..j]. If the entire prefix is a palindrome, dp[j] = 0 with no cut at all. Otherwise the last piece is some palindromic s[i..j] with i >= 1, costing one cut plus dp[i-1]. Every palindrome question inside that loop is now a single table lookup, so the whole algorithm is O(n^2) time - fast enough for the 2000-character limit.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Return 0 immediately for a string of length 0 or 1.
2. Allocate pal as an n x n boolean table, all False.
3. Fill it with i running from n-1 down to 0 and j from i up to n-1: pal[i][j] is True when s[i] == s[j] and (j - i < 2 or pal[i+1][j-1]).
4. Allocate dp of length n, where dp[j] = fewest cuts for the prefix s[0..j].
5. For each j: if pal[0][j] then dp[j] = 0, otherwise start best = j and for every i in 1..j with pal[i][j] relax best = min(best, dp[i-1] + 1).
6. Store dp[j] = best and finally return dp[n-1].

complexity.time: O(n^2) - one quadratic pass to build the palindrome table and one quadratic pass to relax the cuts, with O(1) lookups inside
complexity.space: O(n^2) for the boolean palindrome table plus O(n) for the dp array

Palindrome Partitioning II.tests:
assert minCut("aab") == 1                      # "aa" | "b"
assert minCut("a") == 0                         # single character, already a palindrome
assert minCut("ab") == 1                        # "a" | "b"
assert minCut("aabbaa") == 0                    # the whole string is a palindrome
assert minCut("abcde") == 4                     # worst case: cut everywhere
assert minCut("") == 0                          # edge case: empty string
assert minCut("noonabbad") == 2                 # "noon" | "abba" | "d"

Kth Largest Element.title: Kth Largest Element
Kth Largest Element.problemStatement: You are given an unsorted array of integers `nums` and an integer `k`. Your job is to return the k-th largest element of the array. Important: this is the k-th largest element in the SORTED ORDER of the values, not the k-th largest *distinct* value. So if the array is [2, 2, 2, 2] and k = 3, the sorted-descending view is [2, 2, 2, 2] and the third entry is still 2. You do not have to modify the array, and you may return the value only (not its index). The array always has at least k elements, so a valid answer always exists. The interesting part of the problem is doing this faster than a full sort: you are asked for one position in the order, so paying O(n log n) to arrange every element is more work than the question actually requires.

examples.explanation: Sort the values descending to see the ranking: 6 (1st largest), 5 (2nd), 4 (3rd), 3 (4th), 2 (5th), 1 (6th). We want k = 2, so the answer is 5. The optimal solution never builds this full ranking: it keeps a min-heap of size 2. After 3 and 2 it holds {2, 3}; 1 arrives, is pushed and immediately evicted because it is the smallest of the three; 5 arrives and pushes 2 out leaving {3, 5}; 6 arrives and pushes 3 out leaving {5, 6}; 4 arrives and is itself evicted. The heap ends as {5, 6} and its root -- the smaller of the two -- is 5.
Descending order is 6, 5, 5, 4, 3, 3, 2, 2, 1. The 4th entry is 4. Notice the two 5s each occupy their own rank, which is why duplicates are not collapsed.
With a single element the largest element is that element itself.

constraints: The answer is guaranteed to exist (k never exceeds the array length).
edgeCases: k == 1 (just the maximum) and k == n (just the minimum) -- both are valid and the size-k heap logic must not special-case them.
Heavy duplicates such as [2,2,2,2] with k=3 -- tricky because a solution that de-duplicates values silently returns the wrong rank.
All-negative arrays -- tricky if you initialise a running maximum with 0 instead of nums[0] or -infinity.
n == 1 with k == 1 -- the heap never exceeds its budget, so the eviction branch never runs and heap[0] must still be returned.
Very large n with tiny k (n = 10^5, k = 2) -- the whole point of the size-k heap: memory stays O(k) instead of O(n).
followUps: Can you get expected O(n) time instead of O(n log k)? (Quickselect / randomised partition around a pivot, keeping only the side that contains rank k.)

The numbers arrive as an infinite stream and you must answer 'k-th largest so far' after every arrival -- how does the size-k min-heap solve this in O(log k) per element? (This is exactly LeetCode 703.)
The data lives on 100 different machines and does not fit in one memory. How would you compute the global k-th largest with as little network traffic as possible?
What changes if you are asked for the k-th SMALLEST instead, and can you reuse the same code by pushing negated values?
How would you return all k largest elements in sorted order, and what is the extra cost over returning just the k-th?
prerequisites: Python's `heapq` implements a MIN-heap only: `heap[0]` is the smallest item, and there is no max-heap -- the standard trick is to push negated values.
`heapq.heappush` and `heapq.heappop` are both O(log m) where m is the current heap size; `heap[0]` is an O(1) peek that does not remove anything.
A heap is stored as a plain Python list in level order, so printing it shows a valid heap array, NOT a sorted array -- only the root is guaranteed to be the minimum.
The 'bounded heap' pattern: to track the k best of a stream, keep a heap of size k whose root is the weakest survivor, and evict the root whenever the size exceeds k.
Negative indexing on a sorted list: `sorted(nums)[-k]` is the k-th largest -- useful as the easy baseline you should mention before optimising.

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: Forget clever data structures for a moment and ask what 'k-th largest' literally means: remove the largest element, then the largest of what remains, and repeat. Whatever you remove on the k-th round IS the k-th largest, because you have removed exactly k-1 strictly-better-ranked elements before it. Finding a maximum is something we know how to do with a plain linear scan, and removing it is just a list deletion. This costs a full scan per round, so k rounds cost O(n * k), but it needs no new concepts at all and it is the version you should be able to write in ten seconds at a whiteboard before you optimise.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Copy nums into a working list `remaining` so the caller's array is untouched.
2. Repeat the following k times.
3.   Scan `remaining` from left to right, tracking the largest value and its index.
4.   Pop that index out of `remaining`, and remember the value in `answer`.
5. After k rounds, `answer` holds the value removed on the k-th round -- the k-th largest.
6. Return `answer`.
approaches.code:
def find_kth_largest(nums, k):
    # Never mutate the caller's list -- interviewers notice side effects.
    remaining = list(nums)
    answer = None
    # Round r removes the current maximum, so after k rounds we have
    # removed the 1st, 2nd, ... k-th largest values in order.
    for _ in range(k):
        # Linear scan for the biggest value still present.
        current_max = remaining[0]
        max_index = 0
        for idx in range(1, len(remaining)):
            # Strict '>' keeps the FIRST occurrence on ties (either is fine).
            if remaining[idx] > current_max:
                current_max = remaining[idx]
                max_index = idx
        # Physically delete it so the next round sees the next largest.
        remaining.pop(max_index)
        answer = current_max          # last value removed = k-th largest
    return answer

complexity.time: O(n * k) — each of the k rounds does a full O(n) scan plus an O(n) list pop
complexity.space: O(n) — the defensive copy of the input list

approaches.name: Better (Sorting)
approaches.intuition: The brute force wastes work because it rediscovers the maximum from scratch every round. Sorting computes the entire ranking once, and once the array is ascending the k-th largest is simply the k-th element counted from the right end. Python's negative indexing makes that a one-liner: `sorted(nums)[-k]`. This is a genuine improvement, O(n log n) instead of O(n * k), and for small arrays it is what you would actually ship. Its weakness is that it computes far more information than we asked for -- we wanted ONE rank, and we produced all n of them -- which is exactly the wasted work the heap approach removes.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Make a sorted (ascending) copy of nums with `sorted(nums)`.
2. Understand the indexing: index -1 is the largest, -2 the second largest, and so on.
3. Therefore index -k is the k-th largest element.
4. Return `ordered[-k]`, which is valid because the constraints guarantee k <= n.
approaches.code:
def find_kth_largest(nums, k):
    # Sorting puts the numbers in ascending order: nums[0] is smallest,
    # nums[-1] is largest, nums[-2] second largest ... nums[-k] is k-th largest.
