    ordered = sorted(nums)            # Timsort, O(n log n), returns a NEW list
    # Negative indexing counts from the right: -1 -> last, -k -> k-th from the end.
    return ordered[-k]                # exactly the k-th largest value

complexity.time: O(n log n) — dominated by the sort of all n elements
complexity.space: O(n) — `sorted` returns a new list (an in-place `nums.sort()` would be O(1) extra but mutates the input)

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: Here is the aha: to answer 'what is the k-th largest?' you only ever need to remember the k largest numbers you have seen. Everything smaller than all of them is permanently irrelevant. So carry a container of exactly k elements and, whenever a new number arrives, decide whether it deserves a seat. The perfect container is a MIN-heap of size k, because the element most at risk of eviction -- the smallest of our current top k -- is sitting right at the root where we can compare against it in O(1) and remove it in O(log k). After the single pass, the heap holds the k largest values of the whole array and its root is the smallest of those k, which by definition is the k-th largest overall. Time drops to O(n log k) and, crucially, memory drops to O(k) -- so this still works when n is huge or streaming and k is small.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Create an empty list `heap` and treat it as a min-heap via the heapq functions.
2. For each `num` in nums, push it with `heapq.heappush(heap, num)`.
3. If the heap now holds more than k items, `heapq.heappop(heap)` removes the smallest — it cannot be among the k largest, so discarding it is safe.
4. Repeat until the input is exhausted; the invariant 'heap contains the k largest values seen so far' holds after every iteration.
5. Return `heap[0]`: the root of a min-heap is its minimum, i.e. the weakest of the k largest, which is the k-th largest element of the array.
approaches.code:
import heapq                                    # heapq is a MIN-heap: heap[0] is the SMALLEST item

def find_kth_largest(nums, k):
    # Key insight: we do not need the whole sorted order, only a bucket
    # that holds the k largest numbers seen so far.
    heap = []                                  # this list will never grow past k+1 entries
    for num in nums:                           # one single pass over the input
        heapq.heappush(heap, num)              # O(log k) insert, keeps heap order
        if len(heap) > k:                      # we are holding one candidate too many
            heapq.heappop(heap)                # evict the SMALLEST -> it can't be the k-th largest
    # Only the k largest values survived, and the min-heap keeps the
    # weakest of them at the root, which is precisely the k-th largest.
    return heap[0]

complexity.time: O(n log k) — n pushes/pops on a heap that never exceeds size k
complexity.space: O(k) — the heap stores at most k+1 elements at any instant

Kth Largest Element.tests:
assert find_kth_largest([3, 2, 1, 5, 6, 4], 2) == 5
assert find_kth_largest([3, 2, 3, 1, 2, 4, 5, 5, 6], 4) == 4
assert find_kth_largest([1], 1) == 1
# Edge case: duplicates -- the k-th largest is a VALUE, not a distinct value.
assert find_kth_largest([2, 2, 2, 2], 3) == 2
# Edge case: all negatives, and k == n (the k-th largest is the minimum).
assert find_kth_largest([-1, -5, -3], 3) == -5

Top K Frequent Elements.title: Top K Frequent Elements
Top K Frequent Elements.problemStatement: You are given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`. Return the k elements that appear most often in the array. You return the VALUES themselves, not their counts, and each value appears once in the output even if it occurs many times in the input. The answer may be returned in any order — there is no requirement to sort it by frequency — and the problem guarantees that the answer is unique, meaning there is never an ambiguous tie at the k-th position that would give two different valid answers. The array can contain negative numbers and duplicates, and k is always at least 1 and at most the number of distinct values in the array.

examples.explanation: First count everything: 1 appears three times, 2 appears twice, 3 appears once, giving the map {1: 3, 2: 2, 3: 1}. We now want the two values with the biggest counts. Walking the map with a size-2 min-heap: push (3, 1) so the heap is [(3,1)]; push (2, 2) and since 2 < 3 the pair (2,2) becomes the root, heap = [(2,2), (3,1)]; push (1, 3) which is the weakest of the three, so the heap is briefly [(1,3), (3,1), (2,2)] and its size 3 exceeds k = 2, so we pop the root (1, 3) — value 3 with count 1 is out. The survivors are (2, 2) and (3, 1); stripping the counts gives the values [2, 1], which is the correct answer in any order.
There is only one distinct value, so it is trivially the most frequent one.
Counts are {4: 3, 5: 2, 6: 4}. The two largest counts are 4 (for value 6) and 3 (for value 4), so the answer is {6, 4} in any order.

constraints: k is in the range [1, number of distinct elements in nums]
The answer is guaranteed to be unique.
edgeCases: k equals the number of distinct values — every value qualifies, and the heap never actually evicts anything, so the eviction branch must not be required for correctness.
All elements identical, e.g. [5,5,5,5] with k = 1 — tricky because the frequency map has a single key and code that assumes at least k pushes before the first pop would break.
Ties in frequency, e.g. [7,7,8,8] with k = 2 — the problem promises a unique answer, but you should know that with a tie an arbitrary tie-break is used and asserting one exact output would be wrong.
Negative values and zero — tricky only if you tried to index counts by value into a plain list instead of using a dictionary.
n = 10^5 with only two distinct values — the heap stays tiny, showing the cost is really O(n) counting plus O(u log k) heap work where u is the number of distinct values.
followUps: Can you solve it in strictly O(n) time? (Bucket sort: index an array of lists by frequency, since no frequency can exceed n, then walk the buckets from the back.)
Can you get O(n) average time with Quickselect on the (count, value) pairs, partitioning around a pivot count?

The numbers arrive as an unbounded stream and you must report the current top k at any moment — how do you maintain it incrementally, and why does a plain heap become wrong when a count is updated in place?
Memory is too small to hold every distinct value (think trending hashtags). How would a Count-Min Sketch plus a heap give an approximate top k?
What if you must return the answer sorted by decreasing frequency, with ties broken by smaller value first?
prerequisites: `collections.Counter(nums)` builds a value -> count dictionary in one O(n) pass; dictionary get/set is O(1) on average.
Python tuples compare lexicographically: `(2, 9) < (3, 0)` because the first components decide, which lets a heap of `(count, value)` order itself by count automatically.
`heapq` is a min-heap, so `heap[0]` is the least-frequent survivor — exactly the candidate you want to evict when the heap grows past k.
The bounded-heap pattern: keeping only k items gives O(u log k) instead of O(u log u) and, more importantly, O(k) memory.
A heap's list is in heap order, not sorted order, so the returned k values come out unordered — fine here because the problem allows any order.

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: Do exactly what the words say, with nothing but lists. First find which distinct values exist by walking the array and appending any value we have not seen before. Then, for every distinct value, count its occurrences by scanning the whole array again with `nums.count(value)`. Now we have (count, value) pairs, and we pick the winner k times by scanning the pairs for the largest count and removing it — the same selection-sort idea as repeatedly taking the maximum. Nothing here is clever, and the repeated linear scans make it quadratic, but it is correct and it makes the shape of the problem obvious: the real cost is counting, then ranking.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Build a list `uniques` of distinct values by scanning nums and appending values not already present.
2. For each distinct value, compute its occurrence count with `nums.count(value)` and store the pair (count, value).
3. Repeat k times: scan the pair list for the entry with the largest count.
4. Remove that entry from the list and append its value to the result, so the next round finds the next best.
5. Return the k collected values.

complexity.time: O(n * u + u * k) — the `not in` membership test and `count` each scan the data per distinct value (u distinct values)
complexity.space: O(u) — the list of distinct values and their counts

approaches.name: Better (Counter + Sort)
approaches.intuition: The brute force burns time on two avoidable things: membership testing in a list, and recounting the array once per distinct value. A hash map fixes both — one pass over nums and every count is known, because a dictionary lookup is O(1) on average instead of an O(u) scan. Once the counts exist, 'top k' is just 'sort by count descending and take the first k'. This is a big real-world improvement and is usually good enough. The one thing it still overpays for is the sort: it puts ALL u distinct values into perfect frequency order when we only care which k of them are on top, and that surplus ordering is what the heap removes.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Build `freq = Counter(nums)` in one linear pass over the array.
2. Take the list of distinct values `list(freq.keys())`.
3. Sort that list with `key=lambda v: freq[v]` and `reverse=True`, so the most frequent values come first.
4. Slice the first k entries — these are the k most frequent values.
5. Return the slice.
approaches.code:
from collections import Counter

def top_k_frequent(nums, k):
    # Counter does the tallying in one O(n) pass using a hash map.
    freq = Counter(nums)                       # {value: how many times it occurs}
    # Turn the map into a list of values we can order.
    values = list(freq.keys())
    # Sort descending by frequency; the biggest counts land at the front.
    values.sort(key=lambda v: freq[v], reverse=True)
    # The first k entries of that ordering are the k most frequent values.
    return values[:k]

complexity.time: O(n + u log u) — linear counting plus a sort of the u distinct values
complexity.space: O(u) — the counter plus the list of keys

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: Counting is unavoidable — you cannot know the top k without looking at every element once — so the only thing left to improve is the ranking step. The aha is the same bounded-heap idea as 'k-th largest': we never need more than k candidates in hand. Walk the frequency map and push each (count, value) pair into a MIN-heap. Because tuples compare on their first element, the heap orders itself by count for free, and its root is always the least frequent candidate we are still holding. The moment the heap holds k+1 pairs, the root is provably not in the top k, so we pop it. After the walk, exactly k pairs remain and they are the k most frequent values. The ranking cost falls from O(u log u) to O(u log k), and memory falls to O(k) — which matters a great deal when there are millions of distinct values but you only want the top ten.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Build `freq = Counter(nums)` so every distinct value knows its count.
2. Create an empty list `heap` used as a min-heap of (count, value) pairs.
3. For each (value, count) in freq.items(), push `(count, value)` onto the heap.
4. If the heap size now exceeds k, pop the root — it is the least frequent candidate and can be discarded safely, because k other candidates already beat it.
5. When the map is exhausted, the heap holds exactly k pairs: the k most frequent.
6. Return a list of just the `value` component of each surviving pair.
approaches.code:
import heapq                                     # min-heap: heap[0] is always the SMALLEST entry
from collections import Counter                  # hash map counter, O(1) average per update

def top_k_frequent(nums, k):
    # Step 1: tally every value in one linear pass.
    freq = Counter(nums)                        # e.g. [1,1,1,2,2,3] -> {1: 3, 2: 2, 3: 1}
    # Step 2: keep a min-heap of at most k (count, value) pairs.
    heap = []                                   # heap[0] is the WEAKEST candidate we still hold
    for value, count in freq.items():           # at most n distinct values
        heapq.heappush(heap, (count, value))    # tuples compare on count first, so the heap orders by frequency
        if len(heap) > k:                       # holding k+1 candidates is one too many
            heapq.heappop(heap)                 # drop the least frequent -- it cannot be in the top k
    # Step 3: whatever survived IS the answer; strip the counts off the pairs.
    return [value for count, value in heap]     # order among the k winners is unspecified

complexity.time: O(n + u log k) — one pass to count, then u heap operations on a heap capped at size k
complexity.space: O(u) for the counter plus O(k) for the heap

Top K Frequent Elements.tests:
assert sorted(top_k_frequent([1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3], 2)) == [1, 2]
assert top_k_frequent([1], 1) == [1]
assert sorted(top_k_frequent([4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 6, 6, 6, 6], 2)) == [4, 6]
# Edge case: k equals the number of distinct values -> everything is returned.
assert sorted(top_k_frequent([1, 2, 3], 3)) == [1, 2, 3]
# Edge case: negative numbers hash just fine as dictionary keys.
assert sorted(top_k_frequent([-1, -1, -2, -2, -3], 2)) == [-2, -1]

Merge K Sorted Arrays.title: Merge K Sorted Arrays
Merge K Sorted Arrays.problemStatement: You are given k arrays, and each individual array is already sorted in non-decreasing order. Your job is to combine all of them into ONE array that is also sorted in non-decreasing order, containing every element from every input array (duplicates included — nothing is removed). The arrays may have different lengths, some of them may be completely empty, and the list of arrays itself may be empty. You return a brand new list; the inputs are not modified. Let N be the total number of elements across all k arrays. The whole challenge is to exploit the fact that each piece is ALREADY sorted, so that you can beat the obvious 'concatenate then sort' solution.

examples.explanation: Seed a min-heap with the first element of each array, tagged with where it came from: (1, arr0, idx0), (2, arr1, idx0), (3, arr2, idx0). Pop the smallest, 1 — it belongs to arr0 at index 0, so we output 1 and push arr0's next element (4, arr0, idx1). Pop 2, output it, push (6, arr1, idx1). Pop 3, output it, push (5, arr2, idx1). The heap is now {4, 6, 5}: pop 4, then 5, then 6 with no more elements to push. The output built in that exact order is [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]. Notice the heap never held more than 3 entries even though 6 elements flowed through it.
The arrays happen not to interleave at all, so the heap drains one array completely before touching the next.
Two arrays are empty and are simply never seeded into the heap; only the single element 1 is emitted.

constraints: 0 <= length of each array; total elements N <= 10^5
Every input array is already sorted in non-decreasing order.
edgeCases: Some input arrays are empty — tricky because seeding the heap with `arr[0]` blindly raises IndexError, so you must guard with `if arr`.
The outer list itself is empty (k = 0) — the while-loop never runs and the function must return [] rather than crash.

Arrays of wildly different lengths, e.g. [[1,9,10,11],[2],[3]] — tricky because the heap shrinks below k as short arrays are exhausted, which is fine but breaks any code that assumes a fixed heap size.
Duplicate values across arrays, like [[5,5],[5]] — the merge must keep every copy, so a solution that de-duplicates or uses a set is wrong.
k = 1 (a single array) — the answer is a copy of that array, and the code must not depend on there being something to compare against.
followUps: Can you merge the arrays in place inside one output buffer to avoid the intermediate list, and what changes if the result must be written to a memory-mapped file?
Divide-and-conquer merging pairs of arrays also gives O(N log k) without a heap — implement it and explain when you would prefer it (hint: cache locality and no tuple allocation).
The k sources are network streams that never end. How do you turn this into an online merge, and what happens if one stream stalls?
Now the arrays are so large they do not fit in RAM (classic external merge sort). How do you choose k, and how does disk I/O change the analysis?
Return only the smallest M elements of the merge instead of everything — how do you stop early, and what is the new complexity?
prerequisites: `heapq` is a min-heap over any comparable items; pushing tuples `(value, i, j)` makes it compare on `value` first because tuples compare element by element.
The k-way merge invariant: if the heap holds the smallest untaken element of every array, then the heap's root is the smallest untaken element overall.
`enumerate(arrays)` gives you `(index, sub_array)` pairs — you need the index to know which array to pull the replacement element from.
`heappush`/`heappop` cost O(log k) here because the heap never exceeds k entries (one per array), which is what makes the whole merge O(N log k).
Guarding with `if arr:` before touching `arr[0]` — an empty list is falsy in Python, and this one line prevents the classic IndexError on empty inputs.

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: The simplest thing that can possibly work: forget that the arrays are sorted, pour every element into one big list, and sort that list. It is three lines and it is definitely correct. The reason it is the brute force is that it throws away the single most valuable fact we were given — each input is ALREADY in order. Sorting a list that is made of k sorted runs costs O(N log N) with a generic comparison sort, whereas a merge that exploits the runs can do it in O(N log k), and k is usually far smaller than N. (Fun detail worth mentioning in an interview: Python's Timsort actually detects existing runs, so in practice this is faster than the O(N log N) bound suggests — but you cannot rely on that in a language-agnostic answer.)
approaches.algorithm:
1. Create an empty list `flat`.
2. For each sub-array in `arrays`, extend `flat` with all of its elements.
3. Sort `flat` in ascending order with the built-in sort.
4. Return `flat`, which now contains all N elements in non-decreasing order.
approaches.code:
def merge_k_arrays(arrays):
    # Throw away all structure: dump every element into one flat list.
    flat = []
    for arr in arrays:
        # extend copies the whole sub-array; total work is O(N).
        flat.extend(arr)
    # Now sort from scratch, ignoring that the pieces were already sorted.
    flat.sort()                     # Timsort, O(N log N) on N total elements
    return flat

complexity.time: O(N log N) — a generic sort over all N elements, ignoring the pre-existing order
complexity.space: O(N) — the flattened output list

approaches.name: Better (Sequential Two-Way Merge)
approaches.intuition: Now we do use the sortedness. Merging TWO sorted arrays is the classic two-pointer routine from merge sort: look at the front of each, take the smaller, advance that pointer. So merge array 0 with array 1, merge that result with array 2, and so on. Every element ends up in the right place and no comparison sort is needed. The catch is the shape of the folding: the accumulator grows as we go, and each new fold re-copies everything already merged. Array 0's elements get copied k-1 times. Total work is roughly N * k, which is worse than the brute force once k gets large — a great illustration that 'using the structure' is not automatically fast if you use it in a lopsided order. Pairing the arrays up (divide and conquer) instead of folding left-to-right would fix exactly this.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Write a helper `merge_two(a, b)` that merges two sorted lists with two pointers i and j.
2. While both pointers are in range, append the smaller of a[i] and b[j] and advance that pointer.
3. When one list runs out, extend the result with the remaining tail of the other.
4. In the main function, start with `result = []` and fold: `result = merge_two(result, arr)` for every arr.
5. Return the accumulated `result`.
approaches.code:
def merge_two(a, b):
    # Classic two-pointer merge of two already-sorted lists.
    merged = []                      # output for this single pairwise merge
    i = 0                            # read cursor into a
    j = 0                            # read cursor into b
    while i < len(a) and j < len(b):     # while BOTH still have elements
        # '<=' keeps equal elements in a-before-b order (stability).
        if a[i] <= b[j]:
            merged.append(a[i])      # a's front is the smaller candidate
            i += 1                   # consume it
        else:
            merged.append(b[j])      # b's front wins instead
            j += 1                   # consume it
    # Exactly one of these tails is non-empty; both are already sorted.
    merged.extend(a[i:])             # leftover of a (possibly empty)
    merged.extend(b[j:])             # leftover of b (possibly empty)
    return merged                    # sorted union of a and b

def merge_k_arrays(arrays):
    # Fold the arrays into the accumulator one at a time.
    result = []                      # merging with [] returns the other list
    for arr in arrays:
        # Each fold re-copies everything merged so far -- that is the waste.
        result = merge_two(result, arr)
    return result                    # after the last fold this holds all N elements

complexity.time: O(N * k) — the accumulator is re-copied on each of the k folds
complexity.space: O(N) — the accumulator (plus one temporary of the same order during each fold)

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: Think about what you need to know to emit the next output element. You need the smallest element that has not been used yet. Because every array is sorted, that element must be at the FRONT of one of the arrays — an element deeper inside an array can never be smaller than the one in front of it. So there are only k candidates at any moment, one per array. Keep exactly those k candidates in a min-heap, each tagged with which array it came from and where. Pop the root: that is the global minimum, so append it to the output. Then push the next element from that same array as the replacement candidate, restoring the invariant. Every element enters and leaves the heap exactly once, and the heap never exceeds k entries, so we pay O(log k) per element for a total of O(N log k) time and only O(k) extra space beyond the output — a big win over both the O(N log N) sort and the O(N * k) sequential fold.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Create an empty min-heap. For every array index i with a non-empty array, push the tuple `(arrays[i][0], i, 0)` — value, source array, position inside it. Skipping empty arrays avoids an IndexError.
2. Create the empty output list `merged`.
3. While the heap is not empty, pop `(value, i, j)` — the smallest unused element anywhere.
4. Append `value` to `merged`; it is safe because every remaining element is >= it.
5. If `j + 1` is still a valid index in `arrays[i]`, push `(arrays[i][j+1], i, j+1)` so that array is represented in the heap again.
6. When the heap empties, every element has been emitted exactly once — return `merged`.
approaches.code:
import heapq                                              # min-heap: heap[0] is the smallest entry

def merge_k_arrays(arrays):
    # The heap holds ONE candidate per array: its smallest element not yet taken.
    heap = []                                            # entries are (value, array_index, element_index)
    for i, arr in enumerate(arrays):                     # seed with every array's first element
        if arr:                                          # skip empty arrays -- they contribute nothing
            heapq.heappush(heap, (arr[0], i, 0))         # (value, which array, position inside that array)
    merged = []                                          # output, produced in sorted order
    while heap:                                          # run until every element has been consumed
        value, i, j = heapq.heappop(heap)                # globally smallest element still unused
        merged.append(value)                             # safe: nothing smaller can appear later
        if j + 1 < len(arrays[i]):                       # the array we just took from still has elements
            heapq.heappush(heap, (arrays[i][j + 1], i, j + 1))   # push its next element as the new candidate
    return merged                                        # fully merged, fully sorted

complexity.time: O(N log k) — each of the N elements is pushed and popped once on a heap of size <= k
complexity.space: O(k) auxiliary for the heap, plus O(N) for the returned merged list

Merge K Sorted Arrays.tests:
assert merge_k_arrays([[1, 4], [2, 6], [3, 5]]) == [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
assert merge_k_arrays([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6], [7, 8, 9]]) == [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9]
assert merge_k_arrays([[5, 5], [5]]) == [5, 5, 5]
# Edge case: empty sub-arrays must be skipped, not crash on arr[0].
assert merge_k_arrays([[], [1], []]) == [1]
# Edge case: no arrays at all.
assert merge_k_arrays([]) == []
# Edge case: very unequal lengths -- one array outlives all the others.
assert merge_k_arrays([[1, 9, 10, 11], [2], [3]]) == [1, 2, 3, 9, 10, 11]

Merge K Sorted Linked Lists.title: Merge K Sorted Linked Lists
Merge K Sorted Linked Lists.problemStatement: You are given an array `lists` of k linked-list heads. Each individual linked list is already sorted in non-decreasing order by node value. Merge all of them into one single sorted linked list and return its head. Every node from every input list must appear in the output, duplicates included. Some entries of `lists` may be `None` (an empty list), and `lists` itself may be empty, in which case you return `None`. The expected solution re-links the EXISTING nodes rather than allocating new ones, so the output uses O(1) extra node memory. If N is the total number of nodes, the naive approach costs O(N log N); the interview target is O(N log k), which is a large win because k is usually far smaller than N.

examples.explanation: Seed a min-heap with each list's head, tagged with its list index so ties never compare the node objects themselves: (1, 0, node1a), (1, 1, node1b), (2, 2, node2). Pop (1, 0, node1a) — list 0's head — stitch it after the dummy, and push its successor (4, 0, node4a). Pop (1, 1, node1b), stitch, push (3, 1, node3b). Pop (2, 2, node2), stitch, push (6, 2, node6). Continue: pop 3, push 4 from list 1; pop 4 (list 0), push 5; pop 4 (list 1), nothing left in list 1; pop 5, then pop 6. The stitched chain, in the order the nodes left the heap, is 1->1->2->3->4->4->5->6. The heap held at most 3 entries the whole time.
There are no lists at all, so the heap is never seeded, the loop never runs, and dummy.next is still None.
The two None heads are skipped during seeding; only the single node 1 ever enters the heap.

constraints: 0 <= length of each list; total nodes N <= 10^4 * 500
Each individual list is already sorted in non-decreasing order.
edgeCases: `lists` is empty or contains only `None` heads — tricky because the dummy-node pattern is what saves you: `dummy.next` is naturally `None` and no branch is needed.

Duplicate values across different lists, e.g. two lists both starting with 1 — tricky in Python because a tuple `(val, node)` falls back to comparing ListNode objects on a tie and raises TypeError, which is why the list index is inserted as a tie-breaker.
One list is far longer than the rest — the heap shrinks below k as short lists drain, so any code assuming a constant heap size is wrong.
Forgetting `tail.next = None` at the end — the last stitched node may still point at a stale successor from its original list, producing a duplicated tail or an infinite loop when printed.
A single list (k = 1) — the answer is that list itself, and the algorithm must not allocate a parallel copy or lose the head.
followUps: Solve it with divide and conquer instead of a heap: merge lists pairwise in log k rounds. Same O(N log k) time but O(log k) recursion space and no tuple allocation — when is that preferable?
What if the lists are doubly linked, or circular? Which parts of the stitching change?
The k lists are produced by k different threads/streams that append over time. How do you merge lazily and emit the merged head as an iterator?
Can you do the merge with O(1) extra space (no heap at all) if you are allowed O(N * k) time, and would you ever choose that trade?
Explain precisely why the heap solution is O(N log k) and not O(N log N), and what happens to that bound if k approaches N.
prerequisites: The dummy-head pattern: allocate one throwaway `ListNode(0)`, build from `dummy`, and return `dummy.next` — it removes every 'is this the first node?' special case.
Python's `heapq` compares tuples element by element, and ListNode has no `__lt__`, so you MUST include a unique tie-breaker (the list index) before the node in the tuple.
The k-way merge invariant: with the smallest untaken node of every list in the heap, the heap root is the global minimum untaken node.
Re-linking versus rebuilding: assigning `tail.next = node` reuses the existing node, so no new memory is allocated for the output chain.
`heappush`/`heappop` are O(log k) because the heap holds at most one entry per list, which is what gives the O(N log k) total.

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: Linked lists make people nervous, so start by turning the problem into one you already solved: walk every list and copy all the node VALUES into an ordinary Python list. Now you have N plain numbers, so sort them, and finally rebuild a fresh chain node by node. This is guaranteed correct and it is a perfectly good first answer to state out loud. Two things make it the brute force. First, it ignores that the inputs were already sorted, paying O(N log N) to re-derive an order we were handed. Second, it allocates N brand-new nodes and an N-element array, so the extra space is O(N) instead of O(k).
approaches.algorithm:
1. Create an empty list `values`.
2. For each head in `lists`, walk the chain with a cursor and append every `node.val` to `values`.
3. Sort `values` in ascending order.
4. Create a dummy node and a `tail` cursor pointing at it.
5. For each value in the sorted list, allocate a new ListNode, attach it after `tail`, and move `tail` onto it.
6. Return `dummy.next`, which is None when there were no values at all.
approaches.code:
def merge_k_lists(lists):
    # Step 1: harvest every value into a plain Python list.
    values = []
    for head in lists:
        node = head
        while node:                     # walk this list to its end
            values.append(node.val)     # keep only the number, drop the node
            node = node.next
    # Step 2: sort the numbers, ignoring that the inputs were sorted.
    values.sort()                       # O(N log N)
    # Step 3: rebuild a brand new chain from the sorted numbers.
    dummy = ListNode(0)                 # dummy avoids a special case for the head
    tail = dummy
    for v in values:
        tail.next = ListNode(v)         # allocate a fresh node
        tail = tail.next                # move the tail forward
    return dummy.next                   # skip the dummy, return the real head

complexity.time: O(N log N) — the sort dominates the two linear walks
complexity.space: O(N) — the value array plus N freshly allocated nodes

approaches.name: Better (Sequential Two-Way Merge)
approaches.intuition: Reuse the routine you already know from merge sort: merging TWO sorted linked lists is a simple two-pointer splice with a dummy head. So merge list 0 with list 1, merge that result with list 2, and keep folding. Nothing is copied and no sorting is needed — we finally use the fact that each input is sorted, and the extra space drops to O(1). The problem is the shape of the folding. The accumulator grows every round, and each merge re-walks all of it, so the nodes of the first list are traversed k-1 times. That gives roughly N * k work: fine for k = 3, terrible for k = 10^4. This is the approach whose weakness motivates both divide-and-conquer and the heap.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Write `merge_two_lists(a, b)`: with a dummy head and a `tail` cursor, repeatedly attach whichever of a/b has the smaller value and advance that pointer.
2. When one chain runs out, attach the whole remaining chain — it is already sorted.
3. In the main function start with `result = None` (merging anything with None returns that thing).
4. For each head in `lists`, set `result = merge_two_lists(result, head)`.
5. Return `result` after the last fold.
approaches.code:
def merge_two_lists(a, b):
    # Standard two-pointer merge of two sorted chains.
    dummy = ListNode(0)                 # placeholder so we never branch on "is this the head?"
    tail = dummy
    while a and b:
        # '<=' preserves the relative order of equal values (stable merge).
        if a.val <= b.val:
            tail.next = a               # splice a's node in
            a = a.next
        else:
            tail.next = b               # splice b's node in
            b = b.next
        tail = tail.next                # tail always trails the last stitched node
    # At most one list still has nodes; it is already sorted, so attach it whole.
    tail.next = a if a else b
    return dummy.next

def merge_k_lists(lists):
    # Fold the lists into an accumulator, one at a time.
    result = None
    for head in lists:
        # Each fold re-walks everything merged so far -- that is the waste.
        result = merge_two_lists(result, head)
    return result

complexity.time: O(N * k) — the growing accumulator is re-walked on each of the k folds
complexity.space: O(1) — only pointers; the nodes are re-linked, never copied

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: To emit the next node of the answer you need the smallest node not yet used. Because each list is sorted, that node has to be the current HEAD of one of the k lists — a node deeper in a list can never be smaller than the one in front of it. So at any moment there are only k candidates, and a min-heap gives you the smallest of them in O(1) to look at and O(log k) to remove. Pop the winner, splice it onto the growing tail, then push that list's next node so the invariant 'the heap holds every list's smallest untaken node' is restored. Each node is pushed once and popped once, so the whole merge is O(N log k) with only O(k) extra memory, and the nodes themselves are re-linked rather than copied. One Python-specific trap: two nodes can tie on value, and the heap would then try to compare the ListNode objects and crash with a TypeError — so we store `(value, list_index, node)`, and the always-distinct list index settles every tie before the node is ever looked at.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Create an empty min-heap. For every index i whose head is not None, push `(head.val, i, head)`; the index i is a tie-breaker so two equal values never force a ListNode comparison.
2. Create `dummy = ListNode(0)` and set `tail = dummy`.
3. While the heap is non-empty, pop `(val, i, node)` — the smallest untaken node anywhere.
4. Splice it on: `tail.next = node`, then `tail = node`.
5. If `node.next` exists, push `(node.next.val, i, node.next)` so list i is represented again.
6. After the loop, set `tail.next = None` to cut any leftover pointer from the original list.
7. Return `dummy.next` — the head of the merged chain, or None if nothing was ever stitched.
approaches.code:
import heapq                                        # min-heap: heap[0] is the smallest entry

def merge_k_lists(lists):
    # The heap holds ONE candidate per list: its smallest node not yet taken.
    heap = []                                      # entries are (node value, tie-breaker id, node)
    for i, node in enumerate(lists):               # seed with the head of every list
        if node:                                   # skip empty lists (None heads)
            heapq.heappush(heap, (node.val, i, node))   # 'i' breaks ties so ListNode is never compared
    dummy = ListNode(0)                            # dummy head keeps the stitching branch-free
    tail = dummy                                   # tail always points at the last stitched node
    while heap:                                    # until every node has been placed
        val, i, node = heapq.heappop(heap)         # smallest remaining node across all k lists
        tail.next = node                           # reuse the node itself -- no new allocation
        tail = node                                # advance the tail onto it
        if node.next:                              # that list still has more nodes to offer
            heapq.heappush(heap, (node.next.val, i, node.next))   # its successor becomes the new candidate
    tail.next = None                               # cut any stale pointer inherited from the input
    return dummy.next                              # first real node = head of the merged list

complexity.time: O(N log k) — each of the N nodes is pushed and popped once on a heap of size <= k
complexity.space: O(k) — the heap holds at most one entry per list; no new nodes are allocated

Merge K Sorted Linked Lists.tests:
a = [build_linked_list([1, 4, 5]), build_linked_list([1, 3, 4]), build_linked_list([2, 6])]
assert linked_list_to_list(merge_k_lists(a)) == [1, 1, 2, 3, 4, 4, 5, 6]
assert linked_list_to_list(merge_k_lists([build_linked_list([1, 1, 1])])) == [1, 1, 1]
# Edge case: the outer list is empty -> nothing to merge.
assert merge_k_lists([]) is None
# Edge case: every list is empty (None heads) -> still None.
assert merge_k_lists([None, None]) is None
# Edge case: a None head mixed in with real lists must be skipped, not crash.
assert linked_list_to_list(merge_k_lists([build_linked_list([2]), None, build_linked_list([1])])) == [1, 2]

Find Median from Data Stream.title: Find Median from Data Stream
Find Median from Data Stream.problemStatement: Design a data structure that accepts integers one at a time from a never-ending stream and can report the median of everything seen so far at any moment. The median is the middle value once the numbers are arranged in sorted order: if the count is odd it is the single middle element, and if the count is even it is the average of the two middle elements (so the answer can be a non-integer such as 1.5). You must implement a class with two operations: `addNum(num)`, which inserts a value into the structure, and `findMedian()`, which returns the current median as a float. Both operations can be called any number of times in any interleaving, and `findMedian` is only ever called after at least one `addNum`. The difficulty is that re-sorting the whole collection on each query is far too slow when millions of numbers arrive, so you need a structure that keeps just enough order to expose the middle cheaply.

examples.explanation: Two heaps split the data at the middle: `low` is a max-heap of the smaller half (stored negated) and `high` is a min-heap of the larger half. addNum(1): push -1 into low, then move low's max over to high, leaving low = [] and high = [1]; high is now bigger, so rebalance by moving 1 back, giving low = [-1] (that is the value 1) and high = []. addNum(2): push -2 into low which becomes [-2, -1]; move its max (2) to high, so low = [-1] and high = [2]; the sizes are 1 and 1, so no rebalance. findMedian(): the sizes are equal, so average the two roots: (1 + 2) / 2 = 1.5. addNum(3): 3 travels through low into high giving low = [-1], high = [2, 3]; high is bigger, so move its minimum 2 back into low, giving low = [-2, -1] (values 2 and 1) and high = [3]. findMedian(): low is bigger, so the median is its top, 2.0 — and indeed sorted [1, 2, 3] has middle 2.
With one element the median is that element. After -2 arrives, sorted order is [-2, -1] and the median is (-2 + -1) / 2 = -1.5.
Sorted so far: [1, 3, 5, 15]. Even count, so the median is (3 + 5) / 2 = 4.0.

constraints: findMedian() is only called after at least one addNum().
At most 5 * 10^4 calls to addNum and findMedian combined.
Both operations should be efficient enough to be called interchangeably many times.
edgeCases: The very first addNum — tricky because one heap is still empty, and code that peeks at `high[0]` before checking sizes raises IndexError.
All values identical, e.g. 7, 7, 7 — the median is 7.0 and the balancing must still keep the size invariant even though no comparison ever swaps anything.
Strictly decreasing input like -1, -2, -3 — tricky for the naive 'push to low if num <= low top else push to high' shortcut, which drifts out of balance unless you rebalance every time.
Even versus odd counts — forgetting the float division (using `//` or integer arithmetic) silently returns 1 instead of 1.5.
Negative numbers combined with the negation trick — a sign error makes `low` behave as a min-heap and produces a plausible-looking but wrong median.
followUps: If all numbers are guaranteed to be in the range [0, 100], can you answer in O(1) per query? (Keep a 101-slot count array and scan it — the scan is bounded by a constant.)
If 99% of the numbers are in [0, 100] and the rest are arbitrary, how do you combine a count array for the common range with heaps for the outliers?
Support `removeNum(num)` as well as `addNum`. Why does a plain heap struggle with deletion, and how do lazy deletion with a 'to-delete' counter, or an order-statistic tree / SortedList, fix it?
Generalise to the p-th percentile instead of the 50th — what size ratio must the two heaps maintain?
Support a sliding window of the last W numbers instead of the whole stream. What breaks, and which structure would you reach for?
prerequisites: `heapq` provides only a MIN-heap; the standard max-heap trick is to push `-value` and negate again on the way out.
The two-heap (median maintenance) pattern: split the data into a max-heap of the smaller half and a min-heap of the larger half, so both middles sit at a root.
The size invariant `len(low) == len(high)` or `len(low) == len(high) + 1` is what makes the median a pure O(1) peek — decide it once and enforce it after every insert.
Peeking `heap[0]` is O(1) and does not remove anything, while push/pop are O(log n).
The push-then-transfer idiom `heappush(high, -heappop(low))` routes every new value through `low` first, which guarantees correct placement without any if/else on the value itself.

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: Start with the most literal reading of the problem. `addNum` just remembers the number in a list, which is O(1) and does no thinking at all. Then `findMedian` does all the work: sort a copy of everything seen so far and index into the middle. This is obviously correct and is the right thing to write first, because it pins down the two cases you must handle — an odd count means one middle element, an even count means the average of two. Its problem is the imbalance of cost: inserts are free but every single query is O(n log n), so a workload that alternates add and query on a million numbers becomes hopeless. Recognising that we are re-sorting data that barely changed between queries is the push toward the next approach.
approaches.algorithm:
1. In `__init__`, create an empty list `self.data`.
2. In `addNum`, append the number to `self.data` and do nothing else.
3. In `findMedian`, build a sorted copy of `self.data`.
4. If the count n is odd, return the element at index n // 2 as a float.
5. If n is even, return the average of the elements at indices n // 2 - 1 and n // 2, using float division.

complexity.time: O(1) per addNum, O(n log n) per findMedian — the sort is redone on every query
complexity.space: O(n) — the stored numbers plus the sorted copy made per query

approaches.name: Better (Sorted Insertion with bisect)
approaches.intuition: The waste in the brute force is re-sorting an almost-sorted collection over and over. Flip the cost instead: keep the list sorted at ALL times, so a query is a direct index lookup. `bisect.insort` finds the correct insertion point with binary search in O(log n) and inserts there, which keeps the invariant automatically. Now `findMedian` is O(1): odd count means one middle index, even count means the mean of two adjacent ones. This is a real improvement and is often fast enough in practice. The remaining flaw is physical, not logical: inserting into the middle of a Python list has to shift every element after it, so `addNum` is O(n) even though finding the spot was O(log n). Removing that shift is the last thing the optimal solution fixes.
approaches.algorithm:
1. In `__init__`, create an empty list `self.data` that will always stay sorted.
2. In `addNum`, call `bisect.insort(self.data, num)` — binary search for the position, then insert there.
3. In `findMedian`, read n = len(self.data); no sorting is needed because the invariant holds.
4. If n is odd, return `self.data[n // 2]` as a float.
5. If n is even, return the average of `self.data[n // 2 - 1]` and `self.data[n // 2]`.

complexity.time: O(n) per addNum (the memory shift dominates the O(log n) search), O(1) per findMedian
complexity.space: O(n) — one sorted list of everything seen so far

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: Here is the key realisation: to report a median you do NOT need the numbers fully sorted. You only need to know the boundary in the middle — the largest element of the smaller half and the smallest element of the larger half. 'Largest of a group' is exactly what a max-heap gives you in O(1), and 'smallest of a group' is exactly what a min-heap gives you. So split the stream into two halves: `low`, a max-heap of the smaller numbers, and `high`, a min-heap of the larger numbers, and keep them balanced so their sizes differ by at most one. Then the median is either the top of `low` (odd count) or the average of the two tops (even count) — an O(1) peek either way. Insertion is the elegant part: rather than branching on where `num` belongs, push it into `low`, immediately move `low`'s maximum into `high`, then move back from `high` if that made it too big. Those three unconditional lines always restore both the ordering invariant (every low value <= every high value) and the size invariant, in O(log n). Since Python's heapq has no max-heap, `low` stores negated values and we negate again on the way out.
approaches.algorithm:
1. `__init__`: create `self.low = []` (max-heap of the smaller half, values stored negated) and `self.high = []` (min-heap of the larger half).
2. `addNum` step 1: `heapq.heappush(self.low, -num)` so the new value is ranked inside the small half.
3. `addNum` step 2: `heapq.heappush(self.high, -heapq.heappop(self.low))` — move the current largest of `low` into `high`. This guarantees every value in `low` is <= every value in `high`, whatever `num` was.
4. `addNum` step 3: if `len(self.high) > len(self.low)`, move `high`'s minimum back with `heapq.heappush(self.low, -heapq.heappop(self.high))`, restoring 'low is equal in size or exactly one larger'.
5. `findMedian`: if `len(self.low) > len(self.high)` the count is odd and the extra element is `low`'s top, so return `-self.low[0]` as a float.
6. Otherwise the count is even, so return `(-self.low[0] + self.high[0]) / 2.0`, the average of the two middle values.

complexity.time: O(log n) per addNum (a constant number of pushes/pops) and O(1) per findMedian (two root peeks)
complexity.space: O(n) — every number lives in exactly one of the two heaps

Find Median from Data Stream.tests:
mf = MedianFinder()
mf.addNum(1)
mf.addNum(2)
assert mf.findMedian() == 1.5
mf.addNum(3)
assert mf.findMedian() == 2.0
# Edge case: a single element -- the median is that element, as a float.
mf2 = MedianFinder()
mf2.addNum(-1)
assert mf2.findMedian() == -1.0
mf2.addNum(-2)
assert mf2.findMedian() == -1.5
mf2.addNum(-3)
assert mf2.findMedian() == -2.0
# Edge case: values arriving out of order still give the right median.
mf3 = MedianFinder()
for v in [5, 15, 1, 3]:
    mf3.addNum(v)
assert mf3.findMedian() == 4.0
# Edge case: many duplicates.
mf4 = MedianFinder()
for v in [7, 7, 7]:
    mf4.addNum(v)
assert mf4.findMedian() == 7.0

Set Matrix Zeroes.title: Set Matrix Zeroes
Set Matrix Zeroes.tests:
# 1) classic: a single interior zero wipes its row and its column
m1 = [[1, 1, 1], [1, 0, 1], [1, 1, 1]]
setZeroes(m1)
assert m1 == [[1, 0, 1], [0, 0, 0], [1, 0, 1]], m1

# 2) zeroes sitting ON the first row / first column (the marker strip itself)
m2 = [[0, 1, 2, 0], [3, 4, 5, 2], [1, 3, 1, 5]]
setZeroes(m2)
assert m2 == [[0, 0, 0, 0], [0, 4, 5, 0], [0, 3, 1, 0]], m2

# 3) edge: 1x1 matrix that is already zero — must stay zero, must not crash
m3 = [[0]]
setZeroes(m3)
assert m3 == [[0]], m3

# 4) edge: no zero anywhere — the matrix must come back untouched
m4 = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
setZeroes(m4)
assert m4 == [[1, 2], [3, 4]], m4

# 5) edge: negative values must survive the marking pass unharmed
m5 = [[-1, 0], [-2, -3]]
setZeroes(m5)
assert m5 == [[0, 0], [-2, 0]], m5

# 6) edge: single row — the whole row collapses to zeroes
m6 = [[1, 0, 3]]
setZeroes(m6)
assert m6 == [[0, 0, 0]], m6
prerequisites: In-place matrix problems: you may not allocate another m x n grid, so any 'remember which rows/cols to clear' information has to live inside the matrix itself.

Why a naive one-pass fails: writing a 0 immediately makes that 0 indistinguishable from an original 0, so the very next cell you read would wrongly trigger another wipe — you always need a two-phase (mark, then apply) structure.
Python 2-D lists are lists of row references: `matrix[i][j]` is row i then column j, and `len(matrix)` is the row count while `len(matrix[0])` is the column count.
The first row and first column can be reused as O(1)-space bookkeeping, but cell (0,0) is shared by both — that overlap is exactly why a separate `col0` flag is needed.
Traversal direction matters: the second pass must run bottom-right to top-left so the marker strip is read before it is itself overwritten.

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: The obvious first move is to walk the matrix and, the instant you meet a 0, blank its whole row and column right away. Run that on [[1,1,1],[1,0,1],[1,1,1]] and the entire grid collapses to zeros: the zeros you just wrote look exactly like the one you were given, so the very next cell you inspect fires again and the damage spreads. The real problem is not the clearing, it is that a written zero is indistinguishable from a given zero. So write something else. Pick a sentinel that no genuine cell can hold, here -999999, meaning "this cell is doomed but is not a trigger". Because the sentinel is non-zero, the scanning loop keeps reacting only to the original zeros, and a second sweep can safely convert every sentinel into a real 0. This buys correctness with zero extra memory, but each original zero drags a full walk of one row and one column behind it, so the cost is O(m*n*(m+n)) time for O(1) space.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Read the dimensions m = len(matrix) and n = len(matrix[0]), and fix placeholder = -999999 as the sentinel meaning "must become zero later".
2. Begin the marking pass: scan every cell (i, j) row by row and test whether matrix[i][j] == 0, that is, whether this is an original zero rather than a mark you wrote yourself.
3. On finding an original zero, walk its row with c from 0 to n-1 and set matrix[i][c] = placeholder whenever that cell is not already 0 — the "not already 0" guard leaves genuine zeros intact so they can still fire their own row and column later in the scan.
4. Still handling the same zero, walk its column with r from 0 to m-1 and set matrix[r][j] = placeholder under the identical guard. The invariant held throughout this pass is: a cell is 0 only if it was 0 in the input, and it is placeholder only if it shares a row or a column with some original zero.
5. Run a second full pass over every (i, j) and, wherever matrix[i][j] == placeholder, set it to 0; the original zeros are already 0 and need no work.
6. Return nothing — the grid was edited in place, so the caller already holds the finished matrix.
approaches.code:
def setZeroes(matrix: List[List[int]]) -> None:  # mutates the grid in place; nothing is returned
    # Get matrix dimensions
    m, n = len(matrix), len(matrix[0])  # m rows by n columns; grid is assumed rectangular
    placeholder = -999999  # a value no real cell holds, so marks stay distinguishable
    
    # pass one only marks; erasing now would cascade wrongly
    for i in range(m):  # visit every cell hunting for the ORIGINAL zeros
        for j in range(n):
            if matrix[i][j] == 0:  # a genuine zero: its whole row and column must die
                # Mark non-zero cells in the same row
                for c in range(n):  # walk the row of this zero, left edge to right edge
                    if matrix[i][c] != 0:  # skip real zeros so they still trigger their own row/col
                        matrix[i][c] = placeholder  # marked for death, but still non-zero to the outer scan
                # Mark non-zero cells in the same column
                for r in range(m):  # now walk the column of the same zero, top to bottom
                    if matrix[r][j] != 0:  # same guard: never overwrite an original zero
                        matrix[r][j] = placeholder  # queued; the marker survives until the second pass
                        
    # pass two commits every mark to an actual zero
    for i in range(m):  # safe now: no new zeros can trigger more marking
        for j in range(n):
            if matrix[i][j] == placeholder:  # only markers change; original zeros are already 0
                matrix[i][j] = 0  # O(m*n*(m+n)) time but O(1) extra space, hence brute force

complexity.space: O(1) using placeholder marker

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: The sentinel brute force fixes the cascade - a written zero looking exactly like a given zero - but it still walks the full row and the full column for every zero it meets, so a matrix seeded with zeros costs O(M x N x (M + N)) writes, and it stakes correctness on -999999 never being a real input value. The observation that removes both problems: no cell needs its own mark. A cell dies if and only if its row is doomed OR its column is doomed, which is M + N facts, not M x N. And M + N cells that can hold those facts are already inside the matrix - row 0 and column 0 - because the moment any cell in row i is zero, matrix[i][0] is doomed anyway and its old value no longer matters. So store the row flags down column 0 and the column flags across row 0. Only matrix[0][0] is contested, since it would have to mean 'row 0 dies' and 'column 0 dies' at once; the extra variable col0 takes over the column-0 job and matrix[0][0] keeps the row-0 job. Correctness rests on the traversal direction: filling from the bottom-right upward means every marker is READ before the pass that overwrites it, and column 0 of a row is written only after that row's interior is finished. Cost: two full passes, O(M x N) time, O(1) extra space - traded for an algorithm whose correctness now depends on a stated order of writes rather than on separate storage.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Read m and n and set the flag col0 = 1. It exists because matrix[0][0] would otherwise have to serve as the marker for row 0 and for column 0 at the same time; col0 takes over the job for the first column.
2. Sweep forwards with i over the rows. First test matrix[i][0] == 0 and, if so, set col0 = 0. Then scan j from 1 to n-1 and, for every zero found at matrix[i][j], write matrix[i][0] = 0 to record 'row i must die' and matrix[0][j] = 0 to record 'column j must die'.
3. After that sweep the following holds - an invariant, meaning a statement guaranteed true at this exact point in the algorithm: matrix[i][0] == 0 means row i must be cleared, matrix[0][j] == 0 for j >= 1 means column j must be cleared, and col0 == 0 means the whole first column must be cleared.
4. Now walk the matrix backwards, i from m-1 down to 0 and j from n-1 down to 1, setting matrix[i][j] = 0 whenever matrix[i][0] == 0 or matrix[0][j] == 0. Going in reverse is essential: the marker row and marker column are consumed last, so they are still readable while the interior cells are being overwritten.
5. At the end of each row i, if col0 == 0, set matrix[i][0] = 0. This clears the first column only after its markers have already been used for that row.
6. Return nothing; the matrix now satisfies the rule using only the flag col0 as extra memory.

complexity.time: O(M * N)
complexity.space: O(1) strictly in-place

Set Matrix Zeroes.problemStatement: You are given a rectangular matrix of integers with m rows and n columns. Wherever a cell holds the value 0, every other cell that shares its row and every other cell that shares its column must also be turned into 0. The rule refers to the zeros present in the ORIGINAL matrix only: a cell that you blank out during the process must not itself trigger the clearing of its own row and column, otherwise a single zero would cascade until the whole grid was wiped. The matrix must be modified in place and nothing is returned, so the caller reads the answer out of the same object it passed in.

Reverse Linked List.title: Reverse Linked List
Reverse Linked List.tests:
# 1) the standard case
assert linked_list_to_list(reverseList(build_linked_list([1, 2, 3, 4, 5]))) == [5, 4, 3, 2, 1]

# 2) two nodes — the smallest case where anything actually moves
assert linked_list_to_list(reverseList(build_linked_list([1, 2]))) == [2, 1]

# 3) edge: a single node reverses to itself and must NOT self-link into a cycle
one = reverseList(build_linked_list([7]))
assert linked_list_to_list(one) == [7]
assert one.next is None

# 4) edge: an empty list must return None instead of crashing
assert reverseList(None) is None

# 5) duplicate values must keep their multiplicity
assert linked_list_to_list(reverseList(build_linked_list([2, 2, 1]))) == [1, 2, 2]
prerequisites: A singly linked node only knows its successor: once you overwrite `curr.next` the rest of the list is unreachable unless you saved that pointer first — this is why `next_node = curr.next` comes before the re-wiring.
The three-pointer idiom `prev / curr / next_node` and the exact order of the four statements inside the loop; swapping any two of them loses nodes or creates a cycle.
The loop ends when `curr` becomes None, at which point `prev` (not `curr`) is sitting on the last node — so `prev` is the new head.
Python assignment binds names to the same objects: `prev = curr` does not copy a node, it just makes a second name for it.
Edge handling: `head = None` and a one-node list must both flow through the same code without a special case, and the new tail's `next` must end up None.

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: Forget pointers for a second. If somebody handed you the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 on paper and asked for them backwards, you would just read them all down, flip the paper, and copy them back. That is exactly this approach: walk the list once and dump every value into an ordinary Python list, reverse that list (an array knows how to reverse itself cheaply because it has random access), then walk the chain a second time overwriting each node's value with the mirrored one. The node objects and the .next wiring never move at all — only the payloads change. It is correct and easy to believe, but it pays O(n) extra memory for a copy of the data, and in a real interview the follow-up 'now do it without the array' arrives within ten seconds. It is still the perfect first answer because it separates the idea (reverse the order) from the hard part (re-wiring pointers safely).
approaches.algorithm:
1. Walk the list from head to tail with a cursor and append every node's `val` into a Python list `values`.
2. Reverse `values` in place, so `values[0]` is now the value that must sit in the first node.
3. Reset the cursor back to `head` and set an index `i = 0`.
4. Walk the list a second time; at each node write `node.val = values[i]` and advance both the cursor and `i`.
5. Return `head` — the same physical node is still first, but the list now reads backwards.
approaches.code:
def reverseList(head: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
    # ---- Pass 1: copy every value out of the chain into a plain array ----
    values = []                 # will hold the values in ORIGINAL order
    node = head                 # cursor we can move without losing `head`
    while node:                 # stops as soon as we fall off the tail (None)
        values.append(node.val) # read the payload, ignore the wiring
        node = node.next        # hop to the next node

    # ---- Flip the array: arrays have random access, so this is cheap ----
    values.reverse()            # [1,2,3,4,5] becomes [5,4,3,2,1]

    # ---- Pass 2: write the mirrored values back into the same nodes ----
    node = head                 # restart the cursor at the front
    i = 0                       # index into the reversed value array
    while node:                 # walk the identical chain a second time
        node.val = values[i]    # overwrite the payload only
        i += 1                  # next value in the reversed array
        node = node.next        # next node in the chain

    # No pointer was ever re-wired, so the ORIGINAL head is still the head
    return head                 # for an empty list this is simply None

complexity.time: O(n) — two full passes over the list plus an O(n) array reverse, which is still linear overall.
complexity.space: O(n) — the `values` array holds a copy of every payload in the list.

approaches.name: Better (Recursion)
approaches.intuition: Here is the recursive way of seeing it: a list 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5 is just the node 1 glued in front of the smaller list 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5. Suppose a magic helper already reversed that smaller part into 5 -> 4 -> 3 -> 2 and handed you its new head, 5. What is left to do? Node 2 is now the TAIL of that reversed piece, and happily `head.next` is still pointing at node 2 — so `head.next.next = head` staples node 1 onto the end, and `head.next = None` makes node 1 the new tail. Return the head the helper gave you (5) unchanged, because the front of the answer never changes as the recursion unwinds. The base case is a list of zero or one node, which is already its own reverse. This costs no explicit array, but the call stack silently stores one frame per node, so it is O(n) space in disguise — which is exactly why the iterative version below is the real optimum.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Base case: if `head` is None (empty list) or `head.next` is None (single node), the list is already reversed — return `head`.
2. Recursively reverse everything after the head: `new_head = reverseList(head.next)`. Trust that this returns the head of the reversed tail.
3. `head.next` still points at the node that is now the LAST node of that reversed tail, so `head.next.next = head` appends the head to it.
4. Set `head.next = None` so the old head becomes the new tail and the list terminates properly (skipping this creates a 2-node cycle).
5. Return `new_head` untouched — it is the deepest node, and it stays the answer all the way up the call stack.
approaches.code:
def reverseList(head: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
    # Base case: an empty list or a single node is already its own reverse
    if head is None or head.next is None:
        return head                 # nothing to flip, hand it straight back

    # Recurse on the REST of the list first (1 -> [2,3,4,5])
    # We trust this call to return the head of the reversed remainder (node 5)
    new_head = reverseList(head.next)

    # head.next is still the node that is now the TAIL of the reversed part.
    # Example: for head = 1, head.next = 2, and 2 is currently the last node.
    head.next.next = head           # staple `head` onto the end: ... -> 2 -> 1

    # `head` is the new tail, so its own next must terminate the list.
    head.next = None                # forget this and 1 <-> 2 becomes a cycle!

    # The front of the answer was decided at the deepest call — pass it up
    return new_head                 # always the original tail node

complexity.time: O(n) — one recursive call per node, each doing O(1) pointer surgery.
complexity.space: O(n) — the recursion stack holds one frame per node until the deepest call returns.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: The brute force copied the values out and the recursion copied the stack; the insight that removes both is that reversing a list needs no memory at all beyond three names, because a link only has to be flipped once. Walk the chain with `curr`, and keep `prev` pointing at the piece you have already reversed. At every node you do one job: make `curr.next` point backwards at `prev`. The catch is that this overwrites the only reference to the rest of the list, so you must stash it in `next_node` FIRST — that single temporary variable is the whole trick. Then slide both names one node to the right and repeat. When `curr` falls off the end and becomes None, `prev` is standing on what used to be the tail, which is now the head of the reversed list, so that is what you return. One pass, no allocation, no recursion depth.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Initialise `prev = None` (the reversed part is empty) and `curr = head` (the un-reversed part is everything).
2. Loop while `curr` is not None — the loop ends exactly when every node has been flipped.
3. Save the rest of the list before destroying the link: `next_node = curr.next`.
4. Flip this node's pointer backwards: `curr.next = prev`.
5. Slide both names one node right: `prev = curr`, then `curr = next_node`.
6. When the loop exits, `curr` is None and `prev` is the old tail — return `prev` as the new head.
approaches.code:
# Definition for singly-linked list.
# class ListNode:
#     def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
#         self.val = val
#         self.next = next

def reverseList(head: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
    prev = None # Tracks the reversed list head
    curr = head # Tracks the current traversal node
    
    # Traverse through all nodes
    while curr:
        next_node = curr.next # Save next node reference
        curr.next = prev      # Reverse pointer link
        prev = curr          # Move prev pointer forward
        curr = next_node     # Move curr pointer forward
        
    return prev # prev ends up as the new head of reversed list

complexity.time: O(n) — each node is visited exactly once and its pointer flipped in O(1).
complexity.space: O(1) — only the three pointers prev, curr and next_node, regardless of list length.

Reverse Linked List.problemStatement: You are given the head node of a singly linked list. Each node holds a value and a single `next` pointer to the node after it; the final node points at nothing. Your job is to flip the direction of the whole chain so that the node that used to be last becomes the first, the node that used to be second-to-last comes next, and so on down to the original head, which becomes the final node and must point at nothing. Return the head of this reversed list. You are not asked to build a copy or to move the values around inside the existing nodes -- the expected solution rewires the existing `next` pointers so the same node objects are reused in the opposite order. An empty list (head is None) and a one-node list are both valid inputs and should simply come back unchanged.

Pascal's Triangle.title: Pascal's Triangle
Pascal's Triangle.tests:
# 1) the canonical 5-row triangle
assert generate(5) == [[1], [1, 1], [1, 2, 1], [1, 3, 3, 1], [1, 4, 6, 4, 1]]

# 2) smallest non-trivial input
assert generate(1) == [[1]]
assert generate(2) == [[1], [1, 1]]

# 3) edge: zero rows requested -> an empty triangle, not a crash
assert generate(0) == []

# 4) structural invariants for a bigger triangle: row r has r+1 cells,
#    the edges are 1, and every inner cell is the sum of its two parents
t = generate(8)
assert len(t) == 8
for r in range(8):
    assert len(t[r]) == r + 1
    assert t[r][0] == 1 and t[r][-1] == 1
    for c in range(1, r):
        assert t[r][c] == t[r - 1][c - 1] + t[r - 1][c]

# 5) row 7 of Pascal's triangle is the known binomial row
assert t[7] == [1, 7, 21, 35, 35, 21, 7, 1]
prerequisites: Pascal's triangle rule: row r has r+1 entries, both ends are 1, and every interior entry is the sum of the two entries diagonally above it.
The same entry equals the binomial coefficient C(r, c) = r! / (c! * (r-c)!) — that identity is what makes the factorial brute force correct, and `math.factorial` / `math.comb` implement it directly.
Why factorials are the slow route: they compute huge intermediate numbers and throw away all the shared work between neighbouring cells, whereas the DP row reuses the row you just built.
Python idiom `[1] * (r + 1)` creates a pre-filled row so you only have to overwrite the interior indices 1..r-1.
Indexing care: the loop `for c in range(1, r)` is deliberately empty for r = 0 and r = 1, which is exactly why the first two rows need no special-casing.

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: The triangle has a closed-form description that is very tempting to use directly: the cell in row r, column c is the binomial coefficient C(r, c), the number of ways to choose c items out of r, which equals r! / (c! * (r - c)!). That formula means you never have to look at any other cell — each position can be computed in isolation purely from its own coordinates. So the whole problem collapses into two nested loops over coordinates with one formula in the middle, and there is essentially no state to get wrong. What makes it a brute force is the cost of that convenience: there are about n^2/2 cells, and every single one rebuilds three factorials from scratch, multiplying up to r numbers each time. That extra factor turns an O(n^2)-sized answer into roughly O(n^3) work, and the intermediate factorials grow into huge integers long before the triangle's own entries do.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Create an empty list `triangle` that will collect one list per row.
2. Loop `r` from 0 to numRows - 1; this is the 0-based row index, so the row being built will hold r + 1 numbers.
3. Start a fresh empty list `row` for this iteration — the defining property of this approach is that no row ever reads a previously built row, so each `row` is independent.
4. Loop `c` from 0 through r inclusive, written as `range(r + 1)`, and compute `val = math.factorial(r) // (math.factorial(c) * math.factorial(r - c))`, which is exactly the binomial coefficient C(r, c); the floor division is exact because that quotient is always a whole number.
5. Append `val` to `row`, which keeps the entries in left-to-right order.
6. When the inner loop ends, append the finished `row` to `triangle`.
7. After the outer loop completes, return `triangle`, which now holds all numRows rows.
approaches.code:
import math  # factorial lets us compute a cell without the row above it

def generate(numRows: int) -> List[List[int]]:  # return the first numRows rows as a list of lists
    triangle = []  # accumulates one list per row
    # row index r is 0-based, so row r has r+1 entries
    for r in range(numRows):  # each row is built independently of its neighbours
        row = []  # fresh row; nothing here reuses the previous row's work
        # column index c walks across the current row
        for c in range(r + 1):  # range stops at r inclusive, hence the +1
            # cell (r, c) is exactly the binomial coefficient C(r, c)
            val = math.factorial(r) // (math.factorial(c) * math.factorial(r - c))  # integer // division: the quotient is always a whole number
            row.append(val)  # append keeps the row in left-to-right order
        triangle.append(row)  # row done; recomputing factorials is what makes this slow
    return triangle  # O(n^2) cells, each costing factorials, so brute force

complexity.space: O(N^2) for the results

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: Recomputing factorials per cell is wasted effort once you notice the recurrence the triangle is actually built on: an interior cell (r, c) equals cell (r-1, c-1) plus cell (r-1, c), and the first and last entry of every row are always 1. That single observation replaces an expensive factorial evaluation with one addition. It also fits the order we are already generating in — because rows are produced top to bottom, the row we need to read, row r-1, was finished on the previous iteration and is already sitting inside `triangle`, so nothing has to be recomputed or stored specially. Each cell therefore costs O(1) instead of O(r), and the total drops from O(n^3) to O(n^2), which is as good as possible since the output itself contains that many numbers. As a bonus the arithmetic stays small: we never construct an enormous factorial only to divide most of it away again.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Start with an empty list `triangle`.
2. Loop `r` from 0 to numRows - 1 and create `row = [1] * (r + 1)`; prefilling with 1s means the two boundary cells, index 0 and index r, are already correct and need no special casing.
3. Loop `c` over `range(1, r)`, which visits only the interior positions of the row; for r = 0 and r = 1 this range is empty, so those short rows are finished as soon as they are created.
4. Set `row[c] = triangle[r - 1][c - 1] + triangle[r - 1][c]`, reading the two cells diagonally above. The loop invariant that makes this safe is that `triangle` always already contains every completed row 0 through r-1 by the time row r is being filled.
5. Append the finished `row` to `triangle` so it becomes available to the next iteration.
6. Once the outer loop has produced all numRows rows, return `triangle`.
approaches.code:
def generate(numRows: int) -> List[List[int]]:
    triangle = []
    
    # Generate row by row
    for r in range(numRows):
        # Initialize row filled with 1s
        row = [1] * (r + 1)
        # Fill inner cells
        for c in range(1, r):
            # Sum elements from previous row
            row[c] = triangle[r - 1][c - 1] + triangle[r - 1][c]
        triangle.append(row)
        
    return triangle

complexity.space: O(N^2) to store values

Pascal's Triangle.problemStatement: You are given a single integer numRows. Build and return the first numRows rows of Pascal's triangle as a list of lists, where the row at 0-based index r contains exactly r + 1 numbers. Every row begins and ends with the value 1, and each interior entry equals the sum of the two entries diagonally above it in the row before. So row 0 is [1], row 1 is [1, 1], row 2 is [1, 2, 1], and row 3 is [1, 3, 3, 1]. The returned structure must keep the rows in top-to-bottom order and the numbers inside each row in left-to-right order.

Next Permutation.title: Next Permutation
Next Permutation.tests:
# 1) plain ascending array -> swap the last two
a = [1, 2, 3]
nextPermutation(a)
assert a == [1, 3, 2], a

# 2) edge: fully descending array is the LAST permutation -> wrap to the smallest
b = [3, 2, 1]
nextPermutation(b)
assert b == [1, 2, 3], b

# 3) duplicates must be handled (the pivot uses >= so equal values are skipped)
c = [1, 1, 5]
nextPermutation(c)
assert c == [1, 5, 1], c

# 4) edge: a single element has no next permutation and must stay unchanged
d = [1]
nextPermutation(d)
assert d == [1], d

# 5) pivot in the middle with a descending suffix that must be reversed
e = [1, 3, 5, 4, 2]
nextPermutation(e)
assert e == [1, 4, 2, 3, 5], e

# 6) edge: two equal elements are already the last permutation -> unchanged
f = [2, 2]
nextPermutation(f)
assert f == [2, 2], f
prerequisites: Lexicographic (dictionary) order on arrays: [1,3,2] comes after [1,2,3] because the first differing position holds a bigger value — 'next permutation' means the immediate successor in that order.
Key structural fact: a non-increasing (descending) block is already the LARGEST arrangement of its own values, so the change must happen at the first index that breaks the descent — the pivot.
Reversing a descending block turns it into the ascending, i.e. smallest, arrangement of those values — that is why an O(n) reverse can replace an O(n log n) sort in the final step.
The problem is in-place and returns nothing: use `nums[i], nums[j] = nums[j], nums[i]` and slice assignment `nums[:] = ...`; rebinding `nums = [...]` would silently do nothing to the caller.

Watch the comparison operators: `>=` in the pivot scan (skip equal values) but `>` (via `<=` in the loop guard) when hunting the successor, otherwise duplicates produce a swap that does not increase the permutation.

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: The definition of 'next permutation' is literally: list every arrangement of these numbers in dictionary order, find where ours sits, and take the one right after it (wrapping to the very first arrangement if ours is the last). So the most honest brute force just does that definition word for word — generate every permutation with itertools.permutations, de-duplicate them with a set (needed when the input has repeated values, otherwise the same arrangement appears several times and the 'next' one could be a copy of itself), sort them lexicographically, locate ours, and copy the following one back into nums. This is guaranteed correct because it IS the definition, which makes it a great sanity oracle for testing the clever version. It is also completely unusable: for n = 12 there are almost half a billion permutations. Writing it first, though, is what reveals the pattern the optimal solution exploits — that only a short descending suffix ever changes.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Snapshot the current arrangement as a tuple so we can search for it later: `current = tuple(nums)`.
2. Generate every permutation with `itertools.permutations(nums)`, drop duplicates with `set(...)`, and sort the result lexicographically.
3. Find the position `idx` of `current` inside that sorted list.
4. The answer is the entry at `idx + 1`; use modulo arithmetic so the last permutation wraps around to the first (the smallest arrangement).
5. Copy that tuple back into `nums` using slice assignment `nums[:] = ...` so the caller's list is modified in place.
approaches.code:
from itertools import permutations

def nextPermutation(nums: List[int]) -> None:
    # Remember the arrangement we were given (tuple = hashable + comparable)
    current = tuple(nums)

    # Build EVERY arrangement of these numbers.
    # set(...) removes duplicates, which matter when nums has repeats:
    #   permutations([1,1,5]) yields (1,1,5) twice, and we want it once.
    # sorted(...) puts them in dictionary (lexicographic) order.
    all_perms = sorted(set(permutations(nums)))

    # Where does our arrangement sit in that ordered catalogue?
    idx = all_perms.index(current)

    # The next one in dictionary order.
    # The % wraps the LAST permutation back to the FIRST (smallest) one,
    # which is exactly the behaviour the problem asks for.
    nxt = all_perms[(idx + 1) % len(all_perms)]

    # Slice assignment mutates the caller's list in place (nums = list(nxt) would not)
    nums[:] = list(nxt)
