complexity.time: O(n! * n * log(n!)) — we materialise all n! permutations and sort them, each comparison costing O(n).
complexity.space: O(n! * n) — every permutation is stored in memory at once.

approaches.name: Better (Break Point + Sort Suffix)
approaches.intuition: Staring at the brute-force output reveals the pattern: to get the NEXT arrangement you want to change the rightmost part of the array, because changing something on the left jumps you far ahead in dictionary order. Scan from the right and you will find a maximal descending suffix (like 5, 4, 2 in 1, 3, 5, 4, 2) — a descending block is already the largest arrangement of its own values, so nothing inside it can be increased. The first index that breaks that descent, here nums[1] = 3, is the pivot: it is the only digit we are allowed to bump up. Swap it with the smallest suffix value that is still strictly bigger than it (4), and the prefix is now minimally larger. Everything after the pivot should then be as small as possible, so we simply SORT the suffix ascending. That sort is the only wasteful bit — O(n log n) instead of O(n) — but the logic is much easier to trust than the reverse trick, so it is the natural stepping stone to the optimal.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Scan from index n-2 leftwards while `nums[i] >= nums[i+1]` to find the pivot index `i` — the first place where the array stops descending.
2. If no such index exists (`i < 0`), the whole array is descending, i.e. the last permutation: sort it ascending to wrap to the smallest and return.
3. Otherwise scan from the right for the last index `j` with `nums[j] > nums[i]`; because the suffix descends, that is the smallest suffix value still greater than the pivot.
4. Swap `nums[i]` and `nums[j]` — the prefix is now the smallest value that is strictly larger than before.
5. Sort the suffix `nums[i+1:]` ascending so the tail is the smallest arrangement of the remaining values, and write it back with slice assignment.
approaches.code:
def nextPermutation(nums: List[int]) -> None:
    n = len(nums)

    # --- Step 1: find the pivot, the first index (from the right) that
    # breaks the descending run. Everything to its right is non-increasing.
    i = n - 2                              # start at the second-to-last index
    while i >= 0 and nums[i] >= nums[i + 1]:
        i -= 1                             # still descending, keep walking left

    # --- Step 2: no pivot => the array is fully descending => it is the
    # LAST permutation, so we wrap around to the smallest one.
    if i < 0:
        nums.sort()                        # ascending = smallest arrangement
        return                             # done, nothing else to do

    # --- Step 3: find the rightmost value that is strictly bigger than the
    # pivot. Because the suffix descends, the rightmost such value is also
    # the SMALLEST value that still beats the pivot - exactly what we want.
    j = n - 1                              # start from the very last index
    while nums[j] <= nums[i]:
        j -= 1                             # too small to be the successor

    # --- Step 4: swap them. The prefix has now grown by the least possible amount.
    nums[i], nums[j] = nums[j], nums[i]

    # --- Step 5: the suffix should be as SMALL as possible, so sort it.
    # (The optimal version replaces this O(k log k) sort with an O(k) reverse.)
    nums[i + 1:] = sorted(nums[i + 1:])    # slice assignment keeps it in place

complexity.time: O(n log n) — the two scans are O(n), but sorting the suffix dominates in the worst case.
complexity.space: O(n) — `sorted(nums[i+1:])` builds a temporary copy of the suffix.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: This is the 'Better' approach with its one remaining inefficiency removed. We still find the pivot by scanning right-to-left for the first index where the descent breaks, and we still swap it with the smallest suffix value that beats it. The improvement is in the final step: the Better version SORTED the suffix, but that sort is unnecessary because the suffix is guaranteed to still be in non-increasing order after the swap. Why? It was descending before the swap, and we exchanged nums[i] for the last element greater than it, which drops a value into a slot where it still fits the descending pattern. A descending sequence reversed is an ascending one — the smallest arrangement of those values — so an O(k) two-pointer reverse does exactly what an O(k log k) sort did. The no-pivot case falls out for free: `i` ends at -1, so `left` starts at 0 and the reverse flips the entire array, wrapping the last permutation back to the first.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Scan from index n-2 leftwards while `nums[i] >= nums[i+1]` to find the pivot — the first index where the array stops descending.
2. If `i >= 0` a pivot exists: scan from the right for the last index `j` with `nums[j] > nums[i]`, which (because the suffix descends) is the smallest value still greater than the pivot.
3. Swap `nums[i]` and `nums[j]`, so the prefix increases by the least possible amount and the suffix is STILL non-increasing.
4. Set `left = i + 1` and `right = n - 1`, then reverse that suffix in place by swapping the ends and stepping inward.
5. Because a reversed descending run is ascending, the suffix is now the smallest arrangement of its values — and when no pivot was found, i = -1 makes step 4 reverse the whole array, correctly wrapping to the first permutation.
approaches.code:
def nextPermutation(nums: List[int]) -> None:
    # 1. Find the break point
    n = len(nums)  # how many elements we are permuting
    i = n - 2  # start one before the last index
    while i >= 0 and nums[i] >= nums[i + 1]:  # walk left over the descending tail
        i -= 1  # still descending -> keep going
        
    # If break point found
    if i >= 0:  # a pivot exists => this is not the last permutation
        # 2. Find next greater element to swap
        j = n - 1  # hunt the successor from the far right
        while nums[j] <= nums[i]:  # nums[j] too small to beat the pivot
            j -= 1  # step left and try again
        # Swap break point with next greater
        nums[i], nums[j] = nums[j], nums[i]  # prefix grows by the SMALLEST possible amount
        
    # 3. Reverse the suffix to get smallest permutation
    left, right = i + 1, n - 1  # the suffix that must become ascending
    while left < right:  # mirror the suffix in place
        nums[left], nums[right] = nums[right], nums[left]  # swap the two ends of the window
        left += 1  # close in from the left
        right -= 1  # close in from the right

complexity.time: O(n) — at most three single passes (find pivot, find successor, reverse suffix), with no sorting at all.
complexity.space: O(1) — everything is done by swapping inside the input array; only index variables are stored.

Next Permutation.problemStatement: You are given an array of integers nums holding one particular arrangement of those numbers. Imagine writing down every possible arrangement (permutation) of exactly the same multiset of numbers and sorting that entire catalogue of arrangements in dictionary (lexicographic) order, the way words are ordered by comparing the first position where they differ. Your task is to rearrange nums into the arrangement that comes immediately after the given one in that catalogue. If the given arrangement is already the very last one - the numbers sit in non-increasing order, so no greater arrangement exists - then wrap around and produce the smallest arrangement instead, which is the same numbers sorted in non-decreasing order. The result must reuse exactly the same numbers with the same multiplicities, and the classic form of the problem asks for the rearrangement to be done in place using only a constant amount of extra memory.

Maximum Subarray Sum (Kadane's Algorithm.title: Maximum Subarray Sum (Kadane's Algorithm)
Maximum Subarray Sum (Kadane's Algorithm.tests:
# 1) the textbook example: best subarray is [4, -1, 2, 1] = 6
assert maxSubArray([-2, 1, -3, 4, -1, 2, 1, -5, 4]) == 6

# 2) edge: a single element is its own answer
assert maxSubArray([1]) == 1
assert maxSubArray([-9]) == -9

# 3) edge: ALL negative -> must return the largest single element, never 0
assert maxSubArray([-3, -1, -7]) == -1

# 4) all positive -> the whole array is the answer
assert maxSubArray([5, 4, -1, 7, 8]) == 23
assert maxSubArray([1, 2, 3]) == 6

# 5) a dip that is worth riding through vs one that is not
assert maxSubArray([2, -1, 2]) == 3
assert maxSubArray([2, -5, 3]) == 3
prerequisites: A subarray is CONTIGUOUS (a slice), unlike a subsequence — so the answer is always described by one start index and one end index.
The problem requires a non-empty subarray, which is why every approach seeds its answer with nums[0] instead of 0; seeding with 0 silently breaks all-negative inputs.
Kadane's core decision: at each element you either extend the previous run or start a brand-new run at this element — `current_sum = max(x, current_sum + x)` encodes exactly that choice.
The invariant to hold in your head: `current_sum` is the best sum of a subarray ENDING at the current index, while `max_sum` is the best over all indices seen so far — two different quantities.
A running sum that has gone negative can only hurt whatever comes next, so discarding it is always safe — that is the one-line proof that Kadane is correct.

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: A subarray is fully described by where it starts and where it ends, so the most literal way to answer 'what is the largest subarray sum' is to try every possible (start, end) pair, add up the numbers between them, and keep the biggest total you ever see. Three nested loops do it: the outer two pick the boundaries i and j, the inner one walks from i to j adding elements. Nothing clever is happening, which is the point — it is impossible to get wrong and it doubles as a reference implementation you can test the fast version against. The catch is that it recomputes overlapping sums endlessly: the sum of nums[2..7] is calculated from scratch even though we just finished computing nums[2..6]. Seed the answer with nums[0] rather than 0, otherwise an all-negative array would wrongly report 0 for the empty subarray, which the problem does not allow.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Initialise `best = nums[0]` — never 0, because the array may be entirely negative and a subarray must contain at least one element.
2. Loop `i` over every possible starting index from 0 to n-1.
3. For each `i`, loop `j` over every possible ending index from `i` to n-1.
4. For each (i, j) pair, run a third loop over `k` from `i` to `j` accumulating `total = total + nums[k]`.
5. If `total` beats `best`, update `best`; after all pairs are exhausted return `best`.
approaches.code:
def maxSubArray(nums: List[int]) -> int:
    n = len(nums)
    # Seed with the first element, NOT 0: an all-negative array like [-3,-1]
    # must answer -1 (the best single element), never 0 (the empty subarray).
    best = nums[0]

    # Try every possible START index of a subarray
    for i in range(n):
        # ...paired with every possible END index at or after it
        for j in range(i, n):
            total = 0                 # rebuild this window's sum from scratch
            # Third loop: literally add up nums[i], nums[i+1], ..., nums[j]
            for k in range(i, j + 1):
                total += nums[k]      # this is the wasted, repeated work
            # Keep the running champion
            if total > best:
                best = total          # a new best subarray sum

    return best                       # the largest sum over all n*(n+1)/2 windows

complexity.time: O(n^3) — O(n^2) start/end pairs, each re-summed in O(n) by the innermost loop.
complexity.space: O(1) — only the scalars best, total and the loop counters are stored.

approaches.name: Better (Running Sum)
approaches.intuition: Look at what the brute force throws away. After computing the sum of nums[i..j], the very next thing it does is compute the sum of nums[i..j+1] — which is just the previous total plus nums[j+1]. There is no need to walk the window again. So we delete the innermost loop entirely: for each fixed start i, carry a `total` that grows by one element per step as j slides right, and compare it to the best after every extension. That single change drops the cost from O(n^3) to O(n^2), a huge practical win, and it is a pattern worth internalising — whenever an inner loop recomputes something that only changed by one term, replace it with an incremental update. This version is already fast enough for n in the low thousands, but Kadane's insight (that you never need to revisit a start index at all) is what finally makes it linear.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Initialise `best = nums[0]` so all-negative arrays are handled correctly.
2. For each start index `i` from 0 to n-1, reset a running accumulator `total = 0`.
3. Extend the window one element at a time: for `j` from `i` to n-1, do `total += nums[j]` — this is the sum of nums[i..j] with no re-walking.
4. After each extension compare `total` against `best` and keep the larger.
5. When both loops finish, `best` holds the maximum over every window; return it.
approaches.code:
def maxSubArray(nums: List[int]) -> int:
    n = len(nums)
    # Same seeding rule as before: start from a REAL element, not 0
    best = nums[0]

    # Fix the starting index of the window
    for i in range(n):
        total = 0                     # sum of nums[i..j], grown incrementally
        # Slide the end of the window rightwards one element at a time
        for j in range(i, n):
            total += nums[j]          # O(1) extension instead of an O(n) re-sum
            # Every prefix of this start is itself a candidate answer
            if total > best:
                best = total          # record the new champion

    return best

complexity.time: O(n^2) — n starting indices, each extended at most n times with O(1) work per extension.
complexity.space: O(1) — a couple of integer accumulators, no extra arrays.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: The O(n^2) version still restarts from every index. Kadane's insight kills that outer loop entirely with one observation: if the best subarray ending at position i-1 has a NEGATIVE sum, then dragging it along into position i can only make things worse, so the best subarray ending at i is just nums[i] by itself. And if that running sum is positive, extending it is always at least as good as starting over. That means at each element there are only two candidates, not i of them: extend the previous run (`current_sum + x`) or start fresh at this element (`x`) — and `max` picks the winner in O(1). So we keep two numbers: `current_sum`, the best sum of a subarray ENDING here, and `max_sum`, the best over everything seen so far. They are different quantities and confusing them is the classic bug. One pass, two variables, and the answer falls out.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Seed both `max_sum` and `current_sum` with `nums[0]` — never 0, so an all-negative array still returns a real element.
2. Iterate over the remaining elements `x` from index 1 onwards.
3. Make the only decision there is: `current_sum = max(x, current_sum + x)` — start a new run at x, or extend the existing one, whichever is larger.
4. Update the global record: `max_sum = max(max_sum, current_sum)`, keeping the two quantities strictly separate.
5. After the single pass, `max_sum` holds the largest sum over every possible subarray — return it.
approaches.code:
def maxSubArray(nums: List[int]) -> int:
    max_sum = nums[0]  # seed with a REAL element, never 0 (all-negative arrays)
    current_sum = nums[0]  # best sum of a subarray ENDING at the current index
    
    # Traverse remaining elements
    for x in nums[1:]:  # index 0 is already seeded, so start from the second element
        # Add current element or start fresh if previous sum is negative
        current_sum = max(x, current_sum + x)  # extend the old run, or abandon it and restart at x
        max_sum = max(max_sum, current_sum)  # remember the best run seen anywhere so far
        
    return max_sum  # the maximum subarray sum over the whole array

complexity.time: O(n) — one pass, with a constant-time decision at each element.
complexity.space: O(1) — only the two running integers max_sum and current_sum are stored.

Maximum Subarray Sum (Kadane's Algorithm.problemStatement: You are given an array of integers that may freely mix positive numbers, negative numbers and zeros. A subarray here means a block of one or more elements that sit next to each other in the original order: you may choose where the block starts and where it ends, but you may not skip elements in the middle and you may not reorder anything. Every such block has a sum, and among all of them exactly one value is the largest. Return that largest sum itself, as a single integer, rather than the block that produced it. Because the chosen block must contain at least one element, an array made up entirely of negative numbers still has a well-defined answer: the single least-negative element in it.

Sort Colors.title: Sort Colors
Sort Colors.tests:
# 1) the classic mixed input
a = [2, 0, 2, 1, 1, 0]
sortColors(a)
assert a == [0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 2], a

# 2) one of each, worst-possible starting order
b = [2, 0, 1]
sortColors(b)
assert b == [0, 1, 2], b

# 3) edge: a single element, and an empty array (must not crash or hang)
c = [0]
sortColors(c)
assert c == [0], c
d = []
sortColors(d)
assert d == [], d

# 4) edge: all elements identical — no swap should ever be needed
e = [2, 2, 2]
sortColors(e)
assert e == [2, 2, 2], e

# 5) already sorted input must stay sorted, and a reversed one must flip
f = [0, 0, 1, 2, 2]
sortColors(f)
assert f == [0, 0, 1, 2, 2], f
g = [2, 2, 1, 0, 0]
sortColors(g)
assert g == [0, 0, 1, 2, 2], g
prerequisites: The Dutch National Flag pattern: three pointers carve the array into four zones — [0, low) is all 0s, [low, mid) is all 1s, [mid, high] is unexplored, and (high, n-1] is all 2s.
That zone invariant is the whole proof: the loop condition `mid <= high` says 'the unexplored zone is non-empty', so the algorithm terminates exactly when every element has been classified.

Crucial asymmetry: after swapping with `high` you must NOT advance `mid`, because the value that just arrived from the back has never been inspected; after swapping with `low` you may advance, because that value is guaranteed to be a 1.
The input contains only the values 0, 1 and 2 — that bounded universe is what allows an O(n) solution to beat the O(n log n) comparison-sort lower bound.
Python tuple-swap `nums[i], nums[j] = nums[j], nums[i]` evaluates the right side first, so it is safe even when i == j; and the function mutates in place and returns None.

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: Strip away the story about red, white and blue balls and the task is simply: sort an array. So the first answer any beginner should give out loud is 'call sort'. Python's Timsort rearranges the list in place in O(n log n) and it is unquestionably correct for 0s, 1s and 2s just like for any other numbers. Saying this out loud in an interview is not a mistake — it establishes the baseline that everything else must beat, and it makes the interviewer state the real constraint: no library sort, single pass, constant space. It also frames why the problem is interesting at all: a general comparison sort has to pay log n because it knows nothing about the values, whereas here we know there are exactly THREE distinct values, and that extra knowledge is worth a whole logarithmic factor. Note this approach does not even look at the values — it would behave identically on any input.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Observe that the required output is exactly the sorted order of the input, because 0 < 1 < 2.
2. Call `nums.sort()`, which sorts the list in place using Timsort — no new list is created, so the caller sees the change.
3. Return nothing: the problem mutates the input rather than producing a new array.
4. Note the cost: O(n log n) comparisons, and a general sort cannot exploit the fact that only three distinct values exist.
5. Treat this as the correctness baseline that the counting and Dutch-flag approaches must reproduce exactly.
approaches.code:
def sortColors(nums: List[int]) -> None:
    # The required output IS the sorted order, because 0 < 1 < 2.
    # list.sort() is Timsort: it rearranges the SAME list object in place,
    # so the caller's array is modified (that is what the problem wants).
    nums.sort()

    # Why this is only the baseline:
    #   * O(n log n) comparisons - a general sort learns the order by comparing,
    #     while we already KNOW there are only three possible values.
    #   * Most interviewers explicitly ban it, which is the whole point of
    #     the follow-up: "now do it in one pass with O(1) space".
    # Nothing is returned - the mutation is the answer.

complexity.time: O(n log n) — Timsort's comparison-sort bound; it cannot exploit the fact that only three values exist.
complexity.space: O(1) auxiliary in practice for this input size — `list.sort()` sorts in place (Timsort may use O(n) scratch in the worst case).

approaches.name: Better (Counting Sort, Two Passes)
approaches.intuition: Since the array only ever contains 0, 1 and 2, we do not need to compare anything — we just need to know HOW MANY of each there are. One pass tallies three counters, and then the sorted array is completely determined: write count0 zeroes, then count1 ones, then count2 twos, straight over the original array. This is counting sort restricted to a universe of three values, and it is O(n) time with O(1) space (three integers), which already beats the library sort. The reason it is still labelled 'better' rather than 'optimal' is the two passes: we read the whole array once to count and write the whole array once to fill. If the data were arriving as a stream, or the elements were heavy objects rather than the labels 0/1/2 (so that overwriting them would destroy real data), the counting trick would break down — and that is precisely the situation the Dutch National Flag algorithm handles by swapping elements instead of overwriting them, in a single pass.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Initialise three counters `count0 = count1 = count2 = 0`.
2. Pass 1: walk the array once and increment the counter matching each value.
3. Pass 2 begins: write the value 0 into indices 0 .. count0-1.
4. Then write the value 1 into the next `count1` slots, i.e. indices count0 .. count0+count1-1.
5. Finally write the value 2 into the remaining slots; the array is now sorted and every index has been written exactly once.
approaches.code:
def sortColors(nums: List[int]) -> None:
    # --- Pass 1: tally how many of each of the only three possible values ---
    count0 = 0                      # how many reds (0)
    count1 = 0                      # how many whites (1)
    count2 = 0                      # how many blues (2)
    for value in nums:              # one linear scan, no comparisons needed
        if value == 0:
            count0 += 1
        elif value == 1:
            count1 += 1
        else:                       # value must be 2 by the problem constraints
            count2 += 1

    # --- Pass 2: the sorted array is fully determined by the three counts ---
    index = 0                       # write cursor moving left to right
    for _ in range(count0):         # first block: all the 0s
        nums[index] = 0
        index += 1
    for _ in range(count1):         # second block: all the 1s
        nums[index] = 1
        index += 1
    for _ in range(count2):         # third block: all the 2s
        nums[index] = 2
        index += 1
    # Every slot was written exactly once, so nums is now sorted in place.

complexity.time: O(n) — one counting pass plus one writing pass, 2n operations total with no comparisons.
complexity.space: O(1) — only three integer counters and a write cursor, regardless of n.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: Counting sort needed two passes because it read the whole array before writing anything. The Dutch National Flag algorithm gets it down to one pass by SWAPPING instead of overwriting, which also means it works when the elements are real objects rather than the bare labels 0/1/2. Three pointers carve the array into four regions: [0, low) is settled 0s, [low, mid) is settled 1s, [mid, high] is still unknown, and (high, n-1] is settled 2s. `mid` is the scanner. A 0 gets swapped down to the `low` boundary and both low and mid advance — advancing mid is safe because whatever came back from `low` was necessarily a 1. A 1 is already where it belongs, so mid just steps over it. A 2 gets swapped up to the `high` boundary and high shrinks, but mid must NOT advance, because the value that just arrived from the back has never been inspected. That asymmetry is the one detail everybody gets wrong.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Initialise `low = 0`, `mid = 0`, `high = len(nums) - 1`, establishing the four zones (0s, 1s, unexplored, 2s).
2. Loop while `mid <= high`, i.e. while the unexplored zone still contains at least one element.
3. If `nums[mid] == 0`: swap it with `nums[low]`, then increment BOTH `low` and `mid` — the incoming value is guaranteed to be a 1, so it needs no re-inspection.
4. Else if `nums[mid] == 1`: it is already inside its own zone, so just increment `mid`.
5. Else (it is a 2): swap it with `nums[high]` and decrement `high`, but deliberately leave `mid` where it is so the unexamined value swapped in from the back gets classified next turn.
6. When `mid` passes `high` the unexplored zone is empty and the array is sorted in place.
approaches.code:
def sortColors(nums: List[int]) -> None:
    low, mid, high = 0, 0, len(nums) - 1  # boundaries of the 0s / 1s / unexplored / 2s zones
    
    # Sort in a single pass
    while mid <= high:  # loop while the unexplored zone [mid..high] is non-empty
        if nums[mid] == 0:  # a 0 belongs in the front zone
            nums[low], nums[mid] = nums[mid], nums[low]  # send it to the low boundary
            low += 1  # the 0s zone just grew
            mid += 1  # safe to advance: whatever came back was a 1
        elif nums[mid] == 1:  # a 1 is already in its correct middle zone
            mid += 1  # nothing to swap, just step over it
        else: # nums[mid] == 2
            nums[mid], nums[high] = nums[high], nums[mid]  # park the 2 at the back of the array
            high -= 1  # the 2s zone grew - and mid deliberately does NOT move

complexity.time: O(n) — every iteration either advances mid or decreases high, so at most n steps run in total.
complexity.space: O(1) — three index variables and in-place swaps; nothing is allocated.

Sort Colors.problemStatement: You are given an integer array nums in which every element is guaranteed to be one of exactly three values: 0, 1 or 2, standing for the colours red, white and blue. Rearrange the elements of that same array so that all the 0s come first, then all the 1s, then all the 2s — in other words, sort the array into non-decreasing order so that equal colours end up adjacent to one another. The work must be done in place: you modify nums itself rather than building and returning a new list, and the function returns nothing, so the caller reads the answer by looking at nums after the call. The expected solution does not call a built-in sorting routine and does not count occurrences in one pass and overwrite in a second pass; it settles the whole array in a single sweep using only a constant amount of extra memory.

Two Sum.title: Two Sum
Two Sum.tests:
# 1) the canonical example
assert twoSum([2, 7, 11, 15], 9) == [0, 1]

# 2) the answer is not at the front, and the indices must be ascending
assert twoSum([3, 2, 4], 6) == [1, 2]

# 3) edge: two EQUAL values form the pair — the same element must not be reused
assert twoSum([3, 3], 6) == [0, 1]

# 4) edge: no pair sums to the target -> empty list, no crash
assert twoSum([1, 2, 3], 100) == []

# 5) negatives and a zero target
assert twoSum([-3, 4, 3, 90], 0) == [0, 2]

# 6) edge: fewer than two elements can never form a pair
assert twoSum([5], 5) == []
assert twoSum([], 0) == []
prerequisites: Python dict lookups (`key in d`, `d[key]`) are O(1) on average thanks to hashing — that single fact is what turns the O(n^2) pair scan into an O(n) one.
The complement trick: instead of asking 'do these two add to target?', ask 'have I already seen target - num?' — one question per element instead of one per pair.
Order matters in the one-pass version: check the map BEFORE inserting the current number, otherwise an element could pair with itself (e.g. nums=[3], target=6 would wrongly match).
`enumerate(nums)` yields (index, value) pairs, which is how you keep positions while iterating over values.
You must return indices, not values — so any approach that sorts the array first has to carry the original index alongside each value.

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: The question asks for two positions whose values add to the target, so the most direct answer is to test every pair. Fix the first index i, then try every index j strictly to its right (starting at i+1 rather than 0 avoids both re-testing pairs in the opposite order and the illegal case of using the same element twice), and check whether nums[i] + nums[j] equals the target. The moment a pair matches we can return immediately, because the problem guarantees at most one valid answer. This needs no extra memory at all and is impossible to get wrong, which makes it the right thing to say first. Its weakness is obvious once you count: with 10,000 elements you perform about 50 million additions. The fix is to notice that the inner loop is really asking one question over and over — 'does the value target - nums[i] exist somewhere?' — and a hash map answers that in O(1).
approaches.algorithm:
1. Let n be the length of nums, and loop `i` from 0 to n-2 as the index of the first element of the pair.
2. For each `i`, loop `j` from `i + 1` to n-1 so the second index is always strictly after the first — this both prevents reusing one element and prevents reporting the same pair twice.
3. Test whether `nums[i] + nums[j] == target`.
4. On the first match, return `[i, j]` immediately (indices in increasing order).
5. If both loops finish without a match, return an empty list to signal 'no such pair'.
approaches.code:
def twoSum(nums: List[int], target: int) -> List[int]:
    n = len(nums)

    # Pick the FIRST index of the pair. It can stop at n-2 because
    # a pair needs at least one element after it.
    for i in range(n - 1):
        # Pick the SECOND index. Starting at i + 1 does two jobs at once:
        #   * it never reuses the same element twice (i != j), and
        #   * it never re-checks a pair we already tried in the other order.
        for j in range(i + 1, n):
            # The only test there is
            if nums[i] + nums[j] == target:
                # The problem promises at most one answer, so the first
                # match is THE answer - return straight away.
                return [i, j]

    # Fell through every pair: no two numbers add up to the target
    return []

complexity.time: O(n^2) — roughly n*(n-1)/2 pairs are examined in the worst case (when no pair matches).
complexity.space: O(1) — nothing is stored beyond the two loop counters.

approaches.name: Better (Sorting + Two Pointers)
approaches.intuition: If the array were sorted, you could stop testing pairs blindly: put one pointer at the smallest value and one at the largest, add them, and let the comparison tell you which pointer to move. Too small means the only way to grow the sum is to raise the left pointer; too big means you must lower the right one. Each step eliminates a whole column of pairs, so the scan finishes in O(n). The catch is that the problem wants ORIGINAL indices, and sorting destroys them — so before sorting we pair every value with the index it came from, and sort those (value, index) tuples by value. When the pointers finally land on a matching pair we read the remembered indices back out and return them in ascending order. Overall O(n log n), dominated by the sort, with O(n) extra space for the tuple array. It is a genuine improvement over the quadratic scan and it is the exact machinery that powers 3 Sum — but a hash map removes the sort entirely and gets us to O(n).
approaches.algorithm:
1. Build a list of `(value, original_index)` tuples so the original positions survive the sort.
2. Sort that list by value (Python sorts tuples lexicographically, so the value is the primary key).
3. Place `left` at 0 and `right` at the last position, and loop while `left < right`.
4. Compute `total = pairs[left][0] + pairs[right][0]`. If it equals the target, return the two stored indices sorted ascending.
5. If `total < target` move `left` right (the only way to increase the sum); if `total > target` move `right` left. If the pointers meet, return an empty list.
approaches.code:
def twoSum(nums: List[int], target: int) -> List[int]:
    # Sorting throws away positions, so bolt each value to the index it came from
    pairs = [(value, index) for index, value in enumerate(nums)]

    # Sort by value (tuples compare on the first element first)
    pairs.sort()

    left = 0                        # points at the smallest remaining value
    right = len(pairs) - 1          # points at the largest remaining value

    # Squeeze the window from both ends
    while left < right:
        total = pairs[left][0] + pairs[right][0]

        if total == target:
            # Found it - recover the ORIGINAL indices we stored alongside
            # the values, and report them in ascending order.
            return sorted([pairs[left][1], pairs[right][1]])

        if total < target:
            # Sum too small: the left value is the smallest available,
            # so no pair using it can work - discard it.
            left += 1
        else:
            # Sum too big: symmetric argument on the largest value.
            right -= 1

    # Pointers crossed without a match
    return []

complexity.time: O(n log n) — building the tuple list and the two-pointer sweep are O(n), but the sort dominates.
complexity.space: O(n) — the array of (value, index) tuples is a full-size copy of the input.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: Both earlier approaches did more work than the question requires. The brute force asked 'do these two add up?' n^2/2 times; the sorting version paid O(n log n) to impose an order we never actually needed. Flip the question around: while standing on `num`, the partner it needs is completely determined — it is `target - num`. So the only thing we need is a structure that answers 'have I already seen this value, and where?' instantly, and that is exactly a dict. Walk the array once, keeping a map from value to the index it was found at. At each element compute the complement and look it up; a hit means the pair is complete and we return the stored index followed by the current one. Insert the current number only AFTER the lookup — otherwise a single 3 with target 6 would match itself. One pass, O(1) average work per element, and the trade is O(n) memory for the map.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Create an empty dict `lookup` that will map each value already seen to the index where it was found.
2. Iterate with `enumerate(nums)` so both the index `i` and the value `num` are available.
3. Compute `complement = target - num` — the one value that would complete the pair with this element.
4. If `complement` is already a key in `lookup`, the pair exists: return `[lookup[complement], i]`, earlier index first.
5. Otherwise record `lookup[num] = i`. Doing this AFTER the check is what prevents an element from pairing with itself.
6. If the loop finishes with no hit, return an empty list — no pair sums to the target.
approaches.code:
def twoSum(nums: List[int], target: int) -> List[int]:
    lookup = {} # Maps value to index
    
    # Single pass search
    for i, num in enumerate(nums):  # enumerate gives index and value together
        complement = target - num  # the partner this number needs
        if complement in lookup:  # O(1) average lookup - have we already passed it?
            return [lookup[complement], i]  # earlier index first, current index second
        lookup[num] = i  # store AFTER the check so a number never pairs with itself
    return []  # no pair adds up to the target

complexity.time: O(n) — a single pass with O(1) average-time dict lookup and insert per element.
complexity.space: O(n) — in the worst case every value is stored in the hash map before a match is found.

Two Sum.problemStatement: You are given an array of integers called nums and a single integer called target. Somewhere in that array there are two entries, sitting at two different positions, whose values add up exactly to target. Your job is to return the positions (the 0-based indices) of those two entries, not the values themselves. The two indices must be different from each other, which means a single element cannot be paired with itself to reach the target, although two separate positions that happen to hold the same value are perfectly legal. The array is not assumed to be sorted, values may be negative, and the pair may be returned in either order.

Longest Consecutive Sequence.title: Longest Consecutive Sequence
Longest Consecutive Sequence.tests:
# 1) the canonical example: 1,2,3,4 is the longest run
assert longestConsecutive([100, 4, 200, 1, 3, 2]) == 4

# 2) edge: empty input -> 0 (no run exists at all)
assert longestConsecutive([]) == 0

# 3) edge: duplicates must NOT inflate a streak
assert longestConsecutive([1, 1, 1]) == 1
assert longestConsecutive([1, 2, 2, 3]) == 3

# 4) two separate runs, the longer one wins, and negatives are handled
assert longestConsecutive([9, 1, 4, 7, 3, -1, 0, 5, 8, -1, 6]) == 7

# 5) single element, and a run given in reverse order
assert longestConsecutive([5]) == 1
assert longestConsecutive([4, 3, 2, 1]) == 4
prerequisites: Position is irrelevant here: the answer depends only on WHICH values exist, which is why a set (an unordered membership structure) is enough and a sort is overkill.
`set(nums)` gives O(1) average membership tests and silently removes duplicates — both properties are load-bearing for the optimal solution.
The start-of-run guard `if num - 1 not in num_set` is what keeps the algorithm linear: without it every element would re-walk its whole run, making it quadratic.
Amortised counting argument: because each run is walked only from its smallest element, every value is visited by the inner while-loop at most once across the entire run of the algorithm.
Edge conventions: an empty array must return 0, and duplicates contribute a length of 1, not more — both fall out naturally once you deduplicate into a set.

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: The definition says: find the longest chain of numbers x, x+1, x+2, ... that all appear somewhere in the array (their positions do not matter at all). So the literal approach is to take each value in turn, pretend it is the start of a chain, and then keep asking 'is the next number also present?' — searching the raw list each time. Every 'is it present?' question costs a full linear scan because an unsorted list has no faster way to answer, and we ask that question once per link of every chain we try, from every possible starting value. That is a lot of repeated scanning, which is exactly why this is the slow version. But it is worth writing because it names the two separate costs cleanly: (a) membership testing, which a hash set makes O(1), and (b) restarting the same chain from the middle over and over, which the 'only start when num-1 is absent' guard removes.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Initialise `longest = 0`, which is also the correct answer for an empty array.
2. For every value `num` in the array, assume it starts a consecutive run: set `current = num` and `streak = 1`.
3. While `current + 1` can be found in the array (a full linear scan each time), increment `current` and increment `streak`.
4. When the chain stops growing, update `longest = max(longest, streak)`.
5. After trying every starting value, return `longest`.
approaches.code:
def longestConsecutive(nums: List[int]) -> int:
    longest = 0                       # also the right answer for an empty array

    # Try EVERY value as a possible start of a consecutive run
    for num in nums:
        current = num                 # cursor walking forward along the run
        streak = 1                    # the run contains at least `num` itself

        # `x in nums` on a LIST is a linear scan - this is the expensive part.
        # We repeat it once per link of the chain, for every starting value.
        while current + 1 in nums:
            current += 1              # the next number exists, extend the run
            streak += 1               # ...and count it

        # This run is finished; is it the best one so far?
        longest = max(longest, streak)

    return longest                    # length of the longest consecutive run

complexity.time: O(n^3) in the worst case — n starting values, each chain up to O(n) long, and every membership test is an O(n) list scan.
complexity.space: O(1) — only scalars are kept; the input list is not copied.

approaches.name: Better (Sorting)
approaches.intuition: Consecutive numbers are only awkward to find because the array is shuffled. Sort it and they line up as neighbours, so a single left-to-right walk can measure every run: if the next value is exactly one more than the previous one, the current run grows; if it is the SAME value, we skip it (duplicates must not inflate a streak — [1,1,2] is a run of length 2, not 3); anything else breaks the run and we restart the counter at 1. We track the best run seen and return it. This is O(n log n) because of the sort, with O(n) extra space if we avoid mutating the caller's list by using `sorted(...)`. It is a big improvement over the brute force and is often good enough in practice, but the sort is doing more work than we need: we never actually care about the total order, only about which values exist — and answering existence questions is precisely what a hash set does in O(1).
approaches.algorithm:
1. If the array is empty return 0 straight away, since the loops below assume at least one element.
2. Build a sorted copy `s = sorted(nums)` so equal and consecutive values become adjacent.
3. Initialise both `longest = 1` and `streak = 1` — with at least one element the answer is never smaller than 1.
4. Walk `i` from 1 to the end: if `s[i] == s[i-1]` skip this duplicate without touching `streak`; else if `s[i] == s[i-1] + 1` increment `streak`; otherwise reset `streak = 1`.
5. After each element update `longest = max(longest, streak)` and return `longest` at the end.

complexity.time: O(n log n) — the sort dominates; the single scan afterwards is only O(n).
complexity.space: O(n) — `sorted()` allocates a full copy so the caller's list is not mutated.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: Sorting was overkill: we never needed the total order, only the answer to 'does the value x exist?'. A set answers that in O(1), so drop every number into one — which conveniently removes duplicates too. Now the naive plan would be to count a run forward from every element, but that re-walks the same run once per member and is quadratic. The fix is a single guard: only start counting when `num - 1` is NOT in the set, because that means `num` is the smallest element of its run. Every run therefore gets measured exactly once, from its left end, and every other member is dismissed by one O(1) check. The amortised argument is what makes it linear despite the nested while-loop: across the entire algorithm the inner loop advances a total of at most n times, since each value belongs to exactly one run and is stepped over only when that run is being measured.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Build `num_set = set(nums)` — this gives O(1) membership tests and silently drops duplicates.
2. Initialise `longest = 0`, which is also the correct answer for an empty input.
3. For each `num` in the set, test whether `num - 1` is absent; if it is present, `num` sits mid-run and is skipped immediately in O(1).
4. If `num` IS a run start, set `current_num = num` and `current_streak = 1`, then walk forward with a while-loop as long as `current_num + 1` is in the set, incrementing both.
5. When the run stops growing, update `longest = max(longest, current_streak)`.
6. Return `longest`; because every run is counted only from its smallest element, the total inner-loop work across the whole algorithm is O(n).
approaches.code:
def longestConsecutive(nums: List[int]) -> int:
    num_set = set(nums) # Load numbers into hash set
    longest = 0  # also the correct answer for an empty input
    
    for num in num_set:  # the set already dropped duplicates for us
        # Check if current number is start of a sequence
        if num - 1 not in num_set:  # nothing precedes num => it is a run's smallest element
            current_num = num  # cursor that walks forward along this run
            current_streak = 1  # the run contains at least num itself
            
            # Count sequence size
            while current_num + 1 in num_set:  # O(1) membership test, not a scan
                current_num += 1  # the next number exists - extend
                current_streak += 1  # ...and count it
            longest = max(longest, current_streak)  # each run is measured exactly once, from its start
            
    return longest  # length of the longest consecutive run

complexity.time: O(n) — each value is examined once by the for-loop and stepped over at most once by the while-loop (amortised).
complexity.space: O(n) — the hash set stores every distinct value from the input.

Longest Consecutive Sequence.problemStatement: You are given an array nums of integers in no particular order, and the array may contain duplicates. Consider any group of values drawn from that array which forms a run of consecutive integers, meaning each is exactly one greater than the previous one, such as 3, 4, 5, 6. Your job is to return the length of the longest such run that can be assembled out of the values present in nums. The elements do not have to sit next to each other in the array and their positions are irrelevant; only which values exist matters. If nums is empty the answer is 0, and if no value has a neighbour one higher or one lower, the answer is 1.

Find Middle of Linked List.title: Find Middle of Linked List
Find Middle of Linked List.tests:
# 1) odd length -> the single middle node
assert middleNode(build_linked_list([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])).val == 3

# 2) even length -> the SECOND of the two middles (4, not 3)
assert middleNode(build_linked_list([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6])).val == 4

# 3) the returned value must be a real node of the chain, so the caller can walk on
assert linked_list_to_list(middleNode(build_linked_list([1, 2, 3, 4, 5]))) == [3, 4, 5]

# 4) edge: a single node is its own middle
assert middleNode(build_linked_list([1])).val == 1

# 5) edge: an empty list has no middle -> None, not a crash
assert middleNode(None) is None

# 6) two nodes -> the second one
assert middleNode(build_linked_list([1, 2])).val == 2
prerequisites: Linked lists have no random access: reaching position k costs k `.next` hops, which is why 'just index the middle' is not available.
The slow/fast (tortoise and hare) pattern: when fast moves two nodes per turn and slow moves one, fast reaches the end in n/2 turns and slow is therefore exactly halfway.
Loop-guard order matters: `while fast and fast.next` must test `fast` FIRST, because Python short-circuits and `None.next` would raise AttributeError.
This exact guard also decides the even-length convention — it returns the second middle (node 4 of 1..6); using `while fast.next and fast.next.next` would return the first middle instead.
The function returns a NODE, not a value, so the caller can continue traversing from it — assertions should read `.val` or convert with `linked_list_to_list`.

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: A linked list is painful here only because you cannot jump to position k — there is no indexing, just .next hops. So the crudest fix is to give ourselves indexing: walk the chain once and push every node reference into an ordinary Python list. Now `nodes[k]` is instant, and finding the middle is arithmetic rather than traversal — `nodes[len(nodes) // 2]` is the middle for an odd length and, because integer division rounds down, the SECOND of the two middles for an even length, which is exactly what the problem asks for (for 1,2,3,4,5,6 it gives index 3, i.e. node 4). Note we store the nodes themselves, not their values, because the function must return an actual node so the caller can keep walking from it. The price is O(n) extra memory for a list of n references, which is a real cost for a million-node list and completely avoidable.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Handle the empty list first: if `head` is None there is no middle node, so return None.
2. Create an empty Python list `nodes` and walk the chain from `head`, appending each NODE (not its value) as you go.
3. After the walk, `len(nodes)` is the length of the list and the array gives O(1) random access.
4. Compute `mid = len(nodes) // 2`; floor division automatically selects the second middle when the length is even.
5. Return `nodes[mid]`, which is a real node from the original chain, so the caller can traverse onwards from it.
approaches.code:
def middleNode(head: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
    # An empty list has no middle node at all
    if head is None:
        return None

    # --- Pass 1: give ourselves random access by copying the NODE
    # references (not the values - the caller needs a real node back).
    nodes = []
    node = head
    while node:                       # walk until we fall off the tail
        nodes.append(node)            # remember this node
        node = node.next              # hop forward

    # Integer division picks the middle index:
    #   length 5 -> 5 // 2 = 2  -> the 3rd node  (the single middle)
    #   length 6 -> 6 // 2 = 3  -> the 4th node  (the SECOND middle, as required)
    mid = len(nodes) // 2

    # O(1) lookup now that we have an array
    return nodes[mid]

complexity.time: O(n) — a single traversal to build the array, then one O(1) index lookup.
complexity.space: O(n) — the array holds a reference to every node in the list.

approaches.name: Better (Count Then Walk)
approaches.intuition: We do not really need to store the nodes — we only needed the LENGTH. So walk the list once just to count nodes, then walk it a second time from the head and stop after `length // 2` hops. That lands on exactly the same node the array version returned (index length//2 counted from 0), and it uses only two integers of extra memory instead of an n-element array. This is a genuinely good solution: O(n) time, O(1) space, and very easy to explain. Its only blemish is that it reads the list TWICE, which matters when the list is huge and cache-cold, or when the data is a one-shot stream you cannot rewind. The slow/fast pointer trick below removes that second pass by making one pointer travel at double speed, so that when the fast one reaches the end the slow one is automatically halfway.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Return None immediately if `head` is None, so the counting loop has something to walk.
2. Pass 1: set `length = 0` and a cursor at `head`, then advance the cursor to the end incrementing `length` at every node.
3. Compute `steps = length // 2` — the number of `.next` hops needed to reach the middle from the head.
4. Pass 2: reset the cursor to `head` and hop exactly `steps` times.
5. Return the cursor, which now points at the middle node (the second of the two middles for an even length).
approaches.code:
def middleNode(head: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
    # Nothing to find in an empty list
    if head is None:
        return None

    # --- Pass 1: count the nodes. We keep the count, not the nodes,
    # so memory stays O(1) no matter how long the list is.
    length = 0
    node = head
    while node:                       # walk to the tail
        length += 1                   # tally this node
        node = node.next

    # How many .next hops from the head to reach the middle?
    #   length 5 -> 2 hops -> node index 2 (the 3rd node)
    #   length 6 -> 3 hops -> node index 3 (the SECOND middle, as required)
    steps = length // 2

    # --- Pass 2: walk exactly that many hops from the head
    node = head                       # rewind to the front
    for _ in range(steps):            # take `steps` single steps
        node = node.next

    return node                       # this is the middle node

complexity.time: O(n) — two sequential passes over the list, which is 2n hops, still linear.
complexity.space: O(1) — only an integer counter and a node cursor are stored.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: Both earlier versions had to learn the length before they could use it — one by storing every node, the other by reading the list twice. The tortoise-and-hare trick gets the middle in a single pass by exploiting a ratio instead of a count: run one pointer at one node per turn and another at two nodes per turn, starting together. After k turns the slow pointer has covered k nodes and the fast one 2k, so at the exact moment the fast pointer runs out of list (2k has reached n), the slow pointer is sitting at n/2 — the middle — without anyone ever counting anything. The loop guard `while fast and fast.next` does double duty: it stops the walk at the right moment AND protects both dereferences, since Python's `and` short-circuits so `fast.next.next` is only evaluated once `fast.next` is known to exist. For an even-length list this guard lands slow on the SECOND middle, which is the convention the problem asks for.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Point both `slow` and `fast` at `head` so they start from the same place.
2. Loop while `fast` and `fast.next` are both non-None — checking `fast` first is what makes `fast.next.next` safe.
3. Inside the loop advance `slow` by one node: `slow = slow.next`.
4. Advance `fast` by two nodes: `fast = fast.next.next`, so the gap between the pointers grows by exactly one per turn.
5. The loop exits when fast reaches the end (odd length) or falls off it (even length); at that moment slow has covered exactly half the list.
6. Return `slow` — the middle node, or the second of the two middles when the length is even.
approaches.code:
def middleNode(head: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
    slow = head # Moves 1 step
    fast = head # Moves 2 steps
    
    # Traverse list
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next.next
        
    return slow # Points to the middle node

complexity.time: O(n) — the fast pointer traverses the list once and the loop runs about n/2 times.
complexity.space: O(1) — just the two node pointers, no array and no second pass.

Find Middle of Linked List.problemStatement: You are given the head pointer of a singly linked list, in which every node stores a value plus a reference to the next node, and the last node points to null. Return the middle NODE itself, not just its value, so the caller can carry on walking the rest of the chain from that point. When the list holds an odd number of nodes the middle is unambiguous. When the length is even there are two equally central candidates, and the rule is to return the second of them, so a list of four nodes returns the third node and a list of six returns the fourth.

Merge Two Sorted Linked Lists.title: Merge Two Sorted Linked Lists
Merge Two Sorted Linked Lists.tests:
# 1) the canonical example, with a duplicated value on both sides
assert linked_list_to_list(
    mergeTwoLists(build_linked_list([1, 2, 4]), build_linked_list([1, 3, 4]))
) == [1, 1, 2, 3, 4, 4]

# 2) edge: both lists empty -> None, which converts to []
assert linked_list_to_list(mergeTwoLists(None, None)) == []
assert mergeTwoLists(None, None) is None

# 3) edge: exactly one list empty -> the other one comes back untouched
assert linked_list_to_list(mergeTwoLists(None, build_linked_list([0]))) == [0]
assert linked_list_to_list(mergeTwoLists(build_linked_list([1, 2]), None)) == [1, 2]

# 4) fully disjoint ranges: every node of one list is drained before the other starts
assert linked_list_to_list(
    mergeTwoLists(build_linked_list([5]), build_linked_list([1, 2, 3]))
) == [1, 2, 3, 5]

# 5) all values equal -> nothing is lost or duplicated
assert linked_list_to_list(
    mergeTwoLists(build_linked_list([2, 2]), build_linked_list([2, 2]))
) == [2, 2, 2, 2]

# 6) the result must be a properly terminated chain (no cycle, correct length)
merged = mergeTwoLists(build_linked_list([1, 3, 5]), build_linked_list([2, 4, 6]))
assert linked_list_to_list(merged) == [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
prerequisites: Both inputs are already sorted — the merge step of merge sort exploits exactly that, so no comparison sort is ever needed.
The dummy (sentinel) head idiom: allocating one throwaway node removes the 'is this the first node?' special case, and the real answer is `dummy.next`.
Splicing vs copying: you can build the answer by re-pointing existing nodes (O(1) extra space) instead of allocating new ones — that is the whole advantage of a linked list.
Use `<=` not `<` when comparing heads so equal values preserve the first list's node — this keeps the merge stable and avoids an unnecessary branch swap.
After the loop, at most one list can be non-empty and it is already sorted, so `curr.next = list1 if list1 else list2` finishes the job in O(1) — no final loop required.

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: Ignore that the inputs are already sorted and ignore that they are linked lists — just get all the numbers into one place, sort them, and build a fresh chain. Walk list1 collecting values, walk list2 collecting values, call sorted() on the combined array, then create a new node per value and link them up. It is undeniably correct and takes about five lines, which makes it a perfectly reasonable first answer. Two things are wasteful though. First, sorting costs O((n+m) log(n+m)) even though the inputs were ALREADY sorted — we are paying to rediscover order we were handed for free. Second, we allocate n+m brand-new nodes and let the originals be garbage collected, whereas the whole point of a linked list is that you can splice existing nodes together by changing pointers. The optimal solution fixes both by comparing the two heads and stealing whichever node is smaller.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Create an empty Python list `values` and walk list1 from its head, appending every `val`.
2. Walk list2 the same way, appending into the same `values` array.
3. Sort `values` ascending — correct, though it re-derives order the inputs already had.
4. If `values` is empty (both inputs were None) return None.
5. Build a fresh chain: create a node for the first value, keep a `tail` cursor, and for each remaining value attach a new node and advance the tail; return the first node.
approaches.code:
def mergeTwoLists(list1: Optional[ListNode], list2: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
    values = []                      # will hold every value from BOTH lists

    # --- Drain list1 into the array ---
    node = list1
    while node:                      # None terminates the walk
        values.append(node.val)
        node = node.next

    # --- Drain list2 into the same array ---
    node = list2
    while node:
        values.append(node.val)
        node = node.next

    # Re-sort everything. This is the wasteful step: both inputs were
    # ALREADY sorted, so we are paying O(k log k) to rediscover that.
    values.sort()

    # Both inputs empty -> the merged list is empty too
    if not values:
        return None

    # --- Build a BRAND NEW chain (the originals are discarded) ---
    head = ListNode(values[0])       # first node of the result
    tail = head                      # cursor at the end of the new chain
    for v in values[1:]:             # every remaining value, in order
        tail.next = ListNode(v)      # allocate and attach
        tail = tail.next             # the new node is the new tail

    return head

complexity.time: O((n+m) log(n+m)) — draining both lists is linear but the sort dominates.
complexity.space: O(n+m) — the value array plus n+m freshly allocated nodes.

approaches.name: Better (Recursion)
approaches.intuition: Now use the sortedness. Whichever of the two head values is smaller must be the first node of the merged list — there is nothing anywhere else that could beat it, because both lists ascend. So: pick the smaller head, and the rest of the answer is 'merge what is left', which is the same problem on a shorter input. Written recursively that is three lines: if one list is empty return the other (base case), otherwise compare the heads, and set `smaller.next = mergeTwoLists(rest, other)`. No new nodes are allocated — we re-point existing ones — and no sorting happens, so the time drops to O(n+m). The remaining flaw is invisible in the source: every recursive call keeps a stack frame alive until the very end, so a merge of two 100,000-node lists will blow Python's recursion limit. Turning that recursion into a while-loop with a dummy head is the last step to the optimal.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Base case: if `list1` is None, the merge is just `list2` — return it. Symmetrically, if `list2` is None return `list1`.
2. Compare the two head values. Use `<=` rather than `<` so that equal values keep list1's node first, which makes the merge stable.
3. If `list1.val <= list2.val`, that node is the answer's head: set `list1.next = mergeTwoLists(list1.next, list2)` and return `list1`.
4. Otherwise `list2` owns the head: set `list2.next = mergeTwoLists(list1, list2.next)` and return `list2`.
5. Each call consumes exactly one node, so the recursion depth is n + m — correct, but a stack-overflow risk on long lists.
approaches.code:
def mergeTwoLists(list1: Optional[ListNode], list2: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
    # --- Base cases: if one side is exhausted, the answer is the other side.
    # Nothing left to compare, and the remaining chain is already sorted.
    if list1 is None:
        return list2
    if list2 is None:
        return list1

    # Both lists ascend, so the smaller of the two HEADS is the global
    # smallest remaining value - it must be the head of the merged list.
    if list1.val <= list2.val:       # <= keeps list1 first on ties (stable)
        # Keep list1's node, and let recursion merge everything after it
        list1.next = mergeTwoLists(list1.next, list2)
        return list1                 # this node is the head of the answer
    else:
        # Symmetric case: list2's node wins this round
        list2.next = mergeTwoLists(list1, list2.next)
        return list2

    # Note: no new nodes are created - we only re-point existing ones.
    # The hidden cost is the call stack: one frame per node consumed.

complexity.time: O(n + m) — every node from both lists is consumed by exactly one recursive call doing O(1) work.
complexity.space: O(n + m) — the recursion stack holds one frame per node until the base case is reached.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: The recursion had the right idea — repeatedly take the smaller head — but paid for it with one stack frame per node. Turn that recursion into a loop and the space collapses to O(1). The awkward part of an iterative merge is the very first node: until you have compared the heads you do not know which list owns it, so every 'append' would need an `if this is the first node` special case. A dummy sentinel node removes that entirely: start the merged chain at a throwaway node, keep `curr` on the chain's tail, and unconditionally do `curr.next = <winner>` every round. At the end the real answer is simply `dummy.next`. And because both inputs are sorted, once one list is exhausted the other is already in final order, so a single pointer assignment `curr.next = list1 if list1 else list2` appends the entire remainder in O(1) — no cleanup loop needed. Nodes are spliced, never copied, so no memory is allocated at all.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Create a throwaway `dummy = ListNode(0)` and set `curr = dummy`; `curr` will always mark the tail of the merged chain.
2. Loop while BOTH `list1` and `list2` still have nodes — the loop ends as soon as either runs out.
3. Compare `list1.val <= list2.val`; using `<=` rather than `<` keeps list1's node first on ties, making the merge stable.
4. Splice the winning node in with `curr.next = <winner>` and advance that list past the node it just gave up.
5. Move the tail forward with `curr = curr.next` so the next node attaches in the right place.
6. After the loop at most one list is non-empty and it is already sorted, so `curr.next = list1 if list1 else list2` appends the whole remainder at once; return `dummy.next` to skip the sentinel.
approaches.code:
def mergeTwoLists(list1: Optional[ListNode], list2: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
    dummy = ListNode(0) # Dummy start node
    curr = dummy  # curr always marks the tail of the merged chain
    
    # Iterate both lists
    while list1 and list2:  # stop as soon as either list runs out
        if list1.val <= list2.val:  # <= keeps list1 first on ties (stable merge)
            curr.next = list1  # splice the existing node in - no allocation
            list1 = list1.next  # consume it: advance list1
        else:  # list2 owns the smaller value this round
            curr.next = list2  # splice list2's node instead
            list2 = list2.next  # consume it: advance list2
        curr = curr.next  # the node we just attached is the new tail
        
    # Append leftover nodes
    curr.next = list1 if list1 else list2  # at most one list is left, and it is already sorted
    return dummy.next  # skip the throwaway dummy - this is the real head

complexity.time: O(n + m) — every node from both lists is inspected and spliced exactly once.
complexity.space: O(1) — only the dummy sentinel and the curr pointer; existing nodes are re-linked, never copied.

Merge Two Sorted Linked Lists.problemStatement: You are given the heads of two singly linked lists, and each list is already sorted in non-decreasing order on its own. You must produce one single linked list that contains every node from both inputs and that is itself sorted in non-decreasing order, then return the head of that merged list. The rule connecting input to output is a simple ordering rule: at every position of the result, the next node emitted is whichever of the two remaining front nodes carries the smaller value, and when the two front values are equal either one may go first. The result is expected to be built by splicing the existing nodes together -- relinking their `next` pointers -- rather than by allocating a fresh list of copies. Either input may be empty, in which case the answer is simply the other list.

Detect Cycle in Linked List.title: Detect Cycle in Linked List
Detect Cycle in Linked List.tests:
# 1) a plain terminated list has no cycle
assert hasCycle(build_linked_list([3, 2, 0, -4])) is False

# 2) same list, but the tail is wired back to index 1 -> a real cycle
h = build_linked_list([3, 2, 0, -4])
tail = h
while tail.next:
    tail = tail.next
tail.next = h.next            # -4 now points back at node 2
assert hasCycle(h) is True

# 3) edge: an empty list cannot contain a cycle
assert hasCycle(None) is False

# 4) edge: a single node pointing at itself is the smallest possible cycle
solo = ListNode(1)
solo.next = solo
assert hasCycle(solo) is True

# 5) repeated VALUES must not be mistaken for repeated nodes
assert hasCycle(build_linked_list([1, 1, 1, 1])) is False

# 6) two nodes looping to each other
a = ListNode(1)
b = ListNode(2)
a.next = b
b.next = a
assert hasCycle(a) is True
prerequisites: Floyd's tortoise-and-hare: a fast pointer moving 2 steps and a slow pointer moving 1 step close the gap between them by exactly one node per turn, so inside a cycle they must eventually collide.
That gap argument is the termination proof — the hare can never 'jump over' the tortoise, because their separation shrinks by one, not two, each iteration.

The loop guard `while fast and fast.next` protects both dereferences (`fast.next` and `fast.next.next`) and is also what makes an acyclic list terminate; Python's `and` short-circuits so the order matters.
Compare NODES, not values: `slow == fast` on ListNode objects falls back to identity comparison, which is what we want — a list of four 1s has no cycle.
Edge conventions: `head = None` and a single node with `next = None` must both return False, while a node pointing at itself must return True.

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: A cycle means that while walking the list you eventually arrive at a node you have already stood on. So the most direct detector is to write down every node you visit and check, before each step, whether this one is already on your list. Store the NODES themselves in a Python set, never their values: two different nodes can hold the same number, and a list like 1 -> 1 -> 1 -> None has no cycle at all, so a set of values would report a false positive. Node objects are hashable by identity by default, which is exactly the comparison we want. If we ever fall off the end and reach None, there is no cycle; if we ever see a repeat, there is. The logic is airtight and runs in O(n) time, but it stores a reference to every node — O(n) memory for a problem that Floyd's two pointers solve with two variables.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Create an empty set `visited` that will hold node OBJECTS (identity-hashed), not values.
2. Start a cursor `node` at `head` and loop while `node` is not None.
3. At each node, first check `if node in visited` — if it is, we have arrived somewhere we already stood, so a cycle exists: return True.
4. Otherwise add `node` to `visited` and advance with `node = node.next`.
5. If the loop ends because the cursor became None, we reached a real tail, so return False.
approaches.code:
def hasCycle(head: Optional[ListNode]) -> bool:
    # Store NODE OBJECTS, not values! Two distinct nodes can hold the same
    # number, so a set of values would call 1 -> 1 -> None a cycle.
    # Python hashes objects by identity by default, which is exactly right.
    visited = set()

    node = head                      # cursor walking the chain
    while node:                      # None means we found a real tail
        # Have we stood on this exact node before?
        if node in visited:
            return True              # revisiting a node => there is a cycle

        visited.add(node)            # remember it and carry on
        node = node.next             # one hop forward

    # We fell off the end, so the chain terminates: no cycle
    return False

complexity.time: O(n) — each node is visited at most once, and set membership/insert are O(1) on average.
complexity.space: O(n) — the visited set grows to hold a reference to every node in the list.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: The hash-set version works but remembers every node it has seen, which is O(n) memory for a yes/no question. Floyd's tortoise-and-hare answers it with two pointers and nothing else. Run `slow` at one node per turn and `fast` at two. If the list genuinely terminates, `fast` simply falls off the end and the loop stops — no cycle. If there IS a cycle, both pointers eventually end up inside it, and from that moment the hare closes the gap on the tortoise by exactly one node per turn. A gap that shrinks by one can never be jumped over, so it must eventually reach zero and the pointers must land on the same node — which is why `slow == fast` is a proof of a cycle and not a coincidence. Crucially the comparison is between node OBJECTS, so Python falls back to identity: a list of four nodes all holding the value 1 correctly reports no cycle.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Start both `slow` and `fast` at `head`.
2. Loop while `fast` and `fast.next` are both non-None; this guard both terminates the walk on an acyclic list and makes the double dereference safe.
3. Advance `slow` by one node and `fast` by two, so their separation changes by exactly one node per turn.
4. Compare `slow == fast`. On ListNode objects this is an identity check, so it is True only when both pointers really are on the same node — return True.
5. If the loop instead exits because fast reached None, the chain has a genuine tail, so return False.
approaches.code:
def hasCycle(head: Optional[ListNode]) -> bool:
    slow = head  # tortoise: one node per turn
    fast = head  # hare: two nodes per turn
    
    # Traverse list with two speeds
    while fast and fast.next:  # test fast BEFORE fast.next - Python short-circuits
        slow = slow.next  # tortoise crawls
        fast = fast.next.next  # hare sprints; safe because of the guard above
        
        # Pointers meet -> cycle detected
        if slow == fast:  # == on nodes compares IDENTITY, not values
            return True  # same node twice => the hare lapped the tortoise
            
    return False  # fell off the tail, so the list terminates

complexity.time: O(n) — with no cycle fast reaches the end in n/2 turns; with a cycle the gap shrinks by one per turn so they meet within one lap.
complexity.space: O(1) — two node pointers, no visited set no matter how long the list is.

Detect Cycle in Linked List.problemStatement: You are given `head`, a pointer to the first node of a singly linked list, where each node holds a value and a `next` pointer. Normally the final node's `next` is null, but the list may instead have been wired so that some node's `next` points back at an earlier node, which turns the tail into a loop. Your task is to report whether such a loop exists: return true if repeatedly following `next` from `head` would go around forever, and false if the walk eventually reaches a null and stops. You are not asked where the cycle starts or how long it is, only whether one is present. An empty list contains no cycle.

3 Sum.title: 3 Sum
3 Sum.tests:
def _norm(res):
    # Different approaches emit triplets in different orders, so compare a
    # canonical form: each triplet sorted, and the whole list sorted.
    return sorted([sorted(t) for t in res])

# 1) the canonical example: exactly two unique triplets
assert _norm(threeSum([-1, 0, 1, 2, -1, -4])) == [[-1, -1, 2], [-1, 0, 1]]

# 2) edge: no triplet sums to zero
assert _norm(threeSum([0, 1, 1])) == []
assert _norm(threeSum([1, 2, 3])) == []

# 3) edge: fewer than three elements can never form a triplet
assert _norm(threeSum([])) == []
assert _norm(threeSum([0])) == []
assert _norm(threeSum([0, 0])) == []

# 4) edge: four zeroes must yield [0,0,0] exactly ONCE, not four times
assert _norm(threeSum([0, 0, 0, 0])) == [[0, 0, 0]]

# 5) heavy duplicates must not produce duplicate triplets
assert _norm(threeSum([-2, 0, 1, 1, 2])) == [[-2, 0, 2], [-2, 1, 1]]

# 6) all triplets returned must genuinely sum to zero and be pairwise distinct
out = threeSum([-4, -2, -2, -2, 0, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 6, 6])
assert all(sum(t) == 0 for t in out)
assert len(set(tuple(sorted(t)) for t in out)) == len(out)
prerequisites: Sorting first is what makes everything else possible: it groups duplicates together (so they can be skipped in O(1)) and it gives the two-pointer sweep its direction rule.

The two-pointer invariant on a sorted array: if the current sum is too small only moving `left` right can help, and if it is too big only moving `right` left can help — each move safely discards a whole block of pairs.

Three separate duplicate guards are needed: skip a repeated anchor (`nums[i] == nums[i-1]` for i > 0), and after recording a hit skip repeated `left` and repeated `right` values — miss any one and duplicate triplets leak out.
The answer is about VALUES, not indices, so [-1,-1,2] appearing at two different index pairs counts once — that is why de-duplication is part of the problem, not an afterthought.
`nums.sort()` mutates the caller's list in place; if that matters, sort a copy with `sorted(nums)` instead.

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: The problem says 'find all unique triplets that sum to zero', so the literal translation is three nested loops over indices i < j < k, testing whether the three values add to zero. Keeping the indices strictly increasing is what stops us from using the same element twice and from reporting the same triplet in six different orders. There is still a duplicate problem though: different index triples can hold the same VALUES, for example [-1, 0, 1] appearing twice in [-1, 0, 1, 2, -1, -4]. The standard fix is to sort each matching triplet and drop it into a Python set, which de-duplicates by value; at the end we convert the set back into a list of lists. This is correct and makes a great oracle for testing, but the cost is brutal: n = 3000 means roughly 4.5 billion iterations. The way out is to fix only ONE element and turn the remaining search for a pair into a two-pointer sweep on a sorted array.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Create an empty set `found` that will store each matching triplet as a SORTED tuple, so value-duplicates collapse automatically.
2. Loop `i` from 0 to n-3, then `j` from `i+1` to n-2, then `k` from `j+1` to n-1 — strictly increasing indices, so no element is reused.
3. If `nums[i] + nums[j] + nums[k] == 0`, sort those three values and add the resulting tuple to `found`.
4. After all three loops finish, convert every tuple in `found` back into a list.
5. Sort the resulting list of triplets so the output order is deterministic, and return it.

complexity.time: O(n^3) — every combination of three indices is examined, with O(1) work (plus a 3-element sort) per combination.
complexity.space: O(k) — the `found` set holds one tuple per unique triplet (k triplets, up to O(n^2) of them).

approaches.name: Better (Hashing)
approaches.intuition: The innermost loop of the brute force is just asking 'does the value -(a + b) exist further along the array?', and that is a membership question a hash set answers in O(1). So fix the first element with an outer loop over i, then sweep j through the rest while keeping a set `seen` of every value between i and j. For each j the third value we need is `third = -(nums[i] + nums[j])`; if it is already in `seen` we have a valid triplet, because everything in `seen` sits at an index strictly between i and j and is therefore a genuinely different element. That drops one whole factor of n, giving O(n^2) time. We still have to de-duplicate by value, so each hit is sorted into a tuple and dropped into a set, and that set is the O(n) extra memory this approach costs. Sorting the array up front and using two pointers achieves the same O(n^2) time while needing no hash structure at all — that is the optimal below.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Create a set `found` for unique sorted triplets, exactly as in the brute force.
2. Loop `i` over every index as the first (anchor) element of the triplet.
3. For each anchor, create a fresh empty set `seen` and loop `j` from `i+1` to the end.
