    # (a chain of n nodes) that copying happens at every level, so we pay O(n) work n times.
    return left_part + [root.val] + right_part     # left, then root, then right

complexity.time: O(N^2) worst case — list concatenation copies up to N elements at each of up to N levels (O(N log N) on a balanced tree).
complexity.space: O(N^2) allocated overall in the worst case; O(N) live at any moment plus O(H) recursion frames.

approaches.name: Better (Iterative with an Explicit Stack)
approaches.intuition: Recursion is doing two things for us: remembering which node to come back to, and remembering that we still owe it a visit. We can do both by hand with a list used as a stack, which removes any dependence on Python's recursion limit — important because a skewed tree of 100000 nodes would otherwise raise RecursionError. The loop has three clear phases. Dive left as far as possible, pushing every node you pass so you can return to it. When you cannot go left any further, pop the top node: its left subtree is by construction finished, so this is the moment to visit it. Then move the cursor to its right child and repeat. The outer condition `while node or stack` keeps going while either there is somewhere to walk or something to come back to.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Keep an answer list, an empty stack, and a cursor node starting at the root.
2. Loop while the cursor is not None OR the stack is non-empty.
3. Inner loop: while the cursor is not None, push it and move the cursor to its left child.
4. Pop the stack into the cursor — that node's left subtree is fully processed — and append its value to the answer.
5. Move the cursor to that node's right child and repeat the outer loop.
6. Return the answer list once both the cursor and the stack are exhausted.
approaches.code:
def inorderTraversal(root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> List[int]:
    ans = []                                       # values collected in inorder
    stack = []                                     # nodes whose value has not been taken yet
    node = root                                    # a cursor walking the tree
    # Better: run the SAME algorithm but manage the "call stack" ourselves, so a tree
    # 100000 nodes deep cannot blow Python's recursion limit.
    while node or stack:                           # work remains while either is non-empty
        # Phase 1 - dive as far LEFT as possible, remembering the path on the stack.
        while node:
            stack.append(node)                     # come back to this node later
            node = node.left                       # keep descending to the left
        # Phase 2 - the top of the stack is the deepest node with no unvisited left child.
        node = stack.pop()                         # its left subtree is completely finished
        ans.append(node.val)                       # VISIT it (this is the "root" step)
        # Phase 3 - now handle its right subtree exactly the same way.
        node = node.right                          # may be None, which the outer loop handles
    return ans                                     # left, root, right for the whole tree

complexity.time: O(N) — every node is pushed once and popped once.
complexity.space: O(H) — the stack holds at most one node per level, which is O(N) for a skewed tree.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: The first instinct is to picture the tree on paper and read the values off from left to right, but code has no eyes. At any instant your program is holding exactly one node reference and can only step to node.left or node.right, so the real question is: standing on a single node, how do I emit an entire subtree in the correct order? The observation that unlocks everything is that the definition of inorder is already the algorithm. The inorder list of a node is the inorder list of its left child, followed by the node's own value, followed by the inorder list of its right child. Written as a recursive helper, you never have to reason about the shape of the whole tree at once; you trust the recursive call to handle a strictly smaller subtree and you only have to place three things in the right order, letting the empty-child base case stop the descent. The price is one visit per node, so O(N) time, plus the call stack, which grows to the height of the tree and reaches O(N) on a completely skewed tree.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Create an empty list `ans`; it is the only shared state the recursion writes into, and its final contents are the answer.
2. Define the inner helper `dfs(node)`, which returns immediately when `node` is None — an empty subtree contributes nothing, and this is the base case that terminates every branch of the recursion.
3. Inside `dfs`, first call `dfs(node.left)` so that the entire left subtree is appended before the current node is touched at all.
4. Then append `node.val` to `ans`. Invariant: at this exact moment `ans` already holds every value that must precede this node in inorder order, so appending here keeps `ans` correct at all times.
5. Then call `dfs(node.right)` so the whole right subtree is appended after the current node's value.
6. Kick the walk off with `dfs(root)` and return `ans`, which now holds one value per node in inorder sequence.
approaches.code:
# Definition for a binary tree node.
# class TreeNode:
#     def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
#         self.val = val
#         self.left = left
#         self.right = right

def inorderTraversal(root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> List[int]:
    ans = []
    
    def dfs(node):
        if not node: return
        dfs(node.left)    # Traverse Left
        ans.append(node.val) # Visit Root
        dfs(node.right)   # Traverse Right
        
    dfs(root)
    return ans

complexity.time: O(N)
complexity.space: O(N) recursion depth call stack

Inorder Traversal.problemStatement: You are given the root reference of a binary tree, where every node stores an integer value and has up to two children reached through the pointers left and right. Return a flat list containing every node's value, arranged in inorder sequence. Inorder means that for each node, all of the values in its left subtree come first, then that node's own value, then all of the values in its right subtree, and the same rule is applied recursively at every level of the tree. If the tree is empty (root is None) the answer is an empty list; otherwise the returned list contains exactly one entry per node in the tree.

Search in BST.title: Search in BST
Search in BST.tests:
root = build_tree([4, 2, 7, 1, 3])
assert tree_to_level_list(searchBST(root, 2)) == [2, 1, 3]
assert tree_to_level_list(searchBST(root, 7)) == [7]         # a leaf returns just itself
assert tree_to_level_list(searchBST(root, 4)) == [4, 2, 7, 1, 3]
assert searchBST(root, 5) is None                            # edge: value absent -> None
assert searchBST(None, 1) is None                            # edge: empty tree -> None
prerequisites: The BST invariant: every value in a node's left subtree is smaller than the node, and every value in its right subtree is larger — this holds recursively for the whole subtree, not just the direct children.
That invariant is what lets one comparison discard an entire subtree, turning an O(n) search into an O(h) walk down a single root-to-leaf path.
The function returns the NODE (and therefore its whole subtree), not a boolean — so the answer is compared by converting it back with a level-order helper.
A balanced BST has height h = O(log n), but a BST built from already-sorted inserts degenerates into a chain with h = n, making search O(n) again.
Two base cases must be handled together: `not root` (fell off the tree, return None) and `root.val == val` (found it) — `if not root or root.val == val: return root` covers both.
The recursion is a TAIL call, so it converts to a simple `while root:` loop if you need O(1) space.

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: Suppose you did not know, or did not trust, that the tree is ordered. Then the target value could sit anywhere, and the only safe plan is to visit every node until you find it. That is a plain depth-first search: check the current node, then search the whole left subtree, and if that comes back empty search the whole right subtree. It returns the correct node for ANY binary tree, ordered or not, which is precisely its value as a teaching baseline — it isolates what the BST property is actually buying us. The cost is that it touches all n nodes in the worst case (and always, when the value is absent), instead of the O(h) nodes on one root-to-leaf path.
approaches.algorithm:
1. If the current node is None, return None — this branch is exhausted.
2. If the current node's value equals the target, return that node immediately.
3. Otherwise recurse into the left subtree and keep the result.
4. If the left recursion returned a node, propagate it upwards straight away.
5. If not, return the result of recursing into the right subtree, which is either the node or None.
approaches.code:
def searchBST(root: Optional[TreeNode], val: int) -> Optional[TreeNode]:
    # Brute force: pretend the ordering property does not exist and treat this as an
    # ordinary binary tree, where the target could be hiding absolutely anywhere.
    if not root:                                   # walked off the bottom of the tree
        return None                                # nothing to report on this branch
    if root.val == val:                            # this node is the one we were asked for
        return root                                # return the whole subtree rooted here
    left_hit = searchBST(root.left, val)           # search the ENTIRE left subtree
    if left_hit:                                   # the target was somewhere on the left
        return left_hit                            # bubble that node back up the call chain
    # Not found on the left, so the only remaining place is the right subtree
    # (which returns None itself if the value is absent there too).
    return searchBST(root.right, val)              # search the ENTIRE right subtree

complexity.time: O(N) — every node may be visited, and always is when the value is absent.
complexity.space: O(H) — one recursion frame per level, up to O(N) on a skewed tree.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: A beginner's instinct is to treat this like any other tree and visit every node — a full DFS or BFS that stops when it stumbles on val. That is correct, but it throws away the single most valuable fact about this tree, and it costs O(N) even though the data is already organised for you. The specific insight is the ordering invariant: at any node, everything on the left is strictly smaller and everything on the right is strictly larger. So one comparison against root.val is enough to prove an entire half of the remaining tree cannot contain the key. If val < root.val, no node on the right can possibly equal val, so the right subtree is discarded without ever being touched; if val > root.val, the left subtree goes. This is binary search, just walking pointers instead of array indices. Each step drops one level, so the cost is O(h) where h is the height — about O(log N) on a balanced tree, and O(N) in the degenerate case where the BST has collapsed into a chain. Recursion uses O(h) stack frames.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Check the two stopping conditions together: if root is None, or root.val == val, return root. This single line returns None when the key is absent and returns the matching node when it is found.
2. Otherwise compare val against root.val to pick a direction; the loop invariant is that val, if it exists anywhere, must lie inside the subtree currently being examined.
3. If val < root.val, the key can only be smaller than everything on the right, so return searchBST(root.left, val) and discard the entire right subtree in one step.
4. Otherwise val is strictly greater than root.val, because equality was already handled in step 1, so return searchBST(root.right, val) and discard the entire left subtree.
5. Each recursive call returns its result straight up the chain unchanged, so whatever the deepest call produces — the found node or None — becomes the answer of the original call.
approaches.code:
def searchBST(root: Optional[TreeNode], val: int) -> Optional[TreeNode]:
    # Base case: node is empty or matches value
    if not root or root.val == val:  # both stopping conditions in one test
        return root  # None when absent, the node itself when found
        
    # Recurse left or right based on key comparison
    if val < root.val:  # target is smaller, so it can only be on the left
        return searchBST(root.left, val)  # the entire right subtree is discarded in one step
    else:  # target is larger (equality was already handled above)
        return searchBST(root.right, val)  # the entire left subtree is discarded in one step

complexity.time: O(log N) average, O(N) worst case
complexity.space: O(log N) stack bounds

Search in BST.problemStatement: You are given the root of a binary search tree and an integer val. A binary search tree obeys one rule at every node: every value stored in its left subtree is smaller than the node's own value, and every value in its right subtree is larger. Your job is to locate the node whose value equals val and return that node, which effectively hands the caller back the whole subtree hanging beneath it. If no node in the tree carries that value, return null (None in Python) instead. You are not asked to modify the tree or to return a boolean — the return type is a tree node, so an absent key is signalled by returning the empty node rather than by raising an error.

BFS Traversal.title: BFS Traversal
BFS Traversal.tests:
assert bfsOfGraph(5, [[1, 2], [0, 3], [0, 4], [1], [2]]) == [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]
assert bfsOfGraph(5, [[1, 2, 3], [], [4], [], []]) == [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]
assert bfsOfGraph(1, [[]]) == [0]                  # edge: a single isolated vertex
assert bfsOfGraph(3, [[1], [0], []]) == [0, 1]     # edge: vertex 2 is unreachable from 0
assert bfsOfGraph(4, [[1, 2], [0, 2], [0, 1], []]) == [0, 1, 2]   # a triangle plus an island
prerequisites: BFS explores in layers: every vertex at distance k from the source is emitted before any vertex at distance k+1, which is why BFS gives shortest paths in unweighted graphs.
Mark a vertex visited at ENQUEUE time, not at dequeue time — otherwise a vertex with two discovered edges gets pushed twice and appears twice in the output.
`collections.deque` gives O(1) popleft(); a plain list's `pop(0)` is O(V) because it shifts every remaining element.
A boolean array indexed by vertex gives O(1) membership tests, whereas `x in some_list` is an O(V) linear scan.
Total cost is O(V + E) because each vertex is dequeued once and each adjacency list is walked once.
Starting only from vertex 0 means vertices in other connected components are never reported — a disconnected graph needs an outer loop over all start vertices.

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: The first BFS almost everyone writes uses a plain Python list as the queue and another plain list to remember who has been seen. It produces exactly the right traversal, so it is not wrong — it is just slow in two specific and very instructive ways. First, `queue.pop(0)` removes from the FRONT of a list, and Python has to shift every remaining element one slot left, costing O(V) per dequeue instead of O(1). Second, `neighbor not in visited` on a list is a linear scan through everything seen so far, so each of the E edge checks costs up to O(V). Together those turn a linear-time algorithm into a quadratic one. Seeing the same logic side by side with the optimal version makes clear that the algorithm and its data structures are separate design decisions.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Create an empty answer list, an empty visited LIST, and a queue list seeded with vertex 0.
2. Mark vertex 0 as visited immediately so it can never be enqueued a second time.
3. While the queue is non-empty, remove the front element with pop(0) and append it to the answer.
4. For each neighbour in that vertex's adjacency list, test membership with `not in visited` (a linear scan).
5. If it is unseen, append it to visited and push it onto the back of the queue.
6. Return the answer list once the queue drains.
approaches.code:
def bfsOfGraph(V: int, adj: List[List[int]]) -> List[int]:
    # Brute force: the CORRECT BFS order, but built from the two data structures a
    # beginner reaches for first - a plain list as the queue and a list of visited nodes.
    bfs = []                                        # the traversal order we will return
    visited = []                                    # a LIST of visited vertices, not an array
    queue = [0]                                     # plain Python list pretending to be a queue
    visited.append(0)                               # vertex 0 is discovered before we start
    while queue:                                    # keep going while something is scheduled
        # list.pop(0) removes the FRONT, which shifts every remaining element left: O(V).
        node = queue.pop(0)                         # dequeue the oldest vertex
        bfs.append(node)                            # record it in visit order
        for neighbor in adj[node]:                  # look along every outgoing edge
            # 'in' on a LIST is a linear scan, so each membership test costs O(V).
            if neighbor not in visited:
                visited.append(neighbor)            # mark at DISCOVERY time, not at pop time
                queue.append(neighbor)              # schedule it behind everything already queued
    # Same answer as the optimal version - only the constant factors are terrible.
    return bfs

complexity.time: O(V^2 + V*E) — every pop(0) shifts O(V) elements and every one of the E membership tests scans O(V) entries.
complexity.space: O(V) — the queue, the visited list and the answer each hold at most V vertices.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: If you just start walking the graph without a plan you naturally recurse into the first neighbour, then into its first neighbour, and you end up deep in one branch before you ever look at the second neighbour of the start vertex. That is depth-first, and it gives the wrong order here. The observation that makes breadth-first work is that layer order is exactly the order in which vertices are discovered, so if you keep discovered-but-not-yet-expanded vertices in a first-in-first-out queue and always expand the oldest one, every vertex at distance d is popped before any vertex at distance d+1. The second, easy-to-miss observation is when to mark a vertex as visited: it must happen the moment you enqueue it, not when you pop it, otherwise a vertex with two parents in the same layer gets pushed twice and printed twice. A boolean array gives that check in O(1), and a deque gives popleft in O(1), where a plain list would cost O(V) per removal. The total cost is O(V + E) time, since each vertex is expanded once and each edge examined once, with O(V) memory for the queue and the flags.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Create an empty list `bfs` for the traversal order and an array `visited` of V booleans, all False, so membership checks are O(1).
2. Initialise the queue as `deque([0])` and immediately set `visited[0] = True`, because the source counts as discovered before the loop begins.
3. Loop while `queue` is non-empty. The invariant is that the queue always holds discovered-but-unexpanded vertices in non-decreasing distance from vertex 0.
4. Inside the loop, pop the oldest vertex with `node = queue.popleft()` (this FIFO choice is what makes the traversal breadth-first) and append `node` to `bfs`.
5. For each `neighbor` in `adj[node]`, if `visited[neighbor]` is False, set it to True at discovery time and `queue.append(neighbor)` so it waits behind everything already queued.
6. When the queue empties, every vertex reachable from 0 has been expanded, so return `bfs`.
approaches.code:
from collections import deque  # deque gives O(1) popleft(); list.pop(0) would be O(V)

def bfsOfGraph(V: int, adj: List[List[int]]) -> List[int]:
    bfs = []  # the traversal order we will return
    visited = [False] * V  # one O(1) flag per vertex, far cheaper than scanning a list
    queue = deque([0]) # BFS queue starting at vertex 0
    visited[0] = True  # the source counts as discovered before the loop starts
    
    while queue:  # keep going while any vertex is still scheduled
        node = queue.popleft()  # popleft() takes the OLDEST vertex, which is what makes this breadth-first
        bfs.append(node)  # record the vertex in visit order
        
        # Enqueue unvisited neighbors
        for neighbor in adj[node]:
            if not visited[neighbor]:  # never enqueue the same vertex twice
                visited[neighbor] = True  # mark at DISCOVERY time, not at pop time
                queue.append(neighbor)  # it waits behind everything already queued
                
    return bfs  # every vertex reachable from 0, in layer order

complexity.time: O(V + E)
complexity.space: O(V) storage

BFS Traversal.problemStatement: You are given a directed graph with V vertices, numbered 0 through V-1, described by an adjacency list adj, where adj[u] is the list of vertices you can reach in one step from vertex u. Starting at vertex 0, produce the Breadth First Search traversal order: visit vertex 0 first, then everything one edge away from it, then everything two edges away, and so on, expanding the graph outwards in layers. Within a single layer, neighbours are visited in the order they appear inside the adjacency list of the vertex that discovered them. Every vertex must appear exactly once in the returned list, and vertices that cannot be reached from 0 by following directed edges do not appear at all.

DFS Traversal.title: DFS Traversal
DFS Traversal.tests:
assert dfsOfGraph(5, [[2, 3, 1], [0], [0, 4], [0], [2]]) == [0, 2, 4, 3, 1]
assert dfsOfGraph(5, [[1, 2], [0, 3], [0, 4], [1], [2]]) == [0, 1, 3, 2, 4]
assert dfsOfGraph(1, [[]]) == [0]                  # edge: a single isolated vertex
assert dfsOfGraph(3, [[1], [0], []]) == [0, 1]     # edge: vertex 2 is unreachable from 0
assert dfsOfGraph(4, [[1, 2], [0, 3], [0], [1]]) == [0, 1, 3, 2]
prerequisites: DFS commits to one neighbour and follows it as deep as possible before ever looking at the next neighbour — that is the whole difference from BFS.
Mark a vertex visited on ENTRY to the recursive call; skipping that in an undirected graph sends you straight back to the parent and into infinite recursion.
A nested helper function closes over `visited` and `dfs`, so all recursive calls share one copy of the state instead of passing it around.
Cost is O(V + E): each vertex is entered once and each adjacency list is scanned once (each undirected edge is looked at twice, once from each end).
The visit order depends entirely on the order neighbours appear in the adjacency list — there is no single "the" DFS order for a graph.
Recursion depth can reach V, so a 100,000-vertex chain needs either an explicit stack or a raised sys.setrecursionlimit.

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: Start with the DFS a beginner writes: the recursion is already right, but the bookkeeping is not. Instead of a boolean array indexed by vertex number, the visited set is kept as a plain Python list and tested with `neighbor not in visited`. That expression walks the entire list from the front every single time, so a membership test costs up to O(V) rather than O(1). Since we run one such test per edge, the whole traversal degrades from O(V + E) to roughly O(V * E). The output is byte-for-byte identical to the fast version, which is exactly the point: the algorithm was never the bottleneck, the data structure was. Fixing it is a one-line change once you can see it.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Keep an answer list dfs and a plain list visited that starts empty.
2. Define a nested traverse(node) helper so it shares both lists with the outer function.
3. Inside traverse, append the node to visited (marking on entry) and to dfs (recording the order).
4. Loop over adj[node]; for each neighbour, test `neighbor not in visited`, which is a linear scan of the visited list.
5. Recurse into any unvisited neighbour immediately, going deep before trying the next one.
6. Call traverse(0) to start and return dfs.
approaches.code:
def dfsOfGraph(V: int, adj: List[List[int]]) -> List[int]:
    # Brute force: the CORRECT depth-first order, but 'visited' is a plain LIST, so every
    # membership test is a linear scan instead of an O(1) indexed lookup.
    dfs = []                                        # traversal order to return
    visited = []                                    # vertices already seen (searched linearly)

    def traverse(node):
        visited.append(node)                        # mark on ENTRY so we can never re-enter
        dfs.append(node)                            # record the visit order immediately
        for neighbor in adj[node]:                  # follow the edges in the given order
            # 'not in' walks the whole visited list: up to O(V) work for EVERY edge.
            if neighbor not in visited:
                traverse(neighbor)                  # go DEEP before trying the next neighbour

    traverse(0)                                     # the traversal always starts at vertex 0
    return dfs                                      # identical output to the optimal version

complexity.time: O(V * E) — one O(V) linear membership scan for each of the E edge checks.
complexity.space: O(V) — the visited list, the answer list, and up to V recursion frames.

approaches.name: Better (Iterative with an Explicit Stack)
approaches.intuition: Recursion is convenient but Python caps it at roughly 1000 frames by default, so a graph shaped like a long chain will crash. Managing the stack ourselves removes that ceiling. The subtlety is order: if we push adj[node] left to right and then pop, the LAST neighbour comes off first, reversing the traversal compared with the recursive version. Pushing `reversed(adj[node])` puts the FIRST neighbour on top, which reproduces the recursive order exactly. The other subtlety is that a vertex can be pushed more than once before it is popped (two different vertices may both discover it), so we mark visited at POP time and skip any stale duplicate we find on top of the stack.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Create the answer list, a boolean visited array of size V, and a stack seeded with vertex 0.
2. While the stack is non-empty, pop the top vertex.
3. If that vertex is already visited, skip it — it is a stale duplicate pushed by an earlier vertex.
4. Otherwise mark it visited and append it to the answer.
5. Push its neighbours in REVERSED order so the first neighbour is explored next, matching the recursive traversal.
6. Return the answer once the stack empties.
approaches.code:
def dfsOfGraph(V: int, adj: List[List[int]]) -> List[int]:
    dfs = []                                        # traversal order to return
    visited = [False] * V                           # O(1) lookups: one flag per vertex
    stack = [0]                                     # an explicit stack replaces the call stack
    # Better: same order, same O(V + E) cost, but no recursion - so a graph with 100000
    # vertices in a chain cannot raise RecursionError.
    while stack:                                    # keep working while anything is pending
        node = stack.pop()                          # LIFO pop is what makes this go DEEP
        if visited[node]:                           # the same vertex can be pushed twice
            continue                                # so skip any stale duplicate
        visited[node] = True                        # mark at POP time in the iterative form
        dfs.append(node)                            # record the visit
        # Push neighbours REVERSED so the FIRST neighbour ends up on TOP of the stack,
        # which reproduces exactly the order the recursive version produces.
        for neighbor in reversed(adj[node]):
            if not visited[neighbor]:               # cheap pre-filter (not needed for correctness)
                stack.append(neighbor)              # schedule it to be explored next
    return dfs

complexity.time: O(V + E) — each vertex is popped and processed once, each adjacency list scanned once.
complexity.space: O(V) — the stack can hold up to O(V) entries plus the visited array.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: A first attempt at walking a graph usually just follows edges from wherever you are, and it hangs forever: an undirected edge u-v is stored in both adj[u] and adj[v], so stepping from u to v and then reading v's neighbours immediately offers u again, and any cycle loops indefinitely. The fix is a single idea: a vertex only ever needs to be expanded once, because whatever is reachable through it is the same no matter which of its edges brought you there. So keep one boolean flag per vertex in `visited` and set it the moment you enter a vertex, not when you leave it, since marking on exit would let the recursion bounce straight back along the edge it just used. With that guard in place, 'depth first' falls out for free from ordinary recursion: appending the node before looping over its neighbours records it at the right moment, and calling traverse on a neighbour immediately means you sink all the way down that branch before the loop even glances at the next neighbour. The call stack is the stack. Every vertex is entered once and every edge is inspected twice, giving O(V + E) time and O(V) space for the flags plus recursion depth.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Create the output list `dfs` and a boolean array `visited` of length V initialised to all False, one O(1) flag per vertex.
2. Define the helper `traverse(node)`; the Python call stack itself acts as the DFS stack, so no explicit stack structure is built.
3. On entry set `visited[node] = True` before anything else, then append `node` to `dfs`, fixing its place in the traversal order. Marking on entry is what stops an undirected edge from sending the recursion straight back where it came from.
4. Loop over each `neighbor` in `adj[node]`, in the order the adjacency list stores them.
5. If `visited[neighbor]` is False, call `traverse(neighbor)` right there, descending completely through that branch before the loop looks at the next neighbour; if it is already True, skip it.
6. Call `traverse(0)` to start the walk at vertex 0, then return `dfs`. Invariant maintained throughout: a vertex is in `dfs` exactly when its `visited` flag is True.
approaches.code:
def dfsOfGraph(V: int, adj: List[List[int]]) -> List[int]:
    dfs = []  # traversal order to return
    visited = [False] * V  # one O(1) flag per vertex
    
    def traverse(node):  # the Python call stack IS our stack here
        visited[node] = True  # mark on ENTRY, or an undirected edge sends us straight back
        dfs.append(node) # Visit current node
        
        # Recurse deep into neighbors
        for neighbor in adj[node]:  # follow the edges in adjacency-list order
            if not visited[neighbor]:  # skip anything already recorded
                traverse(neighbor)  # go DEEP before even looking at the next neighbour
                
    traverse(0)  # the walk always starts at vertex 0
    return dfs  # every vertex reachable from 0

complexity.time: O(V + E)
complexity.space: O(V) recursion stack

DFS Traversal.problemStatement: You are given an undirected graph with V vertices labelled 0 through V-1, described by an adjacency list adj in which adj[u] is the list of vertices directly connected to u by an edge. Starting from vertex 0, you must perform a depth-first traversal and return a list of vertex labels in the exact order they were first visited. Depth-first means that from the current vertex you commit fully to its first unvisited neighbour and explore everything reachable through that neighbour before you come back and consider the next one. The graph is connected, so every vertex is reached, and each vertex must appear exactly once in the returned list.

Implement Trie.title: Implement Trie
Implement Trie.tests:
# --- basic insert / exact search ---
t = Trie()
t.insert("apple")
assert t.search("apple") is True or t.search("apple") == True   # full word stored
assert not t.search("app")            # "app" is only a PREFIX, never inserted as a word
assert t.startsWith("app")            # but the prefix path does exist
assert not t.startsWith("apx")        # no such prefix anywhere

# --- inserting a prefix of an existing word must flip only that node's flag ---
t.insert("app")
assert t.search("app")
assert t.search("apple")              # the longer word is untouched

# --- duplicate insert must not corrupt anything ---
t.insert("apple")
assert t.search("apple")

# --- several words sharing prefixes ---
t2 = Trie()
for w in ["cat", "car", "card", "dog"]:
    t2.insert(w)
assert t2.search("car") and t2.search("card") and t2.search("cat")
assert not t2.search("ca")
assert t2.startsWith("ca") and t2.startsWith("d")
assert not t2.startsWith("cart")

# --- EDGE CASE: the empty string is a legal key ---
t3 = Trie()
t3.insert("")
assert t3.search("")                  # empty word was inserted -> found
assert t3.startsWith("")              # every stored word starts with ""

# --- EDGE CASE: searching an empty structure must never crash ---
t4 = Trie()
assert not t4.search("anything")
assert not t4.startsWith("a")
prerequisites: A trie is an N-ary tree where the EDGE carries the character, not the node — the root itself stores nothing, and a word is spelled out by the path from the root down.
Every node needs a boolean end-of-word flag (`is_word`). Without it you cannot tell an inserted word from a mere prefix, which is the whole difference between `search` and `startsWith`.
Python dict lookups are O(1) average, so `curr.children[ch]` costs the same as an array slot while using memory only for the characters that actually occur.
All three operations share one skeleton: start `curr = self.root` and walk one character at a time; they differ only in what they do when a character is missing and what they return at the end.
Know the cost model you are buying: insert/search/startsWith are O(L) in the word length and completely independent of how many words are stored.
`bisect.bisect_left` on a sorted list returns the leftmost insertion index — useful for the intermediate sorted-array approach and for seeing why the trie still wins.

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: Forget clever data structures for a moment and ask the laziest possible question: what is the least work I can do on insert? Just remember the word. So the whole structure becomes a plain Python list of strings. insert appends, search compares the query against every stored word, and startsWith asks every stored word whether it begins with the prefix. This is genuinely correct and it is worth writing once, because it makes the real cost visible: every query touches every word, and words that share a prefix like "car" and "card" store that shared "car" twice. Those two wastes -- rescanning unrelated words, and duplicating shared prefixes -- are exactly what the trie removes.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Keep a single list self.words that holds every inserted string.
2. insert(word): if word is not already in the list, append it (the 'not in' check itself scans the list).
3. search(word): loop over every stored string and return True on the first exact == match; return False after the loop.
4. startsWith(prefix): loop over every stored string and return True on the first w.startswith(prefix); return False after the loop.
5. Note the cost: with N words of length up to L, both queries are O(N*L) instead of O(L).

complexity.time: O(N*L) per search/startsWith/insert — every call scans all N stored words and compares up to L characters each
complexity.space: O(N*L) — every word is stored in full, with no sharing of common prefixes

approaches.name: Better (Sorted List + Binary Search)
approaches.intuition: The brute force scans all N words on every query, but a sorted list lets us skip almost all of them. Two facts make this work. First, an exact search is a textbook binary search: bisect_left finds in O(log N) the one slot where the word would live, so we only compare one string. Second -- and this is the pretty part -- in dictionary order every word sharing a prefix sits in one unbroken block, and that block begins precisely at bisect_left(prefix). So if the single word at that position does not start with the prefix, no word does. Queries drop to O(log N + L). The remaining wart is insert: keeping the list sorted costs an O(N) shift, and shared prefixes are still stored once per word.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Maintain self.words as a list kept in sorted (lexicographic) order at all times.
2. insert(word): pos = bisect.bisect_left(self.words, word); if the slot already equals word, return (duplicate).
3. Otherwise call self.words.insert(pos, word), which keeps the list sorted but shifts the tail in O(N).
4. search(word): pos = bisect_left(word); return True only if pos is in range AND self.words[pos] == word.
5. startsWith(prefix): pos = bisect_left(prefix); return True only if pos is in range AND self.words[pos].startswith(prefix), because the prefix block, if it exists, must begin exactly there.
approaches.code:
import bisect

class Trie:
    def __init__(self):
        # One list again, but this time we promise to keep it SORTED forever.
        # Sorting is what buys us binary search instead of a linear scan.
        self.words = []

    def insert(self, word: str) -> None:
        # bisect_left tells us, in O(log N), the slot where word belongs.
        pos = bisect.bisect_left(self.words, word)
        # If that slot already holds exactly this word it is a duplicate.
        if pos < len(self.words) and self.words[pos] == word:
            # Nothing to do; the key is already stored.
            return
        # list.insert shifts the tail, so insert costs O(N) -- the price of order.
        self.words.insert(pos, word)

    def search(self, word: str) -> bool:
        # Binary search jumps straight to where the word WOULD live.
        pos = bisect.bisect_left(self.words, word)
        # Present only if that slot exists and holds the exact same string.
        return pos < len(self.words) and self.words[pos] == word

    def startsWith(self, prefix: str) -> bool:
        # Key insight: in sorted order every word sharing a prefix forms one
        # contiguous block, and that block starts exactly at bisect_left(prefix).
        pos = bisect.bisect_left(self.words, prefix)
        # So only the FIRST word at/after the prefix needs to be examined.
        return pos < len(self.words) and self.words[pos].startswith(prefix)

complexity.time: O(log N + L) per search/startsWith — one binary search plus one string comparison; insert is O(N + log N) because of the list shift
complexity.space: O(N*L) — still one full copy of every word; only the lookup got faster, not the storage

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: The sorted list made both queries fast, but it left two things unpaid. First, insert: keeping the list in order means list.insert shifts every word after the new one, so a cheap-looking insert is O(N). Second, storage: apple, apply and app still spell out a-p-p three separate times, and every query re-compares those same shared characters from scratch. The observation that fixes it is to store the spelling paths rather than the strings — let each node stand for one position inside a word, and let its `children` dict map the next character to the next node. Words with a common prefix then physically share the same nodes, and any lookup becomes a walk of one edge per character. Because arriving at a node does not by itself mean a word ended there, each node carries an `is_word` flag, and that flag is the only thing distinguishing `search` from `startsWith`, which otherwise perform an identical traversal. Every operation costs O(L) for a string of length L, regardless of how many words the trie holds.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Define `TrieNode` with two fields: `children`, a dict mapping one character to the child `TrieNode` reached by that character, and `is_word`, a boolean that is True only when some inserted word ends exactly at this node.
2. In `Trie.__init__`, create `self.root = TrieNode()`. The root stores no character; it is simply the shared starting point of every walk.
3. For `insert(word)`, set `curr = self.root` and loop over each `char` of `word`: if `char` is missing from `curr.children`, create a new `TrieNode()` under it, then step down with `curr = curr.children[char]`. Existing paths are reused rather than duplicated. After the loop, `curr` is the node for the word's last character, so set `curr.is_word = True`.
4. For `search(word)`, walk from `self.root` the same way but create nothing: the moment a `char` is absent from `curr.children` the path is broken and you return False. If the walk completes, return `curr.is_word`, so a stored prefix that is not itself a word correctly answers False.
5. For `startsWith(prefix)`, run the identical walk and return False as soon as a character is missing; if the walk completes, return True unconditionally, because here the existence of the path is the entire question and `is_word` is irrelevant.
6. The invariant shared by all three methods is that after consuming k characters, `curr` is the unique node reached by spelling those first k characters out from the root.

complexity.time: O(L) where L is string length
complexity.space: O(Total chars inserted) nodes storage

Implement Trie.problemStatement: Implement a prefix tree, or trie, as a class supporting three operations on strings. `insert(word)` stores a word in the structure. `search(word)` returns true only when that exact word was inserted earlier, and false otherwise. `startsWith(prefix)` returns true when at least one stored word begins with the given prefix, even if that prefix was never inserted as a complete word on its own. The difference between the last two is the whole point: after inserting apple, search(app) must return false while startsWith(app) must return true. Each operation should cost time proportional to the length of the string handed to it, not to how many words are stored.
